lawyer:
Faruque Ahmed, Advocate ------ For the Petitioner. 
Md. Abdul Kuddus Miah, Advocate ------ For the Opposite Parties.
parties:
Sourja Bala Devi ------ Petitioner
Vs.
Habibullah Sheikh ------ Opposite Party
full_judgment:
This Rule under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure calls in question the judgment and order dated 31.5.84 passed by the Subordinate Judge, Lakshmipur in Misc. Appeal No. 242 of 1980 dismissing the appeal and affirming the judgment and order dated 11.12.80 passed by the Munsif Second Court, Lakshmipur in Misc. Case No. 36 of 1976. 

2. The aforesaid Misc. Case was started by one Sarajubala the petitioner herein by making an application under Section 174(3) of the Bengal Tenancy Act, 1885 for selling aside the sale of certain land measuring about 1.35 acre which was sold in auction for a sum of Rs. 19/-being the arrear rent for the land. 

3. It appears from the plaint that the auction took place on 6.2.64 and it was confirmed on 9.3.64 and the application for setting aside the sale mainly on the ground of fraud was made on 29.5.76. The application was contested by opposite party Nos. 1-8 who appear to be the heirs of one Luthfur Rahman. The record shows that this Luthfur Rahman was the auction purchaser and it has been alleged in the plaint that this man was the care-taker of this land sold in auction, on behalf the petitioner Sarajubala. 

4. The trial court dismissed the application holding inter alia that the application suffered from defect of party as all the heirs of deceased Luthfur Rahman were not made a party that the applicant did not deposit under sub-clause (3)(b) of Section 174 of the Bengal Tenancy Act the amount recoverable from the judgment-debtor and that the petitioner failed to prove fraud practiced by the decree holder and auction purchaser in collusion with each other. 

5. Onappeal the Subordinate Judge dismissed the appeal on the ground inter alia that the Bengal TenancyAct, 1885 was repealed by' the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1951 and as such the remedy available under the repealed Act was not available to the petitioner at the relevant time and that though the application was also under Order 21, Rule 19 of the C.P.C. read with Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1908 none of these provisions of law are applicable at all. The learned Subordinate Judge held that the judgment-debtor or the person affected by the auction sale failed to come within six months from the date of sale as required by the provision of Section 174(3) of the Bengal Tenancy Act; as the sale was held in 1964 and the petitioner challenged the sale in 1976 the application was hopelessly barred by the limitation of this section. Moreover in the opinion of the appellate court, the provision of Section 174(3)(b), the mandatory provision of the said Act regarding money to be deposited by the judgment-debtor had not been complied with. Further the appellate court expressed surprise as to how the case under the Bengal Tenancy Act was entertain able in the year 1976 when the Act had no existence being repealed by the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, and therefore the learned Subordinate Judge did not find any reason to interfere with the judgment and or- der of the trial court. 

6. The legality of this judgment and order pI' the appellate court was challenged here by the petitioner, Sarajubala who died on 6.1.87 during the pendency of this Rule and her successor-in-interest were substituted under Order 22, Rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure vide order of this Court dated 7.4.88. 
7. The learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner Sarajubala, submits that the right to apply under Section 174 sub-sec. (3) was available to the petitioner even though the Bengal Tenancy Act stood repealed at the time when the application was made. In support of his submission he refers to a decision reported in 29 D.L.R. 301. In that case the tenancy was sold on 19.3.52 in a Rent Execution Case and the application for setting aside the sale was filed on 2.11.66 under Section 174(3) of the Bengal Tenancy Act. It was held by a Division Bench of this Court that the application was maintainable even though the Bengal Tenancy Act was not in force at that time. It was a reference case made by a Munsif under Section 113 read with Order 46, Rule 2 of the Civil Procedure Code. The reference was answered in the above term and the matter was sent back to the trial court for decision in accordance with the judgment. 

8. With regard to failure of the petitioner to deposit the decrial amount as required under Section 174(3)(b) of the said Tenancy Act the learned Advocate submits that the deposit of money is not a condition precedent for filing but for allowing the application. He further submits that the provision of Section 5 of the Limitation Act is applicable to an application under Section 174(3) of the Bengal Tenancy Act and in support of his contention he relies on a decision reported in Q D.L.R. 89. In that case the question for determination was whether the pro- vision of Section 5 of the Limitation Act was applicable to an application under Section 174(3) of the Bengal Tenancy Act. His Lordship referred to Section 185 of the Bengal Tenancy Act which reads:- 

"Sections 6, 7,8 and 9 and sub-section (2) of section 29 of the Limitation Act, 1908 shall not and, subject to the provisions of this Chapter, the remaining provisions of that Act, shall apply to all suits, appeals and applications specified in Schedule III annexed to this Act." and held that Section 5 was applicable as per provision of this section not only to applications and suits but also to appeals specified in Schedule III of that Act. It was contended in that case that when the appellate court admits the appeal through mistake in spite of the fact that the appellant had not made necessary deposit under Section 174(5) of the Bengal Tenancy Act the appeal was incompetent and the appellate Court had no power to condone the delay under Section 5 of the Limitation Act in making the deposit but his Lordship did not accept the contention and held that the learned Subordinate Judge acted properly in condoning the delay under Section 5 of the Limitation Act. 

9. It is to be needhere however that sub- section (5) of Section 1-n of the Bengal Tenancy Act makes the deposit a condition precedent for ad- mission of the appeal. It lays down :-
"An appeal shall lie against an order setting aside or refusing to set aside a sale: Provided that where the Court has refused to set aside the sale on the application of the judgment-debtor or any person whose interests are affected by the sale and the amount recoverable in execution of the decree is not in deposit in Court, no such appeal shall be admitted unless the appellant deposits such amount in Court." 

It was decided in the case under reference that Section 5 of the Limitation Act would be applicable to such an appeal. 

10. It was further contended by the learned Advocate for the petitioner relying on a decision reported in 5 D.L.R. 451 that an appeal under Section 174(5) even if registered without the deposit may be admitted for hearing in suitable circumstances by giving the appellant an opportunity of making the required deposit. This view is also supported by a decision reported in 8 D.L.R. 258 where the view taken that the deposit could be made after filing of the appeal but before it was admitted. In this connection it was observed :-"If it is admitted behind the back of the appellant or in his presence soon after it is filed, say, on the very day it was filed, without considering the question of the deposit the appellant does not get an opportunity to make the deposit. It is a failure on the part of the Court to see if the required deposit is there before the appeal is admitted for which the appellant should not suffer. In such circumstances the only course open in revision is to send the case back on remand to the lower appellant Court, to admit the appeal according to law after receiving the required de-posit from the appellant before the appeal is set down for hearing under Order 41 Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure as has been done in the case of Sasadher Ghose reported in 53 C.W.N. 694 at 699 in the circumstances of that case." 

11. With regard to the allegation of fraud made by the petitioner it was contended by the learned Advocate for the petitioner with reference to a case re-ported in 5 D.L.R. 43 that a gross under-valuation of the property put up for sale amounts to a fraud and in such a case the judgment-debtor is entitled to claim the benefit of Section 18 of the Limitation Act. 

12. The learned Advocate for the opposite party on the other hand submits with reference to two cases reported in 6 D.L.R. 434 and 9 D.L.R. 394 that admission of appeal under Section 174 sub-section (5) of the Bengal Tenancy Act without the deposit is without jurisdiction. The deposit of the decrial amount is a condition precedent for the ad mission of the appeal. He further submits that the trial court did not raise the question of repeal of the Bangla Tenancy Act it raised the question only of deposit as required under sub-section (1) of Section 174 of that Act and the question of limitation and that fraud could not be proved and there was defect of parties. 

13. Having gone through the judgment of both the courts below and the deposition on record and having heard the learned Advocates of either side it appears that the appellate court below approached the whole question involved in the appeal from a wrong angle and came to an erroneous conclusion on points of law. The courts started on the premise that since Bengal Tenancy Act 1885 was repealed the right given to a judgment-debtor under it could not be enforced. This is clearly an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of jus-tice as it would be evident from the decision reported in 29 D.L.R. 301 referred to above. It is, however, to be noted that it is one thing to entertain an application or register an appeal and it is quite different thing to dispose it of on merit. With regard to the requirement of deposit also the approach of both the courts below is erroneous from the point of view of law as has been indicated above. 

14. It is also to be noted that the land sold in auction included bhiti land comprising an area of 1.35 acre for a paltry sum of Rs. 19/- only and the auction purchaser is one Luthfur Rahman who has been described in the main petition as a caretaker of the land in question on behalf of the petitioner herself. But unfortunately this important question has been overlooked by both the courts below; it has not been decided by them as to whether the said Luthfur Rahman was her caretaker or not, although this has been denied by the defendants opposite party the heirs of said Luthfur Rahman in their written objection. 

15. In the facts and circumstances of the case it ought to have been made an issue as to whether said Luthfur Rahman was really the care-taker on be-half of the petitioner Sarajubala because the nature of the auction-purchase would depend largely on the determination of this question on the basis of evidence on record. It was also stated in the main petition that the petitioner was all along in possession of the said land and she produced rent receipt to show her ownership in respect of the land even for the period after the alleged auction sale which was challenged by her. 

16. In this connection the question of possession of the disputed land was also very much relevant and also who paid rent in respect of the disputedland after the said auction sale that is to say after the alleged auction sale who exercised the right of ownership by paying rent and/or remaining in possession. All these are very relevant questions to be decided on the basis of evidence on record. But these have not resolved and it has occasioned a total failure of justice. 

17. It is, therefore, ordered that the judgment and order passed in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 242 of 1980 by the Subordinate Judge, Lakshmipur be set aside and the appeal is remanded to the said court and it is directed that the appeal be heard afresh in accordance with law in the light of the observation made above taking into consideration also the provision of Order 41 Rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure. 

In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs. 

End.

lawyer:
M. H. Khondker with A. Rahim ----- For I Petitioner
Syed I. R. Mudassir Hossain, Assistant Attorney General ----- For the Respondent No. 1.
parties:
Md. Abul Hossain Sarder ----- Petitioner
Vs.
Government of Bangladesh and others ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
Sultan Hossain Khan, J: This rule under Article 102 of the Constitution is directed against an order dated 16.1.70 declaring certain property as Enemy Property and leasing out the same to the respondents Nos. 5-23.

2 Facts in short are that the property in question measuring in total 22 acres with structures thereon in the town of Jessore belonged to Ajit Kumar Halder. While Ajit Kumar Halder was in seisin of the property having perfect right and title therein, he entered into an agreement on 15.6.63 to sell the said property to the petitioner at a price of Rs.10,000/- and on receipt of Rs. 6,000/-out of that price he executed on 15 6.63 a deed of agreement which was registered on 16.7.63 in favour of the petitioner stipulating, inter alia, that he would execute and register the necessary kabala after obtaining Income Tax Clearance Certificate, The Income Tax Clearance Certificate, however, could not be obtained but under pressing need of money Ajit Kumar Halder, the said Vendor, again took Rs.1,000/- on 21.8.63 from the petitioner. The balance amount of Tk. 3,000/- was also paid to him on 11.2.64 by the petitioner under a receipt duly granted. The aforesaid vendor on receipt of the entire consideration money handed over possession of the property to the petitioner on 11.2.64 i.e. the day of payment of the balance of consideration money of Rs. 3,000/- and the petitioner took possession of the property in part performance of the contract pending execution and registration of the sale. The petitioner having paid the entire consideration money obtained from the aforesaid vendor a power of Attorney, registered on 12.2.64, appointing the son of the petitioner as constituted Attorney for the purpose of registering a kabala already executed in favour of the petitioner. The Disturbed Persons Ordinance 1964 (Ordinance No 1 of 1964) in. the mean-time having lapsed, the petitioner filed a suit for specific performance of contract against the said vendor being Other Class Snit No 108/69. The said suit was decreed on 24.11.70, and in execution of the said decree, the petitioner got a kabala executed and registered on 26.6.71 and 24.7.71 respectively through Court in respect of the disputed property. While the petitioner was thus in possession of the property respondent No. 2 by an order dated 16.11.70 declared the aforesaid property as 'Enemy Property' and issued notice upon the tenants of the petitioner and others to surrender the Property to the Assistant Custodian of Enemy Property. The petitioner having learnt about the matter made representations to the Authorities but without any success. Soon after the liberation, the petitioner stated, he suffered mental shock resulting in mental disorder and he recovered from his illness in December, 1974 on an enquiry from the Office of the respondent No. 2 he came to learn that by successive orders the respondent No. 2 granted leases of the property to several persons. The petitioner, therefore, decided to file an application in this Court under Article 102 of the Constitution and in fact the petitioner prepared Writ Petition No. 120/75 for release and restoration of the property to him. The petitioner however was advised to exhaust his remedy before the respondent No. 1 by way of an appeal against the orders of the respondent No. 2 and as such the petitioner did not move the said Writ Petition before this Hon'ble Court. An appeal was preferred before respondent No. 1 who by an order dated 14.3.79 rejected the same and refused to release the property. This order has been challenged in this Rule.

3. Respondent No. 1 appeared to contest the Rule and filed an affidavit-in-opposition contending, inter alia, that Ajit Kumar Halder, the vendor was a literate man and he always used to transact business in English and monthly rent receipts granted to tenants by him were always signed in English and that Bengali signature on the alleged bainapatra dated 16.3.63 was very unusual in view of the fact that the said vendor left erstwhile East Pakistan in 1961 and did not return again. He denied that Ajit Kumar executed a bainapatra on 16.7.63. It has been alleged by the respondent that the petitioner was a turbulent type of man and he used to realise rents from the tenants of Ajit Kumar and that the property in question was recorded in the name of original owner Ajit Kumar and Ajit Kumar having left for India in 1962 and never returned back, the property in question was lawfully declared to be Enemy Property and that the property vested in the Assistant Custodian of Enemy Property in terms of the Notification No. 199 dated 3.12.65. The respondent alleged, that the bainapatra and all the documents of the petitioner were fabricated and false, and those were never produced before the respondents and that the respondents rightly refused to release the property from the list of enemy property. With regard to possession the respondent has alleged that Ajit Kumar did not hand, over possession of the property to the petitioner and that Ajit Kumar was not present in East Pakistan at the time the suit for the specific performance of contract was decreed by the Civil Court.

4. Mr. M. H Khondker, learned Advocate for the petitioner has submitted that the petitioner undisputedly being a citizen of Bangladesh and permanently residing in the town of Jessore, the property acquired and possessed by him on the basis of the kabala executed and registered through Court in a suit for specific performance of contract entered into in 1963, cannot be declared to be an enemy property under law. He has further submitted that the property in question being in lawful possession of the petitioner on the basis of a registered agreement to sell since 11.2.64, i.e. before the promulgation of Deface of Pakistan Ordinance and the Rules, 1965 the order declaring and treating the property as enemy property was without any lawful authority and is of no legal effect. The learned Advocate for the petitioner has also submitted that apart from the question of his possession on the basis of part performance of contract to sell, the petitioner acquired perfect right and title in the property on registration of the kabala in 1977 and the title and interest of the petitioner having taken effect from 15.6.63, i.e. the date of agreement, the order declaring the property as enemy property should be held to billets and without lawful authority. He has also submitted that the vendee in law became the owner on payment of the entire consideration money on 11.2.64 and that on payment of the entire consideration money the vendor bad no right in the property expecting to discharge his obligation to execute and register a kabala, and that there remained nothing to be vested in the respondents. He has lastly submitted that in view of the agreement to sell followed by part performance of the contract and delivery of the property to the petitioner in pursuance thereof, there remained nothing with the vendor which coat be vested in the respondents. In support of his contentions be has referred to the decisions in the cases reported in 34 C.L.J. 79, 20 DLR (HC) 976, 25 DLR (Dacca) 1, 30 DLR (SC) 139, 16 DLR (SC) 706, 32 DLR (AD 29 and 29 DLR (HC) 239.

<u>5. It is not disputed that the petitioner is a Bangladeshi citizen and a permanent resident of this country The petitioner alleged that be entered into an agreement with Ajit Kumar Halder, the owner of the property on 15.6.63 for transfer of the same to him at a price of Rs. 10,000/-, and on receipt of Rs. 6,000/ out of the said price on 16.3.63 he executed a deed of agreement which was registered on 16.7A2. The petitioner further alleged that he paid the entire consideration money and the last balance of Rs. 3,000/- was paid on 11.2.64 and the said vendor on receipt of the entire consideration money executed a kabala in favour of the petitioner. The vendor also executed and registered a power of attorney appointing the son of the petitioner as constituted attorney for the purpose of registering the said kabala. The kabala, however, could not be registered in view of the provisions of Ordinance No. 1 of 1964 which, however, lapsed in 1969. The respondent on the other hand has alleged that the Bainapatra, the Power of Attorney and the kabala were all fabricated and that Ajit Kumar Halder did not execute and register the documents. These are disputed questions of fact but nonetheless in appropriate cases where the evidence are patently acceptable the court can enter into and decide questions of fact in a writ of mandamus but may not decide the question of title in the property. We would not have accepted the facts alleged by the petitioner in his affidavits if a decree for specific performance of contract was not passed by a competent civil, court against the Vendor. It is seen that the petitioner filed a suit for specific performance of contract in the local civil court being other Class suit No. 108/69 in which he obtained a decree on 24.11.70 and the kabala was executed and registered through court on 26.6.71 and 24.7.71 respectively. In view of the nature of the transaction in this case which were done by registered documents in 1963 and 1964 we have no reason to reject those documents in this proceeding for the purpose of adjudicating as to whether the possession of the petitioner in the property was unlawful since 196f. It appears that the petitioner-entered into a lawful agreement with Ajit Kumar, the admitted owner of the property for transfer of the same to him. This agreement was executed on 15.6.63 and registered on 16.7.63 It is also seen that in part performance of the said agreement and on receipt of the entire consideration money the said vendor put the petitioner in possession of the property and the petitioner received the same in part performance of the contract. It has been held in the case of Messrs M. M. Ispahani Ltd. Vs. Deputy Custodian of Enemy Property reported in 20 DLR (Dacca) 493 that a person in occupation of the property on the basis of a lawful agreement cannot be ousted from his possession unless and until his possession has become unlawful and unauthorised It appears to us that the petitioner in the instant case was in possession of the property in part performance of the contract and his possession could not be said to be unlawful. A similar view has been taken in the case of Ananda Mohan Kundu Vs the Province of East Pakistan reported in 20 D.L.R (Dac.) 976 In that decision their Lordships have held as follows:-</u>

<u>"Mere vesting of the enemy property in the Custodian does not transgress on the title or the ultimate right of the real owner and a person in possession of the enemy property by virtue of a document of however limited or imperfect nature it may be cannot he said to be a trespasser and be cannot be ousted from it by the Custodian."</u>

<u>In this view it cannot be said that the possession of the petitioner in the property was unlawful so as to enable the Respondents to declare the property as enemy property or to refuse release of the same in favour of the petitioner.</u>

6. Mr M. H Khandker has further submitted that on registration of the kabala through Court right and title of the petitioner in the property vested from the date of agreement i.e. from 15.6.63 and as such there remained nothing for the Custodian to vest in him. In support of his contention Mr. M. H. Khandker has referred to a decision reported in 34 Cr.L.J. 79 in which it has been held that a suit for specific performance of contract for transfer of immovable property is ended by a final decree transferring the title and that title relates to the date of the agreement on which the suit is based, and that the Court will not permit its decree to be rendered negatory by an intermediate conveyance.

<u>7. Mr. Khondker has further submitted that the aforesaid agreement to transfer the property, followed by delivery of possession of the property to the petitioner in part performance of contract, has created an unimpeachable right of possession against any act of dispossession by the Respondents through the vendor in view of the provision of section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act. He has further submitted that the petitioner has not only a right to protect his possession in the property but has a right to enforce his right of possession therein as the vendee. In this connection, he has referred to the decision reported in the case of Mrs. June Ferguson Vs. Aminur Rashid Chowdhury reported in 25 DLR (Dacca) 1. Agreeing with the views expressed in the decision we hold that on the basis of the registered agreement dated 15.6.63 and the power of attorney registered on 12.2.64 followed by possession of the property to the petitioner in part performance of the contract the petitioner has acquired an indefeasible right of possession in the property by operation of section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act and the petitioner is entitled to enforce such right against a person claiming through the vendor. The provision of section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act have created a bar against enforcement of any right of the transfer in respect of the property in question which he would have apart from the agreement. In view of the provisions of section 53A of the Act the vendor or his successors in-interest are prevented from dealing with the property provided the vendee has performed his part of the contract and in pursuance thereof has taken possession of some immovable property. We are also of the view that the vendee or any person through the vendor is not entitled to continue aggression upon the property in question and the Vendee in the present case is entitled to protect his own possession by invoking the provisions of section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act and by instituting a suit as has been done in the present case.</u>

<u>8. Mr. Khondker has next cited a decision in the case of Joydeb Agarwala Vs. Baitulmal Karkhan Ltd. 16 DLR (SC) 706 on the question of rights and obligations of the Vendor of a property in respect of which he had entered into an agreement to transfer in favour of Vendee, Their Lordships on this question held that when there is a contract to sell land at a certain price the transferee becomes the owner of the land subject to his obligation to perform his part of the contract by paying the purchase money and subject to that the land is the land of the purchaser. In the instant case, before us, the petitioner, the vendee, having paid the entire consideration money and had performed his part of the obligation in terms of contract the vendor lost all his right and interest In the property and which devolved upon the petitioner subject to execution and registration of the deed of sale by the Vendor. In view of our findings made above further discussions of the remaining cases cited by the learned Advocate for the petitioner is not call for.</u>

9. Though ordinarily an application for writ restoration of property is not an appropriate remedy where question of title is involved, yet on the basis of penalty acceptable documents writs may issue in appropriate cases. Our expression of views on the documents should not be construed as our opinion on the questions of title of the petitioner in the property and if incidentally we have indicated our opinion as to title it would not be binding in a suit. There are series of decisions of superior Courts in this sub-continent to the effect that questions of title and complicated questions of fact should not be gone into in writ jurisdictions and proper remedy is regular suit and the finding of the High Court in writ jurisdiction with regard to title shall not be binding in a suit. Reference for our views may be made to the cases reported in 1969 SCMR 283 1968 SCMR 145 ; AIR 1957 ; S.C. 529 ; AIR 1966 S.C. 142 (145) ; 11 DLR S.C. 53.

10. The upshot of our discussion is that the proceeding taken and all actions done by the respondents including the order dated 16.11.1970 treating and declaring the property in question as enemy property must be declared to have been taken and done illegally and without lawful authority and is of no legal effect. The Rule is, therefore, made absolute. All orders treating and declaring the property and leasing out the same to the respondent Nos. 5-23 and others are set aside. The respondents are directed to release the property forthwith and deliver possession of the same to the petitioner within two months from date. In view of the facts f the case we do not make any order as to cost.

End.

lawyer:
Asrarul Hossain, Senior Advocate instructed by Sharifuddin Chaklader, Advocate-on-Record ------ For the Appellant. 
Abdus Salam, Advocate instructed by Nawab Ali, Advocate-on-Record ------ For the Respondent Nos. 1-3. 
Ex parte ------ Respondent No.4
parties:
Abdul Motalib -------------- Pre-emptee-Appellant.
Vs.
Iman Ali Mollah and ors ----------------- Pre-emptor-Respondents.
case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 16.5.1985 passed by the High Court Division, Dhaka in Civil Revision No. 616 of 1984).
full_judgment:
Mustafa Kamal, J. : The pre-emptor respondents instituted Miscellaneous Case No. 159 of1976 for pre-emption under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act in the 6th Court of Munsif, Dhaka, resisted by the pre-emptee appellant on the ground, inter alia, of limitation. The trial Court allowed pre-emption, but the lower appellate Court refused pre-emption. Both the Courts held that the question of limitation did not arise. In revision a learned Single Judge of the High Court Division, Dhaka set aside the lower appellate Court's judgment in the absence of the pre-emptee appellant in Civil Revision Case No. 616 of 1984 on 16.5.85. A Review Petition was also dismissed on 28.7.85.

<u>2. Leave was granted to the pre-emptor appellant to consider whether notice of the Rule issued in the Civil Revisional Case was served upon the father of the appellant when the former was in death-bed resulting in the disposal of the revisional case in the absence of the appellant and without his knowledge.</u>

<u>3. Leave was also granted to consider whether the trial Court ignored the provision of law in holding that limitation would start from the date when the fact of registration was entered into the Registration Book.</u>

4. On the question of notice, the following evidence of O.P.W. 1 Abdul Khaleque (father of the appellant) is instructive:-

"I am 70-75 years old, Motalib (appellant) is my son and I am looking after his property since his absence. My son is outside Bangladesh. My son executed a power of attorney in my favour for conducting the case. This is the power of attorney signed by my son Ext. I"

5. The High Court Division in disposing of the review petition on 28.7.85 clearly finds that the notice of the Rule was received by the father of the appellant in his full sense by putting his signature in the return in presence of witnesses. Nothing has been shown to the High Court Division that the appellant's father was ill and senseless when he received the notice. Hence no interference is called for with the finding .of the High Court Division that the appellant was aware of the Rule.

6. Coming now to the second point the kabala under pre-emption was presented for registration on 26.2.76. Before it was registered under section 60 of the Registration Act the pre-emptor-respondents came to know about the sale on 16.12.76 and they filed Miscellaneous Case No. 159 of 1976 for pre-emption on 22.12.76. The kabala under pre-emption was registered under section 60 of the Registration Act on 13.4.78 and delivering his judgment on 5.5.82 the learned Munsif held that as registration of the kabala was entered in the Volumes on 13.4.78, the registration was complete during the pendency of the miscellaneous case and as such the question of bar of limitation did not arise. The lower appellant Court also held so.

7. Mr. Asrarul Hossain, learned Counsel for the appellant, submits that a "transfer" of pre-emptable land effected by a registered document is to take effect under section 47 of the Registration Act and in view of sub-section (3) of section 75 of the Registration Act, it shall take effect at least from 26.2.76 after its registration on 13.4.78. The miscellaneous case having been filed on 22.12.76 is obviously barred by limitation, Mr. Hossain submits.

8. Mr. Abdus Salam Khan, learned Counsel for the respondents, submits, on the other hand, that it is well-established by now that the right of pre-emption accrues on not the date of execution or presentation of the deed for registration, but on the date of its registration under section 60 of the Registration Act.

<u>9. We find that a long line of decisions of the erstwhile Dhaka High Court has followed the principle that when registration is compulsory, the date of accrual of the right of pre-emption is not the date of execution of the deed of sale or any earlier date or the date of presentation for registration but the date on which the deed of sale is registered and the title effectively passes. The earliest case is that of Noab Mian Bhuiyan. V. Golam Hossain. 13 DLR 889. In the case of Muhammad Meher Ali Mondal V. Muhammad Karam Ali Laskar. 17 DLR 365. J. Sayem (as his Lordship then was) delivering the Division Bench judgment, pronounced as follows:-</u>

<u>"It is section 60 of the Registration Act which supplies the answer to the question as to when a document is considered to be registered In our view, the language of section 60 admits of no doubt that it is the certificate in compliance with the provision of this section that makes a document a registered document. The document can not be regarded as registered before the certificate is endorsed thereon and signed, sealed and dated in terms of section 60, nor has it to wait for acquiring the character of a registered document till after compliance with the other provisions that follow section 60. Their Lordships of the Privy Council having had an occasion to refer to this section in the case of Muhammad Ewaz V. Birj Lal (ILR 1 All 465) observed that, "the certificate is that which gives the document the character of a registered instrument."</u>

<u>To the same effect is the case of Ajimuddin Pramanik V. Najemuddin Mondal, 17 DLR 231. Azimuddin Bhuiyan V. District Registrar. Dhaka 20 DLR 355 and Abdur Rahman V. Baser Ali, 21 DLR 599.</u>

10. It is in this light that the decision of this Division in the case of Abdur Rahman @ Abdul Rahman V. Maklis Ali, 31 DLR (AD) 118, is to be looked into. In the cited case the pre-emption case was filed on 8.8.72. The kabala under pre-emption was presented for registration on 29.7.72 and it was registered under section 60 of the Registration Act on 11.8.72. As a proposition of law the earlier decisions of the erstwhile Dhaka High Court were accepted and it was affirmed that the cause of action for pre-emption accrues on date of registration of the kabala where registration is compulsory. Also it was held that the pre-maturity of the pre-emption case was cured during its pendency.

11. This Division has since followed Abdur Rahman's case in the cases of Lebu Miah V. Ganesh Chandra, 34 DLR(AD) 220 and Aftab Mia V. Wahab Ali, BCR 1982 AD 87.

<u>12. Section 47 of the Registration Act, relied upon by Mr. Asrarul Hossain, has no application. It is also well-established that section 47 of the Registration Act is called in aid to decide the claims of b two competing kabalas from the same vendor. It is designed to protect a vendee from the fraudulent operations of a vendor. This section applies when the same vendor successively transfers the same property to different purchasers at different times. The cases of Jainullah and another Vs. Anu Miah and others, 9 DLR 258 followed by Abdur Rahman V. Baser Ali, 21 DLR 599 have long gained acceptance and the case cited by Mr. Hossain, Mir Abdul Ali V. Md. Rafiqul Islam. 40 DLR (AD) 75 is the last such case along these lines having nothing to do with accrual of right of pre-emption.</u>

<u>13. The question of law that the right of pre-emption accrues on the date of registration of the deed of sale, when registration is compulsory, has stood the test of time and is now a stare decisis an established precedent handed down by past judges. Mr. Asrarul Hossain submits that it takes a longer time these days, months invariably, years too, to get a document registered under section 60 after presentation. Just when the pre-emptee is secure in his belief that he can relax with his ownership and possession of purchased land arrives the notice of a pre-emption case as a rude awakening. Surely, he submits, the pre-emptor cannot be given such a long rope with which to hang the pre-emptee after such a lapse of time. Mr. Hossain, however, hastens to add that delays in the application of law cannot be a ground for a different interpretation of law.</u>

<u>14. We are thus left with no compulsive argument to depart from the past and initiate a break. Difficulties complained of call for improvement in the administration of law, not a changed interpretation of law.</u>

15. The trial Court and the lower appellate Court correctly decided the issue of limitation. The appeal is dismissed without any order as to costs.

End.

lawyer:
Rafiqul Hoque, Fazlul Hoque, Md. Aminul Hoque ------ For the Petitioner 
H.K. Abdul Hye ------ For the Respondent.
parties:
M.A. Hai------Petitioner.
Vs.
Trading Corporation of Bangladesh------Respondent.
full_judgment:
Shahabuddin Ahmed, J.-This rule under Article 102 of the Constitution is directed against an order dated 13.4.78 of the respondent, the Bangladesh Trading Corporation, briefly, the Corporation, removing the petitioner from his service on the ground of negligence of duty which resulted in theft of the employer's property worth Tk. 83,096,00.

2. The Petitioner was, at the relevant time, Store Officer in-charge of the Bangladesh Trading Corporation's go down at Siddique Bazar, Dacca. On 6.9.74 a theft was detected in this go down and it was found, on verification that 111 rolls of synthetic fabrics had been missing from the go down. The petitioner suspects the chowkidars on duty and himself lodged a First Information Report to the Police against them. The police after investigating the case submitted final report against the chowkidars. The Corporation suspected the petitioner also and drew up a departmental proceeding against him asking him to show because why disciplinary action would not be taken against him for misappropriating the properties in question. He submitted explanation denying the allegations whereupon an enquiry was held into the allegations. The Enquiry Officer found him not guilty of the charge of misappropriation but held him guilty of negligence of duty which resulted in the said theft which was found committed through a big opening or gap above the door of the go down, and that the petitioner, who was in charge of the go down, had neglected his duty in the normal course of his work to get the gap covered up or repaired. The Enquiry Officer recommended a minor punishment but the authorities while accepting the finding of the Enquiry Officer rejected his recommendation for minor punishment and awarded the impugned punishment in view of the heavy loss involved in the matter. Being dissatisfied with the order the petitioner moved this court and obtained the rule.

<u>3. The petitioner is not a government servant but is an employee of a statutory corporation engaged in performing function of public nature. No statutory rules have been made by the Corporation for regulating the terms and conditions of service of its officers and employees. But the Corporation has been following the Government Servants (Discipline and Appeal) Rules, 1976 in the cases of its officers and employees. This, however, has not been done by any statutory instrument or notification in the Gazette but by way of a working arrangement. As such application of the Government Servants (Discipline, and Appeal) Rules cannot be enforced by a Court in the case of violation of any terms and conditions of service of the Corporation's officers and employees. The Corporation has not yet made its own Service Rules in pursuance of the statute, the P.O. No. 68 of 1972. The position of the petitioner is, however, not that of an employee under a private employer governed under the ordinary law of "Master and Servant". A decision of the Appellate Division in the case reported in 29 DLR 41 is the guiding principle in respect of matters like this and in the absence of any statutory rules the principles of natural justice shall be applicable to an employee of a statutory corporation in the case of his dismissal, removal or termination. Principles of natural justice as propounded by their Lordships of the Appellate Division in the said case in 29 D.L.R. require that before an officer or employee of a statutory corporation in dismissed or removed from service or his service is terminated, he should be given an opportunity to show cause against the proposed action and that he shall not be condemned unheard. Case of the petitioner before us is that he has been condemned unheard as no opportunity was given to him to defend himself. It is to be seen whether this contention has got substance.</u>

4. Mr Rafiqul Huq, the learned Advocate for the petitioner has assailed the impugned order of removal of the petitioner taking the ground that the petitioner was not given any opportunity to cross-examine the witnesses examined against him in his absence and that he was also not heard in person. Mr. H.K. Abdul Hye, the learned Advocate appearing for the respondent Corporation has, on the other hand, referred to the record of the case and pointed out that the petitioner was given as many as 3 show-cause notices containing the allegations brought against him and he, in a very lengthy statement in reply, gave his explanation denying the allegation and that the Enquiry Officer after considering the materials against the petitioner held him guilty of negligence of duty and on that finding the petitioner was removed from service. Principles of natural Justice as propounded in the case of (1977) 29 D.L.R. as referred to above, were fully complied with, Mr. Bye has added.

5. Annexure 'A' of the petition is a show-cause notice dated 16.4.77 issued under the signature of the Chairman of the Corporation himself; it contains the allegation against the petitioner that he misappropriated 111 rolls of Japanese synthetic fabrics valuing TK. 83,096/- and in it the petitioner was asked to show-cause within 10 (ten) days why he would not be removed from service and the value of the property should not be recovered from him. It further shows that one Mr. Ayeenul Haque, Senior Executive (Import) was appointed to enquire into the matter. Annexure B is a similar show cause notice dated 25.4.77 issued in continuation of the show-cause notice Annexure 'A', by the Enquiry Officer asking the petitioner to show-cause why disciplinary action as proposed in Annexure 'A' should not be taken against him. Annexure 'C' is the explanation in lengthy details submitted by the petitioner in reply to the show-cause notices denying the allegation and stating, inter alia, that the chowkidars against whom he had lodged the Ejahar hefted the responsibility of theft upon him. In that explanation he particularly mentioned that the theft was committed in all probability through the gap above the two doors of the go down without opening or breaking, their locks. Annexure 'F' is the report of enquiry held by Mr. Ayeenul Hoque. This shows that the Enquiry Officer after examining some witnesses including one referred to by the petitioner held that the petitioner was not guilty of actual misappropriation but was guilty of grave negligence of duty which resulted in the theft; that it was the duty of the petitioner who was in charge of the go down to get this gap above the door repaired in time but he neglected to do so and as such he was responsible for the theft. Annexure 'F' dated 26.11.77 is another show-cause notice issued by the Chairman upon the petitioner provisionally holding him guilty on the basis of the report, Annexure 'F', and proposing to remove him from service. The petitioner accordingly showed cause against the proposed action submitting his explanation, Annexure 'G' denying the allegation once again and claiming to be heard in person and also to cross-examine the witnesses examined by the Enquiry Officer. The explanation was rejected, petitioner's requests were not conceded to and he was removed from service by the impugned order, Annexure 'H'.

6. From these documents it is clear that the petitioner was given opportunity to show-cause against the proposed action. He submitted his explanation denying the allegations but the authorities after considering his explanation passed the impugned order.

7. Mr. Rafiqul Haque, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, contends that from the records as referred to above, particularly the notices, Annexures A, B and F, it is clear that the petitioner was not given "reasonable opportunity" to defend himself by cross-examining the witnesses who had deposed against him and also he was not heard in person. These are requirements la principles of natural justice, Mr. Haque further contends. In support of his contention be has referred to a number of decisions, particularly a decision of the Pakistan Supreme Court in the case of University of Dacca Vs. Zakir Ahmed (1964) 16 DLR (SC) 722, a decision of the Indian Supreme Contort in A.L.R. (SC), 1957, 882; a decision of this court in the case reported in (1974) 26 DLR 27; three recent decisions of the Appellate Division in C.A. Nos. 52 of 1977, 106 of 1977 and 138 of 1977, the first one being already reported in (1979) 31 D.L.R. (Appellate Division), 33 and a decision of the Calcutta High Court reported in A.I.R. 1970 Cal. 179.

8. In the case of Zakir Ahmed, 16 D.L.R. a student of the Dacca University was expelled on the ground that he had taken part in an unruly demonstration in the University campus during the Convocation as reported by the Provost of his hall. The University authorities simply acted on the report of the Provost who stated that he had recognised the student among forty others who had made demonstration. The student was not heard about it nor was given any opportunity to defend himself. The action of expulsion was successfully challenged in the High Court under Writ Jurisdiction, and in an appeal by the University Authorities the Supreme Court held that principles of natural justice were applicable to the case of the student and that as he was not given any opportunity to show cause against the expulsion, the impugned order violated the principles of natural justice. Mr. R. Huq has referred to paragraphs 28 and 29 of the judgment of the Supreme Court in which it has been stated, among other things, as follows : "In order to ensure the "elementary and essential principles of fairness" as a matter of necessary implication, the person sought to be affected must at best be made aware of the nature of the allegations against' him, he should be given a fair opportunity to make any relevant statement putting forward his own case, and to correct or controvert any relevant statement brought forward to the prejudice."

9. This part of the observations in the judgment has been referred to by Mr. Haque to emphasize his ground that the petitioner before us was not allowed to cross-examine the witnesses examined against him in his absence by the Enquiry Officer. As has been already pointed out, the petitioner's case is not governed by any statutory rules requiring that in the domestic enquiry witnesses should be examined in his presence or allowing him a right to cross-examine them. This aspect of the matter was taken into consideration by their Lordships of the Supreme Court of Pakistan in the case of Zakir Ahmed in which it was observed "What these principles of natural justice are it is not possible to lay down with any exactness, for, they have been variously defined in various cases, as was pointed out by the Judicial Committee in the case of the University of Ceylon V. Fernando, Tucker L J. said in Russell V. Duke of Norfolk (11), "the requirements of natural justice must depend on the circumstances of the case, the nature of the enquiry, the rules under which the tribunal is acting, the subject matter that is being dealt with, and so forth."

10. The Indian Supreme Court also held similar view as appears from its decision in the A.I.R. 1957 (SC) 882 on which Mr. Haque has placed reliance. It has been stated there as follows:

"Tribunals 'exercising quasi-judicial functions are not courts and, therefore, they are not bound to follow the procedure prescribed for trial of exciters in Courts nor are they bound by strict rules of evidence. They can unlike Courts, obtain all information materials without being fettered by rules and procedures which govern proceedings in courts. The only obligation which the law casts on them is that they should not act on any information which they may receive unless they put it to the party against whom it is to be used and give him a fair opportunity to explain it. What is a fair opportunity must depend on the facts and circumstances of a case."

11. It may be mentioned that this case was decided under Article 226 of the Indian Constitution as the person affected by an order of dismissal in that case was a government servant whose conditions of service were protected under Article 311 of the Indian Constitution. He was dismissed on a charge of attempt of bribing a person in authority but the order of dismissal was challenged in Writ Jurisdiction of the High Court which set aside the order of dismissal on the ground that the principles of natural justice were not followed in that case, but in appeal the Supreme Court cancelled the Writ and restored the order of dismissal on finding that principles of natural justice, read along with the provisions of the Indian Constitution regarding government servants, were fully followed. The case in A.I.R. (1970) Cal, 179 was also decided accordingly to Rules made under the Indian Constitution. In the case of Zakir Ahmed, 16 D.L.R. (SC) 722, as already referred to, the Court's decision as to natural justice was based on the admitted fact that the student was not given any show cause notice at all before he was expelled, whereas, in the instant case before us, as many as three show cause notices were given to the petitioner and he submitted in detail his version of the case denying the allegation of misappropriation or theft.

<u>12. In the three recent cases including C.A. No. 52 of 1978 reported in 31 D.L.R. A.D. 33, the question of principles of natural justice was considered and the decision in each case has been based on interpretation of Article 7 of the Government of Bangladesh (Services Screening) Order, P.O. 67 of 1972, The Rules Made under the P.O. 67 of 1972 do not provide for examination of witnesses in presence of the accused officer nor their cross-examination by him, whereas Article 7 of the parent law provides that an accused officer shall be given a reasonable opportunity to show cause against any proposed action. Their Lordships of the Appellate Division in construing Article 7 observed that the language of Article 7 clearly contemplates giving the delinquent officer all chances to defend himself and ensure fair trial and it is in disregard to the principles of natural justice in that case that the delinquent officer was denied the right to cross-examine the witnesses who were examined in his absence by the Screening Board constituted under the President's Order No. 67 of 1972. The Screening Board is a statutory body which is required to act according to the statute and when the statute itself, by necessary implication, provided for cross-examination of witnesses, then the Screening Board, it was held, acted illegally by denying the accused officer the right of cross-examination of the witnesses. The observations of the Appellate Division in those three cases decided by the Screening Board can hardly help the petitioner before us who was found guilty in a domestic enquiry which was not held under any statutory rules. The principles of natural justice in his case requited that the tragic be brought to his notice and he should i. e given an opportunity to submit his defence. He, in fact, submitted his defence denying the allegations but the authorities were not satisfied with his explanation. The authorities were also not bound to hold any enquiry but got every power to dispose of the case on consideration of his explanation, and if any enquiry was held there was no requirement of law that witnesses should be examined in his presence or that they should be cross-examined by him. For, these are requirements of statutes and not requirements of principles of natural justice. As to personal hearing, it is also net a requirement of the principles of natural justice. The petitioner did not pray for personal hearing when he submitted his explanation, Annexure C; he asked for personal hearing when he showed cause (Annexure G) against the proposed punishment. The authorities said not allow this prayer as it was too late. Be that as it may, in a case like the petitioner's, where there are no statutory rules making examination of cross-examination of witnesses or personal hearing of an accused mandatory, but disciplinary measures against him are governed only by the principles of natural justice, requirements of princes of natural justice are limited to giving him an opportunity to show cause why he will not be punished for the allegation as brought against him. If a detailed enquiry according to procedure followed in a court of law is contemplated then statutory rules embodying these requirements will be superfluous, principles of natural justice taking their place. In this case, it cannot be said that the petitioner has been condemned unheard. His version of the case was also taken into contract erotic by theta the rites who, however, did not accept his version.</u>

13. The last contention of Mr. Haque is that when the petitioner was given a higher punishment than recommended by the Enquiry Officer the authorities were required to record specific reasons for differing with the Enquiry Officer's recommendation, and in support he has referred to the case in (1974) 26 DLR decided by the High Court as referred to. That the authorities got power to disagree with the Enquiry Officer is not deserted. In the instant case the authorities are found to have given reason for awarding the higher punishment stating that the negligence of the petitioner had resulted in a huge loss of the Corporation's properties to the extent of TK. 83,096.00. We do not think that any Legality has been committed by tale authorities in awarding the higher punishment. The petitioner was, no doubt, charged with misappropriation but in absence of any direct evidence this charge failed, but failure of the charge of misappropriation did not in any way prevent the authorities from holding him guilty of a inner offence, such as negligence of duty.

14. On consideration of the materials produces before us we are of the view that the petitioner was not condemned unheard but was given opportunity to show cause against the proposed punishment and that the principles of natural justice as in the case (of (1977) 29 D.L.R. AD 41 are found to have been complied with etc. is nothing to interfere with the impugned order. In the result, the rule is discharged without any cruder as to costs.

Abdul Matia Khan Chowdhury J—I agree.

End.

caseno: Appeal from Appellate Decree Nos. 106 & 107 of 1965.
lawyer:
Md. Shamsul Huq Chowdhury ----- For the Appellant. 
No one ----- For the Respondents.
parties:
Moulvi Ruhul Amin ----- Appellant.
Vs.
Bazal Huq and others ----- Respondents.
full_judgment:
These two appeals arise out of judgment and decrees passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Chittagong dated 10.3.64 in other Appeal Nos. 311 and 312 of 1963 affirming those passed by the learned Mansif North Roasan Chittagong dated 3-7-63 in other Suit Nos. 123 and 124 of 1962 and arise out of two suits for redemption in both the appeals the plaintiff is the common and the respondents were different. Both were tried analogously by the Courts below and covered by the same judgment. Here also both the appeals will be covered by the same judgment.

2. The case of the plaintiff was to the effect that the properties of both the suits belonged to Aminur Rahman, Abidur Rahman, Nabidur Rahman, and Azizur Rahman who along with Tamanna Khatun, wife of Abidur Rahman, took loan of Rs. 100/- for their cushy from Sukur Ali, predecessor of defendent Nos. 1-9 of Title Suit No. 123 of 1962 by mortgaging the suit land with an area of 1 kani 12 ganda 1 kara on 11.2.30 A.D. The same persons also took a loan of Rs. 200/- on the same date as in the previous case from the defendant No. 1 of Title suit No. 124 of 1962 by mortgaging the lands of that suit comprising an area of 3 kanis 4 ganda 2 karas for their necessity. The mortgage deed for the loan of Rs. 100/a was taken by Sukur Ali in the same of his mother Hafizunnessa. The said Hafizunnessa died leaving Sukur Ali as only heir. Possession of mortgaged property was delivered in favour of mortgagees who with their heirs had been possessing the suit land even now. The said Jamana Khatun had no interest in the mortgaged property. The mortgagors i.e. Abdur Rahman and others sold the disputed property in both the suits to the plaintiff who thus became owner of the suit properties. The mortgagees and their heirs have already been enjoying double the amount of the principal by enjoying the usufruct of she mortgaged property. In spite of demands the mortgagees and their heirs the defendants are not vacating the possession of the disputed property in favour of the plaintiff. Hence these suits for redemption.

3. Defendants 1 to 5, 7, 9 of other Suit No. 123 of 1962 and defendant No. 1 of other Suit No. 724 of 1962 contested the suits by filing written statements. Their case was to the effect that the aforesaid four mortgazors namely Abidur Rahman, Azizur Rahman, Aminur Rahman and Nabidur Rahman sold the disputed property to Sukkur Mia the predecessor of defendant Nos. 1 to 9 of other suit No. 123 of 1962 and defendant No. 1 Nurul Huq of Title Suit No. 124 of 1962 by sale deeds Exts. B and B(1) for consideration of Rs. 100/- and Rs. 200/- respectively with a condition to repurchase within certain period. They contended that the transactions were out and out sale deeds with condition of repurchase and are not in any way mortgaged by conditional sale. They further contended that the plaintiff's alleged kabala with respect to the disputed property were collusive and fraudulent. The plaintiff did not acquire any title on the basis of such Kabala as his vendors had no interest in the suit land, and the plaintiff has no locus standi to bring the present suits. The defendants are in possession of the disputed property in their absolute debt.

4. The learned Munsif dismissed the suits of the plaintiff. He found that the transactions by documents Ext's. B and B(1) were out and out sale deeds with a condition of repurchase within a certain period and not mortgage and the plaintiff's kabala by which he purchased the suit land was a collusive document and by virtue of the same the plaintiff did not acquire any title.

5. The learned Subordinate Judge on appeal affirmed judgment and decree passed by the learned Munsif, also held that the documents Exts. B and B(1) were out and out sale with condition of repurchase and were not mortgage by conditional sale. As against the same the present second appeals have been preferred. Mr. Md. Shamsul Huq Chowdhury, the learned Advocate appeared on behalf of the plaintiff, appellant but the defendants have not appeared in spite of notice upon them.

<u>6. Mr. Md. Shamsul Huq Chowdhury, the learned Advocate for the appellant submits that the Courts below erred in law in holding that the documents Ext. B and B(1) were documents of out and out sale with condition of repurchase. He submits that on a reading of documents themselves it will transpire that by these documents the predecessor of the plaintiff mortgaged the suit land and the document: were not deeds of absolute sale with a condition of repurchase: that these were covered by section 58(c) and were mortgages by conditional sale. He further submits that the Courts below have misconstrued the documents Ext. B and B(1) and therefore judgments and decrees passed by the Courts below are not maintainable. Mr. Chowdhury, the learned Advocate has taken me through the documents and he has pointed out that though the documents showed that those were documents of ostensible sale but actually the details incorporated in the documents would tend to show that absolute right was not transferred and those were not documents of sale but mortgage by Conditional sale. Mr. Chowdhury, the learned Advocate, submits that though the documents Exts. B and B (1) stated that the mortgage shall have absolute right in the land transferred; the same was subject to following conditions;</u>

<u>“প্রকাশ থাকে যে মেয়াদ ১৫ বৎসরের মধ্যে ৮ বৎসর ভোগ করার পর যে সনের ফাল্গুন মাস উক্ত আসল টাকা আমরা কি আমরার পরাধীকারগন আপনি কি আপনার পরাধিকারগনকে আদায় করিলে উক্ত দলিল সহ জমি আমরার মালী কি দখলীতে ছাড়িয়া দিবা। যদি ম্যাদ মতে উক্ত টাকা আদায় না করি তবে অগ্র দলিল বরবাদ সিদ্ধক্রমে আসল কবলা পরিণত করিয়া লইতে আমরার কোন আপত্তি থাকিবে না।”</u>

<u>and these conditions are the same in both Exts. B and B(1). This condition proves that the Kabala though ostensibly showed that those were sale deed but actually they were mortgage by conditional sale. The condition referred to above clearly shows that if money is not paid within the stipulated period of 15 years the purchaser shall have the right to force on these documents and convert the same into a document of purchase. The sentence, is to the effect that “দলিল বরবাদ সিদ্ধক্রমে আসল কবলা পরিণত করিয়া। বরবাদ সিদ্ধক্রমে means "by way of foreclosure" and this condition refers to section 67 of the Transfer of Property Act by which right of foreclosure is given to the mortgagee. Section 67 of the Transfer of Property Act is to the effect that "in the absence of a contract to the contrary, the mortgage has, at any time after the mortgage money has become due to him, and before a decree has been made for the redemption of the mortgaged property or the mortgage money has been paid or deposited as hereinafter provided, a right to obtain from the Court a decree that the mortgagor shall be absolutely debarred of his right to redeem the property, or a decree that the property be sold". Thus we find that the said contents in the documents Exts. B and B(1) are in consonance with the provisions of section 67 of the Transfer of Property Act. The mention of the term; “দলিল বরবাদ সিদ্ধক্রমে আসল কবলা পরিণত করিয়া” definitely speaks of a final Kabala by virtue of a suit for foreclosure. Though in the earlier part of the documents Exts. B and B(1) absolute right has been given to mortgagor those rights were subject to the latter portion which has been quoted above. As such this was nothing but an ostensible sale. It may be noted that in the said documents the mortgagors ostensibly sold the property on condition that on such repayment being made the sale shall become void. One of the terms in the document were to the effect that if the consideration money is paid back after 8 years of the execution of document, within 15 years the mortgagees shall return the documents as also the mortgaged property to the mortgagors. The conditions were also embodied the same document in terms of proviso to section 58(C), T.P. Act. The stipulation mentioned for return of the document with the mortgaged laid to the mortgagors together with the condition of foreclosure proves categorically that the said documents exts B and B(1) were mortgage by condition of repurchase. Thus, on a proper consideration of the deeds Exts B and B(1) I find that the Courts below tried in law construing those documents and as such they erred in holding that the said documents were out and out sale deeds, with condition to re-purchase. It may also be noted that the time that was given for redemption was a longer time i.e. 15 years and the price that was paid was loan. These are also circumstances which prove that the nature of the documents were not sale deed but mortgage.</u>

The result, therefore, is that these appeals are allowed. The judgments and decrees passed by the Courts below are hereby set aside and the suits are deemed. There will be no order as to costs.

End.

lawyer:
Syed Mohammad Ali ----- For the Appellant.
H.H. Rasul ----- For the Respondent.
parties:
Sajeda Khatoon ----- Appellant.
Vs.
Mostafa Khatoon and others ----- Respondents.
full_judgment:
D. C. Bhattacharya, J. - This appeal is directed against an order of rejection of an application under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

The appellant who was Defendant No. 7 in Partition Suit No. 45 of 1959/partition suit No. 37 of 1960 of the Additional Court of Subordinate Judge, Chittagong which was instituted by Mostafa Khatun the Respondent No.1 and predecessor of Respondent Nos. 2 to 5, for partition of the properties in suit on the allegation that the said properties belonged to one Ajaluddin who died leaving Defendant respondent No. 6, as the son and one Jamiran as the daughter by one of his wives and Respondent No. I Mostafa Khatun the plaintiff, as the other daughter, by another wife of the said Ajaluddin, that Jamiran subsequently died leaving Defendant Respondent No.7 as her husband and Defendant Nos. 3 to 8 including the present appellant as her sons and daughters. The said was contested by Defendant No. 1, 11, 13 and 14 and was ultimately decreed on contest against the said defendants and on admission against Defendants 3 (kha), 4, 5 and 8 who appeared in the suit and prayed for sahams and expert against the rest in a preliminary form on 14-1-61. The main contest was by Defendant No. 1 who disputed the fight, title and interest of the plaintiff on the allegation that Ajaluddin had only, one legally married wife, who was the mother of Defendant No.1, and Jamiran, the predecessor of Defendant Nos. 2 to 8. This plea was, however, rejected by the trial Court. After the decree, Defendant No. 1 preferred an appeal to the Dacca High Court being F. A. No. 33 of 1962. Plaintiff- respondent No.1 Mostafa Khatun appeared in the said appeal and the said appeal was dismissed after full hearing by a Bench of the Dacca High, Court on 6-6-1967 comprising B.A. Siddiky and Mahmud Husain, JJ.

2. Thereafter on 26-12-67 an application purporting to be under Order 9 Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure was filed by Defendant No.6 and Defendant No.7 for setting aside the exparte decree passed against them in Partition Suit No. 45 of 1959 /Partition Suit No. 37 of 1960 of the allegation that the notices of the suit were fraudulently suppressed and that they were not aware of the decree until 20-12-67 This application was contested by the plaintiff by filing a written objection in which the material allegations made in the application were denied.

3. In support of the petition, Sajeda Khatun the petitioner No.2 examined her husband as P. W. No. 1 and examined herself as a witness on commission as P. W. 3. On behalf of the opposite parties, opposite party No.5, Jani Alam who, happens to be a full brother of the petitioners was examined as P. O. W. 1 and Nur Mia, husband of the plaintiff, Mustafa Khatun was examined as O. P. W. 2.

4. It is, however, interesting to note that petitioner No. 1 Ayesha Khatun, (defendant No. 6) virtually withdrew from the proceeding by filing a petition on 23-1-68 in the trial Court stating that her signature was taken by her maternal uncle, Defendant No.1, on a misrepresentation that her signature was necessary for withdrawal of money deposited in a L. A. Case and that she was not a petitioner in the application under Order 9 Rule 13 C. P. C. and she prayed that her name might be struck off from the record. Her husband, Saleh Ahmed, was examined as P. W. 2 in support of the allegations made in that application.

5. It was argued on behalf of Petitioner No. 2 that the petitioners who were married ladies were residing at the address of their husband whereas in the plaint they were shown to be the daughter of Saleh Ahmed residing at the address of their father. As it was shown in the Process Server's report as to the service of notice upon Defendant Nos. 6 and 7 that they were received by their father Defendant No. 2 on their behalf, the learned Subordinate Judge has Come to the conclusion that the petitioners having been married ladies and there having been nothing on record to show that Defendant No. 2 had authority to receive the summons on behalf of their daughters. Petitioner Nos. 1 and 2, there is no escape from the conclusion that the petitioners were not served with the summons in the partition suit according to law.

6. On the question of limitation, however, the learned Subordinate Judge, relying upon the evidence of O. P. W. 1 Md. Jani Alam, the brother of the petitioners, that their father received summonses and copies of plaint on behalf of all his sisters as well as on their behalf and then delivered their summonses to respective parties and that thereafter Defendant Nos. 3, 4, 5 and 8 appeared in the partition suit and on the other evidence on record has come to the finding that Petitioner No. 2 (Defendant No. 7) was aware of the present decree right from the very beginning and the application was barred by limitation. The present appeal has been filed by Defendant No. 7 as against the said order of the dismissal.

7. Mr. Syed Mohammad Ali, the learned Advocate for the appellant, has contended that the learned Subordinate Judge has committed an error in failing to notice that palpable fraud was committed by giving a wrong address of the petitioner and making a show of service upon her at a wrong address, which has also been found by the learned Subordinate Judge himself. According to the learned Advocate, that finding is sufficient for establishing fraud within the meaning of section 18 of the Limitation Act and as such the learned Subordinate Judge who has held that the onus was upon the plaintiffs to show by positive evidence that the petitioner had no earlier knowledge was patently wrong.

<u>8. We do not think there is any substance in this contention of the learned Advocate. In order to establish fraud mere non-service of notice is not sufficient. The party seeking to establish fraud should not only make specific allegations as to the nature of the fraud, but should also give cogent evidence in support thereof. It is essential in such a case to give the particulars of the persons who are alleged to have committed the fraud and also the positive steps taken by them towards furtherance of the said object.</u>

9. In the present suit, if the plaintiffs were minded to suppress notice of the suit by practicing fraud so that they could get an easy decree they should have suppressed notice on all the defendants who might have been expected to contest the suit, particularly Defendant No.1. It appears that all the defendants who are interested to defeat the claim of the plaintiff did appear in the, suit and one of them seriously contested by filing a written statement and by adducing evidence. Some others who are the brothers and sisters of the appellant petitioner appeared in the suit, admitted the allegations of the plaintiffs and prayed for sahams. It is difficult to imagine what conceivable motive the plaintiffs might have had to suppress the notice only upon Defendant No. 7 and not upon the others. Even the co-applicant of the application under Order 9 Rule 13 being her sister admitted that she had received the notice. Having regard to the facts and circumstances of the case we are definitely of opinion that there is no material on record from which an act of evil design of the plaintiffs could be inferred. We are there for of the view that the learned Subordinate Judges properly appreciated the evidence on record and rightly found that Defendant No.7 petitioner was aware of the decree from the very beginning.

10. One other fact as to the knowledge of Defendant No. 7 might have been noticed for the purpose of disposal of the Order 9 proceeding. In the First Appeal which was filed in the High Court against the decree made in the Partition Suit Defendant No. 7 was also a party as Respondent No. 7. There is a presumption that the official acts were regularly done and therefore it could have been very well presumed that Respondent No. 7 of the said appeal received the notice of the said appeal also, and was thereby fastened with the knowledge of the decree made in the said partition suit.

11. The disposal of the First Appeal referred to above, however, raises a very important question, which requires consideration, as. it appears that there is some conflict of judicial views on this question. The decree which was passed in the partition suit and which has been sought to be set aside in the Misc. Case under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure was the subject matter of the appeal preferred to the High Court as F. A. No. 33 of 1962 at the instance of Defendant No.1. The questions which were agitated in the trial Court were again argued before the High Court in the appeal and the Division Bench which heard the appeal negatived the contentions of the appellant and dismissed the appeal affirming the judgment and decree of the trial Court by its judgment dated 6-6-67. In view of the well-known principle that after the disposal of an appeal preferred against a decree made by the trial Court the decree of the Trial Court merges into the decree of the appellate Court and the Trial Court's decree ceases to exist. a very pertinent question arises as to whether the ex parte decree, as contemplated in Order 9 rule 13 of the Code still subsists and as to whether the Trial Court still retains jurisdiction to entertain a proceeding for setting aside such a decree.

<u>12. The decree against which the appeal is preferred may have been an exparte decree in respect of all the defendants or it may have been exparte in respect of only one or some of the parties. Whether there has been a complete merger of the trial Court's decree in the decree of the appellate Court is to be determined with reference to die nature of the subject matter of the appeal in each case. But if it is found that the entire decree of the trial Court was brought before the appellate Court, which has decided the appeal on merits" according to the preponderant judicial view, the trial Court's decree becomes merged in the decree of the appellate Court, and the trial Court does not retain thereafter any jurisdiction to exercise powers under Order 9 rule 13 C. P. Code to set aside the exparte decree, which has in the meantime, become non-existent.</u>

<u>13. The principle involved in this question was the basis of a decision by the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in the case of Brij Narain Vs. Tajbal Bikram Bahadur, in L. R. 37 Indian Appeal page 70 same case I.L.R. 32 Allahabad 295 same case 14 C.W.N. 667. In the said case a mortgage decree was passed in a suit by the Court of a Subordinate Judge under section 88 of the Transfer of Property Act, which gave future interest on the amount decreed and it was affirmed on appeal by the High Court. Subsequently on the application of the judgment-debtor, the, Subordinate Judge, despite objections by the decree holders amended the decree by striking out the future interest on the ground that such interest was not in accordance with the judgment on which the decree was based. The decree-holder one of them being a transferee made separate applications to the High Court for revision of the Subordinate Judge's order. A Bench of the Allahabad High Court held on the application of the transferee decree-holder that the Subordinate Judge had no jurisdiction to amend a decree which had been affirmed by the High Court and on the, said view set aside the order but only so far as it affected the transferee decree-holder. With regard to the other decree-holder, the same Bench refused to exercise their discretionary power of revision. The matter having been taken before the Judicial Committee; it was of the view that if the decree of the First Court was made without jurisdiction for altering a decree after it had been affirmed in appeal in the case of one decree-holder, so also the alteration in the case of the other decree-holder was equally ineffectual and ought not to have been allowed to stand.</u>

<u>14. Although the view as expressed by the Judicial Committee in the said case was characterized by extreme brevity of language but it did not leave any body guessing as to there content of its decision. After a decree of the trial court has been affirmed in the appeal by the appellate Court, the trial Court loses its jurisdiction to amend its decree which it had under the law, as, by virtue of the decree of the appellate Court, it has ceased to be the decree of the Trial Court.</u>

15. Several years before the aforesaid decision of the Judicial Committee, a Bench of three Judges of the Calcutta High Court had to deal with the question of jurisdiction of the trial court to set aside its decree a part of which was affirmed by two appellate Courts under section 108 of the old code, in the case of Monmohini Choudhurani vs. Nara Narayan Roy Chowdhury, in 4 C.W.N. 456. A decree was passed in the said case against Defendants No. 1 and 2 on contest and exparte against others, who were tenant defendants. It was only Defendants No. 1 and 2 who appealed against the decree to the Court of the District Judge and also the High Court without making other defendants parties to the said appeals, but the said appeals were dismissed.
