There after on an application made by some of the tenant defendants against whom the decree was made exparte, the court of Munsif set aside the exparte decree and directed denovo trial of the suit as a whole So far as the exparte decree was concerned it apparently did not merge in the decree of the appellate Court, so no exception could be taken to the setting aside of the exparte part of the decree which was not before the two Courts of appeal, but so far as the contested part of the decree as affirmed by the appellate Courts, was concerned, the trial Court had clearly no Jurisdiction. Maclean C. J. expressed the view of the Bench in the following words:

"Sec. 108 of the Code contemplates the case of the Court which actually made the decree setting aside its own decree, and not setting aside that of another and a higher tribunal, otherwise We should be landed in the absurdity that if Defendants No. 1 and 2 had taken the case to her Majesty, and, as against them, the decree had been, affirmed, the Munsif on the application of other Defendants could set aside the decree of Her Majesty in Council. This can scarcely be."

16. The next case in which the Calcutta High Court had to consider a similar question is the case of Dhonai Sardar Vs. Tarak Nath Chowdhury in 12 C.L.J. page 53 where the said High Court held that an exparte decree having been affirmed by the appellate Court could not be set aside by the Court of the first instance. But the reasoning in support of the view taken in this case was that after an appeal had been preferred, the original Court could not continue to exercise any jurisdiction in respect of the suit and the case of Saakara Bhatta Vs. Subraya Bbatta and others, D.L.R. 30 Mad 535 which held that after an appeal was filed against a decree of the lower Court, the power to set aside the original decree under section 108 of the old Code became vested in the Appellate Courts, was referred to in support of the view of the Court which however, was not the correct view of law as has been held subsequently.

17. In another early case, viz. Brija Lal Singh Vs. Mahadeo Prasad, 12 I. C.669, the Calcutta High Court took the view that in spite of the appellate decree to which the defendant against whom the decree was made exparte was made a proforma respondent, the exparte decree of the trial Court was not superseded as the plaintiff’s appeal was confined to the contesting defendants only.

18. The Allahabad High Court in the case of Mathura Prasad Vs, Ram Charan Lal, in I. L. R. 37 Allahabad 208 same case A.I.R. 1915 Allahabad page 2 held that although the application for setting aside the exparte decree was made, in the original Court, before any appeal had been filed against the said decree, the said Court did not have jurisdiction to entertain such application after the appeal had been disposed of because the decree of the lower Court had been superseded by the decree of the appellate Court

19. This question came up for consideration before a Division Bench of the Calcutta High Court again in the case of Kalimuddin Vs. Esabakuddin, in I.L.R. 51 Cal.715 same case 28 C. W. N. 795 same case A.I.R. 1924 Cal. 830 in which M. N. Mukherjee J on an analysis of the various decisions of different High Court, laid down his view very clearly in the following words:

"When the ex parte decree has been confirmed or otherwise disposed of in appeal, the Court which passed the exparte decree has no longer any power to entertain an application to set it aside, even though the application was made before the appeal was filed: Mathura Vs. Ram Charan, I.L.R. 37 All. 208.

The same principle will hold good, even if the appeal has been preferred by a party other than the defendant against whom the decree was passed exparte, provided the decree was one and indivisible (Dhonai Sardar Vs.Tarak Nath Chowdhury, 12 C.L.J. 53) Now, the test to be applied is to determine whether the Subordinate Judge had jurisdiction to vacate the exparte decree over which the Subordinate Judge had control. The answer to the question would depend upon the scope of appeal by which expression is meant not merely the value of it. but a variety of other things as well, viz., the subject matter involved, the parties concerned therein and the .manner of its disposal. "

21. In the facts of that case it was, however, held that the decree of the first Court did not merge in the decree of the appellate Court dismissing the appeal as the only question which was decided in the appeal was that it was not maintainable in the absence of the minor legal representatives of a deceased respondent, against whom the appeal was dismissed earlier for non-payment of the costs of the Deputy Registrar.

22. In the case of Abdul, Khalef Molla and others Vs. Bama Charan Chatterjee, and others, in 36 C.W.N. 747 same case A.I.R. 1932 Cal. 773 another Division Bench of the Calcutta High Court appear to have accepted the principle that if a decree of the original court being affirmed by the Appellate Court merges in the decree of the appellate Court, a defendant against whom the original decree was made exparte is incompetent to apply under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil procedure, but in the case the original decree having been passed on contest against some of the defendants and ex parte against others and some of the contesting defendants having preferred an appeal against the said decree without impleading the other defendants, in the appeal, the defendants, against whom the decree was passed exparte, and who were not made parties in the appeal, were held to be competent to apply to set aside the exparte decree passed against them, even though the appeal filed by some of the contesting defendants in the Court of the District Judge was dismissed after hearing and the Second appeal filed in the High Court was Summarily dismissed, under Order 41 rule 11 C.P. Code, as, in the opinion of the said Bench, the defendants against whom the decree was made exparte having not been made parties in the first appeal as well as in the, Second Appeal, the said exparte decree did not merge in the appellate decrees.

23. The same question came up for consideration in the case of Monomohan Kundu Vs. Nripendra Nath Nandi and others before a, Division Bench of the Calcutta High Court consisting of Nasim Ali and Edgley JJ, reported in 41 C.W.N. 1271 same case A.I.R. 1937 Cal/548 same use 172 I. C.608, in which the ratio of the case was stated in the following words:

"By rule 13 of Order 9, C.P. Code the Court which passes an exparte decree has authority to set aside the exparte decree. The exercise of the power presupposes the existence of an  ex parte decree. If an appeal is preferred against the ex parte decree the exparte decree continue till the appellate Court has determined the rights of the parties in controversy. After such, determination by the Court of appeal, the decree of the trial Court ceases to exist. If the decree of the trial Court is affirmed in appeal it merges in the decree of the Court of appeal and consequently ceases to have any existence. See the case in L. R. 37 I.A. 70."

24. In the said case, although the original decree was, passed against some of the defendants. on ton test and exparte against others, and some of the contesting defendants preferred an appeal impleading all the remaining defendants, the decree of the trial Court having been affirmed in appeal was found to have merged in the decree of the Court of appeal and to have ceased to subsist any longer, and as such it was held that there was no exparte decree subsisting which could be set aside under Order 9 rule 13, C. P. Code.

25. All the High Courts of the Indian sub-continent except that of Madras appear to have conformed to the view that after a decree of the original Court, which may be contested or exparte or partly exparte and partly contested has merged in the decree of the appellate Court, the original Court does not retain jurisdiction to set aside the exparte decree. Whether the decree of the first Court has merged in the decree of the appellate Court is to be ascertained from the scope and subject matter of the appeal the manner of its disposal in each case.

26. The judgment of Abdur Rashid J. of the Lahore High Court in the case of Sohan Singh and others Vs. Mool Singh and others, in A.I.R. 1934 and Lah. 1016 has been some times referred quite wrongly in support of the view adopted by the Madras High Court. As a matter of fact, the learned Judge has specifically observed in the said case that the ruling of the Madras High Court reported in A.I.R. 1927 Mad. 722 did not lay down sound law and was opposed to the view taken by the other High Courts and then proceeded to hold that the principle underlying the various rulings of different High Courts is that where the appellate, Court has adjudicated regarding the rights and liabilities of the person against whom an exparte decree has been passed, the exparte decree against such person cannot be set aside by the trial Court but that where there has been no adjudication regarding the rights and liabilities of such person in the appellate Court, the trial Court is entitled to entertain an application for the setting aside of the exparte decree against him.

27.  The Allahabad High Court has taken similar view in the case of Ram Rakhan and another Vs. Mohant Gobind Das, reported in A.I.R. 1945 Allahabad 352 in holding that where a party against whom a decree has been made exparte has not been made party in the appeal and the appeal has been disposed of in the absence of the said party, the trial Court's decree against the non-impleaded party may not be deemed to have merged in the decree of the appellate Court.

28. A Division Bench of the Nagpur High Court in the case of Kikabhai Vs. Mt. Safia Bibi reported in A.I.R. 1939 Nail. 381 and Division Bench of the Sind Chief Court in the Case of Vatoomal Thanwerdas Vs. Godhumal Mulchand, reported in A.I.R. 1948 Sind 10 have been of the view that even in a summary dismissal of an appeal under Order 41 rule. 11 C.P. Code the trial Court's decrees is superseded and that as such the trial Court is no longer competent to entertain an application for sets ting aside the exparte decree.

29. The same view appears to have been taken by the High Court of Madyabharat and the High Court of Bombay of Indian Jurisdiction in the cases of Palbhim Rao Vs. Alkh Murarilal, reported in A.I.R. 1954 Madhya-Bharat 4 and Kantilal Vs. Chiba Bays, reported in A.I.R. 1967 Bombay 310, respectively. These High Courts have accepted the principle laid down in the decisions of the majority of the High Courts of the sub-continent and expressed their dissent from the view of the Madras High Court.

30. The judicial history as to the consequences which may befall an aggrieved party's right to set aside an exparte decree, as a result of the disposal of the appeal affirming the said decree on appeal, so far as the High Court of Madras is concerned, appears to have followed an entirely different course. In the case of Ramanadhan Chetty Vs. Ramayanan Chetty, reported in I.L.R. 27 Mad. 602, a view was expressed to the effect that after an appeal had been preferred the trial Court lost its jurisdiction to deal with the decree of the lower court by way of review, as the entire litigation and all matters are transferred to and placed under the control of the appellate Court. This view was reaffirmed in Sankara Bhatta Vs. Subrayar Bhatta, I.L.R. 30 Mad. 535, while dealing with the power of the trial Court to set aside an exparte decree, after an appeal had been filed against the said decree. It may be noticed that in these cases, the trial Court's decree was not superseded by the decree of the appellate Court, but even then it was held that merely after the filing of an appeal, the trial Court became incompetent to set aside an exparte decree. In the Full Bench case of Chenna Reddi Vs. Peddasha Reddi I.L.R. 32 Mad. 416 (F.B.) it was however pointed out that if an appeal was filed after an application for review has been filed, the trial Court did not lose jurisdiction to deal with the application for review and I.L.R. 27 Mad. 602 was held to be incorrectly decided, although no such opinion was expressed in respect of I.L.R. 30 Mad. 535.

31. In the case of Palaniappa Reddy Vs. Subramanla Chetty, A.I.R. 1922 Mad. 33, a Division Bench took the view that even where a defendant had been a party to the appeal which had been disposed of an application by him to set aside an exparte decree passed against him did not lie in the appellate Court but ought to have been filed in the first court. It does not appear that the said Bench paid any attention to the principle that the exparte decree of the trial Court had merged in that of the appellate Court and that the exparte decree had become non-existent because of the said merger. Neither the decision of the Judicial Committee nor the reasoning’s given in support of the contrary view taken by the other High Courts were adverted to.

32. " A Single Bench decision of the said High Court in the case of Subramania Iyer Vs. Varada Rajalu Naidu, reported in A.I.R. 1927 Mad. 722 merely followed the Palaniappa Chetty's case, as it was Division Bench decision. Another Single Bench of the same High Court in the case of In re Vinkata Subraramian, reported in A.I.R. 1944 Mad. 576 also merely followed the earlier decisions in A.I.R. 1922 Mad. 33 and A.I.R. 1927 Mad. 722.

33. In none of these decisions which lay-down an opinion quite contrary to the view expressed by the other High Courts of the sub-continent, some of which are well reasoned and very lucidly expounded, there is any adequate consideration of the basic principle involved in such cases.

34. This question appears to have come up for consideration before the Dacca High Court in 3 cases, namely, Abdul Jalil Bhuiyan and others Vs. Majibar Nessa Bibi and others reported in 12 D.L.R. (Dacca) 581, Makhan Lal Dutta Vs. Joytun, reported in 16 D.L.R. (Dacca) 130 and Atul Chandra Das Vs. Bhagabati Das and others reported in 18 D.L.R. (Dac.) page 81.

35. In the case reported in 12 D.L.R. 581, Hasan J, who decided the said case relying upon the decisions of the Calcutta High Court in the case of Monmohini Choudhurani Vs. Narayon Ray Chowdhury and others 4. C.W.N. 456 Kalimuddin Vs. Easbakuddin, A.I.R. 1924 Cal. 830 and Monmahan Kundu Vs. Nripendra Nath Choudhury and others A.I.R. 1937 Cal. 548, accepted the principle that the trial Court loses the jurisdiction to exercise powers under Order 9 rule 13 C.P.C. if the dial Court's decree has merged in the appellate Court's decree passed in an appeal from the said decree. But on the facts of that case the learned Judge came to the conclusion that since the appeal was in respect of only apart of the decree passed by the trial Court, there was no merger of the exparte decree with regard to the share of the defendant who sought to have the said decree set aside under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

36. In the case of Mallin Lal Vs. Joytun which arose. out of a proceeding under section 96 .of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and was decided by Asir J, sitting singly, the learned Judge appears to have preferred the view of the Madras High Court and held that the trial Court can exercise the power under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside an exparte order even after the appeal which was preferred against the said order has been disposed of. It may be noted that the applicant in the proceeding under Order 9 rule 13 C.P.C. and the appellant against the exparte order was the same person. It appears that the view of Hasan J, as expressed in 12 D.L.R. (Dacca) 581 was not brought to the notice of this Court. The reasoning of the learned Judge has been expressed in the following words:

"I am inclined to think that the function of the trial Court upon an application under Order 9 rule 13 C.P.C. is not dependent upon the function of the appellate Court while exercising its jurisdiction over an appeal preferred against a decree which stands a chance of being set aside under Order 9 rule 13 C.P.C. As such, the trial Court which has been given special power and jurisdiction under the statute cannot be supposed to lose such jurisdiction simply because the original decree as passed by the trial Court has merged in the decree of the appellate Court before the disposal of the application under Order 9 rule. 13. C.P.C.

37. In a subsequent case before another learned Single Judge, Sayem, J. (as his lord- ship then was) a similar question arose, but his lordship though inclined in favour of the view of the Madras High Court, was unable to agree with the view expressed in the case of Makhan Lal Dutra Vs. Joytun Bibi as the applicant himself was the appellant, and the matter was referred to a Division Bench consisting of Murshed C.J. and Abdullah J. and the said Bench has expressed itself in the said case, which has been reported has Atul Chandra Vs. Bhagabat Das and others in 18 D.L.R. (Dacca) 81, generally in favour of the view that the original court does not lose Jurisdiction to dispose of a proceeding under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code even after an appeal preferred against the said exparte decree has been disposed of by the appellate Court, although OD the facts of that case, the learned Judges were of the view that the defendants in question were not entitled to any relief in the proceeding under Order 9 rule 13 C.P.C. In the said case, a decree was passed ex parte against Defendants No. 4-7, on contest against Defendant Nos. 8 and 10 and without contest against the rest. Defendants Nos. 4 to 6 filled an application in the Trial Court under order 9 rule 13 C.P.C. to set aside the exparte decree and also filed an appeal against the said exparte decree. The appeal was heard before the disposal of the application under Order 9 rule 13 and was dismissed affirming he judgment of the Trial Court. The Misc. Case under Order 9 rule 13 in the meantime was dismissed for default but the petitioners preferred a Misc. Appeal as against the said order. The appellate Court dismissed the appeal on the ground that after the dismissal of the appeal against the decree, the application under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure was no longer maintainable. The Division Bench, which ultimately heard the rule obtained under section 115 C.P. Code against the said order of dismissal, discharged it on the view that the petitioners had complete opportunity of mooting the points, raised by them in their written statement, in the appeal filed by them and that after having obtained an adverse decree the petitioners were not entitled to have this matter considered again. The learned Judges, however, even after dismissal of the application proceeded to discuss the question of law which according to them, was referred to the larger Bench because of the conflicting and some what rather irreconcilable decisions and proceeded to give their opinion on the question.

38. Chief Justice Murshed who has delivered the judgment of the Bench also failed to notice the judgment of Hasan, J. as reported in 12 D.L.R. (Dacca) 581, but has referred to the judgment of Asir, J. as reported in 16 D.L.R. (Dacca) 130, the judgment of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in 37 I.A. 70, several decisions of the High Courts, of preparation India and also a subsequent decision of the Indian Jurisdiction in A.I.R. 1954 Madhya Bharat 4, and expressed the view of the Bench Oil this question in the following manner:

"It is true that the original decree loses its identity in the appellate decree which suppliants the original decree a1Id wipes out its existence. But the right conferred under Order 9 rule 13 is of a different nature, namely, a right by a party who has not at all been beard in respect of the decree that has been passed against such party to apply to the trial court to set aside the decree. It is a right specially conferred by law without which no such right could have existed. It is a statutory relief of a special kind arising out of the mandate of law."

Before we proceed to appreciate the reasoning of the Bench in support of their view as quoted above we may with great respect point out that if the trial Court does not really lose jurisdiction to entertain an application for setting aside an exparte decree under Order 9 rule 13 C.P. Code after the said exparte decree has merged in the decree of appellate Court the view expressed by the said Bench that the defendant who has suffered an exparte decree passed against him should not be lowed any relief under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code as he had full opportunity of being heard in the appeal on all points which he intended to canvass in the trial Court does not seem to be supported by any legal principle or any authority.

39. This view does not appear to have taken sufficient notice if we may say so with respect of the difference between the scope of a suit restored to file as a result of the setting aside of an exparte decree under Order 9 rule 13 C.P. Code and that of an appeal preferred against the said exparte decree. The scope of such an appeal is very much limited as it is to be decided ordinarily on the basis of the exparte evidence adduced by the plaintiff, whereas in the suit which may have been restored as a result of the setting aside of the ex parte decree, the defendant will be free to take any objection and adduce any evidence in support of his case and as such its scope is much wider, However, it is not necessary for us to dilate more on this point as in our opinion, the basic premise of the view viz, the continuance of the trial Court's jurisdiction to set aside an ex parte decree even after the merger of the; said decree in the decree of the appellate Court, does not appear to be well founded. The learned Chief Justice has no doubt expressed the opinion of the Bench in very firm and emphatic terms but the only rational which has been put forward.in order to lend support to the said view seems to be that light conferred under, and the remedy provided In Order 9 rule 13 C.R Code is a statutory relief of a special kind arising out of the man date of law and is not likely to be defeated because of any extraneous consideration.

<u>40. It can hardly be disputed that this remedy, as all remedies are is a creature of a Statute and in founded upon the well recognised principle of Justice that no one shall suffer any peril unheard. This remedy may however be invoked only within the terms of the statute creating such a remedy and it shall be available to an aggrieved party so long it does not become repugnant to any basic Judicial concept.</u>

<u>41. The power which has been conferred upon the trial Court under Order 9 rule 13 C.P. Code is for the purpose of setting aside an exparte decree, and therefore subsistence of an exparte decree is a necessary precondition to the exercise of such a power. If as a matter  of fact the ex parte decree of the trial Court has merged in the decree of the appellate Court, there is no independent existence of the trial Court's decree which the appellate Court has made his own and it has virtually become nonest. How can the trial Court separate the exparte decree out of the ambit of he decree of the appellate Court and exercise its power by setting it aside. By setting aide the exparte decree in such a case, the trial Court Will be virtually undoing the decree of the appellate Court, which having been passed in presence of the party concerned or after giving him proper notice, as has happened in the instant Case, is otherwise binding upon the parties. Terms of the rule in question dearly contemplate the existence of a decree or the trial Court and such a power as has been given in the said rule can be exercised only if an exparte decree is alive and available for the exercise of the said power.</u>

42. The learned Chief Justice noticed the case of Brij Narain Vs. Tejbal, L.R. 37 I.A. 70, decided by the Judicial Committee and sought to distinguish it on the ground that the said case involved the question of amendment of a decree which was not drawn up in accordance with the Judgment while the right conferred under Order 9 rule 13 C.P. Code was a special right of different nature. With great respect to the view of the learned Chief Justice it may be pointed out that basically there is hardly any difference between the exercise of these two powers, excepting that the power under Order 9 rule 13.C.P.Code is of more drastic character. The view of the Judicial Committee was that such a power of amendment although created by statute for correction of certain mistakes which could be due not to the default of the party but to the Court itself could not be exercised if the said decree had already merged into a decree of the appellate Court. The power granted to the trial Court for amendment of a decree for correction of a mistake in the decree is also a statutory remedy and beneficial to the party in the same way as the one contemplated under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

<u>43. We, therefore, fired ourselves unable to accept the view expressed by the learned Chief Justice that the said case of the Judicial Committee was an authority only for the proposition that first court's decree became merged in the decree passed by the appellate Court and that it could not be the basis for the proposition that no application under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure could be made after an appeal from the original decree had been disposed of.</u>

<u>44. The learned Judges of the Dacca High Court deciding the case reported in 16 D.L.R. (Dacca) 113 and 18 D.L.R. (Dacca) 81 have failed to properly notice the inevitable legal consequences, which flow from the merger of the trial Court's decree in the decree of the appellate Court namely, that there is no separate existence of the trial Court's decree apart from that of the appellate Court. The effect of such a consequence upon a proceeding under Order 9 rule 13 C.P. Code, which has not received adequate attention in the said cases, is that there is no subsisting decree of the trial Court which can be set aside by such a court, as was observed by Nasim Ali, J in the case reported in A.I.R. 1937 Cal. 548, and that if the trial Court exercises the power under the said rule, it will set aside a decree which is not its own, but is that of a superior court, as so clearly pointed out by Maclean C.J., in 4 C.W.N. 456. We have given anxious consideration to the different views expressed in the various decisions referred to above and we are definitely of the view that after the merger of the trial Court's decree in the decree of the appellate Court the trial Court's decree cases to exist for the purpose of a proceeding under Order 9 of the Code and as such there cannot be any exercise of the power under the said Order by the trial Court for setting aside such a decree which has already been superseded. In the instant case, the entire decree of the trial Court was brought before the High Court in the First Appeal which was preferred to it and in which all the defendants were made parties, and as such when the High Court dismissed the appeal arid affirmed tried the decree of the trial Court, there is no room for doubt that the entire decree of the trial had merged in the decree of the Court of appeal made in F.A. No. 33 of 1962.</u>

<u>We are, therefore, of the view that the application under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code was not maintainable in the circumstances of the case. The result, therefore, is that this appeal is dismissed with costs.</u>

S.M. Mohsen Ali, J.-I agree.

End.

(From the Judgment and order dated 11-12-94 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.25 of 1984 (Comilla) Civil Revision No.839 of 1990 (Dhaka).
full_judgment:
Latifur Rahman J: Civil Appeal No. 22 of 1997 by the defendant-appellant, Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Comilla by leave and Civil Appeal No. 23 of 1997 by Abdul Karim as defendant-lessee by leave are disposed of by a common judgment as those arise from a common judgment and order dated 11-12-94 passed by a learned Single Judge of the High Court Division making the Rule absolute in Civil Revision No. 24 of 1984 (Comilla)/838 of 1990 (Dhaka) and Civil Revision No. 25 of 1984 (Comilla)/839 of 1990 (Dhaka), setting aside the Judgment and decree of the Additional District Judge, First Court Comilla in Title Appeal No. 233 of 1990 on 11-12-90, reversing those of the Subordinate Judge, First Court, Comilla in Title Suit No. 64 of 1972, decreeing the suit of the plaintiff-respondent.

2. Respondent No. 1 as plaintiff instituted the aforesaid Title Suit against the appellant and respondent Nos. 2-5 for declaration of his title to the property in schedule annexed to the plaint and confirmation of possession therein and alternatively recovery of khas possession of the same. The plaint case is that, respondent No. 4 Rabindra Kumar Dey had purchased the suit land from the original owner, the Eastern Commercial Bank Ltd in the benami of his elder brother respondent No. 3 Birendra Kumar Dey who did not pay any consideration, by registered kabala dated 24-8-44 AD as he was indebted to many persons at the relevant time. Rabindra Kumar raised structures and let out the same to monthly tenants. Rabindra paid rents and taxes in the name of his brother Birendra Kumar and after he left this country Rabindra got his own name mutated in the settlement papers and in the municipality and ever since paid rents and taxes in his own name. The Government realised rent from Rabindra who paid up the certificate dues in Certificate Case No. 28330 of 1960-61. Rabindra''s brother Birendra had sworn an affidavit on 7-5-64 before the Presidency Magistrate, Calcutta, declaring that he was simply a benamder of Rabindra Kumar who was the real owner of the property. Rabindra sold the property to respondent No. 1 for a consideration of Rs. 15,000.00 by a registered kabala dated 20-11-63 AD. Respondent No. 1 after purchase mutated his name in the office of the Government and the municipality, and accordingly, paid rent and taxes. Respondent No. 1 filed suits for ejectment of monthy tenants and at this stage, the tenants set up one Asmat Ali who filed an application before the Assistant Custodian of Enemy Property (L&B), Comilla praying for taking lease of the same as enemy property whereupon enemy property Case No. 274 of 1969 was started and after enquiry the Assistant Custodian of Enemy Property by his order dated 21-4-69 held that the suit property was not an enemy property. But subsequently, the tenants of the plaintiff managed to influence the Assistant Custodian and obtained an order dated 5-5-69 behind the back of respondent No. 1 declaring the suit property as enemy property. On coming to know about the aforesaid order respondent No. 1 filed Title Suit No. 263 of 1969 in the Court of Munsif, 3rd Court, Comilla challenging the legality of the order dated 5-5-69 but the suit was withdrawan and Writ Petition No.177 of 1969 was filed for speedy relief. The Rule in the Writ Petition was discharged on 3-6-76 as not maintainable. Thereafter respondent No. 1''s Civil Petition for leave to appeal was also dismissed on 24-11-76. During the pendency of the aforesaid Writ Petition respondent No. 1 instituted the instant suit.

3. Respondent No. 5, Abdul Karim (appellant in Civil Appeal No. 23 of 1997) got himself added as defendant No. 5 in the suit on filing an application under rule 10 Order 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure and contested the suit.

4. The Assistant Custodian, defendant-appellant and the said added defendant Abdul Karim contested the suit by filing identical written statements. Their common case is that respondent No. 3 Birendra Kumar was a First Class Contractor and he purchased the suit property with his own fund and owned and possessed the same on payment of rents and taxes in his own name. He left for India in 1958 forever. Respondent No.4 used to pay rent and taxes in his name and realised rents from the tenants on his behalf as care-taker. Taking advantage of the absence of Birendra, Rabindra, respondent No.4 managed to have his name recorded in the settlement records and also got his name mutated in municipal record and thereafter paid rents and taxes in his own name. Rabindra never purchased the suit property in the benami of his brother Birendra and he was not the owner of the property and, as such, by purchase on 22-11-63 from him, the plaintiff did not derive any title to the property and he was also not in possession through tenants as alleged. One Asmat Ali applied on 8-2-69 for taking lease of the property as enemy property but through oversight the said property was released on 11-4-69, where after persons in possession of the property filed a petition for review of the order and the Assistant. Custodian, on consideration of the materials on record, declared the suit property as enemy property by order dated 5-5-69. The plaintiff failed to establish his claim in writ petition and lost upto the Appellate Division. The property has been leased out to different persons including respondent No. 5 and they are possessing as lessee under the Assistant Custodian of Enemy Property. The suit is liable to be discharged.

5. The suit was decreed by the trial Court holding that the Government accepted Rabindra as the real owner and recorded his name in the record of rights as early as 1960-61 and realised rent from him amicably and also by issuing certificate case. Rabindra was openly and uninterruptedly exercising all right as the real owner since 1960-61 without any objection or opposition from any quarters and upon holding as aforesaid, the learned Subordinate Judge declared that the suit property is not an enemy property. The trial Court also found that DW 1, the Tahsildar stated in his deposition that the suit land was listed as enemy property in the census list in the year 1967 but he could not produce any paper to prove it. The trial Court further found in respect of the genuineness of the transaction of the plaintiff that it is an admitted fact that he purchased the suit land by registered deed, realised rent, mutated his name in the municipality. His purchase was also proved by PW 2. There is no evidence to believe that the purchase of the plaintiff is a sham and bogus transaction. The tenants who admitted him as landlord are no more possessing the suit land in the capacity of tenants but as lessees of the Government.

6. Against the aforesaid decree, the appellant preferred Title Appeal No. 233 of 1980 and added respondent No. 5 appellant preferred Title Appeal No. 3 of 1981 and both the appeals were heard and disposed of analogously by the Additional District Judge, Comilla. The learned Court of appeal below reversed the findings of the trial Court after holding that Birendra was the real owner of the property and since Birendra was living in India at all material times, the same was rightly declared as enemy property and, as such, the plaintiff derived no title by his purchase from Rabindra. The affidavit of Birendra Kumar sworn in Calcutta is inadmissible having not been processed through the diplomatic channel as required by law.

7. Mr. Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, learned Additional Attorney-General, appeared in Civil Appeal No. 22 of 1997 and Mr Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed, learned Advocate appeared in Civil Appeal No. 23 of 1997 on behalf of a lessee under the vested property authority.

8. Leave was granted to consider primarily on two grounds. First, whether learned Single Judge of the High Court Division in exercise of his revisional jurisdiction acted wrongly in setting aside the findings of fact of the lower appellate Court which is the final court of fact and has taken a contrary view on reassessment of the evidence by disregarding the settled principles for exercising of such revisional jurisdiction under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

9. Secondly, leave was granted to consider whether Ext. 9, the affidavit sworn by defendant No. 3 Birendra Kumar Deb brother of defendant No. 4 Rabindra Kumar Deb before the Presidency Magistrate, Calcutta on 7-5-64, though admitted into evidence without objection is per se inadmissible in evidence as the same was not legally notarized/certified by the Consulate in Calcutta in India and whether the learned Single Judge acted wrongly in considering this inadmissible evidence in the case.

10. Mr. Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed adopts the argument of the learned Additional Attorney-General and elaborates on the legal aspect of Ext. 9, the affdavit sworn in Calcutta, India.

11. The material point for consideration in these petitions is the determination whether Rabindra Kumar Deb purchased the property in the benami of his elder brother Birendra Kumar.

12. The lower appellate Court on consideration of the materials on record held that the plaintiff failed to prove the case of benami whereas the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division in revision found that the benami was proved by the plaintiff and consequently decreed the suit.

13. As the plaintiff set up the case that he purchased the property from defendant No. 4 treating it to be the property of defendant No. 4, the story of benami must be proved by the plaintiff.

14. The original kablaa dated 24-8-44 by which Rabindra Kumar Dey purchased the property in the benami of his brother Birendra Kumar Dey from Eastern Commercial Bank Ltd, Comilla could not be produced by the plaintiff as the same was lost. The certified copies of the kabala were filed by the parties. The kabala of the plaintiff was marked as Ext. 1, while the copy of the defendant was marked as Ext. A. The lower appellate Court found that the plaintiff while deposing as PW 1 said that he lost the original kabala from his custody as it was stolen away by thieves but no GD entry was filed by the plaintiff. Thus the lower appellate Court found that the original deed could not be produced from the custody of the plaintiff. On the contrary the plaintiff procured Ext. 1, the certified copy of the kabala on 3-7-64. The learned Single Judge held that no legal inference could be made for disbelieving that the deed had been stolen simply because no GD Entry was made. The original kabala of the plaintiff''s vendor having been lost he procured the certified copy of the kabala. This explanation was given by the plaintiff for non-production of the original kabala. The suit was filed by the plaintiff long after the theft of his vendor''s kabala from the custody of the plaintiff. Non-production of this original kabala of the plaintiff''s vendor and not filing of the GD Entry weighed heavily on the mind of the lower appellate Court.

<u>15. In the plaint it has been averred that defendant No. 4 used to pay rents and taxes initially in the name of his brother proforma-defendant No. 3. This assertion in the plaint is in keeping with the story of benami as set up in the plaint by the plaintiff. The lower appellate Court found fault as no rent receipts or tax receipts have been filed to show payment of rent or taxes by proforma defendant No. 4 in the name of proforma defendant No. 3 as marfatdar. This finding of the lower appellate Court was reversed by the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division by holding as follows:</u>

<u>"It appears that the appellate Court found that initially the municipal and other taxes were paid in the name of defendant No. 3 and not in the name of defendant No. 4 as marfatdar of defendant No. 3 and, therefore, held that the real owner is defendant No. 3. This is again a wrong conclusion arrived at from the exhibits. When a property is purchased benami the benamder is the ostensible owner and in order to maintain the fiction of benami, the receipts and payment continue to be in the name of the benamder. Therefore, the appellate Court''s contention that the absence of the name of defendant No. 4 as ''marfatder'' of defendant No. 3 disclosed that defendant No. 3 was the real owner is erroneous."</u>

<u>Thus, the learned Single Judge was correct in holding that this finding was erroneous as it is not based on legal inference but on mere surmise and conjecture.</u>

16. It is on record that Birendra Kumar Dey left Bangladesh in 1958 and Rabindra Kumar Dey was staying in Bangladesh. SA Khatian, Ext. 8 was prepared in the year 1960-62 in the name of Rabindra. Municipal assessment holding, Ext. 3 was also made in the name of Rabindra Kumar Dey in the year 1962-63. The receipt of municipal taxes, Ext. 4 series show that taxes were paid by Rabindra Kumar Dey in the year 1962-63, Exts. 5-5A, rent receipts show payment of rent by vendor. Rabindra Kumar Dey after preparation of SA Khatian, Ext. 8. The learned Single Judge found that these documents are all prior to 1965 before the Indo-Pak War and before anybody''s contemplation of coming into force of the Enemy Property Law in this country. The learned Single Judge further found from Ext. 6, that defendant No. 5 (appellant in Civil Appeal No. 23 of 1997) paid rent to Birendra Kumar Dey as monthly tenant. Thereafter he paid rent to Rabindra Kumar Dey and his father. Thus, the learned Single Judge found that defendant No. 5 was aware that Rabindra Kumar Dey was the real owner and to him he was paying rent. It is also on record that defendant No. 5 was paying rent to the plaintiff admitting him as owner after his purchase from Rabindra Kumar Dey. Ext. 7 to 7 (f) are the agreements of the tenants with the plaintiff" as the landlord. Ext 10 also showed that other tenants filed petition admitting that they were tenants under defendant No. 4. Defendant No. 5 also admitted in his cross-examination that he paid rent to the plaintiff. Ext. 10 showed that other tenants filed petition admitting that they were tenants under defendant No. 4 and they never denied that the plaintiff''s vendor was not the real owner. The rent-receipts and tax receipts submitted by the plaintiff were found by the appellate Court to have been initially paid in the name of defendant No. 3 who was, in fact, the benamder and subsequently all these documents were corrected in the name of defendant No. 4, the real owner.

<u>17. The lower appellate Court held that there was no paper to support the question of benami from 1944 till the preparation of SA Khatian in the name of Rabindra Kumar Dey and consequently disbelieved the story of benami. The learned Single Judge of the High Court Division considered the oral evidence in this regard and believed the story of benami and found that the lower appellate Court without considering the material evidence both oral and documentary and on wrong assumptions disbelieved the case of benami. Herein we will consider the relevant evidence of benami on which the learned Single Judge has made reliance in his judgment after due consideration of the evidence of PW 2 Aboni Mohan Dey. The learned Single Judge held as follows:</u>

<u>"The evidence of PW 2 a man of 72 years who was the Secretary of Ram Krishna Orphanage and paid Taka 60/70 thousand as income tax who stated in his deposition that it was defendant No.4 Rabindra Kumar Dey who purchased the suit land in the benami of his brother Birendra Kumar Dey and it was defendant No. 4 who paid the consideration amount. This PW 2 also deposed that the defendant No.4 after purchase possessed the suit land through the tenants and sold it to the plaintiff".</u>

<u>This vital piece of oral evidence was not at all considered by the lower appellate Court. The learned Single Judge found that both PWs 2 and 3 were present at the time of execution of kabala in 1944. The learned Single Judge further found that the lower appellate Court on wrong assumptions held that a person who was in debt cannot purchase the property in benami of his brother. The appellate Court just surmised that it is not a believable story that a person who was in debt could have the capacity for paying the consideration for the said kabala when he purchased the property in the benami of his brother Birendra Kumar Dey. The learned Single Judge rightly held that it was only a guess of the lower appellate Court that defendant No. 4 could not purchase the property in the benami of his brother defendant No. 3. As a matter of fact there was averment in the pleading that in order to avoid debtor such purchase in the benami of brother was made.</u>

<u>18. The learned Single Judge also reversed the finding of the lower appellate Court that the preparation of SA Khatian No. 83, Exhibit 8, municipal assessment in 1961-62 are all collusively done in 1960-61 prior to 1965 when enemy property Ordinance came into force. The learned Single Judge held that it was a mere presumption of the lower appellate Court to hold that in order to save the property from being treated as enemy property all these corrections of SA Khatian and municipal Assessment Register were made. The learned Single Judge also reversed the finding of the lower appellate Court with regard to the plaintiff''s kabala Ext. 1(A) dated 22-11-63 executed by defendant No. 4 by holding that there was no recital that defendant No.4 was the real owner and his brother Birendra defendant No. 3 was simply a name lender. The property is being sold by the real owner and this omission is not very material. Rabindra Kumar Dey possessed the property and let it out to tenants and tenants paid rent to Rabindra Kumar Dey and, as such, Rabindra Kumar Dey treated the property as his own property for all practical purposes. Further, in the sale deed dated 22-11-63 there is a clear recital by vendor Rabindra Kumar Dey that he purchased the property with his own money and for his own interest and owning in his own right. This recital also indirectly reflects that the property was in the benami of his brother.</u>

<u>19. In the case of Hasan Ali Mollah vs. Jonendra Mohan Biswas, 1984 BLD (AD) 307 it has been held that the question of actual possession or receipt of the rents is one of the most important evidence of benami transaction. In the present case it is on record that Rabindra Kumar Dey was in possession of the land and his brother left the country in 1958. Rabindra Kumar Dey himself was possessing through various tenants. The tenants also admitted that they paid rents to Rabindra Kumar Dey and subsequently to the plaintiff. In the present case, the plaintiff had successfully proved that the purchase money was given by Rabindra Kumar Dey who also possessed the property and the relationship between the parties are that of full brothers and the conduct of Rabindra Kumar Dey in dealing with the property and subsequent sale is evidence of the fact that Rabindra Kumar Dey was the real owner and his brother was only a name-lender. Mr Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, learned Advocate for the respondent, also brought to our notice that the property was purchased in the benami from Commercial Bank, Comilla and for the purchase admittedly payments were made in installment and in such a case it is indeed difficult to bring evidence of actual payment of money when the transaction was with a bank. The learned Single Judge rightly determined the effect of benami transaction from all the documents and surrounding facts and circumstances.</u>

20. The defendants adduced two witnesses, namely, DW 1 Tahsilder and DW 2 Abdul Karim (defendant No. 5), a lessee under the vested property authority. DW 1 testified that in the census list of 1967 the disputed property was enlisted as enemy property but he could not produce any paper. He joined office in 1976 for the first time and he only deposed that SA Khatian which was prepared in 1961-62 was wrong. DW 2 Abdul Karim said in his cross-examination that he paid rents to Barindra but he could not produce any rent receipts on the plea that those were burnt. He admitted that on his application Government has granted lease to him and before that he used to pay rent to the plaintiff. This is all the oral evidence on record on behalf of the defendants.

21. It is on record that Certificate Case No. 28330/1960-61 was started against defendant No. 4 Rabindra Kumar Dey and the rent was realised from him by the Government as he was in possession and the Government also treated him as the owner of the land. It is also on record that the tenants recognized Rabindra Kumar Dey as the real owner and paid rents to him. The tenants also paid rent to the plaintiff but subsequently they filed an application to treat the property as enemy property as the plaintiff wanted to enhance the rent. It is on the application of the tenants that the Assistant Custodian treated the property of the plaintiff as enemy property and subsequently released the same on 11-4-69 as its inclusion was wrong. It is also found from the record that the order dated 114-69 was passed on the basis of a report submitted by Tahsilder. The Assistant Custodian, Enemy property again reviewed his earlier order and included the property as an enemy property on 5-5-69 without serving any notice to the plaintiff-owner of the property. Such inclusion without serving any notice to the plaintiff when he acquired a vested right is illegal. It was the tenants who were instrumental in listing the property as enemy property.

<u>22. Mr. Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, learned Additional Attorney-General submits that there being no reciprocal arrangement for recognition of notarial act done by Foreign Notary under section 14 of Notary Ordinance, 1961, the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division wrongly accepted Ext. 9, the affidavit sworn before the Presidency Magistrate at Alipur, Calcutta, India. In support of his contention he cited the case of Nurun Nessa and others vs. Babar Ali Bepari and others, 33 DLR (AD) 124. Under section 14 of the Notary Ordinance 1961 Notarial acts in a reciprocal country is recognized in Bangladesh when reciprocal arrangement exists. In the present case the affidavit was authenticated before the Magistrate, Alipur, Calcutta, India and it was produced before the court in Bangladesh but without validating it with local stamp. Section 18 of the Stamp Act, 1889 provides that instruments other than bill and notes executed out of Bangladesh may be stamped within 3 months after it has been first received in Bangladesh. Section 35 of the Stamp Act provides that instruments not duly stamped are inadmissible in evidence. According to the learned Advocate for the appellant, the affidavit being insufficiently stamped is not admissible in evidence. No such objection having been raised at the trial Court, the plaintiff did not get any opportunity for payment of proper stamp duty with penalty. A failure to comply with the stamp duty as provided under the Stamp Act may entail penalty but the instrument cannot be thrown away for want of stamp as inadmissible in evidence not being duly stamped. Thus it appears that the finding of the lower appellate Court that Ext. 9 was inadmissible is not legally correct and the learned Single Judge rightly considered this document in evidence and set aside the erroneous finding of the lower appellate Court on this score. The case of 33 DLR (AD) 124 (Supra) relates to a General Power of Attorney executed in India and authenticated by a Magistrate in India. In that decision, section 14 of the Notary Ordinance, 1961 was held to be a permissive section and the decision lays down the conditions of acceptance of foreign notarial acts. This Division held that there was no prohibition or exclusion of accepting such a document. The case was remanded to prove the document as per relevant provisions of law to discharge the onus of proof. In the reported decision the power of attorney was authenticated before a Magistrate, Alipur, India and it was produced before the court of Bangladesh after validating it with the local stamp. In the present case the original affidavit was filed in the court of Bangladesh and marked as exhibit without validating with local stamp, though it was duly sworn before a Magistrate in India. The plaintiff having duly proved the same as an exhibit without any objection whatsoever had discharged the onus of proof and, as such, it would be wrong to hold that the document is not admissible in evidence.</u>

23. In the present case, proforma defendant No. 3 had already left for India in 1958 and Rabindra Kumar Dey sold the property to the plaintiff on 22-11-1963 and to prove the same along with other evidences the plaintiff has also produced Ext. 9, affidavit sworn by Birendra Kumar Dey before the Presidency Magistrate''s Court, Calcutta acknowledging that defendant No. 4 Rabindra Kumar Dey was the real owner and that he was merely a benamder. This exhibit is an important piece of evidence. The lower appellate Court did not consider this document on the ground that the document was inadmissible as it did not come through diplomatic channel and did not contain any notary certificate. The learned Single Judge found that the affidavit sworn outside Bangladesh needed to be notarised by our Embassy or High Commissioner abroad. It appears that Ext. 9 was admitted as exhibit without any objection from the defendants. The learned Single Judge found that no objection having been taken as to the admissibility of the said affidavit on the ground that it was not notarized and certified by the Embassy of Bangladesh on any ground, Ext. 9 was properly and legally admitted in evidence. The learned Single Judge thus correctly found that the appellate Court thus comitted an error of law in holding that Ext. 9 was prima fade inadmissible in evidence. In the case of Abdullah and 3 others vs. Abdul Karim and another 22 DLR 205 it has been held that the objection as to formal proof of a document has to be taken at the earliest point of time and it cannot be taken subsequently and suddenly put in appeal. It was further held in that decision that if a document has been marked as exhibit without objection it becomes admissible in evidence and it should be taken into consideration. The learned Single Judge has rightly considered Ext. 9 as a vital piece of evidence to show that Birendra Kumar Dey, full brother of Rabindra Kumar Dey, clearly stated that the property belonged to his brother and he paid consideration for the same. It cannot be argued that affidavit by itself is an inadmissible piece of document. The affidavit has been sworn before a Magistrate in accordance with law. There may be some omissions as to the fact that it was not duly stamped and it contained no notarized certificate. But these are matters of formal nature and at the trial no objection was taken with regard to these formalities. In such view of the matter we are of the view that the learned Single Judge was correct in holding that non-consideration of this vital document has resulted in a serious failure of justice. In the case of Joynal Abedin and others vs. Mafizur Rahman and others, 44 DLR (AD) 162, it has been held by this Division that a document having been filed and marked as exhibit without any objection the question of inadmissibility of that document cannot be raised at a subsequent point of time and the courts below acted wrongly in not considering that document and the same has materially affected the decision in that case.

24. A word need to be said with regard to the argument of Mr Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed as he referred to section 2 of the Evidence Act. Section 2 of the Evidence Act speaks that it applies to all judicial proceedings except affidavit. Section 139 of the Code of Civil Procedure provides that an affidavit may be administered by a court of magistrate, which has been done in this case. This exhibit has been filed as a documentary evidence in this case and duly proved. The onus of rebuttal that the affidavit is not validly executed and authenticated is on the defendants and they having not done so it is admissible as a piece of documentary evidence.

<u>25. Thus on a careful consideration of the oral and documentary evidences, attendant facts and circumstances of the case, we hold that the lower appellate Court in fact did not consider certain material evidence in this case and the surrounding facts and circumstances relevant for consideration of determining the nature of benami transaction and fell into an error of law occasioning failure of justice calling for interference by the High Court Division in its revisional jurisdiction.</u>

Consequently, both the appeals are dismissed without any order as to costs.

End.

full_judgment:
ATM Afzal CJ: This is a defendants' appeal by leave which arises out of an order of the trial Court rejecting their application under Order VII rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure and affirmed by the High Court Division in revision.

2. Plaintiff-respondent No.1 who was a driver of the Sonali Bank and at the relevant time posted at the Kishoreganj Branch instituted OC Suit No. 289 of 1986 in the Court of 'Subordinate Judge, Kishoreganj for a declaration that the letter dated 24 September, 1981 terminating his service was void, illegal, inoperative, etc. and further that the plaintiff's service as driver of the Sonali Bank was continuing with its salaries and facilities on the allegation, inter alia, that the termination of his service was the result of a high-handed action on the part of the Regional Manager.

3. Defendant Nos.4 and 6 filed an application under Order VII rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure for rejection of the plaint on the grounds that the suit was barred by reason of the Administrative Tribunals Act, 1980 which got exclusive jurisdiction to try such a matter, that the suit was barred under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, that the matter was triable by the Labour Court and that the suit was barred under the Limitation Act.

4. The learned Subordinate Judge, among others, relying upon the case of Assistant General Manager, Rupali Bank vs. Nazrul Islam, 39 DLR 167 held that the plaintiff was not a 'worker' and, as such, his case was not triable by the Labour Court. The other contentions of the defendants were also rejected by the learned Subordinate Judge and consequently their prayer for rejection of the plaint was also rejected by order dated 11-11-89. Being aggrieved by the said order the appellants moved the High Court Division in revision Civil Revision No. 261 of 1990, in which a Division Bench by the impugned judgment and order dated 3rd April, 1994, discharged the Rule and upheld the order of the learned Subordinate Judge.

5. It appears that the only point, which did not succeed in the trial Court, argued before the High Court Division was that since the plaintiff was a 'worker' his remedy lay in the Labour Court and the jurisdiction of the civil Court was impliedly barred. The appellants relied on MD Rupali Bank vs. Tafazal Hossain 44 DLR (AD) 260 in support of their submission. The learned Judges extensively took notice of the said decision but upon considering the 'proviso' to section 25(1) (b) of the Employment of Labour (Standing Orders) Act, 1965 (Act VIII of 1965), briefly the Act, came to the conclusion that it was the Labour Court which was barred for any relief for the plaintiff and, as such, the civil Court has jurisdiction to entertain the suit of the plaintiff challenging the order of his termination from service.

<u>6. The correctness of the decision of the High Court Division is the subject-matter in this appeal and it is found that a number of grounds were raised by Mr. Asrarul Hossain, learned Counsel, while obtaining leave to appeal from this Division. Mr. Ajamalul Hossain, learned Counsel, (son of Mr. Asrarul Hossain) who is now appearing for the appellants, has, however, submitted fairly that it will be difficult for him to press the points incorporated in the leave order and also to assail the impugned judgment seriously inasmuch as the view taken by the High Court Division of section 25 of the Act has not been directly questioned. Mr. Hossain has also fairly pointed out that the termination of the plaintiff's service was done not under the Act but under rule 17(ii) of the Bank's (Staff) Service Rules which is permitted under section 3 of the Act. Although the action was taken under the Bank's Service Rules the remedy for the plaintiff lay before the Labour Court as he was a 'worker' by definition under the Act. Mr. Hossain reiterated the failed argument that the plaintiff respondent was required to proceed under section 25 of the Act and not in the civil Court but he ran out of breath when he reached the 'proviso' to section 25(1)(b) upon which the impugned decision of the High Court Division turned. He could not pursue the appeal any further.</u>

7. The reasons given by the High Court Division for departing from the decision of this Division in 44 DLR (AD) 260 may now be taken notice of. That was also a case of termination of an Assistant Cashier of the Rupali Bank who got a decree from the civil Court in his favour and the same was upheld by the High Court Division. Leave was granted to consider whether the whole proceeding including the decree of the Civil Court suffered from 'coram non-judice' in view of the Administrative Tribunals Act, 1980. It was, however, found that the Administrative Tribunals Act was not applicable in that case, inter alia, because the termination in question took place in 1981 and the Rupali Bank was brought into the ambit of the Act in 1984. It was then found that the plaintiff was a 'worker' and his remedy lay before the Labour Court under section 25(1) of the Act. On the well settled principle that a particular remedy available under a special law excludes any remedy under the general law, it was held that the civil Court's jurisdiction to entertain the suit of a 'worker' against termination of his service was ousted, not expressly but by implication, because of the remedy provided under the Act which a 'worker' was obliged to follow. It was held that the decision by the Single Judge reported in 39 DLR 167 was palpably erroneous but the decision by the other Single Bench in 41 DLR 94, Md. Shahabuddin vs. Janata Bank & others, was perfectly correct. In the former case civil Court's jurisdiction was found not to be ousted in case of termination of a 'worker' while in the latter case it was found it was.

<u>8. The High Court Division in the present case referred to the 'proviso' to section 25(1)(b) of the Act, which it was observed, was not brought to the notice of this Division while deciding the case in 44 DLR (AD) 260. The 'Proviso' originally stood thus:</u>

<u>25(1) (a) ...........</u>

<u>Provided that no complaint shall lie against an order of termination of employment of a worker under section 19, unless the worker concerned is an officer of a registered trade union and his employment is alleged to have been terminated for his trade union activities or unless the worker concerned, whether an officer of a registered trade union or not, has been deprived of the benefits specified in that section.</u>

<u>The 'Proviso' was substituted by Ordinance No.XVI of 1985 as follows:</u>

<u>25(1)(b)  ...........</u>

<u>Provided that no complaint shall lie against an order of termination of employment of a worker under section 19, unless the services of the worker concerned is alleged to have been terminated for his trade union activities or unless the worker concerned has been deprived of the benefits specified in that section;</u>

<u>9. It is clear from the above original 'proviso' which was in force when the plaintiff's service was terminated in 1981 that he could not make any complaint against the order of his termination before the Labour Court as his case did not fall within the exceptions mentioned in the said 'proviso', that is to say, he was not an officer of a registered Trade Union and his employment was not alleged to have been terminated for his Trade Union activities nor he was alleged to have been deprived of the benefits specified under section 19 of the Act. The plaintiff brought the suit for a declaration that the order of termination was illegal, void, etc. which relief could not be prayed before the Labour Court.</u>

10. The High Court Division having noticed the said 'proviso' and the facts of the case correctly took the view that the door of the Labour Court was closed to the plaintiff and, as such, the decision in 44 DLR (AD) 260 would not be a binding precedent in the present case. The High Court Division noticed rightly that in the case reported in 41 DLR 94 which was found to be correctly decided by this Division in 44 DLR (AD) 260, the office-bearers of the Trade Union were aggrieved persons unlike in the present case. It may be observed that in 39 DLR 167 it was, inter alia, found that the plaintiffs were not 'workers' within the meaning of the Act and as such, the civil Court's jurisdiction was not ousted. If the 'proviso' as above was considered in the decision in 44 DLR (AD) 260 it would have been difficult to resist the view taken by the High Court Division in the present case that the Labour Court itself was barred for the plaintiff and as such, the civil Court's jurisdiction could not be said to be ousted on the principle referred to in the said decision.

11. It is found that the High Court Division went on to take notice of Bangladesh Small Industries Corporation vs. Mahbub Hossain 29 DLR SC 41 in which it was, inter alia, held that if an employee of a statutory body of public character viz. Bangladesh Small Industries Corporation and Janata Bank is dismissed or terminated from service in contravention of a mandatory statutory provision, the employee has a right of action either in a superior Court in its writ jurisdiction or in a Civil Court. Reference was also made to Karnafuli Paper Mills Sramik Karmachari Union vs. Registrar of Trade Union 42 DLR 329 where it was held that if there is no remedy for the grievance of the plaintiff in the Industrial Relations Ordinance then the civil Court will have jurisdiction to try the matter. The plaintiff in the present case having been found to have no other forum either under the Act or the Industrial Relations Ordinance 1969 (Ordinance No.XXIII of 1969) to challenge the order of his termination from service was found to have been entitled to go to the civil Court.

<u>12. There is another aspect of the matter which also deserves consideration. Admittedly in the present case, the plaintiff's service was not terminated under section 19 of the Act but under the Bank's (Staff) Services Rules. The 'proviso' to section 3 of the Act says that any shop or commercial or industrial establishment may have its own Rules regulating employment of 'workers' or any class thereof, but no such Rules shall be less favourable to any 'worker' than the provisions of the Act. In sub-section (1) of section 3 it is provided that in every shop or commercial or industrial establishment, employment of 'workers' and other matters incidental thereto shall be regulated in accordance with the provisions of the Act. Now, if there is a termination of a 'worker' under the Act (section 19) there is no doubt that, if at all, he has to follow the grievance procedure as laid down in section 25 of the Act, because section 25(1) provides that any individual worker "who has a grievance in respect of any matter covered under this Act and intends to seek redress thereof under this section, shall observe the following procedure. The question is: Is the termination of the plaintiff under the Bank's Service Rules a matter which is covered under the Act? True, the Act also provides for termination but is that the same thing as provided under the Service Rules of the Bank which are separate? The terms of section 19 of the Act providing for termination of a 'worker' and those of rule 17 (ii) of the Bank's Service Rules are found to be different and therefore, it is difficult to say that a termination under the service rules of the Bank is covered under the Act. In such view of the matter also the plaintiff cannot be said to have a remedy under the Act.</u>

13. For the reasons aforesaid, there is no valid ground to interfere with the impugned judgment.

The appeal is, accordingly, dismissed without any order as to costs.

End.

lawyer:
M.A. Baqui Mallick with M.A. Wahab Miah ------ For the Petitioner. 
Abdus Subhan ------ For opp. party No. 1.
parties:
Khan Saifur Rahman & ors  ------ Petitioner.
Vs.
Abdul Kader Sikder & ors  ------ Opp. Parties.
full_judgment:
This rule is directed against the order dated 18-1-75 passed by Mr. Z. Islam, Munsif Jhalakati in Miscellaneous Case No. 58 of 1973 under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of civil Procedure.

2. The facts giving rise to the rule, in brief, are that the plaintiff-opposite parties petitioners instituted titled Suit No. 254 of 1967 against the opposite parties in the 3rd Court of the Munsif, Barisal for partition of some lands, which being transferred 10 the Court of Munsif at Jhalakati, was renumbered as Title Suit No. 452 of 1971. The suit was decreed in preliminary form on 23-10-68. The opposite party No.2 instituted Miscellaneous Case No. 137 of 1969, under Order 9, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure which was dismissed. Subsequently, on the prayer of the plaintiff-petitioners an advocate Commissioner was appointed and the suit lands were partitioned by metes and bounds and the suit was finally decreed on 8-11-71 but that final decree was set aside in view of the President's Order No. 12 of 1972 as being passed expert during the Liberation War. The suit was again decreed finally on 21-7-72. The plaintiff-opposite parties petitioners through execution of the decree took possession through Court on 6-5-73.

<u>3. Thereafter, the defendant-petitioner opposite parties instituted Miscellaneous Case No. 58 of 1973 under Order 9, rule 13 and section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure on 3-1-75. The learned Munsif allowed the Miscellaneous case and set aside the final decree and ordered that the preliminary decree was to be restored subject to payment of Taka 120/- to thepetitioners within 14 days (expiring on 17-1-75) of the order failing which the case would stand as dismissed. On the expiry of the said 14 days i.e. on 18-1-75 as payment could not be made by the defendant petitioner opposite parties, the learned Munsif again passed an order on 18-1-75 dismissing the said Miscellaneous Case for default. On 27-1-75 the defendant opposite parties filed a petition under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure praying for allowing them to deposit the said amount after setting aside the dismissal order dated 18-1-75. The learned munsif was pleased to allow time upto 30-1-75 for depositing money and then they deposited the amount on 29-1-75.</u>

<u>Thereafter the plaintiff petitioners filed Revisional application in this Court challenging the legality of the order dated 28-1-75 passed by the learned Munsif and they obtained the present Rule.</u>

4. Mr. M.A. Baqui Mallick, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioners contends before me that the order dated 28-1-75 allowing the defendant opposite parties to make payment of Rs. 120/- within 14 days with default clause i.e. the case would stand dismissed if the opposite parties failed to make payment of money within the time was the final order in the case. As the opposite parties defaulted to make payment within time the learned Munsif again passed final order on 18-1-75 dismissing the Miscellaneous Case for default. Hence the learned Munsif became funtus officio and he had no jurisdiction to pass order dated 18-1-75 allowing the extension of time up to 30-1-75.

5. Mr. Abdus Subhan the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite parties contends before me that section 148 of the Code of Civil Procedure vested jurisdiction on the learned Munsif to allow extension of time even though the period for payment allowed by him already expired.

6. Mr. Mallick, in support of his contention refers to the cases of Darogali Sk, and ors. Vs. Melatan Nessa Bibi and ors.(1976) 28 DLR 9, case of Bhutnath Das and ors. Vs. Sahodeb Chandra Fanja, 66 C.W.N. 645, case of Girish Chandra Das Vs. Annandamoni Dasi, 43 C. W. N., 553 and the case of Rajendra Shirali and others Vs. Mahadev Shirali (1975) 27 DLR 232.

Mr. Abdus Subhan, refers to the case of Joytish Chandra Sen Vs. Pukmini Ballav Sen and ors, 62 C.W.N. 588 and the case of Afaz uddin Molla and others Vs. Abdur Rahman Sk, and another (1959) 11 DJ.R 23.

The learned Munsif in his order referred to the case of Shah Wali Vs. Ghulam Din alias Gaman and Mohamad Din, (1967) 19 DLR (S.C.) 143.

7. In the case of 66 CW.N. 645 it is held that where the Court made an order for specific performance of a contract on a certain sum of money being put in within a specified time and has further ordered that if the said sum be not deposited within that date, the suit would stand dismissed, it has no jurisdiction to extend the time. In the case reported in 43, C.W.N. 553, an auction held under section 174 of the B. T. Act was set aside per order dated 28.2.38 on the condition that the applicant would deposit the amount recoverable in execution of the decree within seven days from the date of the decree in default, the application would stand dismissed. The amount was not paid within the time. On the last date an application was filed for extension of time to make the deposit and on the next date the petition was granted. It was held that the order dated 28. 2. 1938 was the final order of the Court and this order should not have been modified except in the manner provided by Order 20, rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure. In the case reported in 27 D.L.R. 232, extension of time under section 148 C. P. C. in various aspects of cases was considered. D. C. Bhattacharya, J. who delivered the judgment in that case differed with the view taken be Ali J. in the case of Ashraf Ali alias Uddin Mondal and another Vs. Bayla Hasda and others (1965) 17 D.L.R. (D) 593 in which Ali J. disagreed with the views taken in the case of Shaikh Ayezuddin Vs. Priya Sankar Chowdhury, (1954) 6 D.L.R. 595. The relevant portion of the judgment delivered by Bhattacharya J. in the case reported in 27 D.L.R. 232 runs as follows:

"Relying upon a Bench decision of the Madras High Court, namely, Abdul Shakerb Saheb Vs. Abdur Rahman Sahib, reported in I.L.R. 46 Mad., 148, same case A.I.R. 123, Mad. 284 and a Single Judge decision of Nagpur High Court, namely, Gokul Prosad Vs. Fattalal, reported in A.I.R. 1946 Nag, 29.

Mr. Justice Ali held:-

It is thus clear that the decree in an action for specific performance of contract, no matter whatever may be The form in which It may be drawn up, is, in the eye of law, a preliminary decree, and as such, even when default clause is attached  thereto, is not dead but pending though in a condition. Necessarily, the Court retains control over the action and has therefore jurisdiction to enlarge time regardless of the said default clause. In laying down the proposition quoted above, Mr. Justice Ali did not notice that there was no default clause in the decree dealt in the Madras case, of the same nature as in the case dealt by him. It was clearly indicated by the terms of the decree before him that there could be automatic dismissal of the suit without any further interven1ion of the Court, on failure to comply with the direction for deposit by a particular date, and so far as this part of the decree is concerned it cannot be said that it was in the nature of a preliminary decree. It is true that a decree for specific performance of a contract for sale, ordinarily, has been regarded to be in the nature of a preliminary decree and the practice of making such a decree in the final form has been disapproved in a number of cases, unless time is the essence of the contract in a particular case, because in case of a default in payment of the balance of the consideration it is open to the other side to apply for rescission of the contract under section 35 of the Specific Relief Act. The nature of such a decree as did not contain a default clause in terms of finality came up for consideration before a Division Bench of this Court, to which I was a Party, in the case of Chowdhury Md. Sarwar Vs. Shahadat Hossain Khan and others (F.M.A. 16 of 1970), decided on 25. 1. 73 and it has been held in the said case that it is in the nature of a preliminary decree. But the introduction of a default clause of the nature referred to above, whether it is done rightly or wrongly, undoubtedly transforms the character of the decree, and it becomes final, so far as that particular part of the decree is concerned and the Court passing the decree does not retain any jurisdiction to grant any extension of time, either under section 148 of the Code or under any other provision, unless mistake of the Court or Court's Officer leading to some injustice is involved. It is however perfectly within the powers of the Court of appeal to grant any extension of time in super session of the default clause, when it is seized of the entire case on an appeal from the decree itself. So far as the Nagpur case is concerned the learned Judge of the Dacca High Court did not notice that in that case there was an appeal at the instance of the plaintiff against the decree itself as well as a Revision case at the instance of the defendant against the order of the Trial Court granting extension of time for making the deposit, notwithstanding the default clause in terms of finality. Although the learned Single Judge of the Nagpur High Court Naygi made some observations in the nature of obiter dicta on which Ali J. relied, he exercised his powers in the appeal by granting an extended period for making the deposit by modifying the decree itself and held that the argument that the Lower Court had no Jurisdiction to extend the term fixed by a decree did call for any consideration in view of the modification of the lower Court's decree in the appeal."

The question regarding extension of time under section 48 of the Code of Civil Procedure came up for hearing in the case of Darogali Sk. and others Vs. Melatan Nessa Bibi (1976) 28 DLR 9, S. M. Mohsen Ali J. who delivered the judgment in that case did not disagree with the views taken by D. C. Bhattacharya J. in 27 D.L.R. 232, but S. M. Mohsen Ali J. distinguished shed the case before him on the ground that a petition praying for extension of time was filed in that case on the last date of the period allowed for depositing the money.

8. The decision in the case reported in 11 D.L.R. 23, referred to by Mr. Abdus Subhan does not appear to have application in the facts and circumstances of the present case for the reason that the order of dismissal for default in that was passed before expiry of the time granted to the petitioner for payment of the money. The case reported in 62 C.W.N. 588 referred to by Mr. Abdus Subhan was discussed in 27 D.L.R. 232. Decision in that case is also not applicable in the facts and circumstances of the present case. In other cases as well as in the cases of Bhupendra Nath Vs. Probhat Kumar 63 C.W.N. 460, the same as A.I.R. Cal. 75, Printing and Industrial Machinery Ltd. Vs. Swastika Press Ltd. in 90 C.L.J. 105 and Bokaro and Ramgarh Ltd. Vs.
