State of Bihar in A.I.R. 1965 Cal. 308, it was pointed out that the Court retains seisin over the principal action even though the interlocutory proceeding has come to an end and has jurisdiction in such cases to give an extension of time.

<u>9. In the instant case, Miscellaneous Case was allowed on 3. 1. 75 with default clause; on that date an order was passed for passing the final order on 18.1.75. As the payment was not made within the time allowed, final order dismissing the Miscellaneous Case with default clause was passed on 18. 1. 75. The very order passed on 3.1.75 with default clause itself was the final order in the case. Moreover, passing of an order on that very date expressly stating that final order would be passed on 18. 1. 75, undoubtedly shows that the Court did not intend to retain any control over the case on passing the final order. The case reported in 27 D.L.R. 232 followed the principle of law laid down in the case reported in 19 D.L.R. (S.C.) 143, that Court has no jurisdiction to make any alteration by extending time limit after it becomes functus afficio. The observation of Mohsen Ali J. in the case reported in 28 D.L.R. 9 quoting from the decision in the case of Malsanath Ram Das Ys. Gana Das reported in A.I.R. 1961, (S.C.) 882 that "It is in my opinion a procedural order though preemptory and in essence, is terrorem so that dilatory litigants might put themselves in order and avoid delay does not appear to be applicable in respect of the order dated 18.1.75 even if it was applicable in respect of the order dated 3.11.75, for, time was allowed under order dated 3.1.75 with default clause, but, the Court also expressed its intention by a separate order to pass the final order subsequently on 18.1.75. Hence after passing of the final order on 18.1.75 the learned Munsif became functus officio. He had no jurisdiction to pass an order on 18.1.75 allowing the extension of time.</u>

<u>In the result, the Rule is made absolute with costs. Impugned order dated 28.1.75 passed by the learned Munsif is hereby set side.</u>

End.

lawyer:
Md. Lutfor Rahman Majumder, Advocate ----- For the Petitioner. 
AK Mujibur Rahman, Deputy Attorney-General ----- For the Respondent No.2
MI Faruqui with M Saleem Ullah, Advocates ----- For the Respondent No.4
parties:
Nurjahan Begum ----- Petitioner
Vs.
Bangladesh and others ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
Habibur Rahman Khan, J.: At the instance of the petitioner Mrs. Nurjahan Begum a Rule Nisi was issued by this Court on 4.6.89 calling upon the respondent Nos. 1 and 2 to show cause as to why the notice dated 1.4.89 issued by the respondent No. 2 should not be declared to have been made without any lawful authority and is of no legal effect or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper. Pending hearing of the Rule an ad-interim injunction was passed against the respondent Nos. 1 and 2 directing them not to interfere with the petitioner's possession in the house in question.

2. The case given out by the petitioner in the application, in short is as follows:

The House No. L-C/8-6, Mirpur, Police Station Mirpur, Dhaka was allotted to the petitioner's husband Shamsul Islam with effect from 1.5.72 at a monthly rental of Taka 65.00 and he was also directed to deposit the total amount of Taka 2080.00, out of which half of total amount to be deposited by 14.1.75 and the rest half amount by 29.1.75 to the Bangladesh Bank and the allottee complied with the order and since then the petitioner's predecessor and thereafter the petitioner has been residing in the said house on payment of rents thereof. To the utter surprise of the petitioner, the respondent No. 2 issued an urgent notice on 1.4.89 vide letter No. APP-11/79/82/149 dated 1.4.89 asking the, petitioner's husband late Shamsul Islam to vacate the house and hand over possession to the said authority.

The said house had been declared abandoned under President's Order 16/72 and subsequently it was recorded in the abandoned list as a result of which the Government made enquiries to ascertain these facts. On enquiry it was found that Shamsul Islam died and thereafter his wife, the petitioner with her 5 school going children had been living and paying rents thereof. To the knowledge of the petitioner the house in question was declared as an abandoned property and the Government had been in possession and control of the same from 1972 and accordingly, the demand notice was issued to the allottee vide No. 1/C-69 dated 7.1.75. The petitioner came to know subsequently that the respondent No. 4 obtained the judgment and order from the Court of Settlement by which the property was released from the abandoned list. By the majority decision the learned Court of Settlement found that the house in question docs not fall within the definition of abandoned building and hence passed order for the release of the property with an order for the restoration of the property to the respondent No. 4.

3. In the case filed by the respondent No. 4, the present petitioner was not made a party, neither she could or did appear before the Court of Settlement claiming any interest in the property ordered be the released. The petitioner being aggrieved by the order made by the respondent No. 2 and communicated vide memo No. AP-11/79/82/149 dated 1.4.89 (Annexure-'D' to the petition) has filed the instant application challenging the notice issued by the respondent No. 2 with a prayer for a declaration that it was made without lawful authority and is of no legal effect and obtained the instant Rule.

<u>4. Mr. Md. Lutfar Rahman Majumder, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner, at the very outset challenged the judgment and order of the Court of Settlement on the ground that it is not unanimous rather the chairman of the Court of Settlement gave dissenting verdict. It is submitted that since the decision is not unanimous the Chairman having not agreed with the majority view of the other members of the Court of Settlement and put his signature in the judgment as such, the judgment and order is not a judgment of the Court of Settlement in the eye of law. The learned Advocate cited the case of Fatema Begum Vs. Government of Bangladesh and others reported in 42 DLR 342 wherein it is held:</u>

<u>"In view of the provision for constitution of the Court of Settlement order passed by the Court in the absence of one member is not lawful. No provision has been made in the Ordinance that the order passed in the absence of one member shall not be invalid. It is clear that it was the intention of the Legislature that the Court of Settlement must be constituted to hear and dispose of matters with 3 members including the Chairman. Unless an order is passed by a properly constituted court it has no effect and it is no order in the eye of law even if it is otherwise proper."</u>

5. Section 9 of the Abandoned Buildings (Supplementary Provision) Ordinance LIV of 1985 regarding the constitution of the Board of Settlement Court provides as follows:

"9. Court of Settlement (I) The Government shall by notification in the Official Gazette, establish one or more Courts of Settlement for such areas or area as may be specified therein for the purposes of this Ordinance.

(2) The Court of Settlement shall consist of a Chairman and two other members who shall be appointed by the Govt.

(3). The Chairman shall be a person who is, or has been, or is qualified to be a Judge or Additional Judge of the Supreme Court and of two other members, one shall be a person who is or has been a judicial officer not below the rank of Additional District Judge and the other person who is or has been an officer in the service of the Republic not below the rank of Deputy Secretary to the Government."

6. Sub-sections 5 and 6 of section 10 of the Abandoned Buildings (Supplementary Provisions) Ordinance, LIV of 1985 run as follows:

"Sub-section (5)-A Court of Settlement shall, after such enquiry as it may deem necessary and after giving reasonable opportunity to the parties concerned of being heard and also adducing evidence, both oral and documentary, if any, make such decision on the prayer of the applicant as it deems fit"

"Sub-section (6) The decision of the Court of Settlement shall be final and shall be binding on all parties concerned and shall not be called in question in any other Court."

7. The learned Advocate for the petitioner reading out of the above provisions submits that in case the Court of Settlement though constituted with three members but the decision of the Court being divided, two is to one, and there being no consensus of opinion in the judgment; the Chairman having not agreed with the opinion of the two members that the property in question is abandoned, the unanimous decision cannot be treated as a proper judgment in the eye of law.

8. Mr. AK Mujibur Rahman, the learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing for the respondent Nos. 1 and 2 and Mr. MI Farooqui, the learned Advocate appearing for the respondent No. 4 submitted that the principle laid down in the case referred to above is not applicable here as in the present case there is no controversy as regards the constitution of the Court of Settlement. The Court having been properly constituted and the decision having been arrived at by the majority of the members of the Court we find that. the argument of the learned Advocate for the petitioner challenging the propriety of the judgment on this score is of no substance. The learned Advocate for the petitioner then submits that having regard to the fact that the petitioner's husband was found in possession of the house and her possession having been recognised by the Govt, as a tenant and the petitioner has been living in the premises with the other members of the family since the time of her predecessor on payment of rent as demanded by the Government and in that view of the matter the notice issued by the respondent No. 2 asking her to vacate the premises without affording her any opportunity to show cause has offended the principle of natural justice and has been made in violation of law relating to eviction. The learned Advocate for the petitioner further submits that the petitioner is entitled to a notice in the manner prescribed before asking her to surrender possession of the property so as to enable her to show cause against such order of surrender but in the instant case no such notice was ever served on the petitioner and thus the law relating to surrender of the abandoned property has been violated by the authority. The learned Advocate has referred to the case of Md. Kamruzzaman Vs. Secretary, Ministry of Public Works and Urban Development, Government of Bangladesh and others reported in 29 DLR 125 wherein it is held:

"It is now well settled that whether in administrative or in judicial matters the principles of natural justice, if consistent with the provisions of the statute, must be duly adhered to and complied with. In all proceedings whether administrative or judicial the principles of natural justice has to be observed if the proceedings result in consequence affecting the person or property or other rights of the parties concerned."

9. The facts and circumstances of the present case is different from the case cited. From the record of this case it appears that the petitioner's predecessor having been found in unauthorised possession of the property was served with the demand notice claiming compensation and accordingly, compensation was realised from him and accordingly, the husband of the petitioner and thereafter the petitioner and other members of her family has been found to have been residing there having no right, title, interest and claim over the property. Furthermore, the house in question has been released from the abandoned list in favour of the respondent No. 4. The petitioner having no independent claim than that under the Government is not entitled to notice as prescribed in Form-1. The case referred by the learned Advocate for the petitioner reported in 34 DLR (AD) 34 also relates to recovery of possession of land by the Government under the Local Authority Lands and Buildings (Recovery of Possession) Ordinance No. XXIV of 1970 and hence is not relevant for the purpose of deciding the point raised in the present petition. The learned Advocate for the petitioner has cited the case of Halima Bibi Vs. Chairman and another reported in 44 DLR 197 wherein it is held:

"It is evident that as per clause 3 of Article 7 of the Order the petitioner before being evicted .is entitled to show cause notice."

10. Regard- being had that the property in question was not found as abandoned property and the petitioner also could not and has not claimed title and has not been able to show that she is not in unauthorised possession of the property, the principle laid down in the above referred two cases are not applicable so as to give her protection from being evicted from the property.

11. In the case of Fatima Begum Vs. Government of Bangladesh and others reported in 42 DLR 342 it is held:

"In view of the provision for constitution of the Court of Settlement orders passed by the Court in the absence of one member is not lawful. No provision has been made in the Ordinance that the order passed in the absence of one member shall not be invalid. It is clear that it was the intention of the Legislature that the Court of Settlement must be constituted to hear and dispose of matters with 3 members including the Chairman. Unless an order is passed by a properly constituted court it has no effect and it is no order in the eye of law even if it is otherwise proper."

<u>12. The case reported in 44 DLR 197 relates to the claim of a person who had valid title but in the present case the petitioner has not claimed any title and her occupation being without any valid title we are of the view that she is not entitled to the notice under Article 7(3) of the Ordinance. The petitioner being an allottee of the Government was not made a party and it is submitted that the Government did not inform the petitioner that the property was going to be released and the property as a matter of fact has been released without letting the petitioner know about it. When it is found by the authority that the property was not abandoned and that the petitioner's husband was in occupation of the property as trespasser direction was given for his removal from the property in question. Though the Govt. appears to have received some money by way of compensation from the husband of the petitioner and allowed him to continue in his occupation temporarily but this type of permissive occupation cannot give him or the petitioner claiming under him the right to continue her stay for an indefinite period in the property which is found to be not abandoned and in that view of the matter that petitioner is not entitled to a notice for eviction. Instead of claiming any legal right in the property the petitioner has in fact challenged the notice dated 1.4.89 issued by the respondent No. 2 asking her to vacate.</u>

13. Mr. M Saleemullah, the learned Advocate appearing for the respondent No. 4, who filed affidavit-in-opposition controverting the statement and allegation made in the petition, challenged the maintainability of the writ petition and also the right of the petitioner to seek relief before this Court by way of filing an application under Article 102 of the Bangladesh Constitution. The learned Advocate submits that the petitioner having no right, title and interest in the property in question and her right having not been infringed or affected, she is not an aggrieved person who could seek enforcement of her right under Article 102 of the Bangladesh Constitution as person aggrieved.

14. Without being required to enter into the merit of the claim we are not to see whether the petitioner is an aggrieved person within the meaning of Article 102 of the Constitution. It appears that the petitioner has no direct interest in the property in question and hence she has not challenged the action of the Government releasing the property from the abandoned property list.

15. In the case of Muhammad Abdus Salam Vs. Chairman East Pakistan Election Authority and others reported in 17 DLR 191 it is held:

"Person aggrieved must be a man who has suffered a legal grievance, a man against whom a decision has been pronounced which has wrongfully deprived him of something, or wrongfully refused him something, or wrongfully affected his title to something."

16. In the case before us the petitioner having not lodged any claim of title in the property already declared as not an abandoned property, has suffered no loss and therefore not an aggrieved person. In this connection cases reported in 45 DLR 301, 39 DLR (AD) 111 have been reported. In all the decisions it has been consistently held that an aggrieved person can invoke the aid of the Article 102 of the Constitution if it is found that his right guaranteed under the Constitution has been violated. The petitioner being not an aggrieved person and having not claimed any title in the property, the question of violation of such a right has not arisen. From the facts appearing on the face of the petition and the terms of the Rule, we find that since the property has already been released from the abandoned list by the Court of Settlement on determination of the dispute between the Government and the real owner the petitioner having no locus standi has not claimed any right, title and interest and this writ application has been directed only against the notice which has been issued by the Government in respect of the property against the petitioner. The government having not challenged the order of the Court of Settlement that the property is not an abandoned property but it belongs to the real owner, whatever interest of the petitioner was claimed being in the occupation of the property for continuing her occupation is dependent on the interest of the Government which no more exists and the petitioner's fate is dependent on the rise and fall of the interest of the Government in the property. Considering the facts and circumstances of the case, we are of the view that there is no illegality or impropriety in the impugned notice dated 1.4.89 issued by the respondent No. 2 and the same is not liable to be declared to have been made without lawful authority and is of no legal effect and in that view of the matter the petitioner is not entitled to any relief in the writ petition.

17. In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs.

Let the order of ad-interim injunction passed against the respondent Nos. 1 and 2 directing them not to interfere with the petitioner's possession in the house in question is hereby vacated.

End.

lawyer:
M. G. Bhuiyan, Nurunnabi Khan ------- For the Appellant. 
Sultan Ahmad, Deputy Advocate-General ------- For the Respondents.
parties:
Md. Abdur Rasheed ------- Appellant.
Vs.
Govt. of Bangladesh  ------- Respondent.
full_judgment:
M. H. Rahman J.—This is a second appeal. The appellant, Md. Abdur Rasheed, filed Title Suit No. 36 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Dacca for a declaration that the order dated 22. 2. 66 of the Deputy Director of Public Instructions, Dacca Division, Dacca (defendant No. 2) terminating his service was void, invalid, illegal, ultra vires and without lawful authority and of not legal effect and that he was still in service of the Government.

2. His case, in brief, is that he was appointed as Physical Education Teacher in Nawabur Government High School (Urdu Section) on 31.12. 62 by defendant No. 2 on temporary basis in the scale of Tk. 140-275/- per month with admissible dearness allowances pending final decision after advertisement. The letter of appointment was forwarded to defendant No. 3, the Head Master, Nawabpur Govt. High School, with request to take necessary steps for police verification as to the plaintiff's and defendants. The plaintiff joined his duty on 10. 1. 65. While he was in service there was an advertisement for enrolment of names in the panel of Physical Education Teacher in the Government School. The plaintiff applied to defendant No. 2 for enrolment of his name in the panel of Physical Education Teacher in the scale of Tk. 200-375/-. As directed by defendant No. 2 he appeared before the Selection Committee and was selected as Physical Education Teacher of the Nawabpur Government High School and since then he had been working as an officiating Education Teacher against a substantive post. In 1964, there was a police verification of his antecedents and he learnt from his cousin and next door neighbour Md. Alimuddin that his cousin along with Md. Akkel Ali, a member of Union Council went to the Police Station and supplied necessary formation as to the plaintiff's antecedents whereupon a favourable report was submitted. After three years of satisfactory service the plaintiff's service was terminated by an order dated 22-2-66 of the Deputy Director of Public Instructions, Dacca Division, Dacca with immediate effect due to adverse reports on his confidential antecedents. This, order was communicated to him on 2.3.66. On his representation he was informed that the Home (Political) Department examined his case and considered him unsuitable for appointment. The plaintiff contended that till the filing of the suit he did not know when the other police verification was held and what the report was and when and how it was made by the Police. As he was not given any opportunity to show cause to prove his innocence the impugned order terminating his service violated the principle of natural justice and was liable to be declared to be void.

3. The defendants contested the suit asserting, inter alia, that the plaintiff was appointed on a temporary basis subject to police verification as to his antecedents and his service was terminated according to the terms of the contract; there was only one police verification and that was against the plaintiff; the police report, a secret document was in the custody of the Home (Political) Department and the plaintiff being appointed on a temporary basis. There was no legal requirement for serving notice to show cause before terminating his service and he was not entitled to any relief in the suit.

4. The trial Court, after construing the letter of appointment (Ext. 1) as a whole, held that the appointment was made subject to police verification, disbelieved the plaintiff's assertion that there had earlier been a favorable report from the Police and that the defendants' action was protected under paragraph (b) of clause (2) of Article 177 of the Constitution (of 1962) as the Police report was confidential in nature and no enquiry in respect of the same would have been practicable and the disclosure of the same would have been prejudicial to the security of the country.

5. The appellate Court affirmed the decision of the trial Court and held that the defendants were justified in taking the impugned action and was protected under paragraph (b) of clause (2) of Article 177.

6. Mr. M. G. Bhuiya, the learned Advocate appearing for the appellant, has submitted that the appellant has been condemned unheard and as the order of termination violated the principle of natural justice it is void abinitio. In support of his contention he has referred to the case of the University of Dacca through its Vice-Chancellor and the Registrar, University of Dacca Vs. Zakir Ahmed (1964) 16 DLR (SC) 722 and has drawn our attention to the following observations made therein:

“Wherever any person or body of persons is empowered to take decisions after expost facto investigation into facts which would result in consequences affecting the person, property or other right of another person, then in the absence of any express words in the enactment giving such power excluding the application of the principles of natural justice, the Courts of law are inclined generally to imply that the power so given is coupled with a duty, to act in accordance with such principle of natural justice as may be applicable in the facts and circumstances of a given case.”

Mr. M. G. Bhuiya has then cited to us the case of Abdus Saboor Khan Vs. Karachi University and Controller of Examinations, Karachi University (1966) 18 DLR (SC) 422 wherein the earlier observation was reiterated and it was further observed that "No one can be condemned unheard" is one of the settled principles of law, and such a principle will be read into the relevant law unless its application is excluded by express words", Mr. Bhuiya has also referred to the ease of Bangladesh Small Industries Corporation, Dacca Vs. Mahbub Hossain Chowdhury (1977) 29 DLR (SC) 41 where it was observed that "Precedent hearing or compliance of the principle of natural justice is implicit in the dismissal of employee enjoying some statutory status or holding a statutory post or a post of a public character." Apart from citing these cases Mr. Bhuiyan has also cited to us the case of A. B. M. Habibur Rahman Vs. The Director of Technical Education, East Pakistan and others (1969) 21 DLR (Dac.) 274 wherein termination of service of a temporary employee, terminable at any time without any notice and without assigning any reason whatsoever, was held to have been bad as the order of termination referred to adverse political records against the servant but he was not given an opportunity to show cause as to the aspersion made in the order of termination.

7. Mr. Sultan Ahmed, the learned Deputy Advocate General, has submitted that service of the plaintiff was terminated according to the terms of contract which includes a satisfactory report from the police as to his antecedents; as the plaintiff was appointed on purely temporary basis he was not entitled to any show cause notice or any protection under Article. 177 of the late Constitution and even if he was entitled the Government's action was protected under paragraph (b) clause (2) of Article 177 of the Constitution. He has also contended that the facts of the first.... three cases cited by the learned Advocate for the appellant have got no relevance in the present case and though the fact of 21 DLR 274 appeared to be on all fours with the facts in the present case the decision made therein, according to his submission, was not correctly laid down as the case of Federation of Pakistan Vs. Raja Muhammad Afzal Khan (1959) 11 DLR (SC) 45 was not placed before the Court. The learned Deputy Advocate General has contended that the plaintiff's case is, in fact, a refusal to appointment rather than the termination of service. He has drawn our attention to the following observations made in the case reported in 11 DLR (SC) 45:

“There is no duty upon the employer to give such an employee, whose employment is merely tentative until the contract is completed by satisfaction of all the necessary conditions, an opportunity to clear his character while continuing in such tentative employment. Having received information, upon which the employer can reasonably rely, to the effect that the intending employee is unsuitable for the employment in question, the employer may immediately, refuse to go on with the contract and thus bring it to an end. It is not necessary in such a case that there should be any direct or indirect rescission of the contract, because the contract was never completed. It fell through for lack of satisfaction of a primary and precedent condition”.

The Deputy Advocate General has submitted that had this case been cited in the case reported in 21 DLR 274 the decision could have been otherwise.

8. The facts of the first three cases cited by the learned Advocate for the appellant are, no doubt, distinguishable from those in the present case. The case of 16 DLR (SC) 721 as well as the case of 18 DLR (SC) 422 dealt with question of expulsion of a student and in 29 DLR (SC) 41 the main question was whether the relationship between the servant of a statutory corporation and the statutory corporation was governed by the principle of master and servant. The facts are no doubt distinguishable but the observations made in these cases as to the requirement of observing the principles of natural justice are relevant even in the instant case. The principles of natural justice, particularly the principle that no one should be condemned unheard, have now become, because of the decision of Superior Courts, firmly rooted in our judicial system.

9. These is no doubt that the service of a temporary employee can be terminated according to the terms and condition of the contract. In the instant case, the Government could have terminated the case without showing any cause.

10. It is immaterial whether the police verification was included in the terms of contract or not. An employer is entitled to be satisfied as to the antecedents of an intending employee and may collect information from any source or cause any enquiry in that regard. The process of verifying antecedents of an employee cannot be called a punitive proceeding requiring the employer to give a reasonable opportunity to the employee for representing his views. But when the order of termination of service, even of a temporary employee, casts an aspersion or puts any blame or contains any statement that may adversely affect the employee's career, the employer is obliged to give an opportunity to the employee to place his case. In this regard provision for giving reasonable opportunity is beneficial both to employee as well as to employer and conducive to the cause of justice. The employee gets an opportunity to explain his position and the employer also gets a chance to consider the employee's point of view that might have escaped his notice or was withheld from him.

11. As the plaintiff's employment was terminated on the alleged ground of adverse reports as to his confidential antecedents the plaintiff was entitled to a reasonable opportunity to represent his case. The facts in the present case are distinguishable from the facts in cases. In the latter case the Government employee was offered service on 12th 11 DLR (SC) 45 April, 1956, by a Office Memorandum and he commenced his duties on 19th April, 1956 and later he was sent a copy of the following letter dated 18th June, 1956 of the Ministry of Industries addressed to the Superintending Engineer, Mangla Dam:

“With reference to your letter No. 2836/24 E dated 4th June, 1956 on the above subject, I am directed to say that the Government agrees to terminate the service with immediate effect. In lieu of 15 days' notice he should be given 15 days' pay.”

12. We quote this letter from the High Court decision of the case reported in P.L.D. 1957 (W.P) Lahore 17. It is to be noticed that the order of termination was made within two months from the date the Government servant had commenced his duly. Again, the letter dated 18th June, 1956 on the face of it does not cast any aspersion or blame on the Government servant though it generates suspicion that the- incumbent might have been discharged because of information disclosed in the letter of Superintending Engineer, Mangla Dam. In the present case the plaintiff joined his duty on 10-1-66 and as requested by defendant No. 2 he appeared before the Selection Committee on 4-1-64. The letter of termination shows that the plaintiff was serving as Officiating Physical Education Teacher in the scale of Tk. 200-375/-, a scale higher than the one mentioned in the letter of appointment. This lends support to the claim of the plaintiff that he was selected as Physical Education Teacher and has been working against a substantive post though neither of the parties produced any document how the scale of pay was raised. In the facts and circumstances of the case it cannot be said that the plaintiff's service was inchoate or that the plaintiff had been serving all these years, in advance, as a condition precedent for his appointment.

13. However, from the documents exhibited and evidence led in the case it is not clear whether the plaintiff was appointed for an indefinite period to attract the protection of' Article 177 of the Constitution

14. As the Courts below have concurrently held that the Government is entitled to protection under paragraph (b) of clause (2) of Article 177 of the Constitution and as the learned Deputy Advocate General has laid emphasis on this question of law it is appropriate that we express our Views on the applicability of this constitutional provision. Paragraph (b) of Clause (2) of Article 177 of the Constitution of 1962 makes an exception in respect of requirement of giving a reasonable opportunity to Government servant in case of dismissal, removal or reduction in rank when giving such an opportunity is not practicable or prejudicial to the security of the country. This provision, however, does not empower any authority to cast any aspersion or put any blame on a Government servant. When an order, intending to claim protection under the exception clause, wanders away and casts an aspersion on the Government servant affecting his career, protection under the clause will no longer be available to the Government and will immediately attract the principle of natural justice.

15. In view of the above we hold that the appointing authority ought to have disclosed to the plaintiff the nature of adverse confidential antecedents against him and given him an opportunity to explain his conduct. As the appointing authority did not do so the impugned order of termination of service must be held to have been passed illegally. We set aside the decree passed by the trial Court and upheld by the appellate Court. We decree the suit and declare that the impugned order of termination is illegal and the plaintiff is still in service.

In the result, the appeal is allowed with costs.

Shahabuddin Ahmed J.- I agree.

End.

lawyer:
K.Z. Alam with Latifur Rahman ------- For the petitioner in the three petitions.
Anwarul Huq Chowdhury, Dy. A.G. ------- For the Respondents.
parties:
Mrs. Anwara Begum; wife of Mr. Hannan in (W.P. No. 267/77), Md. Abdul Gafur (W. P. No. 352/77), 
Anwar Mollah (W. P. No. 213/77.)  ------- Petitioners.
Vs.
Govt. of Bangladesh and 2 ors  ------- Respondents.
case_source: In the matter of An application under Article 102 (3)(b)(i) of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh.
full_judgment:
Badrul Haider Chowdhury J.— These three rules challenging the detention of the detenus have been heard analogously as a common question of law is involved and these three writ petitions are disposed by this judgment.

2. In Writ Petition No. 267/77 the detenu is Arijitullah Shaikh and the petition has been filed by his mother-in-law Mrs. Anwara Begum. It is stated that the detenu is detained by an order dated 23-3-77 under rule 5(1)(a) of the Emergency Powers Rules, 1975 (Annexure-A). It is further stated that there is no material for which the detaining authority could pass the order of detention and it is stated that the detenu did not indulge in any prejudicial activity. The respondents by filing affidavit-in-opposition stated that the antecedents of the detenu was considered by the District Anti-Smuggling Committee as his name was mentioned in the agreed list of the smugglers. In reply it is stated that the detenu is a bona fide businessman of Jhaudanga Bazar and it is further challenged in the statement that Anti-Smuggling Committee after considering the reports of various agencies considered the necessity of detaining the detenus was vague. It is further mentioned in reply that had there been any materials against the detenu the respondents would have given the full particulars. In this view of the matter it is contended that the detention is illegal.

3. In Writ Petition No.352/77 the detention of Haji Abu Taleb has been challenged by his son Abdul Gafoor. The detenu has been detained by an order dated 28-5-77 under rule 5(1)(a) of the Emergency Powers Rules. It is stated that the detenu never indulged in any prejudicial activities and there is no specific case against the detenu in any Court. The respondents stated that the name of the detenu is listed as a habitual and veteran smuggler and his antecedents were verified by various agencies and on consideration of reports his name has been placed in the list and that has warranted his detention. In reply it is stated that the list of the anti-smuggling committee had been prepared without any material whatsoever. It is stated that the detenu has been unnecessary harassed and there is no specific case of smuggling against the detenu in any Court.

4. In Writ Petition No.213/77 the detention of Abdullah Dalai has been challenged by his cousin Anwar Mollah, the petitioner. It is stated that the detenu is detained by an order dated 28-3-77 under rule 5(1) (a) of the Emergency Powers Rules. It is stated that the detenu had never indulged in any prejudicial activity. The respondents by filing an affidavit-in-opposition stated that the detention has become necessary because the detenu has been mentioned as a veteran smuggler and his name is mentioned in the list of smugglers which was prepared by the Anti-Smuggling Committee of the Government of Bangladesh. In order to prevent him prejudicing the maintenance of supply and services essential to the life of the community the detention order was passed. In reply, it is stated that the detenu is an inhabitant of village Garakhali which is 500 yrs away from the border intervened by a river Sonai Nadi. It is contended that by itself if should not have been assumed that the detenu is a smuggler and without tangible material the detenu has been detained illegally in colourable exercise of power. Thus in all these three Writ petitions the detaining authority, it is stated, has passed the order of detention as because the Anti-Smuggling Committee of the Government of Bangladesh has mentioned these three detenus as smugglers and therefore, the detention has become necessary under rule 5(1)(a) of the Emergency Powers Rules. These detentions are under challenge.

5. Mr. Latifur Rahman, the learned Advocate appearing for the detenus has argued that rule 5(1)(a) is not at all attracted and, therefore, the detentions are illegal. Further invocation of rule 2(e), (XI) and (XII) in the orders of detentions show that the detenus have been detained for prejudicing the maintenance, supplies and services essential to the life of the community and for prejudicing the economic and financial interest of the State. Mr. Latifur Rahman argued that by invocation of rule 2(e), (XI) and (XII) of the Emergency Powers Rules the detaining authority has passed the order of detention under rule, 5(1)(a) and the detention is, therefore, mala fide.

The learned Advocate has referred to few decisions which will be considered presently.

6. The learned Deputy Advocate General appearing for the respondents has argued that the detention orders were passed with a view to preventing the detenus from acting in a manner prejudicial to the maintenance of supplies and services essential to the life of the community and this being one of the powers that has been conferred upon the Government by section 2 of the Emergency Powers Act for detaining under clause VIII the power of detention is available and no exception can be taken to the detention orders.

7. Now to consider the main argument of Mr. Latifur Rahman, the learned Advocate that if the detenus are smugglers then provision has been made by law for trial of these persons to wit rule 18 of the Emergency Powers Rules which is punishable with death or transportation for life or with rigorous imprisonment for a term which may extend to 14 years. The learned Advocate referred to the case reported in 19 D.L.R. 748, Writ Petition No. 214/76., Writ Petition No. 190/77, Criminal Misc. Case No.69/77 and 29 D.L.R. 5.

Mr. Anwarul Huq Chowdhury, Deputy Advocate General has cited 21 D.L.R. 235 and 28 D.L.R. 172.

8. In the case of Abdur Rahman Vs. Govt. of East Pakistan (1967) 19 DLR 748, a Division Bench of the Dacca High Court considered the detention of a detenu under rule 32 of the Defense of Pakistan Rules, 1965. The order of detention mentioned that the detention was necessary with a view to prevent the detenu "from acting in any manner prejudicial to the security, public safety, maintenance of public order and maintenance of peaceful conditions in the Khulna District, it is necessary that he be detained in Khulna jail." The Division Bench considered that the allegation that he was a member of a gang of smugglers but the detention, order only mentioned the prejudicial activity to the (a) security, (b) public safety, (c) maintenance of public orders, (d) maintenance of peaceful conditions. Nothing was said about the maintenance of essential supply and services. In this view of the matter the Division Bench observed in that context:

“Apart from the question as to how far smuggling activities could be covered by the provisions of rule 32, it seems that the detaining authority has not properly applied its mind to the facts of the case.”

With respect we are in full agreement with this judgment but this decision has no manner of application in the context of the contention that has been advanced by Mr. Latifur Rahman.

9. In Writ Petition No. 214/76, a Division Bench of this Court considered the detention of the detenu under rule 5(1)(a) of the Emergency Powers Rules. In that case the detenu was mentioned as a notorious black-marketer and smuggler and this detenu previously in 1966 was also arrested under Defense of Pakistan Rules on the ground of allegation of black marketing and he was released on execution of bond but since he has been indulging in black marketing, the detention has become necessary. A question was raised whether the detention of a person on the allegation of smuggling and black marketing can be Validly made under rule 5(1) (a), The Division Bench considered, the definition of prejudicial act in rule 2(c) and mentioned that case of smuggling or black marketing may be grounded on clause (xii) prejudiced the economic or financial interest of the state. The Court observed:

“from a reading of the definition of the prejudicial act as contained in rule 2(c) and a language of sub-rule (1) of rule 5, it appears that sub-rule (1) of rule 5 does not cover all the categories of prejudicial acts as enumerated in rule 2(e). Only some of the prejudicial acts have been selected for the purpose of passing an order of restriction of a person, restriction order and detention order......an isolated act of black-marketing cannot be said to be prejudiced in the interest of Bangladesh so the case of the detenu is not covered by clause (iii) of rule 2(c) also. Similarly clause (xi) which provides to prejudice the maintenance, supplies and services essential to the life of the community cannot also be referred to. The clause contemplates altogether a different object. There is no doubt why a case of smuggling or black-marketing does not come within the ambit of clause (xi). Only clause (xii) which provides to prejudice the economic or financial interest of the state may be referred to, to deal with a case of smuggling or black-marketing.”

The Division Bench relied on the 19 D.L.R. 748 and considered the detention illegal,

10. The aforesaid decision in Writ Petition No. 214/76 proceeds from an analysis which was also noticed in the case of Kalipada Hazara Vs. Govt. of Bangladesh (Criminal Misc. Case No. 69/77) by another Division Bench to which one of us was a party. It was noticed that unfortunately attention of the learned Judges was not drawn to section 2, clause (viii) of the Emergency Powers Act which gives vires to rule 5(1)(a). This analysis was based on the decision of Government of West Pakistan Vs. Begum Abdul Karim, (1969) 21 D.L.R. (S.C.) 1 and in the case of Ghulam Jilani, (1967) 19 D.L.R. (S.C.) 417. The decision in Criminal Misc. Case No.69/77 was given on 21-6-77 whereas the decision in petition No. 214/76 was given on 8-12-76. As in the Criminal Misc. Case 69/77 the decision was based on the two Supreme Court decisions, namely, 19 D.L.R. and 21 D.L.R. and as advised at present, we do not see any reason to take a different view.

11. Next case is Writ Petition No.190/77. In this petition a Division Bench considered the detention under rule 5(1) (a) and in the short judgment, if we may say so with respect, the reason is given as under:-

“It appears that the order of detention was passed only for one consideration that is to say to prevent the detenu from indulging in smuggling. Rule 5(1) (a) of the Emergency Powers Rules, 1975 does not, however, provide for preventive detention for smuggling. No other materials has been disclosed in the affidavit-in-opposition of respondent No.1 to attract the application of rule 5(1) (a) of the Emergency Powers Rules, 1965. We are satisfied that the detenu Afazuddiri Dalai is now being detained in Khulna Jail without any lawful authority and in an unlawful manner.”

We have given our anxious consideration to find a reasoning and we could see the Division Bench dismissed the contention of the respondents by holding that rule, 5(1)(a) does not, however, provide for preventive detention for smuggling. With respect we could not persuade ourselves to follow the reasoning that was adopted by the Bench and speaking with great respect we could not persuade ourselves to adopt the reasoning to come to any conclusion.

12. The next case Abdus Sattar Vs. Govt. of Bangladesh, (1977) 29 D.L.R. 187, a Division Bench considered the detention under rule 5(1) (a) of the Emergency Powers Rules. In that case the respondents did not contest the rule and no affidavit-in-opposition as it appears from the reports was filed. Therefore, it is difficult to understand how it will come to help the petitioner in this case because it is settled law that when detention is not challenged by the respondents the detenu is to be released forthwith. If any authority is needed the case of Bihar Vs. Kameswar reported in A.I.R. 1964 (SC) 595 may be relied on.

13. Lastly Mr. Latifur Rahman has relied on Criminal Misc. Case No.69/77 to which one of us were a party. The learned Advocate has relied on this decision specifically to substantiate his contention that the onus is upon the detaining authority u/s. 106 of the Evidence Act and they must bring the materials on record by way of affidavit. In that decision it was held relying on 21 D.L.R. (SC) 1 that the respondents must bring the materials on record by way of an affidavit and section106 of the Evidence Act places the onus upon the respondents.

14. Mr. Anwarul Huq Chowdhury, the learned Deputy Advocate General did not contest this rule of law that has been laid down by the Supreme Court of Pakistan and which was followed by this decision. We shall deal with this case at a later stage. Mr. Chowdhury relied on 21 D.L.R. and 28 D.L.R. 172. In the case of Makhan Lal Sarnakar Vs. Govt. of East Pakistan, a Division Bench of the Dacca High Court considered the case of smuggling The first question was whether the person could be detained under the Defense of Pakistan Ordinance. This decision noticed 19 D.L.R. 748 and considered that that decision has no application in the facts and circumstances of the case. The Court observed:-

“having regard to the activities of the detenu referred to above the act of smuggling too assumes ominous significance for it clearly indicates that the detenu had kept a line of indication open for his activities across the border of Pakistan.”

We accordingly find ample justification for the impugned order of detention."

15. The next case that was relied on by the Deputy Advocate General is the case of Moklesur Rahman Vs. State, (1976) 28 D.L.R 172. In that case the detenu was detained under rule 5(1) of the Emergency Powers Rules. It appears that a F.I.R. was lodged against the detenu about smuggling of 77 tolas of gold. There was, therefore, a specific case and though he was granted bail he could not come out because an order of detention was passed. This detention order was challenged as mala fide. Considering the facts and circumstances of the case our brother Shahabuddin Ahmed, J concluded that the detention was justified. In that case, however, no argument was advanced in the form as has been raised now.

16. The relevant part of the rule 5(1) (a) necessary for the disposal of these rules is whether the power of detention is available for "maintenance of supplies and services essential to the life of the community". It will be seen in section 2 of the Act that this very expression has been mentioned which has empower the Government to make rules for 'maintenance of supplies and services essential to the life of the community", Again the power of detention in clause (viii) was given for maintenance of supplies and services essential to the life of the community. It will be at once noticed though, enabling power was given for protecting the economic life of Bangladesh in section 2 but the power of detention was not given in clause (viii) for such reason, e.g. for prejudicing the economic and financial interest of the state, It has been created as specific offense as "prejudicial act" Vide rule 2(e), (xii). Rule 18 deals with the offense of smuggling, It is thus clear that the Emergency Powers Rules have been framed for preventive detention and punitive detention, Preventive detention has been considered by the House of Lords in the case of Liversidge Vs. Anderson (1942 Appeal Case, 206) as a detention of a person without trial in such circumstances that the evidence in possession of the authority is not sufficient to make a legal charge or to secure the conviction of the detenu by legal proof but yet materials are sufficient to justify his detention. On the other hand, the objective of punitive detention is to punish a person for what he has done. The Indian Supreme Court has noticed in the case of Gopalan and Vs. State of Madras, reported in A.I.R. 1950 (SC) 27 that a person is punitively detained only after a trial for committing a crime and after his guilt has been established in a competent Court. It was further observed that preventive detention is not a punitive but precautionary measure. The object is not to punish a man for having done something but to intercept him before he does it and prevent him from doing it. No offense is proved nor any charge formulated and the justification is suspicion or reasonable probability and not criminal conviction which can only be warranted by legal evidence.

17. The first world war necessitated the enactment of Defense of India (Criminal Law Amendment) Act, 1915 to "provide for special measures to secure the public safety and the defense of British-India and' for the more speedy trial of certain offenses". In 1939 Defense of India Act was passed and Rules were framed under it to provide "for special measures to ensure the public safety and defense of British-India and for trial of certain offenses". It will be noticed that in 1939 Act after the word "public safety" and before the word "defense of British-India" the expression "interest" was inserted. Section 2 of the Act empowered the Central Government to make rules "for securing the defense of British-India, the public safety, the maintenance of public order, or efficient prosecution of war, or for maintaining supplies and services essential to the life of the community". While clause (X) gave the power of detention for public safety or interest, defense of British-India, the maintenance of public order, his Majesty's relations with foreign powers or Indian States, the maintenance of peaceful condition in tribal areas, the efficient prosecution of war, no power was given for detention with a view to prevent from acting prejudicially for maintenance of supplies and services essential to the life of the community. This power was given in clause (xx) for making rules for maintaining supplies and services essential to the life of the community. In part-XII of the Defense of India Rules, 1939 under the heading "Essential Supplies and War" hosts of rules were framed, namely, rule 75(2), 84, Rule 81(3) specifically dealt with maintaining supplies and services essential to the life of the community. Thus, the life of the community was regulated by these rules for maintenance of essential supplies and services to the life of the community and numbers of Orders were framed under rule 81 such as Food Grains Control Order, Kerosene Control Order and contravention of these orders were punishable. In rule 81(d) trading in essential articles were regulated and 'essential articles' was defined as an article which the provincial Government or District Magistrate being of opinion that the maintenance, supplies thereof is essential to the life of the community declares by an order in writing to be an essential article. Number of essential articles were mentioned in the schedule and it was provided that contravention of the rules and orders shall be punishable with imprisonment.

18. When the war ended the Defense of India Act, 1989 was repealed by the Repealing and Amending Act, 1948 but the conditions in the sub-continent following the partition necessitated enactments and orders and the preventive detention for the first time was mentioned in the Constitution, namely, Indian Constitution and in Entry No. 3, List No. 3, it was mentioned preventive detection for reason connected with the security of the State, maintenance of supplies or services essential to the community. The preventive detention was also mentioned in the list No.1 under entry No. 9 as "preventive detention for reasons connected with defense, foreign affairs or security of India, persons subjected to such detention'. Thus the preventive detention was sanctified by the constitutional instrument and power was given both under the list-1 to the Central Government and list-3 to the provincial Govt. that with the difference i.e. the Central Govt. could detain for reasons of defense, foreign affairs or security of India, the State Govt. could detain for the security of the State, maintenance of public orders, or maintenance of supplies and services essential to the community. In India, the preventive detention was thus constitutionally approved and the same position obtained in so far as Pakistan was concerned. The framers of the 'Bangladesh Constitution accorded constitutional approval to the concept of preventive detention subject to constitutional safeguards under article 33 and specifically sub-article (4) which provided "no law providing for preventive detention or authorize the detention of a person for a period exceeding 6 months" unless approved by the Advisory Board. With the proclamation of the Emergency under Article 141(A) right to move the Court was suspended for enforcement of rights guaranteed under Articles 36, 37, 38, 39, 40, and 42. Therefore, the preventive detention was sanctioned by the Emergency Powers Act and both for the purpose of preventive and punitive which we have just analyzed above.

19. The question is what is meant by the "maintenance of supplies and services essential to the life of the community". While the law making authority in the defense of India Act, 1939 did not spell out the scope of activity in this field, either by definitive section or by creating an offense, rule 81(d) simply mentioned the expression and provided for passing regulatory orders contravention of which could be visited with punishment. In the case of Dayanaud Madhi vs. State of Bihar, reported in A.I.R. 1951 (Patna) 47, Justice Das considered that these words were taken from the Defense of India Act, 1939 and 1940. Preventive Detention Act, 1959 provided for preventive detention for reasons connected with the maintenance of supplies essential to the community and maintenance of services essential to the community and concluded pointedly by saying that:

“any activity which directly interferes with or threatens maintenance of the supplies of such primary necessities of life as food or cloth attracts the operation or section 3. The supply of essential commodity cannot be contemplated as entirely divorced from service to the community.”

The learned Judge observed:

“that any apprehension of any black marketing or hoarding will directly affect maintenance as that word is ordinarily understood.”

In that case another argument which will be also relevant for our purpose as the same was advanced by Mr. Latifur Rahman that when there are three courses open to the Government the Government must take recourse of any one of them and not all of them. Justice Das dismissed the contention by saying that it is for State Government to decide which alternative could be adopted and which was most applicable in the circumstances of the case.

20. The next contention that in the English enactment the word "supplies" were used with the word "services" with the conjunctive "and" sometime with disjunctive word though the statute itself used the expression "and" and not "or". The subsequent amendment in 1940 was noticed which inserted "or" in place of word "and". The learned judge on consideration of the use of the expression of "or" and "and" following Maxwell's Interpretation of Statutes concluded that this cannot be considered in watertight compartment. In this view of the matter, the view was taken that wide meaning is to be given to the expression and all activities which hinder or prejudice the maintenance of supplies or services essential to the life of the community will be within the mischief of preventive detention.

21. In the maintenance of internal security Act 1971 power of detention was given with a view to prevent from acting "in a manner prejudicial to the maintenance of supplies and services essential to the community". A detention was challenged in the case of Soshti Chowdhury Vs. State of West Bengal A.I.R. 1972 (SC) 168. The Indian Supreme Court relying on its earlier decisions considered that the detention order was valid.

It observed:-

"It is always open to the detaining authority to pass an order for the detention of a person if the grounds of detention are genuine to the object for which a detention order can legally be made. The fact that the particular act of the detenu which provides the reason for the making of the detention order constitutes an offense under the Indian Penal Code would not prevent the detaining authority from passing the order of detention instead of proceeding against him in a Court of law. The detaining authority might well feel though there was not sufficient evidence admissible under the Indian Evidence Act for securing a conviction, the activities of the person ordered to be detained were of such nature as to justify the order of detention. There would be no legal bar to the making of detention order in such a case.”

22. With respect, if we may say so, we fully subscribe to this view. It will be noticed that in that case the detenu committed theft in respect of some electric wires from the top of the post. Even then the Supreme Court considered it was prejudicial act to the maintenance of supplies and services essential to the community.

23. In the case of Arun Kumar Vs. State of West Bengal the detenu along with his associates cut away 40 metres of copper wire from overhead traction. His detention was challenged that it was mala fide because it could be a case of theft but the Supreme Court rejected the contention by saying:-

“No doubt the removal of overhead traction wire would be a case of theft but it is not to say that such removal would not also be prejudicial to the maintenance of supplies & services essential to the community, especially when indulged on any large scale.”

In the case of Brozan Vs. State of West Bengal, the question was that when a detenu was liable to be tried in a criminal Court for a criminal offense the detention under the Internal Security Act was illegal. The Supreme Court repelled the contention A.I.R. 1972 (SC) 2256. In other words, as case under the criminal procedure whether punitive or preventive depends on the facts which have already taken place whereas a case under the Act providing for preventive detention depends on the satisfaction of the authorities concerned of the likelihood of the person to be detained to act in future in a manner similar to the one seen from his past act, The upshot of the above discussion is that when two modes are available to the executive recourse can be had for any one of them but not for both of them. In other words the executive can detain a person when it sees that sufficient evidence would not be collected or witness could not be procured because of the powerful influence of the detenu as was noticed in the case of Bhimsen Vs. Union of India, A.I.R. 1951 (SC) 481. The reasoning is clear because the clandestine affairs are conducted in the shady hours of the evening and definitely not in public view. Smuggling as a social evil is understood is the ordinary sense which hinders maintenance of supplies or services essential to the life of the community. The offense that has been created under rule 18 is referable to the Customs Act. 1969 but the smuggling which has been noticed by the anti-smuggling committee of the Government of Bangladesh and in pursuance of which District Authorities have maintained a list of smugglers are to be understood in different way and especially when the detention is for the ground that in order to prevent him from prejudicing the maintenance of essential supplies and services to the community. The power is thus available to the Government 'to put them out of circulation to use the expression of Cornelius, C.J. They are simply incapacitated for the time being because the life of the community is the consideration for which the Government exists. The contention that liberty cannot be circumscribed is to be understood in the context of the famous dictum of Hamoodur Rahman, C.J. that "it is being before well-being" that is to be considered (21 D.L.R. SC. 1).

It is emergency which has to be taken as a factor and it has been proclaimed by the President after the fourth constitutional amendment and that emergency is still continuing. Added to it, a proclamation was made on 20th August, 1975 declaring Martial Law and the country is still under the Proclamations of 28th August and 8th November, 1975. The Emergency which was proclaimed in January 1975 has not been lifted.

On the contrary it is continuing. Added to the Martial Law was imposed due to the breakdown, of the constitutional machinery. In this context this liberty is to be understood which we noticed in our decision in the case of Kripa Shindu Hazra Vs. Bangladesh Govt. in Criminal Misc. Case No. 69/77.

24. We now summarise our conclusion- (1) the expression "maintenance of supplies and services essential to the life of the community" is to be understood in the widest import. The activities that hindered the supplies or the essential services will be within the ambit of it and therefore rule 5(1)(a) will at once come into play, (2) when there are two modes of proceedings, namely, by way of criminal prosecution or preventive detention it is for the executive to decide which course to follow but the law does not authorize to follow both simultaneously, (3) the antecedents of the detenu will be relevant in coming to the question of exercising of the jurisdiction honestly to be satisfied for detention and reports of the agencies whose duty is to collect information will be of consideration for coming to its decision as to satisfaction, (4) rule 5(1)(a) has authorized preventive detention while rule 2(e) provides for punitive detention to be tried under rule 10.

25. Now coming to the question of materials which the respondents are u/s. 106 of the Evidence Act bound to place before the Court. In Kripa Shindu Hazra's case we expressed the opinion that it should be brought before the Court on affidavit, Although we noticed a practice of bringing of the file before the Court at the time of hearing which is commendable no doubt but since justice is to be done, it is better that the respondents in future will mention the materials in the affidavit, We have seen the materials in these cases. Arijitullah Sk. was found indulging in these sorts of activities sometime in 1956 and he was recruited as Special Police by the Dist. Anti Corruption Officer. A F. I. R. was lodged u/s. 156 of the Customs Act on 10.3.76 but the criminal case could not be prosecuted because no evidence could be collected and in the F. I R. it is mentioned “কিন্তু রাত্রিতে কোন সাক্ষী পাওয়া যায় নাই”

Haji Abu Taleb is also mentioned in the village crime-book dated 22.7.56 as member of the gang which indulges in smuggling, taking advantage of the position of their homestead which is very close to the border intervened by a river Sonainadi. In the case of Abdullah Dalai he is also mentioned as a habitual smuggler and detention has become necessary. Abdullah Dalai is also mentioned in the village crime book at page 50, Part-III, Vol. V.P.S. Kalaroa, District Khulna. Thus sufficient materials are there to show their antecedents which has given rise to an apprehension in the mind of the detaining authority that with a view to preventing them from acting prejudicially to the life of the community, their detention is necessary.

26. Argument was advanced that there is no time-limit in the detention order and observation has been made in 29 D.L.R. 187 that a person cannot be kept under detention for indefinite period in the absence of any specific case against him. Preventive detention, as we have stated in the beginning portion of this judgment, should have a time-limit but it was sanctified in the constitutional instrument because of social necessity. Though preventive detention is recognized in law now yet the Judiciary in the sub-continent has consistently depreciated it, the opinion that this power should be used sparingly only in exceptional circumstance otherwise the freedom or liberty whatever it means, will be made a mockery of Keeping in mind this sentiment of the eminent judges, we remind the executive that the power of detention is available no doubt but since Government in an organized society exists for the welfare the people, sympathy, consideration and understanding should emanate for it. Because not only it is a source of all power but fountain of mercy also flows from it. In the result therefore the opinion is this detention cannot be declared as illegal and without lawful authority and in this view of the matter we discharge the Rules. It is beyond the province of the Court to say anything further in the matter.

Abdul Matin Khan Chowdhury J.- I agree.

End.

caseno: Appeal from Appellate Decree No. 227 of 1962.
lawyer:
Aminul Huq ----- For the Appellant.
Rabia Bhuiyan ----- For the Respondents.
parties:
Rakhal Chandra Sarkar ----- Appellant.
Vs.
Benode Haldar and ors ----- Respondents.
full_judgment:
This second appeal has been preferred by the plaintiff No. 1 against the decision of district Judge, Khulna in Money Appeal No. 15 of 1960 passed on 10th May, 1961 reversing the judgment of the learned Munsif, 3rd Court, Khulna in Money Suit No. 99 of 1957.

2. The plaintiff's case briefly stated is that one Dijabar Kapalic was owner of the suit land and after his death his widow Solok Moni, who got the lands, settled it by pafta dated 30.9.1943 (Exbt. 1) with plaintiff No. 1, Rakhal Chandra Sarkar, father of plaintiff Nos. 2-6, and plaintiff No. 7, Biswanath Moral and after taking settlement the plaintiffs have been in possession of the suit land by themselves and through bargaders. That the defendants on 27.11.1957 have cut away illegally the paddies grown by the plaintiff on the suit land measuring 2.52 acres in plot Nos. 231, 248 and 127 causing a loss of Rs. 900/-. Hence the plaintiff brought the present suit for recovery of Rs. 900/- as damages from the defendants. Out of 9 defendants, defendant No. 1, Benode Halder and defendant No. 5, Tayeb Ali Molla contested the suit by filing separate written statements. The case of the defendant No. 1 is that the plaintiffs were never in possession of the suit land. That defendant No. 2 has been in possession of the suit plots Nos. 231 and 248 through his bargaders, Tayeb Ali, defendant No. 5 and Sohrab who have grown the paddy thereon and that plot No. 127 was cultivated by the bargader of Solok Moni, namely, the defendant No. 8, Nasaruddin Molla and that the kabuliyat (Exbt. 1) relied upon by the plaintiff is collusive and fraudulent document and was never acted upon. The case of defendant No. 5, Tayeb Ali is that the crop in plot No 127 was grown by Nasaruddin Molla, the bargader of Solok Moni and that the crop in other plots Nos. 231 and 248 was grown by the defendant No. 5 as bargader of Sukhomoy Halder, and that the plaintiffs have no title or possession in the suit land.

The plaintiff have examined 4 witnesses and the defendants have examined 6 witnessed, Both the parties also filed various documents namely, Exbt. 1 to 8 on behalf of the plaintiff and Exbts A to H on behalf of the defendants in support of their respective cases.

3. The learned Munsif found that the entire suit land was sold in auction in the rent sale and the land lord auction purchased the jama; that Exbt. 2(a) (dated 15. 4.25) a mortgage bond shows that Dijabar Kapalic mortgaged the land of the Jama wherein it was stipulated that the lands would remain in possession of the mortgage till Chaitra 1349 B.S., as such, the land was sold in auction while it was in mortgage; and that Exbt. 1, the deed of settlement was executed by Solokmoni in favour of the plaintiffs when the lands were sold in auction. According to him Exbt. 4 (Notice by debt settlement Board) shows that Solokmoni filed D. S. Board Case No. 500 of 1946 for setting aside the rent Sale and got it set aside; that Exbt. 5, certified copy of delivery of possession in Rent Execution Case No. 853 of 1935 shows that Solokmoni got possession of the land through Court on 1.12.1950 and that Biswanath, the plaintiff No. 7, had been an agent of Solkhmoni in Debt Settlement Board Case and identified the suit land at the time of D.P. (delivery of possession). The learned Munsif further found that Exbt. No. 1, which was executed in 1943, if this would not be acted upon then plaintiff No. 7 would not take so much interest for setting aside the sale.

4. The learned Munsif thereafter found that the defendants contention that the landlord had been in possession of the land after auction purchase cannot be believed in the face of Exbt. 2(a). He, therefore, held that the landlords were never in possession of the suit land. The learned Munsif has found that Exbt. 'A', the registered kabala dated 5.11.1947 executed by Solokmoni in favour of Mhomoy, Exbt. B series the barga kabuliyats of different dates taken by the defendant, and Exbt. C, certified copy of kabuliyat, dated 5.11.1947, alleged to have been executed by Solokmoni were all bogus documents. He further found that Exbt. 1 is a genuine document under which the plaintiffs acquired title in the suit land, as according to him, Solokmoni got land in her possession after Ext. 2(a) and as the auction purchaser did not go into possession and Solokmoni cleared the clouds of her title by setting aside the sale.

5. On a discussion of the oral evidence adduced by the parties he was of the view that there was nothing to disbelieve P. W. 1 the plaintiff No. 1, Rakhal Chandra Sarkar. And he found that P. Ws. prove conclusively that plaintiffs grew paddy in the suit land which defendant forcibly cut away, disbelieving the defendants witnesses about their broga cultivation and possession of the suit land.

6. The learned Munsif thereafter considered the question as to the amount of paddy grown in the suit land and its price. According to him 40 mounds of paddies were grown in the suit land and the price of paddy was Rs. 12-1/2 per mound and that of straw Rs. 20/- the plaintiffs are entitled to get in all Rs. 500/- and on this finding he decreed the plaintiff's suit against the contesting defendant and ex-parte against the rest for Rs. 500/- instead of Rs. 900/-.

7. On appeal by the defendants the learned District Judge, Khulna, who heard the appeal reversed the judgment of the learned Munsif holding that plaintiffs have failed to prove that they grew paddy in the suit land in the year 1364 B. S. The lower Appellate Court in arriving at the finding took note of all the exhibits submitted by the parties in the suit though he did not discuss it thoroughly about their implication. The learned Judge directed his attention to the evidence of the witness adduced by the parties with regard to the possession of the land and the growing of paddy. In this connection he found that no borga kabuliyat for the year 1364 B. S. was produced by the plaintiffs and after examining the evidence of P.W. 2, 3 and 4 he was of the view that there was a doubt regarding the truth of the plaintiff's case and that the evidence of P. Ws. is shake and unreliable. He held that the evidence adduced on behalf of the plaintiffs that the plaintiff party has been in possession of the suit land and that they grew the paddy thereon in 1364 B. S. is not worthy of reliance In this connection the learned Judge also took into consideration the evidence of D. W. 3 that Biswanath (plaintiff No. 7) and Rakhal (Plaintiff No. 1) did the works for setting aside the sale and also for delivery of possession through Court under section 37A of the B. A. D. Act but from this circular it cannot be said that the plaintiffs were in possession in 1364 B. S. of the suit land. On a discussion of the evidence of D. Ws. he found almost all of them to be unreliable holding that it is not improbable that defendant No. 5 and D. W. 5 Nowsher Ali, cultivated the suit land in 1364 B. S. and finally came to the conclusion that in the facts, circumstances and evidence in the Case the plaintiffs have failed to prove that they grew paddy in the suit land in the year 1364 B.S. and dismissed the suit.

8. Mr. Aminul Huq the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the appellant has contended that the Lower Appellate Court did not apply its mind to Exbt. 1 to 4 and also to Exbts. A. B. C. which from the basis of the case and upon which the Trial Court has given a finding as to possession in favour of the plaintiff, and that the Lower Appellate Court has erred in law in not considering issues Nos. 2 to 4 and thereby has failed to comply with the provision of Order 20 Rule 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure. According to the learned Advocate, the judgment of the Court of Appeal below is a diffused one and there is no separate finding or decision upon those issues. He has further contended that there is no positive finding by the Court of Appeal below as to who grew the paddy. His submission is, therefore; that judgment of the Lower Appellate Court is not a proper judgment of reversal. In this connection the learned Advocate has referred to the rulings reported in AIR 1963 All. 194 in the case of Ganga Singh and other VS. Sontosh Kumar and another; AIR 1962 (S.C.) 1314 (V. 49C 175) in the case of Sir Chunilal Vs. Mehta & Sons Ltd. Vs. Century Spinning and Manufacturing Co. Ltd. 10 D.L.R. 1 Privy Council in the case of K. M. Perera Vs. H. G. Martin Dias; 65 C. L.J. 270 Privy Council in the case of Pir Ahsanullah Shah Vs. Pir Ziauddin Shah; 27 C.W.N. 749 Privy Council in the case of Mohammad Solaiman VS. Kumar Birendra Chandra Singh & others 21 D.L.R. (S.C.) 448 in the case of Madan Gopal & others. Vs. Maran Bepari & ors 21 D.L.R. Dacca 838 in the case of Mahmuda Khatun Vs. Abu Sayed; 21 D.L.R. Dacca 977 in the case of Tamijur Rahman Vs. Md. Altafur Rahman and ors; A.I.R. 1948 Mad. 488 in the case of Kalabasti Veeramma Vs, Pratti Pati Lakshmayya and others and A.I.R. 1947 Patna 334 in the case of Rambijaya Prasad Singh Vs. Sukar Ahir.

<u>9. In AIR 1963 All. 194 while holding that a finding of fact is illegal if in arriving a it the court completely ignores a relevant and vital piece of evidence, it was observed :-</u>

<u>"Unfortunately, the learned Judge completely ignored a vital piece of direct evidence on this point namely" the oral testimony of several witnesses who appeared for the plaintiffs. One of them was Piarey Lal, the son of Tota Ram, who executed the agreement on behalf of his father Tota Ram, and presented it for registration Another was Ram Chand, also a signatory to the agreement who was present at the time when the transactions were made. The third was Jaipal son of Charan Singh who Was also present. I have read the depositions of these three witnesses. The combined effect of their evidence on this part of the case is overwhelming, for they prove that the parties entered into a contract of sale with an option of re-conveyance. It is significant that there was no cross-examination worth the name of these witnesses on this point. "</u>

<u>In AIR 1962 (S. C.) 1314 it was held:-.</u>

<u>"It is well settled that the construction of document of title or of document which is the foundation of the rights of parties necessarily raises a question of law."</u>

<u>In 10 DLR 1 Privy Council it was observed by Lord Denning as follows:-</u>

<u>"In considering this case, their Lordships call to mind the wise words of Lord Greene, M.R. in Yuill v, Yuill(M) (1945 P. 1 at page 19), when he said ;- "We were reminded of certain well-known observations in the house of Lords dealing with the position of an appellate Court when the judgment of the Trial Judge had been based in whole or in part on his opinion of the demeanor of witnesses It can, of course, only be on the rarest occasions and in circumstances where the Appellate Court is convinced by the plainest considerations that it would be justified in finding that the trial Judge had formed a wrong opinion. But when the Court is so convinced, it is, in my opinion, entitled and indeed bound to give effect to its conviction."</u>

<u>In 65 C. L. J. 270 Privy Council it was held that:</u>

<u>"As the learned Judge has the advantage of seeing the witnesses and watching their demeanor, his finding, so far as it depends on the credibility of oral evidence, cannot be lightly interfered with that the law gives a right of appeal from judgment of the trial Court on questions of fact as well as on questions of law, and the Court of Appeal after carefully. Weighing and considering the judgment has to make up its mind and cannot shrink from overruling it if on a full consideration of all the material, it is satisfied that the judgment is clearly wrong."</u>

<u>10. It may be noted that in the aforesaid two Privy Council Cases the observations made by their Lordships were with regard to the credibility of witness as arrived by the Trial Court depending on their demeanor and, in such case Trial Court's finding should not be lightly interfered with. But their Lordships have further held that in such case as well, if the Appellate Court is satisfied that the judgment is clearly wrong it cannot shrink from overruling it.</u>

<u>In 27 C. W. N. 749 (Privy Council) it was observed as follows:-</u>
