<u>"Before concluding this judgment, their Lordships must allude to the fact that the learned Judges of the High Court, before whom the appeal to their Court was heard, did not express any opinion as to whether the Defendants or any of them were protected from ejectment by any of the exceptions of sec. 37 of Act Xl of 1879, or of sec. Bengal Act VIl of 1968. The issue on that Subject was before them and they should have considered it and found upon it  Their Lordships will quote for the information of those learned Judges what Lord Justice Turner, in delivering the judgment of the Board in Tara Kant Banarjee Vs. Pudda Money Dasee (5 W. R. P. C. 63: 10 M.I.A. 476, 488) said as to the duty of High Court Judges to pronounce their opinions on all important issues in cases before them. The Lord Justice said:- The Case has not been decided in either Court on the principal point-whether the lands formed part of the joke tenure of the Talook. Their Lordships are unfortunately unable to decide this appeal finally by reason of this defect. The Courts below, in appealable cases, by for bearing from deciding on all the issues joined, not infrequently oblige this committee to recommend that a cause be remanded which might otherwise be finally decided on appeal. This is certainly a serious evil to the parties litigants it may involve the expense of a second appeal as well as that of another hearing below. It is much to be desired therefore, that in appealable cases the Courts below, should, .as far as may be practicable, pronounce their opinions on all the important points."</u>

<u>In 21 DLR(S.C.) 448, it was observed with -regard to the concurrent finding of fact and that of river red as follows:-</u>

<u>"The legal position does not admit of any doubt that a concurrent finding of fact reached by the lower Courts will not be disturbed by, the High Court in a Second appeal even if it disagrees with that finding on its own view of the evidence although the concurrent finding of the lower Courts may appear to be grossly erroneous, unless, as laid down in sub-section (c) of section 100, the error or defect discovered is of a substantial character pertaining to the procedure as provided by the Code or by any other law for the time being in force which may possibly have produced an error or defect in the decision of the case upon its merits. Interference would also be justified if the decision of the lower courts is found to be contrary to law or usage having the force of law. If, the finding of fact reached by the first appellate Court is at variance with that of the Trial Court, the former will ordinarily prevail, although it would not possess the same value or sanctity as a concurrent finding. Such a finding by the lower Appellate Court will, be, immune from interference in Second Appeal only if it is found to be substantiated by evidence on the record and is supported by logical reasoning, duly taking note of the reasons adduced by the first Court which have been disfavored in the contrary finding. The finding being at variance with that of the Trial Judge, the two will naturally came in for comparison for their corn operative merits in the light of the facts of the case and the reasons on which the two different findings have respectively proceeded. If the finding of the First Appellate Court cannot be supported on the evidence on record or if it has failed to take into account a material piece of evidence or if it does not reveal a logical basis for differing from the finding of the Trial Court, or is otherwise found to be arbitrary or capricious, it will have to be rejected in Second Appeal.</u>

11. In 21 DLR Dacca 977 while deciding a Second Appeal it has been observed as follows;-

"But the question is when the trial court after considering the, evidence and demeanor of the witnesses came to a finding which has been reversed by the lower Appellate Court without giving due consideration on the proper, aspect of the case. I find no reason why the findings of the 'learned Subordinate Judge on appeal should not be set aside."

In 21 DLR 838, also in a Second Appeal, it was observed;-

": .... it is well settled that interpretation of a document which is the foundation of the claim of a particular party, gives rise to a point of law which can be considered in a Second Appeal. A finding, made on such interpretation is not binding on this Court. This Court is clearly entitled to set aside a finding of the lower Appellate Court on such erroneous interpretation of such a document."

In AIR 1948 Madras 488 it has been observed as follows;-

"Unfortunately many judicial, officers have a habit of clubbing together all most of the issues and writing of diffuse judgment, without bringing their minds to bear on the particular matters that have to be decided under each issue, and then giving their conclusions on the several issues at the end of the judgment. The objector to that form of judgment is not so much that it contravenes the provisions of 0.20 R.5 of the Code, which does not seem to require anything more than that reasons should be given for the findings under the individual issues, but rather that it tends to loose thinking with the result that the Judge does not keep before his mind the essential points to be considered, so that the judgment not only loses clarity, but often leads to wrong conclusions, which would have been avoided, if the Judge had discussed the various issues separately. Having said this, however, I do not find the judgment under consideration so bad that it was impossible for the appellate Court to appreciate that the findings of the trial Court were. In almost every paragraph a point which had to be determined was considered and the learned Munsif's findings given. The Appellate Court would have therefore had no difficulty if it had taken some trouble to ascertain what the findings of the District Munsif were on the various points that had to be considered in the suit and in the appeal and presumably the learned counsel would have drawn its attention in the findings and the reasons given for them."

In AIR 1947 Patna 334 a Special Bench held as follows:-

"It is unfortunate that the trial Court proceeded to dispose of the case on a preliminary point and did not decide all the issues of fact which arose between the parties. As has been repeatedly pointed out by the Court following the observations of their Lordships of the Judicial Committee in 10 M.I.A. 476, 50 I.A. 247 at p. 254 and 60 I.A. 49 at p. 53 the Courts of fact must decide all the issues or fact which arise between the parties so that if the appellate Court takes a different view the parties are saved from further harassment."

Mrs. Rabia Bhuiyan, the learned Advocate appearing for the respondent, has contended on the other hand that the main question involved in this case is one of possession and who grew the paddy, question of title has no bearing in the suit. According to her the ruling cited on behalf of the appellant are not applicable to the facts and circumstances of the case. She submits that the finding of the trial Court that Solokmony got possession of the suit land with the help of plaintiff No. 7 on 1.12.1950 in that case how can she give possession to the plaintiff by Ext. 1 ? Finding of the trial Court that the plaintiffs are in possession basing on Exbt, 1-4, is, therefore, contradictory. According to her the plaintiffs have failed to produce any rent receipts showing payment of rent of the suit land in the year 1364 B.S., the relevant year for which they had brought present suit for damages. The suit is nothing but a test suit without any title and possession and the lower appellate Court has rightly dismissed it on a proper assessment of the facts and circumstances of the case. The learned Advocate, in this connection, has referred to the rulings reported in AIR 1963 (S.C.) 302 (India) in the case of Bamachandra Ayyar and another Vs. Ramalingam Chettiar and another and 12 DLR (SC) 132 in the case of Abdul Mannan Shek and another Vs. Lal Mamud alias & ors.

<u>12. In AIR 1963 (S.C.) 302 a point was raised before the Supreme Court of India that the judgment of the Appellate Court must come into close quarter with the judgment of the trial Court and meet tile reasoning given therein before it can be treated as conclusive between the parties for the purpose of section 100. In this Case their Lordships of the Supreme Court of India after discussing various rulings of the Privy Council observed as follows :-</u>

<u>"It is well known that as early as 1890, the Privy Council had occasion to consider this aspect of the matter in Mst. Durga Chowdhurian Vs. Jawahir Singh Chowdhury, 17 Ind App. 122 (P.C.). In that case it was urged before the Privy Council, relying upon the decision of Calcutta and Allahabad High Court in Futtehma Begum Vs. Moham Ausur, ILR 9 Cal. 309 and Nibvath Singh vs, Bhikki Singh, ILR 7 All. 649 (F .B.), respectively that the High Court would be within its jurisdiction in holding that where the lower Appellate Court has been led to discard or not give sufficient weight to other evidence to which it is not ensured, the High Court can interfere under s. 100. This contention was rejected by the Privy Council and it was observed that an erroneous finding of fact is a different thing from an error or defect in procedure and that there is no jurisdiction to entertain a second appeal on the ground of an erroneous finding of fact; however gross or inexcusable the error may seem to be. Their Lordships added that nothing can be clearer than the declaration in the Code of Civil Procedure that no second appeal will lie except on the grounds specified in S. 584 (corresponding to S.100 of the present Code), and they uttered a word of warning that no Court in India or elsewhere has power to add to or enlarge those grounds. Since 1890 this decision has been treated as a leading decision on the question about the jurisdiction of the High Court in dealing with questions of facts in second appeals."</u>

<u>(Paragraph No. 11, page No. 305).</u>

<u>It was further observed at page 307:-</u>

<u>"In Rani Hemanta Kumari Debi Vs Maharaja Jagadindra Nath Roy Bahadur 16 Mad. LJ 272 (P.C.), the Privy Council has no doubt observed that it is better that the appellate Court whenever it reverses the judgment of the lower Court, comes into close quarters with the judgment of the lower Court and meets the reasoning therein. These observations, however, do not assist us in determining the scope of the provisions of S. 100. They were made in an appeal which went before the Privy Council against the decision of the High Court when the Appellate Bench was dealing with the first appeal filed against the decision of the Judge of the first instance. The High Court had reversed the decision of the first Court; and in considering the propriety or correctness of the said reversing judgment, the Privy Council observed that the appellate judgment did not come into Close quarters with the judgment which it reversed. It would thus be seen that what the Privy Council .has said about the requirements of a proper appellate judgment, cannot assist Mr. Chatterjee in contending that if a proper judgment is not written by the lower appellate Court in dealing with questions of fact, its conclusions of facts can be challenged under S. 100. That question must be considered in the light of S. 100 alone,"</u>

<u>"We must, therefore, hold that Mr. Chatterjee is not right in contending that because the judgment of the lower appellate Court was not as elaborate as that of the trial Judge, or because some of the reasons given by the trial Judge had not been expressly reversed by the lower appellate Court, the High Court was entitled to interfere with the conclusions of the lower appellate Court. The question which arose for the decision of the "Courts of fact, was a simple question of fact-was the release deed executed by respondent No. 2 in favour of the appellate, justified by adequate consideration Had respondent No. 2 independent ad vice at the time when he signed the said document. Did he act bona fide or was he imposed upon? these were the points that arose between the parties on their pleadings. It would be noticed that these points present pure question of fact and their decision depended in the present case on appreciating the oral evidence adduced in support of the rival contentions, documents produced by the parties, their conduct and surrounding circumstances. In other words, what the Courts of fact were called upon to consider and decide were questions of fact in the light of all relevant evidence. That being so, we do not think the High Court was justified in interfering with the finding of fact recorded by the lower appellate Court in favour of the appellants."</u>

13. In 12 DLR (S.C.) 132 in the case of Abdul Majid and others Vs. Khalil Ahmed where in a Second Appeal the concurrent findings of the Courts below as to the application of money in a case of legal necessity were set aside by the High Court on the ground that the Courts below had approached the case from an erroneous view-point, while setting aside that judgment of the High Court it was observed by his Lordship, Munir, C.J. as follows:-

"It is obvious that what the learned Judge intended to say was that for the reasons stated by them the Courts below should not have accepted the evidence which they did and they seem to have assumed that a fallacious method of approaching the evidence is, in second appeal, a good ground for upsetting a finding of fact based on such evidence. With great respect, I am unable to agree With this view, because a fallacy in appraising the evidence as to a fact, unless it amounts to a material mistaken assumption  merely an error has never been held to be an error of law justifying interference in second appeal  had the occasion to examine this question recently in the Lahor High Court in Hadir Shah vs, Lal Shah and others (PLD) 1954 Lah. 447. where suffering for the leading authorities of the Privy Council on this subject I held that the High Court has no jurisdiction to entertain a second appeal on the ground of the erroneous finding of fact however gross and inexcusable the error may seem to be, unless there is an error in the procedure provided by law which may possibly have produced an error or defect in the decision of the case on the mends. I adhere to that opinion which was based on the Privy Council decisions in Durga ChowdhuraDi V. Jewahir Singh Chowdhury; (ILR 18 cal. 23) and Wali Muhammad V. Muhammad Balucb, 11 Lah. 199 which lay down this proposition in clear and unmistakable terms.

14. It is very difficult to follow the reasoning of the learned Munsif. He says that Exbt. 5 shows that Solokmony got possession of the land through Court on 1-12-1950 still he comes to the finding that the landlords were never in possession of the suit land after auction purchase because the evidence of defence witness is contradictory and shaky. His finding that Exbts. A.B. and C are bogus is also abrupt. He also found that Sdlokmony did never possess the lands. If that be so it is difficult to understand how can she give settlement by Exbt. 1. Under these circumstances these documents of title are not worth consideration I find enough force in the argument advanced by the learned advocate appearing for the respondent that these documents are not relevant for the disposal of the Money Suit which is purely based on damages for cutting away paddy alleged to have been grown by the plaintiffs in the disputed land. The learned Advocate has further submitted that had it been found as a fact that the defendant had title in the land in dispute but the paddy was grown by the plaintiffs the defendants could never have escaped the liability for damages if they had cut the paddy illegally. That being so it is equally applicable to the case of the plaintiffs. Omission to make specific mention of the documents as contended by the learned Advocate for the appellant has not affected the case on merits.

<u>15. It is a suit for damages for the alleged cutting away of the paddy the main question is whether the plaintiff is in possession of the land and whether he plaintiff grew paddy. This simple point has been made complicated unnecessarily by going into the question of title and that too in a manner making it more hazy and difficult to follow.</u>

16. Now let me come to the next contention of the learned Advocate for the appellant about the error of the Appellate Court in not considering issues Nos. 2 to 4. These issues are as follows:-

2. Have the plaintiffs acquired any title to the lands in suit?

3. Who are in possession of the lands in suit and who have got better title to possess the lands and to appropriate the usufructs?

4. Have the defendants or any one of them wrongfully cut and appropriately the paddy?

Issue No. 2 is on the point of title and has already been discussed by me and is not at all relevant, so also is the question of better title to possess this land and to appropriate the usufructs in Issue No. 3. Only the question who are in possession in issue No. 3 is relevant. Issue No. 4 is related to issue No. 3 and becomes relevant only if the plaintiff is found to be in possession and to have grown the paddy.

17. The lower Appellate Court has elaborately discussed the evidence adduced on behalf of plaintiffs as well as of the defendants on the question of possession and has comet the finding that the evidence of the P.Ws. is shaky and unreliable, and that the evidence adduced on behalf of the plaintiff that the plaintiff party has been in possession of the suit land and that they grew paddy thereon in 1364 B.S. is not worthy of reliance. The learned Judge has given cogent reasons for arriving at the aforesaid finding  This finding, in my opinion, is sufficient to dispose of the plaintiffs case and I do not find any substance in the argument of the learned Advocate for the appellant that there is no positive finding about who grew the paddy. I do not find any error of law committed by the lower appellate Court in its appreciation of the evidence and there is nothing for me to interfere with the judgment and order passed by the Court of Appeal below. In the result, this appeal this appeal is dismissed but in the facts and circumstances of the case I makes no order as to costs Prayer for Leave to appeal under clause 15 of the Letters Patent is refused.

End.

lawyer:
M. Taleb Au, Advocate ------ For the Petitioner. 
Sajjad Ali Chowdhury Assistant Attorney-General ------ For the Respondents.
parties:
Sirin Begum, wife of detenu Md. Ofazuddin Dewan, son of Late Samiruddin Dewan of GoshalaBazar(Tumal quarter), Police Station & District Lalmonirhat ------ Petitioners 
VS
District Magistrate & anr ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Habibur Rahman Khan. J.	The writ petition under Article 102 (2)(b)(i) of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh has been filed by one Mosammat Siria Begum seeking an order for the release of her husband Md. OfazuddinDewan from detention.

2. On the application of the petitioner a Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause why the detenu Md. Ofazuddin Dewan of Goshala Bazar (Turoal Quarter), P.S. and District Lalmonirhat should not be brought before this Court so that it may satisfy itself that the detenu is not being held in custody without lawful authority or in an unlawful manner. 

3. The petitioner has stated in her petition that the d1enu is the owner of two shops at Goshala Bazar within Lalmonirhat Municipality dealing in food grains and garments with valid license. He was suddenly arrested by the police of Lalmonirhat Police Station on 18.4.87 under section 54 of the Code of Criminal Procedure read with Section 3(2) of the' Special Powers Act, 1974. While in custody, the learned District Magistrate, Lalmonirhat by his Memo No. 33 (Confidential Cell) dated 20.4 .87 un- der Section 3 (2) of the Special Powers Act directed that the detenu be detained in custody for a period of 

30 days on the ground that it was necessary to detain him with a view to preventing him from doing any prejudicial act within the meaning of Section 2(f) (iii)(iv)(v)(vi)(vii) and (viii) of the Special Powers Act. Thereafter, by an order bearing No. 4838 H.M. (Security-1) dated 16.5.87 the Government extended the period of detention of the detenu for 2(two) months with effect from 23.7.87 though the validity of the previous order of detention expired on 20.7.87 and thus the detenu was illegally detained for 2 (two) days without any order. Thereafter presumably on the report of the District Magistrate the Government vide Memo No. 151 H.M. (Security-1) dated 3.8.87 extended the detention of the detenu for 3 (three) months with retrospective effect from 24.7.87 which was also illegal as the order of detention passed earlier already expired on 23.7.87. By another order made on 26.10.87 the Government extended the order of detention with retrospective effect from 24.10.87. On the expiry of the aforesaid order on 24.12.88 the order of detention was again extended by the Government vide order dated 12.1.88 for a period of 3 (three) months with retrospective effect from 24.12.87 on the expiry of which the detenu did not receive any communication from the detaining authority till 4.8.88. Again on 4.8.88 the detenu was served with another order of detention issued by the Ministry of Home Affairs vide Mcmo No. 7581, H.M. (Sccurity-1) dated 20.7.88 purporting to have been made under section 3(1)(a) for 3 (three) months from the date of his arrest. 

4. Notice of the Rule having been served on the respondents, Mr. Sajjad Ali Chowdhury, learned Assistant Attorney-General has appeared on behalf of the respondents but none of the respondents has shown any cause by filing affidavit-in-opposition. Thus statements of the petitioner made in the petition has remained uncontroverted. 

5. The order of detention has been challenged by the petitioner on various grounds. It is contended that the reasons assigned in the order of detention are all vague, indefinite, uncertain and evasive. It is claimed that no grounds have been communicated to the detenu along with the order of detention within fifteen days from the service of the order as required under Section 8 of the Special Powers Act, 1974 the case has been referred to the Advisory Board required under Section 10 of the said Act.. 

6. Mr. M. Taleb Ali Miah, Learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner having taken us through the application made by the petitioner and the order of detention as made by the learned District Magistrate, Lalmonirhat and the subsequent order of detention passed by the Government from time to time, submits that under the provision of Section 8(1) and 8(2) of the Special Powers Act the grounds of detention is required to be communicated to the detenu either at the time while he is detained or, as soon as thereafter as practicable, but not later than fifteen days from the date of making the order and the detaining authority is also to inform the person detained to enable him to make a representation against the order. The learned Advocate further submits that in the instant case the learned District Magistrate who made the initial order of detention in exercise of his powers under sub-section (2) of Section 3 of the Special Powers Act did not serve the grounds of detention on the detenu and did not inform him of his right of making representation within the time prescribed and subsequently also no grounds of detention was communicated to the detenue at any time when detention orders were extended from time to time. The learned Assistant Attorney-General appearing for the respondents could not refute the argument of the Learned Advocate for the petitioner by placing any material from the record that the grounds were communicated to the dctenue and that the detenu was given the intimation within the prescribed time. 

7. Section 8 of the Special Powers Act provides that while a person is detained under Section 3 of the Act the authority making the order shall as seen as thereafter, not later than fifteen days from the date of detention, communicate to the person affected thereby the grounds on which the order has been made to enable him to make representation in writing against the order and it shall be the duty of such authority to inform the person detained of his right of making such representation and to afford him the earliest opportunity in doing so. This is also the constitutional requirements as provided under Article

33(1) of the Constitution of Bangladesh. The object behind it seems to provide and safe-guard the liberty of a citizen against the aribitrary and whimsical exercise of Power of the detaining authority. It may be sometime necessary to detain a person for preventing him from doing any prejudicial acts but the detaining authority must exercise such power according to law and definitely not in an arbitrary and whimsical manner The detenu must know what are the grounds un- der which he is being deprived of his liberty. It has been consistently held in a number of decisions of the High Court Division and also Appellate Division of our Supreme Court that where any or more of the legal requirements as embodied in the Constitution and also in section 80f the Special Powers Act is violated, the detention must be rendered illegal and invalid. In the instant case the grounds under which order of detention was made appears to have never been served on the detenu and the detenu has never been informed of his right of making representation against the order of detention as required under Section 8 of the Act and for that matter the detention must be held to have become illegal for non- compliance of the mandatory provision of Section 8 of the Act. The above view of ours is in line with the decisions taken in the case of Anwar Hossain V s. Government of Bangladesh, reported in 30 D.L.R. 423, and in the case of Sultan Ara Begum Vs. Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs and others, reported in 38 D.L.R. 1986 page 93. 

8. In the case reported in, 30 D.L.R. 423, ithas been observed "Non-service of the grounds of detention as required under Section 8 has been considered as fatal in the proceeding for detention itself, because it deprives the detenu from making necessary representation to the Advisory Board. Mere placing the case before the Advisory Board docs not remove the said defect. Due to non-service of grounds the detention order made under section 3(1) of the Special Powers Act has become illegal." 

9. In the case reported in 38 D.L.R. 93 (RL. it has been laid down by their Lordships. "Mere incorporation of one of the broad definitions of the expression "prejudicial act" as given in section 2 (f) of the said Act in the order of detention without communicating to the per- son affected the details and particulars of the fact and the materials regarding the prejudicial Act does not and cannot mean the communication of the grounds within the meaning of Section 8 of the Act. The word grounds as used in Section 8 means the facts and materials regarding activities of the detenu which satisfied the detaining authority that his detention is necessary in order to prevent him from doing any pre- judicial act and it is imperative that such grounds of detention must be communicated un- der Section 8 to the detenu at the time he is detained or so soon thereafter as is practicable, but not later than fifteen days from the date of detention to enable him to make the necessary representation". 

10. The next point urged by Mr. M. Taleb Ali Miah is that the first order of detention was made on 20th April, 1987 but the grounds of detention were never placed before the Advisory Board in compliance with the provisions of Section IO of the Act though long over 120 days have already elapsed. As the grounds of detention have not been placed before the Advisory Board within 120 days from the date of first order of detention, the detention of the detenu must be held as illegal. In the case before us it appears from the record that neither any Advisory Board was constituted under Section 9 nor the grounds of detention of thedetenu was placed before the Advisory Board and thus the mandatory provision of Section IO has been violated, Reference may be made to the cases, reported in 27 D.L.R. 567, D.L.R. 48 and 40 D.L.R. 21, on the above point. 

11. It is the settled principle of law that requirements of law provided for preventive detention must be strictly followed and scrupulously complied with and failure on the part of the detaining authority to comply with the mandatory requirements of law will render the detention order illegal. 

12.  The next point submitted by the learned Advocate for the petitioner relates to the extension of the order of detention from time to time by the detaining authority always giving retrospective effect after the orders spent its force and validity. From the records it is found that the learned District Magistrate passed the order of detention on 2004.87 and the said order expired on 19.5.87. The Government extended the order of detention for two months on 16.5.87 with effect from 23.5.87 and the validity of the said order expired on 23.7.87. The order of detention of the detenu was extended only on 3.8.87 with retrospective effect from 24.7.87. Thus there appears to be a gap of 10 days and during that period the detenu was held without any valid order of detention. In this way the Government extended the order of detention making orders at a time when the previous orders were found to have expired giving retrospective effect which is not permissible in law. The order of extension of detention order made after the expiry of its validity also becomes illegal and therefore the order of detention purported to have been made in extension of invalid detention order cannot be sustained. In this respect reference may be made to the case of Government of East Pakistan Vs. Roushan Bijaya Shaukat Ali Khan, reported in 18 D.L.R. (SC) 1966 page 214 wherein it has been held "on the face of it the order of detention purports merely to extend the previous detention which has been found to be illegal and consequently the subsequent order of detention must be held to be vitiated." The same view has been taken later on in the case of Abdul Latif Mirza, reported in 31 D.L.R. (AD) 1 and also in the case of Iftekhar Ahmed V s. Government of. Bangladesh, reported in B.L.D. (1988) 157.= 40 DLR 18 

13. The last point submitted by the learned Advocate for the petitioner was that the order of detention passed by the Government on 12.1.88 though expired on 24.3.88 there was no further extension of the order of detention for a long period for which the detenu has been kept in detention illegally without any order of detention. Even after the expiry of the said order of detention on 24.3.88 the detenu was not released but on the contrary the detenu was served with another order of detention made by the Government on 4.8.88 vide Memo No. 7581 H.M. (Security-f) dated 30.7.88 vide Annexure J with a direction to keep the detenu under detention for three months from date of his arrest. It is pointed out by the learned Advocate for the petitioner that the order not only suffers from vagueness and infirmities but it speaks about the absence of application of mind and also the extreme carelessness and callousness of the detaining authority. It is not understood how the order of detention could be made on 30.7.88 for a period of 3(three) months from the date of his arrest without even knowing the date of arrest. It is apparent from the records that the detenu was arrested long before on 24.10.87 and was kept under detention by the orders passed by the Government from time to time. As the detenu has been kept in detention with- out any valid order whatsoever the detention has be- come illegal detention on the expiry of the period, therefore, the illegal detention order cannot be sustained in law. The learned Assistant Attorney- General has found himself helpless in explaining away the inherent anomalies and the apparent infirmities in the order of detention. The respondents though called upon, could not place any material for the satisfaction of the Court. 

14. Having considered the facts and circumstance of the case, the relevant provisions of the Constitution and the Special Powers Act, we hold that the detenu is being held in custody illegally and' in an unlawful manner and as such the order of detention is liable to be declared as illegal and invalid. 

15. In the result, the application succeeds. The Rule is made absolute and it is directed that the detenu Md. Ofazuddin Dewan, son .of Late SamiruddinDewan of Goshala Bazar (Tumal Quarter), P.S. and District Lalmonirhat be set at liberty from Jail custody forthwith, if not wanted in connection with any other case. 

End.

lawyer:
Alimuzzaman Chowdhury with Md. Khurshid Alam Khan, Advocates—For the Petitioner
Md. Awlad Ali, Advocate—For the Opposite Party Nos. 1, 2 and 4-6.
parties:
Nazibunnessa ----- Petitioner
Vs.
Md. Abdus Sobhan Mia and others  ----- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
Mainur Reza Chowdhury J: This Rule was issued calling upon the opposite parties to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and decree dated 30.8.89 and 6.9.89 respectively passed by the Subordinate Judge, Kushtia in Title Appeal No. 198 of 1987 should not be set aside.

2. The facts for the disposal of the Rule are as follows:

The petitioner Most. Nazibunnessa as plaintiff filed Title Suit No. 60 of 1985 in the Additional Court of Assistant Judge, Kushita for declaration that the properties mentional in the schedule "Ka" Kha" "Ga" and "Gha" of the plaint of the suit were not abandoned properties and for a declaration that the lease by defendants Nos. 1 and 2 (Proforma opposite parties No. 7 and 8) in favour of the defendants (opposite parties No. 1-6 and proforma opposite party No. 10) are illegal, ultra vires, void and without jurisdiction.

3. The case of the plaintiff-petitioner was that '08.25 acres of land along with a house thereon appertaining to SA Khatian No. 948/1 of Mouza No. 34 Bahadur Khali District Kushtia as mentioned in schedule 'Ka' belonged to one Zamil Ahmed Ansari, 02.50 acres of land with a building thereon appertaining to SA Khatian No. 936 of the same mouza and district as mentioned in the schedule "Kha" of the plaint belonged to Abdul Latif Ansari and Md. Nazib Ansari equally, 02.97 acres of land along with building thereon appertaining to SA Khatian No. 854 of the same mouza and District as mentioned in schedule 'Ca' of the plaint belonged to Amir Hossain and the houses No. B 101 and B102 in the Kushtia Housing Estate as mentioned in the schedule 'Gha' of the plaint belonged to Najib Ansari and his wife Habiban Nessa. The aforesaid persons were non-Bengali muslims. Amir Hossain Ansari died earlier and was survived by two sons Abdul Latif Ansari and Najib Ansari. Both Abkul Latif Ansari and his son Jamil Ahmed Ansari were killed during the war of liberation on 11.12.1971. The only legal heir of Amir Ansari was then Najib Ansari. Najib Ansari also was killed along with his wife susequently during the said war on 18.12.1971 leaving behind his only daughter the plaintiff since their another daughter Rokeya Banu died earlier during her infancy. On their death, the plaintiff petitioner became the only legal heir of the persons mentioned above and became the absolute owner of the properties mentioned in the schedule 'Ka' to Gha' of the plaint of the suit. The plaintiff was a Bangladeshi citizen and had married a local Bengali. It is stated that the plaintiff who used to live in her father-in-law's house at Jessore came to know about the property being treated as abandoned properties for the first time in 1981 and hence filed the suit for declaration as stated above.

4. The defendant Nos. 1 and 2 (opposite parties No. 7 and 8) contested the suit by filing a written statement stating, inter alia, that Abdul Latif Ansari, Najib Hossain Ansari, Zamil Ahmed Ansari and Amir Hossain Ansari having died during the liberation war and all their properties have been vested in the Government of Bangladesh and the said properties was leased out to the defendant Nos. 4-9 (opposite parties No. 1-6) who are in possession of the scheduled properties. It was further alleged that the plaintiff was not the legal heir of the said persons and was falsely impersonating as daughter of Najib Ansari.

5. The defendant Nos.4 to 9 (opposite parties No. 1-6) filed a separate written statement contending, infer alia that the suit was not maintainable in the present form and was barred by limitation. It was further contended that the property mentioned in the schedule of the plaint belonged to Amir Hossain Ansari who was survived by his only heir Abdul Latif Ansari. Latif Ansari left this country during the liberation war and went to Pakistan where he is survived by his son Jamil Ansari. Jamil Ansari wrote a letter on 15.5.1983 to East Bengali Cloth Store, 10, NS Road, Kushtia and as such the plaintiff was not the legal heir of the deceased persons and had no claim to the scheduled properties. The plaintiff was a fictitious person claiming to be the daughter of Najib Ansari. It was further stated that the defendants were lessees of Latif Ansari and then took lease of the same from the Government as abandoned properties.

6. The learned Assistant Judge after considering the facts and circumstance of the case and evidence on record decreed the suit on contest against defendants Nos. 1 to 10 and declared the right, title and interest of the plaintiff-petitioner in the suit land and for recovery of khas possession by the plaintiff from the defendants within 30 days from the date of the decree amicably, in default the plaintiff would be entitled to take possession of the suit land through Court and further directed the plaintiff to deposit ad valorem court fee of the suit value within 15 days from the date of the judgment. This ad valorem court fee was paid within time as directed by the trial Court. Being aggrieved by the said judgment and decree, the defendant Nos. 4 to 9 i.e. opposite parties No. 1 to 6 preferred an appeal before the District Judge, Kushtia being Title Appeal No. 198 of 1987. Thereafter the defendants 1 and 2 preferred cross-objection. The learned Subordinate Judge, Kushtia by the impugned Judgment and decree dated 30.8.89 and 6.9.89 allowed the appeal and reversed the judgment and decree passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Kushtia in Title Suit No. 60 of 1985, against which the plaintiff-petitioner has obtained the present Rule.

7. It appears that the trial Court on evidence on record was satisfied that some of the previous owners of the suit land were killed during the liberation war and others died earlier, and that the plaintiff petitioner was the daughter of Najib Ansari married to a local Bengali living in Bangladesh and was the sole heir to the scheduled properties in the plaint. Since the prayer was for a simple declaration that the suit lands were not abandoned properties and that the leasing of the said properties by the Government were illegal it was liable to be hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act as no consequential relief was prayed for. The trial Court, therefore directed the plaintiff to pay ad valorem court fee for consequential relief and declared the plaintiff to be the owner of the properties and directed defendant Nos. 1 and 2 to deliver possession of the suit land to the plaintiff-petitioner.

8. The appellate Court allowed the appeal on coming to the following findings amongst others:

That the plaintiff herself had admitted that the property was abandoned; that the suit property being admittedly in the possession of the lessees i.e. defendant Nos. 4 to 9, a suit for a simple declaration that the properties were not abandoned without any prayer for ejectment or any khas possession of the suit properties was not maintainable. It was further found that the plaintiff not having made any prayer for a declaration as to her title and for possession the suit was not maintainable. There being no prayer for consequential relief for restoration of the possession, it was hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. Further, the appellate Court found that the suit was barred by limitation in that the plaintiff did not file any suit within 12 years from the death of her predecessors and during which time the defendants had remained in adverse possession of the suit properties. The appellate Court further found that the plaintiff had failed to prove that she was the daughter of Najib Ansari or that she was married to a local Bengali. The papers submitted by the plaintiff were all dated after 1971.

9. Mr. Md. Awlad Ali, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite parities 1, 2 and 4 to 6, has reiterated the findings of the appellate Court and has further argued that the trial Court in passing the judgment and decree was without jurisdiction in that the buildings having been published in the Gazette as abandoned buildings it was for the Court of Settlement to decide whether the buildings were rightly included as abandoned properties or not. He further argued that no relief could be granted by the trial Court unless such relief was specifically prayed for and for this he relied on Order 7 rule 7 of the Code of Civil Procedure. There being no prayer for declaration of title and prayer for khas possession, the trial Court could not have given this relief for declaration of khas possession. He further argued that the defendants admittedly being tenants the plaintiff was required to file a separate suit for ejectment in accordance with law.

10. Mr. Alimuzzaman Chowdhury, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff petitioner, submits that the appellate Court committed an error of law on the following grounds, amongst others:

On the wrong assumption that by amending the plaint the plaintiff-petitioner accepted the proposition that the suit property was abandoned property. It is submitted that by amending the plaint, the plaintiff petitioner claimed the property to be her own property. In holding that the suit of the plaintiff was barred under the proviso to section 42 of the Specific Relief Act inasmuch as the plaintiff upon direction by the learned trial Court had paid the ad valorem court-fee upon the suit value of the plaint for her declaration of title and recovery of possession and that the appellate Court misapplied the decision in the case reported in 40 DLR 406 and committed serious illegalities in not applying the decision reported in 39 DLR (AD) 55 which was cited before him. The appellate Court under misconception of law held that the suit was barred under Article 142 of the Limitation Act as it was not the case of the defendants that they were in adverse possession for 12 years because their case was that they are tenants of the predecessors of the plaintiff and subsequently tenants of the defendants 1 and 2 after the property was declared as abandoned. The appellate Court did not discuss or consider the evidence on record that the predecessors in interest were killed during the liberation war and that the plaintiff was the only legal heir to have interest in the suit property. The appellate Court without considering the exhibits 3, exhibits 24, and 12 series and other exhibits illegally and accepted the production of the plaintiff's birth certificate and marriage certificate (kabinnama) of her marriage with Kamrul Huq although they were not relevant for the purpose of deciding the suit. The appellate Court illegally taking into evidence a photo copy of the letter from one Jamil Ahmed Ansari which was not formally admitted and which was contrary to written statement filed by defendant Nos. 1 and 2. The appellate Court failed to consider exhibits 2, 12 series 23, 24 and 27 and Succession Certificate granted by the District Judge, Kushtia in Misc. Case No. 59 of 1981 whereupon the District Judge recognized the plaintiff as the successor to Najib Ansari and others and therefore it was not incumbent on the plaintiff to seek such declaration from the trial Court. The appellate Court did not consider that although the plaintiff-petitioner had deposited ad valorem court fee of Taka 1,195.00 on the plaint, the defendant appellants 6 to 10 (opposite parties Nos. 1 to 6) had deposited a fixed court fee of Taka 25.00 only for declaration while filing appeal against the said decree and, as such, the appeal was not maintainable as per law.

<u>11. It appears that the suit was filed on 3.3.85 with a prayer for declaration that the suit properties were illegally included as abandoned properties. Subsequently, the plaint was amended and a decree was sought for a declaration that the suit properties were not abandoned properties and that the grant of lease of the said properties were illegal, ultra vires, void and illegal properties. The appellate Court found that by this amendment, the plaintiff-petitioner had admitted the possession of the defendants and that the suit properties were abandoned properties. This is not correct. Where relief has been prayed for a declaration that the schedule properties are not abandoned properties it cannot be said that such an amendment speaks of admission of the properties being abandoned. The appellate Court held that as the plaintiff did not pray for declaration of title or for possession on the suit properties the suit was not maintainable in the present form which was for a simple declaration that the properties were not abandoned with no consequential relief stated in the plaint. The appellate Court relied on the decision reported in 40 DLR 406 in which it was held that it is the discretion of the court to make a declaration of any status or right uopn a suit being instituted by a person who is entitled to such status or right. But the section at the same time provides a positive bar that no court shall make such declaration where the plaintiff being able to seek further relief than mere declaration of title omits to do so. In this connection Mr. Awlad Ali has cited the case of Haji Yar Ali Khan Chowdhury vs. Mobarak Ali Chowdhury and others reported in 7 DLR 6 in which it was held that in cases where the plaintiff is in possession of the suit property and somebody else from outside tries to interfere with possession, injunction may be a suitable remedy. But where the defendant is in possession, it is wrong to grant a decree for injunction as injunction is a remedy which cannot be utilised for ousting a person from possession who having initially entered into possession in right manner fails to give up possession after the lapse of his right. Where the plaintiff whose right is denied by the defendant is out of possession and the defendant is in possession "further relief" in section 42 of the Specific Relief Act would be recovery of possession and a suit for mere declaration of title without prayer for possession is barred under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. This was supported by the case of Syed Ahmed vs. Prafulla Kumar Dey and others reported in 13 DLR 70. In that case the prayer in the plaint was for declaration that the rent execution proceedings were illegal and ineffective on the ground of fraud. The plaintiff did not ask for recovery of possession of the land. It was not the case of the plaintiff that they were in possession of the suit lands, on the other hand, it was not denied by them that the possession was taken by the auction-purchaser. It was held that in those circumstances the plaintiff's suit must fail under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act inasmuch as being out of possession he had not asked for recovery of possession as a consequential relief. In this connection the case reported in AIR 1952 (AII) 465 was also referred to. As against these decisions Mr. Alimuzzaman Chowdhury has referred to the case of Santosh Kumar Mara and others vs. Hrishikesh Mondal minor and others reported in 13 DLR 278. In that case the plaintiff prayed in his plaint for setting aside the decree on the ground of fraud but did not ask for relief by way of setting aside the sale. It was contended that the plaintiff having failed to ask for relief by way of setting aside the sale it should be presumed to have omitted the same relief and, as such, they were precluded from asking for it again and therefore, the lower appellate Court erred in not only setting aside the decree but also in setting aside the sale. It was held that in view of the provisions of Order 7, rule 7 of the Code of Civil Procedure it lies within the competence of the court to grant an effective relief which may not be inconsistent with the main case as made out in the plaint. Although the relief for setting aside the sale was not formulated in precise terms in the prayer portion of the plaint yet there was nothing irregular for the appellate Court in setting aside the sale as well, in view of the fact that the decree which was foundation of the sale was found to have been vitiated by fraud. This case referred to by Mr. Alimuzzaman Chowdury does not fit into the facts and circumstances of the present case in which consequential relief had to be made out under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and proper court-fee had to be paid for such relief.</u>

<u>12. The question, therefore, before me is where the court itself finds the necessity for making certain prayers and seeking specific relief and orders the plaintiff to pay the necessary ad valorem court fee and the plaintiff having complied with the said order, whether it is still necessary to amend the plaint and seek specific relief. Mr. Awlad Ali, the learned Advocate, has argued that no relief can be granted for which no prayer has been made and the provision in rule 7, Order 7 of the Code of Civil Procedure is quite clear on this point. In the instant case the plaint having not been amended for specific reliefs, the court could not have granted those reliefs without such amendment. The case of Sufia Khanam vs. Faizun Nessa reported in 39 DLR (AD) 46 was referred to. It appears that in case there is an obiter that in a suit under section 42, where consequential relief is found necessary but has not been prayed for the court may either dismiss the suit or direct the plaintiff to pay additional court fee for the purpose. In the case of Kayemat Ali Sakdar and ors vs. jainuddin Talukder reported in 14 DLR 657, it was held that relief to the plaintiff can be given even though it was not specifically asked for in the plaint even without amending the plaint. In that case the plaintiff's case as made out in the plaint was that he was holding the disputed lands under defendant No. 4 (landlord) as a raiyat. The courts below found that in fact the plaintiff was holding some of these lands as under raiyat under defendant No. 4 and in that view of the matter dismissed the suit. It was contended on behalf of the plaintiff-appellant that the courts below acted wrongly in dismissing the plaintiff's suit inasmuch as it having been found that, in respect of some of the suit lands, he was under raiyat under defendant Nos. 1 and 2, it was open to the courts below to give a relief to that extent and not to dismiss the suit altogether. On behalf of the defendants 1 and 2, it was urged that the plaintiff was not entitled to such a relief with the pleading remaining as it was. It was held that there was no doubt that the plaintiff in his plaint might ask for an alternative relief, that is, he might have asked that he might be given a declaration of his under-raiyati right in the disputed lands under the defendants 1 and 2. But this omission could hardly be a sufficient justification for driving the parties to a separate suit for determination of the question determined in the present suit.</u>

<u>13. In the instant case the plaintiff had sought for a declaration that the suit properties were not abandoned and the leasing of such properties by defendants 1 and 2 were illegal. The trial Court has found that the plaintiff ought to have asked for a declaration of her own title and for khas possession of the suit properties and therefore, instead of dismissing the suit directed the plaintiff to pay ad valorem court fee, for this relief, which the plaintiff paid. Keeping the above decision and the obiter expressed in 39 DLR (AD) 46 in my mind it is my opinion that the trial Court having directed the plaintiff to pay ad valorem court-fee, which she paid in compliance of the order, the trial Court was under no bar to give relief for which plaintiff had paid with amending the plaint. In that view of the matter, the contention that the suit was hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and requirement under Order 7, rule 7 of the Code of Civil Procedure being not met are not correct.</u>

<u>14. Mr. Awlad Ali has pointed out that the suit was filed prior to Abandoned Buildings (Supplementary Provisions) Ordinance, 1985 (Ordinance LIV of 1985). During the pendency of the suit this Ordinance was promulgated under which the suit properties were by Gazette Notification enlisted as abandoned buildings. This Ordinance was effective from September, 1985. By the said Ordinance any person claiming interest in any building enlisted as abandoned building might apply to the Court of Settlement within 180 days under the said Ordinance claiming interest in the building and for exclusion of the buildings from enlistment and for release in his favour or for any other relief on the ground that the building is not abandoned property and has not vested in the Government under the President's Order No. 16 of 1972. It has been argued by the learned Advocate for the opposite parties that a special forum having been created by the Ordinance, the present suit was not maintainable in the civil Court. In this connection he has referred to the decision in the case of Madbar Khan and others vs. Province of East Pakistan and others reported in 17 DLR 263 where the High Court held that when the law provides a special forum for adjudicating disputes with regard to any matter under the said law, and if it is the intention of the Legislature that no other forums shall entertain any such dispute, the forum provided by law, and no 'other forum, can have jurisdiction over the dispute. In support of this general principle, he has also referred to the decision in the case of Begum Lutfunnessa vs. Government of Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Works, Dhaka and others reported in 41 DLR 193 where the Writ Bench of the High Court has, inter alia, held that the Court of Settlement has been given the specific power to exclude the disputed property from the list of abandoned buildings. The petitioner has been given a specific right to argue before the Court of Settlement that the building is not an abandoned property, that it was not vested in the Government or that right or interest in the building has not been affected by the provisions of President's Order No. 16 of 1972. When the statute has devised an alternative forum for giving complete relief to the petitioner, the petitioner could not invoke the writ jurisdiction at the first stage without exhausting the remedy provided for in the Ordinance. On appeal, the Appellate Division in its decision reported in 42 DLR (AD) 86 observed that the High Court on examination of the different provisions of the Ordinance including section 7 came to the finding that the section can give the appellant exactly the same remedy which she was praying for in the writ petition, that the Court of Settlement has been given the specific power to exclude the disputed property from the impugned list when the statute devised an alternative forum for giving complete relief to the appellant, she could not invoke the writ jurisdiction without exhausting the remedy provided for in the Ordinance. This view taken by the High Court Division was found to be well in accord with the settled principle governing exercise on discretionary jurisdiction under Article 102 of the Constitution when the law itself provides for a remedy which is to be sought for in the writ petition. The Appellate Division therefore had no reason to interfere with impugned Judgment on the ground that any principle had been laid down which could not be justified. However, the Appellate Division held that it was their opinion that the High Court Division itself interfere, notwithstanding correctly observing that there was an alternative remedy under section 7 of the Ordinance in view of the particular facts of the case. It would thus appear that the jurisdiction was not completely ousted by section 7 of the Ordinance. Further it was observed in that case that the Notification was published on 28.4.86, the Court of Settlement was constituted on 21.10.86 and the appellant filed the writ petition on 19.8.86 apparently at a time when the Court of Settlement was yet to be constituted. To the point taken by the petitioner that the enlistment of the properties under the Ordinance was illegal in that proviso (b) to section 5 of the Ordinance provides that no list published under Ordinance shall include any building in respect of which a suit, appeal, application or other legal proceeding is pending before any Court and immediately before the date of publication of the list in the official Gazette, in which the vesting in, or possession of the government of any building as abandoned property under President's Order has been called in question in any manner whatsoever or any prayer has been made for return or transfer of the building by the Government or by any officer or authority subordinate to it to any person, the learned Advocate for the opposite parties has again relied on Begum Lutfunnessa's case reported in 41 DLR 193. In that case the High Court found that Gazette Notification was first published on 28.4.86 which notice was substituted by publication of another Gazette Notification on 23.9.86. It was therefore, held by the court that the Bangladesh Gazette (Extra Ordinary) on 28.4.86 had been repealed by the subsequent Gazette Notification dated 23.9.86 and that it was not merely a repeal but also a simultaneous re-enactment. That being so, section 6 of General Clauses Act had full application to the facts and circumstances of the case Section 6(a) provides that the repeal shall not receive anything not in force or existing at the time at which the repeal takes effect. It meant that there was no legal proceeding in the High Court regarding the disputed property because the petition which was filed on 19.8.86 against the notification dated 28.4.86 itself was not pending at all and therefore the protection of proviso (b) of section 5 of the Ordinance was not available to the petitioner. In the present case the facts are different in that the suit was pending at the time when the Ordinance LIV of 1985 was promulgated with a prayer to declare that the suit buildings were not abandoned properties. Therefore the decision of Lutfunnessa's case was as just applicable. In that view of the matter I am of the opinion that it is not correct that the suit was not maintainable after the promulgation of Ordinance LIV of 1985. Further in the case of Zaher (Md) vs. Bangladesh and others reported in 42 DLR 430 in which decision I was a party it was held that the suit building was included in the list published in the official Gazette in contravention of section 5(1)(a)(b) of the Ordinance and, as such, the civil Court had jurisdiction to try the suit. The Court clearly fell into error in holding that because of inclusion of the building in the official Gazelle the suit was not maintainable. The plaintiff being entitled to a decree that the suit property was not an abandoned property and the Government having disclaimed the same as requisitioned property, the latter is liable to restore its possession to the plaintiff and also to pay rent/compensation under the Requisition of Property Act for its use and occupation from 14.2.72 till the possession of the property is restored to the plaintiff. I therefore hold that the instant suit was maintainable in the civil Court. It may be mentioned that the question of maintainability was not raised before the trial Court or the appellate Court.</u>

15. Md. Awlad Ali, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite parties, has submitted that the defendant Nos 4 to 10 i.e opposite parties 1 to 6, were tenants of predecessor in interest and subsequently of defendant Nos. 1 and 2. That being the position, the plaintiff was required to file a suit for ejectment in accordance with law, and that present suit being a suit for declaration that the properties were not abandoned, the trial Court could not have passed any order to deliver possession of the suit to the plaintiff. In this connection he has referred to the case of Zahirul Huq vs. Ejamul Huq and others reported in 34 DLR (AD) 25 where the Appellate Division, inter alia, held that release of a property from the category of abandoned property cannot affect the tenancy right of an occupant of a tenant created before the President's Order No. 16 of 1972 came into existence by an order of release which is an executive act. It is therefore, clear that if the property in question is found not to be an abandoned property and is released by an executive order, a lessee or tenant of such property does not ipso facto become unauthorized occupant entitling the Abandoned Property authority to take over possession by ejecting him. If he is in possession under a valid lease or under a valid tenancy relationship, that could only be terminated either under Article 10(1) of the Order, if it applied or by due process of law and then possession may be taken by the law available for the purpose. However the present case is not a case of release of a property from the list of abandoned properties by an executive order. It was order of a Court. I have already held that in addition to the declaration that the buildings were not abandoned properties the trial Court by requiring the plaintiff to pay ad valorem court-fee for consequential relief had rightly passed the release order in favour of the plaintiff. Therefore the decision in Zahirul Huq's case by the Appellate Division with regard to release order by an executing authority, in my opinion, does not apply in the present case.

<u>16. On the question of limitation that this was not pressed by the opposite parties. However it appears that it was not the case of opposite parties that they had been in adverse possession of the suit property. Their case was that they were tenants of predecessor-in-interest and subsequently under lease from the defendant Nos. 1 and 2. That being the position of the opposite parties the question of limitation under Article 142 of the Limitation Act is not applicable.</u>

17. Although Mr Awlad Ali did not go into the findings of the courts below on question of facts it is admitted that the predecessors-in-interest died during the liberation war and some of them died earlier. There is no admitted evidence that there was any other heir of the predecessor-in-interest although a photo copy of a letter had been produced before the court that one Jamil Ahmed Ansari had written a letter from Pakistan who was alleged to be son of Abdul Latif Ansari, but it appears that this photo copy of the letter was not proved before the trial Court and not considered as evidence. Therefore the appellate Court's conclusions that Jamil and Latif Ansari were alive and were living in Karachi were not based on evidence. The appellate Court held that the plaintiff had failed to prove her actual identity as daughter of Najib Ansari on the ground that it was unlikely that she would have remained silent for so many years living in Jessore when her property were treated as abandoned from 1972 and that she only came to know about such treatment only in 1981. It was held by the appellate Court that plaintiff did not examine her alleged husband nor produce any birth certificate or marriage certificate (kabinnama) to prove that she was in fact who she claimed to be that is, she is the only child of Najib Ansari and the only heir of the predecessor-in-interest. But it appears that the trial Court had relied not only on evidence of PWs 2 and 3 to believe that she was wedded to her husband and that she was the only heir to the predecessor-in-interest, but also relied on the Succession Certificate granted by the District Judge in Misc. Case No 59 of 1981 whereby the Court recognised the plaintiff as the only successor to certain sums of money left by the predecessor-in-interest. The appellate Court has not discussed this important evidence produced by the plaintiff to prove her identity and that she was the only heir of the predecessor-in-interest. The appellate Court thereby committed an error in law in not considering the evidence to prove her identity and status.

18. In the light of my discussions and observations, the impugned judgment and decree has to be interfered with.

19. The Rule is therefore made absolute. The Judgment and decree of the appellate Court is hereby set aside and the Judgment and decree of the trial Court is restored.

20. There will be no order as to costs. Send down the LC records at once.

End.
