full_judgment:
AK Badrul Huq J: By these two Rules arising out of Writ Petition Nos. 177 of 1991 and 3424 of 1991 under Article 102 of Constitution, the Notices dated 17-9-88 under section 6 of the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982 issued by the respondent No. 2, the Deputy Commissioner, Chittagong in Land Acquisition Case No. 22 of 1985-86 had been challenged whereupon Rule Nisi had been issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the Notices dated 17-9-88 issued by the respondent No. 2 purported to be under section 6 of the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982 in LA Case No. 22 of 1985-86 and all other proceedings of the said LA Case regarding the property of the petitioners should not be declared to have been issued without any lawful authority and to be of no legal effect and why the same should not be cancelled and the proceedings of LA Case No. 22 of 1985-86 should not be set aside.

2. Common questions of fact and law having been involved in both the Rules, the same are heard consecutively and are being disposed of by this judgment.

3. Mrinalendu Pal is the petitioner in Writ Petition No. 177 of 1991. Sreemati Bhagabati Paul and Sreemati Bharati Paul are petitioners in Writ Petition No. 3424 of 1991. The common case of the petitioners of the writ petitions is set out below: The predecessor in-interest of the petitioner of the respective Rules NN Pal, a leading contractor of British India was the owner of the PS Plot Nos. 226, 210 and 223 recorded in PS Khatian No. 190, 191 and 193 under Ander killa Mouza, Police Station Kotwail, District-Chittagong. The said NN Pal constructed a pucca two storied building and installed family deity ''Radha Madhab'' in the building and Sevapuja of the deity are offered daily. The petitioners are residing in the first floor of the building and the grand floor was let out during Pakistan period to Hillside Kindergarten School now Paharika Girls High School, respondent No. 4, for affording opportunity to educate the children of the locality and some portion of the property has been let out to monthly tenants for defraying their cost of living specially the petitioners Bhagabati Pal and Bharati Pal. In LA Case No. 22 of 1985, notices under section 3 of the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance of 1982 hereinafter referred to as the Ordinance had been issued stating that the property described in the schedule was needed for Paharika Girls High School in the public interest and proposal had been made for the acquisition of the said property. The schedule property of the said notices is PS Plot Nos. 226 (full), 217 (part), 220 (part) and 223 (part) of PS Khatian Nos. 190, 191 and 193 Mouza-Anderkilla, Police Station Kotwali, District-Chittagong. The petitioners filed objection taking the grounds that in the first floor of the building their family deity has been installed and daily Sevapuja are offered there and there is no scope to shift the deity to any other place. The building is their last shelter. The property under the acquisition proceeding are not at all required for Paharika Girl''s School and the Managing Committee of the said School with a malafide motive persuaded the respondent Nos. 1-3 to initiate the acquisition proceeding. Several representations had been made to the respondants praying for dropping the acquisition proceedings but no result came. Thereafter, the impugned notices dated 17-8-88 under section 6 of the Ordinance had been issued upon the petitioners and these notices have been challenged in the writ petitions.

4. The petitioner Mrinalendu Pal in Writ Petition No. 177 of 1991 by way of a Supplementary Affidavit took further grounds that the petitioner as plaintiff instituted Partition Suit No. 35 of 1954, No. 54 of 1956, No. 129 of 1984 in the First Court of Subordinate Judge, Chittagong for partition of his share against his co-sharers. The suit was decreed in preliminary form on 27-3-1957. During the pendency of the suit, the Government of Bangladesh through the Assistant Custodian, Vested Property, treated the undivided share of the property in joint possession of the plaintiff and other co-sharers as vested property and the vested property authority threatened to lease out the undivided portion of the property involved in the writ petition. The prayer for temporary injunction sought against the Government and the vested property authority having been refused by the learned Subordinate Judge, FMA 6 of 1986 had been preferred by the plaintiff before the High Court Division, Chittagong and in the Civil Rule No. 117 (FM) of 1986 arising therefrom, an order of ad interim injunction had been granted restraining the Government from leasing out the part of the disputed land to anybody till the disposal of appeal. It is further stated that the Head Mistress of the School has been adopting all measures sometimes instigating the Government to treat and take over the property as vested property and on the other hand persuading the Government Officials to acquire the same. The power that has been exercised is a colourable exercise of power vested with the Government under the Ordinance.

5. The respondent Nos. 1-3 are the Acquisitioning body and respondent No. 4 is the requiring body. The respondents entered appearances in both the Rules and contested the Rules by filing Affidavits-in- opposition. The averments made in the two Affidavit-in-opposition are common. In the Affidavits-in-opposition it is stated that the writ petitions are not maintainable in view of the fact that the properties claimed by the petitioners have been declared as vested property with the extinguishments of the right, title and interest of the petitioners and the final decision with respect to the acquisition of the property under section 5 of the Ordinance have been made after due compliance of the requirements of law embodied in sections 3, 4 and 5 of the Ordinance and the validity of the actions taken under said sections have not been challenged before any court of law. The petitioner of writ petition No. 177 of 1991 is not a citizen of Bangladesh, rather he is an Indian citizen and thus got no locus standi to file and maintain the writ petition. There is no deity in the building and there is no Shebait for the deity and daily Shevapuja are not offered. The Paharika Girl''s High School has been running from Pakistan period and in view of the increasing number of students more accommodation for school was needed and proposal for the acquisition of land in question had been made to the respondent Nos. 1-3. The acquisition is for public purpose and public interest. The acquisition proceeding is never malafide nor colourable exercise of power nor arbitrary. It is further stated that in PS Khatian No. 190 and 191 there is a total area of 1100 acres with houses thereon. There are other seven plots beyond the four plots under the acquisition proceeding and there are .9814 acres of land in 11 plots and out of which .4000 acres of land are under the acquisition proceeding and the petitioners can be easily accommodated in the rest land of the said Khatians.

6. The petitioners filed Affidavit-in-reply denying all the averments made in the Affidavit-in-opposition and reiterating all the averments made in the petitions.

7. The petitioner of Writ Petition No. 177 of 1991 is represented by learned Advocate Mr SC Das. The petitioner of Writ Petition No. 3424 of 1991 is represented by learned Advocate Mr AF Hasan Ariff. The respondent Nos. 1-3 of both the writ petitions are represented by learned Deputy Attorney-General, Mr KM Saifuddin Ahmed. The respondent No. 4 is represented by the learned Advocate Mr Khondker Mahbuddin Ahmed. The submissions put forward on behalf of the petitioners of both the petitions are common and the submissions advanced on behalf of the respondent Nos. 1-3 and 4 are also common.

8. Since the locus standia and maintainability of Writ Petition No. 177 of 1991 has been seriously challenged on behalf of the respondents, we propose to dispose of the said question first.

9. It has been vehemently contended from the side of the respondents that the petitioner of Writ Petition No. 177 of 1991, Mrinalendu Pal is not a citizen of Bangladesh, rather he is an Indian citizen and being an Indian citizen he got no locus standi to file and maintain the writ petition before this court. This contention raised has been seriously resisted by the petitioners. It is contended that the petitioner Mrinalendu Pal is a permanent resident of Bangladesh and he is never a citizen of India.

<u>10. From the writ petition it appears that the petitioner Mrinalendu Pal himself had sworn Affidavit before the Commissioner of Affidavits, High Court Division, Chittagong. Annexure-J is the impugned notice under section 6 of the Ordinance issued by the Deputy Commissioner, Chittagong wherein his address was shown as of NandanKanon, Chittagong treating him as a resident of Chittagong Town. Annexures-B, C, D and I are objections and representations made by the petitioners Mrinalendu Pal, Bhagabati Pal and Bharati Pal to the respondent Nos.1-3 putting their signatures on the said objections and representations. Annexure-F is a notice issued by the Land Acquisition Officer, Chittagong, addressed to Mrinalendu Pal and others asking them to appear in an enquiry and in the said notice Mrinalendu Pal was shown to be a resident of 23, NandanKanon, Chittagong. All these letters and notices are positive evidences that Mrinalendu Pal is a citizen of Bangladesh and not a citizen of India. Moreover, the petitioner Mrinalendu Pal on 22-5-1997 himself appeared before us and placed his passport. We checked up his passport and compared his signature appearing in the passport and his signature appearing in the writ petition and on comparison it appears that both the signatures are the product of one hand. The respondents failed to place any materials before us to substantiate their contention that Mrinalendu Pal is not a citizen of Bangladesh and he is an Indian citizen. The respondents treating him a citizen of Bangladesh issued all notices at his residence at Chittagong and now they cannot say that he is not a citizen of Bangladesh. The respondents are debarred completely to deny the citizenship of Mrinalendu Pal. Moreover, the property of a citizen of India cannot be the subject matter of any acquisition proceeding. The allegations levelled against Mrinalendu Pal appear to be wild.</u>

11. From all the materials before us, we are satisfied that the petitioner Mrinalendu Pal is a citizen of Bangladesh and he got the locus standi to file and maintain the writ petition.

12. Let us now come back to consider the arguments advanced from both the sides.

<u>13. The first branch of submission on behalf of the petitioners is that under section 15 of the Ordinance, the mandate of law is that when any property is proposed to be acquired for any person other than the Government such person shall enter into an agreement with the Government in such form as prescribed, before a notice under section 3 is published and the requiring body, the respondent No. 4, having not entered into any agreement with the Government before the notice under section 3 of the Ordinance was published, the acquisition proceeding is absolutely illegal and without jurisdiction. In support of this contention, reliance is placed in a decision in the case of Sankar Gopal vs. Additional Commissioner, Dhaka reported in 41 DLR 326.</u>

<u>14. The petitioners nowhere within the four walls of the writ petitions made the averment that the Requiring body, the respondent No. 4, did not enter into any agreement with the Government nor made any such statement in the objections filed by them under section 3 of the Ordinance nor in any representations made to the Acquisitioning authority, the respondents No. 1-3. In the absence of any such averment made in the writ petitions, the respondents got no opportunity to controvert the said allegations in their Affidavits-in-opposition. The petitioners for the first time placed this question by way of only oral submission before this Court. No materials had been placed before us to substantiate the contention that no agreement had been entered into between the respondent No. 4 and the Government. In the cited case of Sankar Gopal vs. Additional Commissioner, Dhaka reported in 41 DLR 326, the fact that no agreement was entered into by the Requiring body with the Government had been specifically set out in the writ petition. In the said case notices under section 3 of the Ordinance was shown to have been issued on 20-6-83 and the agreement between the Requiring body and the Government had been entered on 24-3-86 in respect of the acquisition of the property. In the cited case, the petitioner placed a copy of the agreement dated 24-3-86 to show that the same was executed after the notice under section 3 had been issued. But in this instant case before us no materials has been placed, that no agreement had been entered between the Requiring body and the Government. The cited decision cannot be of any assistance to the petitioners. The first branch of submission from the side of the petitioners, thus, fails.</u>

<u>15. Next comes the second branch of argument. It is argued on behalf of the petitioners that the Acquisitioning Authority failed to apply its mind and the acquisition proceeding fails for non-application of mind. In advancing this argument it is further argued that the Acquisitioning authority has to say whether the property in question is needed or likely to be needed but it cannot say at the same time that it is both needed or is likely to be needed and thus the Acquisitioning authority failed to apply its mind. In reply to the said argument it is argued from the side of the respondents that the respondent No. 4, Paharika Girls High School has been in the land of the acquisition proceeding for more than two decades and number of students is increasing gradually and for the accommodation of ever increasing students in the old school and in order to allow the school to impart education to the children the land was very much needed and no question arises that the land is likely to be needed and the Acquisition Authority duly applied its mind.</u>

<u>16. It is the admitted position that the school is very much on the land under the acquisition proceeding and the number of students are increasing day by day. For accomodation of ever increasing number of students and to impart them education, more land was required and at the instance of the school authority, the acquisition proceedings was initiated and the acquisition matter reached to its finality under section 5 of the Ordinance keeping in view of the school and thus no question of likely to be needed arises at all. So, it cannot be said that there was non-application of mind in issuing notices under sections 3 and 6 of the Ordinance. The contention of the petitioners on this score also does not merit any consideration.</u>

<u>17. Coming now to the third branch of submission on behalf of the petitioners it is contended that respondent No.4, Paharika Girls High School is a privately operated commercial concern and the acquisition of the property in question has been directed to earn profit for small group of persons and the acquisition cannot be for any public purpose and public interest and the impugned notice is a colourable exercise of power vested in the Government under the Ordinance. In support of this contention reliance has been placed upon two decisions (1) in the case of Abdu Mia vs. Bangladesh reported in 32 DLR 290 and (2) the case of Md Ismail vs. Government of Bangladesh reported in 34 DLR 4. The contention raised was seriously resisted by the respondents. It is contended on behalf of the respondents that the school is rendering service to the community in general and the acquisition of land for the expansion of the class rooms and accommodation of the students is public purpose. It is the further contention that the requirements of law had been complied with and the Government took decision under section 5 of the Ordinance which is conclusive and final.</u>

18. In the wake of rival contentions raised from both the sides, the question now falls for determination is whether the acquisition in question is intended to serve "public purpose" and "public interest". It will be profitable to extract the relevant provisions of law of the Ordinance which are as follows:

"3. Publication of Preliminary Notice of Acquisition of Property: Whenever it appears to the Deputy Commissioner that any property in any locality is needed or is likely to be needed for any public purpose or in the public interest, he shall cause a notice to be published at convenient places on or near the property in the prescribed form and manner stating that the property is proposed to be acquired: Provided that no property used by the public for the purpose of religious worship, graveyard and cremation ground shall be acquired.

4. Objection Against Acquisition :(1) Any person interested in any property which has been notified under section 3 as being needed or likely to be needed for a public purpose or in the public interest may, within fifteen days after the publication of the notice, object to the acquisition of the property.

(2) Every objection under sub-section (1) shall be made to the Deputy Commissioner in writing, and the Deputy Commissioner shall give the objector an opportunity of being heard either in person or by an agent and shall, after hearing all such objections and after making such further inquiry, if any, as he thinks necessary prepare a report containing his opinion on the objections.

(3) The Deputy Commissioner shall then—

(a) If the property exceeds 50 standard bighas of land, submit the record of the proceedings held by him, together with his report, for the decision of the Government and

(b) If the property does not exceed 50 bighas of land, submit the record of the proceedings held by him, together with his report, for the decision of the Commissioner or the Divisional Commissioner:

Provided that if no objection is raised within the period specified in sub-section (1), the Deputy Commissioner shall, instead of submitting the records of the proceedings to the Divisional Commissioner, make a decision about the acquisition of the property and such decision of the Deputy Commissioner shall be final and

(5) Final Decision Regarding Acquisition:

(1) The Government or, as the case may be, the Divisional Commissioner after considering the report submitted by the Deputy Commissioner under section 4(3), shall make a decision about the acquisition of the property and such decision of the Government or, as the case may be, the Divisional Commissioner shall be final.

(2) When the Government, the Divisional Commissioner as the case may be, makes a decision for acquisition of the property under subsection (1) or the proviso to section 4(3)(b) as the case may be, such decision shall be conclusive evidence that the property is needed for a public purpose or in the public interest".

19. The expression "public purpose" has not been defined either in the (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948 or in the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982. Section 3 of the Ordinance enjoins that whenever it appears to the Deputy Commissioner that any property in any locality is needed or likely to be needed for any public interest, he shall cause a notice to be published at convenient places or near the property in the prescribed form and manner stating that the property is proposed to be acquired, provided that no property used by the public for the purpose of religious worship, graveyard and cremation ground shall be acquired.

20. The basic concept underlying the expression "public purpose" is the general interest of the community, the test being whether the purpose is primarily and predominantly for general interest of the community or it is mainly or primarily to serve the interest of a few individuals.

21. "What is public purpose?" This question came up for consideration before the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in the case of Hamabai Framjee Petit vs. Secretary of State for India, AIR 1914 PC 20. The oft quoted observations of Batchelor J. are covered in the following terms: "General definitions are, I think, rather to be avoided where the avoidance is possible and I make no attempt to define precisely the extent of the phrase ''public purposes'' in the lease; it is enough to say that, in my opinion, the phrase, whatever else it may mean must include a purpose, that is, an object or aim, in which the general interest of the community, as opposed to the particular interest of individuals, is directly and vitally concerned".

22. The expression public purpose" was considered by a Division Bench of erstwhile East Pakistan High Court in the case of Abdus Sobhan vs. Province of East Pakistan 14 DLR 486. In that case Murshed J, (his Lordship then was) delivering the judgment held: "The expression "public purpose" must include a purpose, that is, an object or aim in which the general interest of the community as opposed to the particular interest of an individual is concerned".

23. "Public purpose" as defined in Willoughby''s ''Constitution of the United States'', volume 3 at page 1740 as reported in 15 DLR 444 is in the following language:

"A public use is one in which the interest of the public is directly and primarily concerned . It may happen, and, indeed, it very frequently happens, that in the exercise of the State''s powers, whether of eminent domain, taxation or police regulation, particular individuals or classes of individuals are benefited. If, however, the action is to be sustained, its aim must be shown to be not merely that this specific result will be reached as a final end, but that the public has itself an interest in securing this benefit to the individual concerned".

24. In the case of suit, Somawanti vs. State of Punjab AIR 1963 (SC) 151, the Supreme Court of India had occasion to examine somewhat similar matter. The Supreme Court of India held "broadly speaking the expression "public purpose" would however include a purpose in which the general interest of the community as opposed to particular interest of individuals is directly and vitally concerned."

<u>25. A broad test, thus, has been formulated by Judicial decisions, and, it is, that whatever furthers the general interest of the community as opposed to the particular interest of the individuals must be regarded as a "public purpose".</u>

26. In this instant case, the respondent No. 4, Paharika Girls'' High School has been running on the ground floor of the two storied building within the land under the acquisition proceeding. It is the positive case of the respondents that with the passage of time the number of the students increased to a great extent and without the expansion of the area of the school education to the students of the school cannot be imparted and for the accommodation purpose the land in question is needed by the school authority. It is not disputed by the petitioners that the school has not been functioning and the number of students are not increasing. The School is imparting education to the students and rendering services to the community in general. In getting the future generation of the country trained up and in imparting education to maximum number of students and children is the State policy of education. Fulfilment of social and public duty definitely get precedence over the individual need and the individual need requires to be sacrificed to the public need.

27. In the case of Abdu Mia vs. Bangladesh 32 DLR 289, the land in question was acquired for a playground of a non-Government Private school and it was held by the High Court Division that the requisition was not intended for the public purpose and the requisition proceeding was declared to be without any lawful authority. In this instant case the acquisition is not for any playground but for the accommodation of the increasing number of students in the class rooms and the fact of the cited case is quite distinguishable in the facts and circumstances of the present case and got no manner of application. In the case of Md Ismail vs. Government of Bangladesh, 34 DLR 4, the petitioner challenged the requisition notice under section 3 of the (Emergency) Requisition of Immovable Property Act, 1948 for the purpose of acquisition of land for the requiring body, namely, Dhaka Housing Corporation Ltd. and other Housing Co-operative society. The Division Bench of the High Court Division presided over by Mustafa Kamal J, (his Lordship then was) held:

"We do not see why construction of houses as per common plan and campus for those members of society who have no land or house in Dhaka City will not serve a public purpose. The beneficiaries under the scheme will be limited in number but it is not the number of beneficiaries which determines public purpose. It is the good that accrues to the community at large that determines public purpose. If 600 allottees are accommodated in a planned manner with common facilities like school, recreation centre, playground, etc. it adds to the planned development of the city and relieves the problem of housing, however slightly".

This decision is of no assistance to the petitioners rather negatives the contention of the petitioners.

28. The question whether the acquisition of land for a private school serves "public purpose" or not became the subject matter of the Appellate Division in the case of Bangladesh vs. Winifred Rubie reported in 1983 BCR (AD) 7. In that case the Additional Commissioner, Land Acquisition requisitioned the premises at 85, Kakrail Road, Dhaka for the accommodation of Little Flower School under the (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948. Legality of the order of requisition was challenged before the High Court Division by the owners of the land in an application under Article 102 of the Constitution. Rule was made absolute with the decision that requisition for a private school run for the benefit of a few is not for public purpose. The Appellate Division set aside the judgment of the High Court Division and held that the requisition for Little Flower School is for public purpose. The Appellate Division in construing the expression "public purpose" discussed and considered the case of HF Petit vs. Secretary of State AIR 1914 PC 20 and Abdus Sobhan vs. Province of East Pakistan 14 DLR 486.

29. It appears from the materials on record that notice under section 3 of the Ordinance (Annexure-A) had been served upon the petitioners. Objection under section 4 (Annexure-B) had been filed by the petitioners to the Land Acquisition Officer. Another objection in the form of prayer for releasing the property from the acquisition proceeding had been filed to the Divisional Commissioner (Annexure-D.) The acquisition proposal has been approved by the Divisional Commissioner on 14-9-88. The order of approval has been given in para-17 of the Affidavit-in-opposition of the respondents No. 1-3. Extract of the order of approval is given below:

“গণপ্রজাতন্ত্রী বাংলাদেশ সরকার

বিভাগীয় কমিশনারের কার্য্যালয়, চট্টগ্রাম।

স্বারক নং-৯৫১৭

তাং-১৫/৯/৮৮

স্বারক নং আর/তিন/৭/৮৮-১৯৮৬ 					তারিখ: (১৪-৯-৮৮ ইং)/(৫-৫-৯৫ বাং)

বিষয়: এল এ নথি নং-২২/৮৫-৮৬ চট্ট্রগ্রাম জেলাধীন কোতয়ালী থানার পাহাড়িকা নিম্ন মাধ্যমিক বিদ্যালয়ের জন্য জমি অধিগ্রহন প্রস্তাব অনুমোদন প্রসংগে।

সুত্র: তাহার স্বারক নং ১৮৯৬ এল এ তারিখ

নিম্নস্বাক্ষরকারী আদিষ্ট হইয়া জানাইতেছে যে, উল্লেখিত বিষয়ে সূত্রে বর্ণিত স্বারকের বরাতে প্রাপ্ত এল এ কেইজ নং-২২/৮৫-৮৬ এ ১৯৮২ ইং সনের ২নং অধ্যাদেশের ৫৯(২) ধারামতে হুকুম দখলের চুড়ান্ত প্রস্তাব অনুমোদন করা হইল।

সূত্রের স্বারক মূলে প্রাপ্ত যাবতীয় কগজ পত্রাদি এতদসংগে ফেরৎ পাঠানো হইল।

স্বাক্ষর+অস্পষ্ট

কাজী মোঃ সামসুল আলম।

সহকারী কমিশনার চট্ট্রগ্রাম বিভাগ

কমিশনারের পক্ষে। ১৪-৯-৮৮।

The Acquisitioning Authority appears to have applied its mind as to the need in initiating the acquisition proceeding for public purpose. Section 5(2) of the Ordinance enjoins that when the Government or the Divisional Commissioner, as the case may be, makes a decision for acquisition of the property under sub-section (1) or the proviso to section 4(3)(b), as the case may be, such decision shall be conclusive evidence that the property is needed for public purpose or the public interest. Thus, it appears that the Acquisitioning Authority applied its mind to the facts and circumstances, considered the pressing need of the school and gave the final decision. We are of this considered view that the requisition was directed for "public purpose" and "public interest."

<u>30. The fourth branch of contention of the petitioners is that in the schedule of land to the notice under section 3 of the Ordinance part of PS Plot Nos. 217, 220 and 223 has been described as land for the acquisition which is illegal when it does not show what specific portion of land is proposed to be acquired. The decision in the case of Aminuddn Ahmed vs. Province of East Pakistan reported in 14 DLR 51 and the case of Ralli Brothers Ltd. vs. Province of East Pakistan reported in 17 DLR (SC) 629 has been referred to by the petitioners in support of the contention. The petitioners did neither take the plea of non-specification and indefiniteness of the proposed acquired land in the writ petitions nor in the objections filed under section 4 of the Ordinance to the acquisitioning authority. Nowhere the petitioners took the ground in their objection under section 4 of the Ordinance against notice under section 3 of the Ordinance that they were unable to make an effective objection against the proposed acquisition. In this instant case, the school is very much within the acquired land and the petitioners are aware which portion of the land is under the acquisition proceedings and they were not prejudiced by the non-mentioning of the specific portion of the land under the acquisition proceeding. Moreover, it appears from Annexure-H to the petition that specific area of the proposed acquired land had been specifically mentioned. In the case of Aminuddin Ahmed vs. Province of Pakistan 15 DLR 51. 1.60 acre of land for the Telephone Exchange was the requirement but 3.20 acres of land had been requisitioned. In that view of the matter the order of requisition was held to be illegal. In the case of Ralli Brothers Ltd. vs. Province of East Pakistan, 17 DLR (SC) 629, the validity of a notice under section 3 of the (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948 was challenged on the ground of inadequate description of the property intended to be taken under the requisition proceeding but in the instant writ petition the validity of the notice under section 3 of the ordinance on the ground of inadequate description of the property has not been challenged. The facts and circumstances of two cited cases are distinguishable and got no manner of application in the facts and circumstance of these cases.</u>

<u>31. The fifth branch of contention advanced on behalf of the petitioners is that in the first floor of the building their family deity ''Radha Madhab'' is installed and daily Shevapuja is offered there and the same having been a place of religious worship proviso to section 3 of the Ordinance is a standing bar as to the acquisition of the said place of religious worship. This contention was seriously contested by the respondents. It is contended that there was no deity ''Radha Madhab'' in the building and even if there is any deity, the same is a family deity and the family members of the petitioners offer puja there and it cannot be said to be a public religious worship and there is no shebait for the purposes of worship. To appreciate the point raised it is necessary to examine once again proviso to section 3 of the Ordinance which runs as follows:</u>

<u>"Provided that no property used by the public for the purpose of religious worship, graveyard and cremation ground shall be acquired".</u>

<u>The plain meaning of the above proviso is that the religious worship must be by the public and not by individuals. In Hindu community of our country in every house there is a family deity where the family members offer puja and the members of Hindu community got no access there. Puzari and shebait are not appointed for offering puja for the family deity. It is alleged that the deity "Radha Madhab" is installed on the first floor of the building and the school is sitting on the ground floor and there arises no occasion as such on the part of other Hindu members of the community to offer Puja to the said deity "Radha Madhab". We think that the place of religious worship as mentioned in the proviso to section 3 of the Ordinance is a place of public religious worship, such as, Temple or Mandir where members of the community assemble for the purpose of worship and, as such, there cannot be any bar in issuing notice under section 3 of the Ordinance with respect to a place where a family deity is installed. We think if the meaning of religious worship as contemplated in the proviso is extended to a place of family worship, then the very object of the Ordinance will be frustrated as because no property of any member of Hindu community can be the subject matter of acquisition. The petitioner''s contention on this score also is devoid of any substance.</u>

32. We are now to deal with the point raised from the side of the respondents that the land under the acquisition proceeding is vested property and the petitioner Mrinalendu Pal being an Indian citizen, his property has been declared as vested property. This point was seriously resisted from the side of the petitioners asserting that no part of the property is vested property and the attempt to declare the property as vested property is absolutely illegal and without jurisdiction. We have earlier found that petitioner Mrinalendu Pal is not an Indian citizen and he is a citizen of Bangladesh. He being a citizen of Bangladesh, his property cannot come under the mischief of the definition of vested property" and the said property is not "vested property."

33. It is the clear assertion of the petitioners that they are in exclusive possession of the entire property including the property under the acquisition proceedings. We see from the statements made in the supplementary affidavit filed by the petitioners and also from Annexure-1 to the petition that petitioner Mrinalendu Pal obtained an order of ad interim injunction in Civil Rule No. 117 (FM) of 1986 arising out of FMA No. 6 of 1986 from High Court Division and the Government and the vested property authority were restrained from leasing out part of the disputed properties till disposal of the appeal. We are informed by the learned Advocates for the petitioners that the said appeal is still pending for disposal.

34. From the materials on record it is evident that the petitioners are in possession of the entire property including the property under the acquisition proceeding. We are constrained to hold that if any portion of the property is treated as a vested property after the disposal of the said FMA, the petitioner''s possession in the remaining land out side the land under the acquisition proceeding must not be disturbed in any way and they should be allowed to take lease of the same as co-sharers of the property.

<u>35. It will be worth while to consider one legal aspect of the matter. Notice under section 3 of the Ordinance had been issued and served upon the petitioner and they filed objection under section 4 of the Ordinance and final decision had been given by the Acquisitioning Authority but the petitioners did not challenge the validity of the said notices under section 3 of the Ordinance and the decision of Acquisitioning Authority under section 5 of the Ordinance. The petitioners only challenged the notice under section 6 of the Ordinance which is only with respect to ascertainment of the shares of the owners and claim of compensation. Our question is can the petitioners do that (?) Our answar is No. we are of this view that the petitioners having not challenged the validity of the notice under section 3 of the Ordinance and the decision given by the Acquisitioning Authority under section 5 of the Ordinance, cannot now challenge the validity of the notice under section 6 of the Ordinance and also the further proceeding of the LA case. The writ petitions thus appear to have suffered from legal infirmity.</u>

<u>36. Before parting with the case we are inclined to observe that the petitioner Sreemati Bhagabati Pal is a widow and the petitioner No. 2 Sreemati Bharati Pal is her daughter. Admittedly, the petitioners are residing on the first floor of the building and their family deity "Radha Madhab" is installed there and the property is their only shelter. There will be much hardship on their part to accommodate themselves to another portion of the property and also to shift their family deity there. Moreover, the property under the acquisition proceeding is situated in the heart of the commercial area of Chittagong town. The hardship and inconvenience of the petitioners along with the situation of the property under the acquisition proceeding must be considered. The petitioners in all fairness can expect adequate compensation from the Acquisitioning Auhourity, the respondents Nos. 1-3. We direct the respondent to give adquaterate of compensation to the petitioners for the property acquired keeping in view of the hardship and the inconvenience of the petitioners and also the location of the property.</u>

37. Having regard to the facts and circumstances of the case and discussion made hereinbefore and also reiewed in the light of the aforesaid principles of law enunciated by the Appellate Division we find no merit in these two Rules.

In the result, these Rules are discharged without any order as to costs with the observations and directions made above.

End.

parties:
Abul Kalam Azad (Md) and 8 others ------ Petitioner
Vs. 
Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh through the Secretary, Ministry of Local Government, Rural Development and Co-Operatives, Bangladesh and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Mainur Reza Chowdhury J: In these Writ Petitions under Article 102 of the Constitution,Rule Nisi were issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the appointment of Administrators and in some case also constitution Members of the Committee to assist the Administrator under sections 18A and 18B respectively of the Pourashava Ordinance, 1977 should not be declared to have been made and issued without lawful authority.

2. As the petitions disclose similar facts and involve same question of law, they are taken up analogously and disposed of by this single judgment.

3. For convenience we will refer to the facts in Writ Petition No. 6365 of 1997.

4. The case of the Writ petitioner is as follows:

5. The petitioner is a citizen of Bangladesh and resident of village Chandina within Ward No. 1 of Paschim Chandina Union Parishad. He was elected Chairman of the said Union Parishad in 1992 and claims to be still holding that office. By Notification issued by the Local Government Division of the Ministry of Local Government, Rural Development and Co-Operatives bearing SRO No. 189-Ain/97 dated 11-9-97 published in the Bangladesh Gazette Extraordinary of the same date Mouzas Chandina (JL No. 236) Maharang (JL No. 235). Harang (JI, No. 233), Chhaikot (part) (JL No. 232) of paschim Chandina Union Parishad; Mouzas Srimontaur (part) JL No. 239, Mouzas Bara-Govindapur (JL No. 237) both within Purba Chandina Union Parishad and Mouza Belashar (JL No. 234) within Uttar Barera Union Parishad was constituted a new Municipality named Chandina Pourashava with effect from 14-8-97 under Rule 5 of the Declaration and Alteration of Municipalities Rule, 1978. The areas of the three Unions being earlier declared as urban areas under the Pourashava Ordinance, 1977. The said Notification being SRO No. 189-Ain/97 was published in the Bangladesh Gazette Extraordinary dated 11-8-91 is annexed to the petition and marked as Annexure-A. The petitioner and others mentioned in paragraph 3 of the petition were earlier elected as Chairman and members respectively of paschim Chandina Union Parishad and Uttar Barera Union Parishad and are still continuing to hold their respective offices.

6. It is stated that Articles 59 and 60 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh were omitted by the 4th Amendment and while the provisions of these Articles of the Constitution were non-existing, Pourashava Ordinance, 1977 was enacted. Subsequently by Pourashava (Amendment) Ordinance, 1981 two new sections being sections 18A and section 18B were inserted in the Pourashava Ordinance, 1977. The new section 18A reads as follows:

"18A. Appointment of an Administrator in certain circumstances, (1) Where an urban area is declared to be a municipality, the Government shall appoint an Administrator to perform the functions of the Pourashava of that municipality till a Pourashava is constituted in accordance with the provisions of this Ordinance.

(2) The Government may, where necessary, appoint a Committee consisting of such number of members as it deems fit to assist the Administrator in the discharge of his functions.

(3) The Administrator and the members of the Committee if any shall respectively exercise the powers of the Chairman and of the Commissioners."

Section 18B says:

"Certain person deemed to be Commissioners,—Notwithstanding anything contained in this Ordinance, where a rural area, after being declared an urban area, is included in a municipality, the person elected as Chairman or member from that area to any Union Parishad, shall be deemed to be a commissioner of the Paurashava of that municipality."

7. By the 12th Amendment of the Constitution effective from 18th September, 1991 Articles 59 and 60 were restored to the Constitution. Article 59 of the Constitution as narrated by the 12th Amendment reads as follows:

"59. (1) Local Government in every administrative unit of the Republic shall be entrusted to bodies composed of person elected in accordance with law.

(2) Everybody such as is referred to in clause (1) shall, subject to this Constitution and any other law, perform with the appropriate administrative unit such functions as shall be prescribed by Act of Parliament, which may include functions relating to-

(a) administration and the work of public officers;

(b) the maintenance of public order ;

(c)the preparation and implementation of plans relating to public services and economic development. "

<u>8. It is submitted that in view of the provision of Article 59(1) requiring elected representative of the areas of local government to function therein, provision contained in section 18A has become ultra vires of the Constitution and also in view of the provision contained in section 18B that when a new area is declared to be a part of a Municipality, the Chairman and members of the Union Parishad concerned (who are mostly concerned with the constituted Paurashava) are entitled to perform the function of the Commissioners of the Paurashava. It is submitted that ignoring the provisions contained in Article 59(1) of the Constitution and the provision contained in section 18B of the Paurashava Ordinance, 1977, Government acted illegally in appointing Mr Kazi Jahangir Alam as Administrator of the newly constituted Chandina Pourashava in purported exercise of power contained in section 18A(1) and in constituting a six-member committee to assist him. It is claimed that the Chairman and the Member of the Committee belonged to the ruling party and some of them are not even residents of the area comprising the Municipality. It is submitted that the Government being influenced by the local political leaders of the ruling party have collusively issued the impugned notification. The notification is, as such, malafide and colourable exercise of authority.</u>

9. The contention of the petitioner is that section 18A was made a part of the Paurashava Ordinance, 1977 when Article 59 and 60 were taken out of the Constitution by the 4th Amendment. But with the inclusion of these two Articles in the Constitution again by the 12th Amendment in 1991 the provision of section 18A is in conflict with the spirit of Articles 59 and 60 and therefore ultra vires of the Constitution.

10. Affidavit-in-opposition has been filed on behalf of the respondent No. 1 denying the contention of the writ petitioner that section 18A conflicts with Articles 59 and 60 of the Constitution. The said section is, therefore, not ultra vires and the respondent acting under section 18A has lawfully appointed the Administrator to hold charge of the newly created Municipality until a Paurashava is constituted. The provision of Article 59 is very clear. It has said in not unambiguous terms that every administrative unit of the Republic shall be entrusted to bodies, composed of persons elected in accordance with law. It is also not denied that the Municipality is an administrative unit and therefore, under Article 59(1) requires to be administered by bodies composed of persons elected in accordance with law. In the instant case, a new Municipality has been created and an election has to be held to meet the requirements of Article 59(1) of the Constitution and until that is done can Municipality be administered by non-elected person that, is by Administrator, and a committee to assist him under section 18A of the Pourashava Ordinance, 1977. Mr. Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, the learned Additional Attorney-General, has taken us through the relevant provisions of the Paurashava Ordinance, 1977 and Article 59 of the Constitution. He has drawn our attention to the words "Local Government" in Article 59. This Local Government in every administrative unit is to be composed of persons elected in accordance with law. In the instant case, the administrative unit is the Municipality and the local Government is the Paurashava. Section 2(28) of the said Ordinance, 1977 says "municipality" means an urban area, declared to be a municipality under this Ordinance. Section 2(33) says "Paurashava" means a Paurashava constituted under this Ordinance by whatever name called. Section 5 of the Paurashava Ordinance provides for constitution of Paurashava and reads as follows:

(1) As soon as may be after the commencement of this Ordinance, there shall be constituted a Paurashava for every municipality in accordance with the provisions of this Ordinance.

(2) Every Paurashava shall be a body corporate, having perpetual succession and a common seal, with power, subject to the provisions of this Ordinance and the rules, to acquire and hold property, both movable and immovable and shall by its name sue and be sued.

(3) The Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, specify the name by which any Paurashava is so specified, it shall be known, and unless the name of a Paurashava is so specified, it shall be known as the Paurashava of the place where its office is situated.

Section 6 of the Paurashava Ordinance reads as follows:

(1) A Paurashava shall consist of-,

(a) Chairman;

(b) such number of elected commissioners as be fixed by the Government; and

(c) three nominated women commissioners and sub-section (2) says that the Chairman and elected commissioners of a Paurashava shall be elected by direct election on basis of adult franchise in accordance with the provisions of this Ordinance and the rules made thereunder."

From the definition and from sections 5 and 6 it is obvious that a Paurashava is distinct from a Municipality. The Additional Attorney-General has submitted that the Paurashava, that is, the local Government of the administrative unit Municipality, has to be administered by elected persons under Article 59 of the Constitution. In the instant case, although an urban area has been declared to be a Municipality that is, an administrative unit, there is no existence of a Paurashava nor there can be a Paurashava until it is constituted after holding the election. The Administrator appointed under section 18A is not a Paurashava and therefore, the provision of Article 59 is not attracted. The Administrator merely discharges the functions of a Paurashava and therefore, it does not make him or the committee appointed to assist him a local government (Paurashava) as emphasized in Article 59 of the Constitution. He has further submitted that if such a provision for appointment of Administrator and Committee are not provided, there will be a Municipality that is, an administrative unit, with nobody to administer. Section 18A merely provides for interim arrangement till the constitution of the Paurashava. Article 59 will begin with the end of section 18A. To elaborate his point, the learned Additional Attorney-General has referred to certain decisions. In the case of Narayan Das Dubey vs. State of Madhya Pradesh reported in 1983 MALI 840; it was, inter alia, held

"1. By virtue of the expression "shall be deemed to be a council for the purposes of this Act" in section 16(1) of the Madhya Pradesh Municipalities Act, the deemed committee, though it is not really a council constituted under the Act, has been fictionally treated to be a council constituted for the purposes of the Act. Legal fictions are created only for some definite purpose, and a legal fiction is to be limited to the purpose for which it was created and should not be extended beyond that legitimate field.

2. Section 19 of the Act provides that a Municipal Council should consist of elected and selected Councilors. It is not possible to have an, elected council immediately for an area which is declared to be a Municipality for the first time. Some time is bound to be consumed in holding the election in the manner provided in the Act after the Municipality has come into being. Thus, to prevent an hiatus in between the period from the coming into being of the Municipality upto the constitution of an elected council, therefore, provision for constituting a committee under section 16(1) is made. Such a committee is a care taker committee to do the work of the Municipality till a council is constituted by election under the Act.

3. By creating a fiction "such a committee shall be deemed to be a council for the purposes of this Act" in section 16 (1) the Legislature intended to assign to it the working functions of an elected council. The legislature did not intend to extend the fiction so as to give the committee an effective nature in the matter of its composition of constitution during the term. This intention is discernible from the non-obstante clause in section 16(4)."

11. In the instant case, there is no deeming clause in section 18A so there is no scope to even consider that the Administrator and the appointed Committee is the Paurashava. In another case of Arun Kumdar vs. Union of India and others reported in AIR 1982 (Rajasthan), 67. The Chief Justice discharging the functions provided under Article 160 cannot be termed to be a Governor within the meaning of Art, 155. That is why provision for payment of emoluments was required to be separately made. The provisions of Article 160 are resorted to prevent an interregnum. Necessary corollary of that is that, stop-gap function need not possess the necessary qualifications for being appointed as a Governor and also does not suffer from the disqualifications attached to that office. He resumes his old office as soon as the new Governor is appointed. If the Chief Justice of India or the senior most Judge of the Supreme Court can be validly appointed to discharge the functions of the President, there is no reason why the Chief Justice of a State cannot be asked to discharge the functions of the Governor of a State in a contingency not provided for in Chapter VI.

12. Reference has been made to the President (Discharge of Functions) Act, 1969 (Act 16 of 1969) of India. Section 3 of the said Act provides for the discharge of President''s functions in certain contingencies. It provides as follows:

"(1) In the event of the occurrence of vacancies in the offices of both the President and the Vice-President, by reason in each case of death, resignation or removal, or otherwise, the Chief Justice of India or in his absence, the senior most Judge of the Supreme Court of India available shall discharge the functions of the President until a new President is elected in accordance with the provisions of the Constitution to fill the vacancy in the office of the President enters upon his office or a new Vice-President so elected begins to act as President under Article 65 of the Constitution, whichever is earlier.

(2) When the Vice-President, while discharging the functions of the President, dies, resigns or is removed or otherwise ceases to hold office, the Chief Justice of India or in his absence, the senior most Judge referred to in sub-section (1) shall discharge the said functions until the President resumes his duties or a new Vice-President is elected as aforesaid, whichever is earlier.

(3) When the Vice-President-

(a) While acting as President, or

(b) While discharging the functions of the President, is unable to discharging the functions of the President owing to absence, illness or any other cause, the Chief Justice of India or, in his absence, the senior most Judge referred to in sub-section (1) shall discharge the said functions-

(i) in the case referred to in clause (a) until a new President elected as aforesaid enters upon his office or until the Vice-President acting as President resumes his duties, whichever is earlier;

(ii) in the case referred to in clause (b) until the President resumes his duties, or the Vice-President resumes his duties, whichever is earlier.

(4) The person discharging the functions of the President under this section shall, during, and in respect of the period while he is so discharging the said functions, have all the powers and immunities of the President and be entitled to such employment, allowances and privileges as may be determined by parliament by law and until provision in that behalf is so made, such employments, allowances and privileges as are specified in the second schedule."

13. While considering the power of the President, it was observed in the Rajasthan case which has been referred to above that, the power under Article 160 of the Constitution makes a stop gap arrangement. Such an arrangement is made till the Governor appointed under Article 155 of the Constitution enters upon his office. The requirement of Article 153 of the Constitution is that there must always be, Governor for a State. In between the expiry of the term of the previously appointed Governor or his removal and the taking over the charge of the office by the newly appointed Governor there can be some time lag and Article 160 of the Constitution is required to be used to cover only the time lag before the successor enters upon his office. The appointment of the Chief Justice to discharge the functions of a Governor by no stretch of imagination can be said to be an inroad of the executive on the judiciary. In a given case if the President makes an attempt to remove a High Court Judge or the Chief Justice of a Court and utilize the provisions of Article 160 of the Constitution as a device to remove an inconvenient Judge or the Chief Justice, the validity of such an appointment can be examined by the Court in a proper case, because then it can be said that the President had neglected to discharge his duties or has failed to act under the Constitution and the Court may find out a remedy for it. The case in hand does not satisfy the need for such an examination as there is nothing on record to hold that the respondent No. 2 is an inconvenient Judge to the Union Government or his appointment as a Governor has been made as a device to remove him once and for all and, as such, an examination. The Courts are not required under Article 226 of the Constitution to examine hypothetical and imaginary questions."

14. In order to distinguish the holder of an office and someone who is merely discharging the functions of that office, the Additional Attorney-General has referred to Article 60 of the Constitution of India which provides oath or affirmation by the President. It provides every President and every person acting as President or discharging the functions of the President shall, before entering upon his office, make and subscribe in the presence of the Chief Justice of India or, in his absence, the senior-most Judge of the Supreme Court available, an oath or affirmation in the following form, that is to say-

swear in the name of God

"I, AB do…………………that I will faithfully execute the office of President solemnly affirm (or discharge the functions of the President of India and will to the best of my ability preserve, protect and defend the Constitution and the law and that I will devote myself to the service and well-being of the people of India."

15. Article 70 provides for discharge of President''s functions in other contingencies —parliament may make such provision as it thinks fit for the discharge of the functions of the President in any contingency not provided for in this Chapter.

<u>16. It has been argued by the learned Counsel for the petitioner that there is no Article equivalent to Article 160 of the Indian Constitution. Article 160 specifically provides that the Parliament may enact such law as to who will act as President in the absence of the President and the Vice-President. It is on the basis of this Article that the President (Discharge of Functions) Act, 1969 was promulgated. The learned Additional Attorney-General argues that although there is no such Article in our Constitution, the Parliament has plenary power under Article 65 to make laws for contingency, not provided in the Constitution. The law of course should not be violative of any provision of the Constitution and for these reasons he submits section 18A does not contravene the provision of Article 59 of our Constitution. It has been suggested by the learned Counsel for the petitioner that in order to comply with Article 59 of the Constitution, the choice of Chairman and Members of the Committee should be from elected persons of that area just as it has been provided in section 18A of the Paurashava Ordinance. It provides that an area after being declared an Urban area is included in a Municipality, the person elected as Chairman or Member from that area to any Union Parishad shall be deemed to be a Commissioner of that Municipality. However we see that what is possible in the case where an area is included to an existing Municipality is not possible where Union is declared to be a Municipality. It is possible for elected Chairman and Members to be deemed to be a Commissioner of an existing Pourashava of a Municipality but this is not possible where no Pourashava exists in a newly declared municipality.</u>

<u>17. The other line of argument on behalf of the petitioners was that in order to comply with Article 59 of the Constitution, the law could provide for election to and constitution of a Paurashava simultaneously with the declaration of an urban area into a Municipality. We have already referred to the case of Narayandas Dubey vs. State where it was held that it was not possible to have an elected Council immediately for an area which is declared to be a Municipality for the first time. Some time is bound to be consumed in holding the election in the manner provided in the Act after the Municipality has come into being. We have found this to be reasonable as there is bound to be a time gap between the declaration of a particular territory to be Municipality and the holding of the election. There may be unforeseen impediments in holding the election. Further the declaration of an Urban Area, a Municipality is created by the Government under law. But the elections are held by an independent body under the Constitution, the Election Commission. Therefore, it may not be practically possible to hold the election simultaneously with the declaration of a Municipality. It has been argued and we have made reference to it that Article 59 was non-existing at the time when section 18A was added to the Paurashava Ordinance, 1977 and therefore, section 18A when added may have been lawful then but it became ultra vires of the Constitution after Article 59 was included by the 12th Amendment in 1991. However, it is pointed out that even when Article 59 was a part of the Constitution prior to its exclusion by 4th Amendment, the Bangladesh Local Government (Union Parishad and Paurashava) Order, 1973 (Presidents Order No. 22 of 1973) recognised the continuous Administrator, for Union Parishad or a Paurashava. Article 4(1) of President''s Order No. 22 of 1973 provides that as soon as may be after the commencement of this order, there shall be constituted Union Parishad and Paurashava throughout Bangladesh in accordance with the provisions of this Order. Clause (2) of Article 4 provides that the Administrator appointed under Article 4 of the Local Councils Order for a Union Parishad or a Paurashava shall make over his charge to the Chairman of the Union Parishad or the Paurashava, as the case may be, as soon as it is constituted under this Order. Similarly, Act IX of 1992 passed after the 12th Amendment included Article 59 of the Constitution provided that where the term of a Paurashava under sub-section(1) expires before the holding of the first meeting of the Paurashava constituted to succeed it, an Administrator appointed by the Government shall perform the functions of the Paurashava until the holding of such meeting. It would thus appear that provision for appointment of Administrator is necessary for certain contingencies not provided for in the Constitution.</u>

<u>18. It was also submitted by the learned Counsel for the petitioners that the provision of section 18A of Paurashava Ordinance, 1997 is being grossly misused by the Government. The purpose and object of Article 59 is being defeated by appointing their henchmen as Administrator and Members of the committee and not holding any election or constituting Paurashava for years together. There is definitely ample scope for section 18A of the Paurashava Ordinance, 1997 to be misused. But the mere scope of an otherwise good and well-intended law cannot be said to be a bad law for being misused. Just as a bad law cannot be said to be a good law simply because it is put to good use. In any event person aggrieved by such misuse is not without remedy. An aggrieved can always seek direction from the competent Court to hold the election to the Paurashava expeditiously. In the case of Awas Samasya Niwaran Sanstha, Indore vs. State reported in AIR 1983 Madhya Pradesh, 12 direction was sought for holding election. The relevant portion of the judgment may be quoted.</u>

<u>"Last elections for the said corporation were held in the year 1965. The corporation was dissolved in the year 1979. As a consequence of its dissolution, as provided in A 423(1) (a) of the Act, all councilors of the corporation vacated their office. Further by virtue of cl. (b) of section 423(1) of the Act, all powers and duties of the corporation are to be exercised and performed until the corporation is reconstituted by such person or a committee of persons as the State Government may appoint in that behalf. The State Government has appointed an Administrator for the purpose, who has been impleaded as respondent No. 3. The petitioners contend that there is a statutory obligation on the respondents to hold elections for reconstitution of the corporation, but they have failed to discharge the obligation in this behalf in spite of expiry of a period of about ten years. Accordingly, the petitioners have prayed for issuance of a Writ of mandamus to compel the respondents to hold elections. Issuance of a writ of q u o warranto restraining respondent No. 3, the Administrator, from exercising powers, is also prayed.</u>

<u>The court held as follows:</u>

<u>Undisputedly the corporation stood dissolved in the year 1970. The consequences of dissolution have been laid down in section 423 of the Act. Clause (b) of sub-section (1) of section 423 of the Act provides that:</u>

<u>"Section 423(1) (b) All powers and duties of the corporation the standing committee and appeal committee under this Act, may until the corporation is reconstituted, be exercised and performed by such person or a committee of persons as the State Government may appoint in that behalf."</u>

<u>From the aforesaid provision it is clear that all the powers and duties of the corporation are intended to be exercised by the person appointed in that behalf by the State Government, who is called the Administrator of the city. It is not the intendment of the framers of the law that the Administrator should function ad infinitum. He can function only until the corporation is reconstituted. It is true that no time limit is fixed within which the corporation is required to be reconstituted. However, when a statue provides no date for holding elections, it has to be inferred that election must be held within a reasonable time and when the authority entrusted with the duty to hold elections abuses its discretion by not holding elections for inordinately long period, the court can control its action by directing it to hold elections and by fixing a date for the same (see Ferris Extraordinary Legal Remedies, p 386).</u>

<u>19. It is therefore, clear, that if the provisions of section 18A of the Paurashava Ordinance, 1977 is abused or misused any aggrieved person may seek remedy in the appropriate Court of jurisdiction. Finally, the petitioners made reference to the observation made by the Appellate Division in the case of Kudrat-e-Elahi Panir vs. Bangladesh, reported in 44 DLR (AD) 319. Chief Justice Shahabuddin Ahmed, as he then was, while delivering the Full Court Judgment observed that Local Government is meant for management of focal affairs by locally elected persons. If Government officers or their henchmen are brought to run the local bodies, there is no sense in retaining them as local government bodies. Considering the origin, growth and development of local government institution at different levels of the administration over one and a half centuries, it is found that local Government is an integral part of the democratic polity of the country.</u>

<u>Justice Mustafa Kamal while concurring with the judgment of the Chief Justice Shahabuddin Ahmed observed that the words ''Local Government" have not been defined in the Constitution. In the absence of any definition and in the absence of any directive to create a local government afresh, the Constitution will be presumed to have referred to the already known concept and institution of and the existing legislations on local government. Local Government, as a concept and as an institution, was already known to have possessed certain common Characteristic, namely, local elections, procedures for public accountability, independent and substantial sources of income, clear areas for independent action and certainty of powers and duties and the conditions under which they would be exercised. I cannot conceive of a local government existing in terms of Articles 59 and 60 and another outside of it. That will make a mockery of Articles 59 and 60 and will be in direct conflict with Article 7(1) of the Constitution. With Articles 59 and 60 in the Constitution local government legislation became very much a subject matter of legislation within the terms of the Constitution. Parliament is not free to legislate on local government ignoring Articles 59 and 60."</u>

<u>20. The Appellate Division in an unambiguous term has declared that the Local Government must be administered by the elected person in accordance with law. The fact in that case was however, different from the facts and circumstances of the present case. In the present case, an urban area had been newly declared to be a Municipality and the Appellate Division by its judgment has not covered such a situation where a newly created Municipality has to be administered until a Paurashava is constituted. We do not think that section 18A of the Paurashava Ordinance, 1977 was intended to defeat the purpose and object of Articles 59 and 60 of the Constitution, but merely provided an interim arrangement to administer declared Municipality until a Paurashava was constituted by elected people. In that view of the matter, we are of the opinion that section 18A of the Paurashava Ordinance, 1977 is not ultra vires of the Constitution i.e. the provision under Articles 59 and 60 of the Constitution.</u>

21. In the light of our above observation and finding, the Rules issued in the above writ petitions cannot be sustained.

22. In the result, the Rules are discharged without any order as to costs.

23. In order to meet the requirement of Article 59 of the Constitution, the Election Commission is directed that it should try to hold the election for the constitution of the Paurashavas of the Municipalities within 3 (three) months.

Let a copy of this judgment be sent to the Election Commission at once.

End.

AJ Mohammad Ali, Additional Attorney-General, (Firoz Shah, Assistant Attorney-General, and Naima Haider, Assistant Attorney-General with him), instructed by B Hossain, Advocate-on-Record - For the Appellant 	
Rokanuddin Mahmud, Senior Advocate, instructed by Fakrul Islam, Advocate-on-Record - For Respondent No. 1.

Vs.

case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 31 August, 1997 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 41 of 1993)
full_judgment:
Md. Ruhul Amin, J: This appeal, by leave is from the judgment and order dated August 31, 1997 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 41 of 1993 making the Rule absolute declaring the judgment of the Court of Settlement dated December 24, 1992 in case No. 397 of 1989 to have been passed without lawful authority and is of no legal effect and further declaring the enlistment of the holding No. NE(C)-2, Road No. 71, Gulshan Model Town, Dhaka in the list of abandoned property published in the Bangladesh Gazette on September 23, 1986 to be illegal and is of no legal effect and directing the respondent-petitioner to release the said holding from the list of abandoned buildings within 60 days from the date of receipt of the copy of the judgment.

2. The Rule was obtained in the aforesaid writ petition impugning the judgment and order of December 24, 1992 of the First Court of Settlement, Dhaka in Case No. 397 of 1989 (Ka-54, Gulshan Model Town, Dhaka) holding No. NE(C)-2 Road No. 71 Gulshan Model Town, Dhaka rejecting the prayer for releasing the aforesaid property from the list of abandoned buildings as published in the Bangladesh Gazette dated September 23, 1986. The list wherein the property in question has been listed as abandoned property was prepared as per provision of Ordinance No. 54 of 1985, hereinafter referred to as the Ordinance, and the Case No. 397 of 1989 seeking release of the property was filed before the Court of Settlement as per provision of section 7 of the Ordinance.

3. The writ petition was filed on the averments, inter alia, that holding No. NE(C)-2 Road No. 71 Gulshan Model Town, Dhaka was leased out to Mr Wali Mohammad by the then Dhaka Improvement Trust (DIT, now RAJUK) on June 23, 1964 by a registered deed of lease. Mr. Wali Mohammad appointed his brother Abdur Rahman (respondent No. 4 attorney by a registered Power of Attorney of March 31,1970 with the authority to construct a building in the said plot as well as to sell and transfer or otherwise dispose of the said property. Mr Wali Mohammad through his attorney Abdur Rahman entered into a contract to sell the said plot of land to the respondent No. 1 (writ petitioner) for a consideration of Taka 1,00,000/- and on receipt of Taka 40,000/- as earnest money executed a deed of agreement on December 29, 1970 and that on that very day delivered possession to the respondent No. 1.

4. Further averment was that respondent No. 1 obtained permission to construct building after obtaining sanction plan from the DIT, now RAJUK. Permission was accorded to him for transfer of the case plot in his name. But before completion of transfer in his name the Sub-Divisional Officer, Sadar (South) Dhaka issued notice upon him under the provision of Lands and Buildings Recovery Ordinance 1972 to vacate the said plot and thereupon he filed Title Suit No. 228 of 1977 in the 3rd Court of Munsif, (now Assistant Judge) Dhaka seeking a decree for permanent injunction and therein obtained an order of temporary injunction. The law enforcing agency in spite of the order of injunction dispossessed him from a portion of the plot, but later on possession was restored to him on July 3, 1979 as per order of mandatory injunction. He tendered balance of the consideration money to the attorney of Wali Mohammad and requested him to execute and register the necessary kabala but he refused to accept the balance of the consideration money and did not execute and register the necessary kabala. He then filed Title Suit No. 282 of 1983 in the 4th Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka seeking decree for specific performance of contract for sale of the plot and obtained decree on February 5, 1989 (later on amended on August 29, 1989). Thereafter pursuant to the decree on August 29, 1989 kabala was executed and registered through the court.

5. It was further averred that respondent No. 1 (in the Writ Petition, herein appellant) most illegally enlisted the property in violation of the provision of section 5 of the Ordinance in the 'Ka' list of abandoned properties at a time while the suit for specific performance of contract was pending and that he (respondent No. 1 herein) filed Case No. 397 of 1989 before the Court of Settlement and that the respondent No. 4 (attorney) also filed Case No. 160 of 1987 claiming the disputed property as his own and the Court of Settlement by the judgment and order of May 6, 1987 dismissed the said case and maintained the inclusion of the property in the list of abandoned property. The Court of Settlement by the judgment and order dated December 24 of 1992 dismissed the Case No. 397 of 1989.

6. Appellant's case before the High Court Division in his affidavit-in-opposition was that lessee Mr Wali Mohammad and his two brothers including Abdur Rahman left erstwhile East Pakistan for the then West Pakistan leaving behind the case property as well as other properties without making any arrangement for its management and possession, that the so-called deed of agreement was executed by Mr Wali Mohammad through his attorney Abdur Rahman sitting in Karachi in the month of December 1970 and that neither in the month of December nor at any time in the year 1971 or after the emergence of Bangladesh Wali Mohammad or Abdur Rahman returned to Bangladesh and, as such, the property vested with the Government as abandoned property under President's Order No. 16 of 1972. It was also the case of the appellant in his affidavit-in-opposition that Wali Mohammad never executed any power of attorney in favour of the respondent No. 4, who filed the case before the Court of Settlement claiming the property as his own and denying the execution of agreement of sale of the case property to the respondent No. 1 as constituted attorney of Wali Mohammad. It was also contended by the appellant that all the papers of respondent No. 1 were forged and collusive.

7. It may be mentioned the Court of Settlement dismissed the case No. 397 of 1989 filed by respondent No. 1 seeking release of the case property from the list of abandoned properties since the said Court by its judgment and order of May 6, 1987 dismissed the case No. 160 of 1987 (filed by respondent No. 4 seeking release of the case property from the list of abandoned properties) rejecting the prayer for release of the case property which was also the subject matter of Case No. 397 of 1997.

8. The respondent No. 1 prior to the filing of Writ Petition No. 41 of 1993 filed Writ Petition No. 2300 of 1990 challenging legality of listing of the holding No. NE(C)-2 Road No. 71 Gulshan Model Town, Dhaka in the list of abandoned buildings and the publication of the list in the Bangladesh Gazette dated September 23, 1986 and also the judgment and order dated May 6, 1987 of the Court of Settlement in Case No. 160 of 1987. The said writ petition was disposed of making observation that the findings and remarks in the said case No. 160 of 1987 would not affect the claim and interest of the respondent No. 1 in the holding. As regard the other relief i.e. relief sought against enlisting of the holding in the list of abandoned buildings, it was observed by the High Court Division that respondent No. 1 would seek his remedy as against the enlistment in the proper forum.

9. The High Court Division made the Rule absolute obtained challenging the legality of the judgment and order of the Court of Settlement in Case No. 397 of 1989 upon observing. "The critical analysis of the aforesaid papers and documents led us to hold that the petitioner is after the suit property since 1890 and showed his immense patience and ultimately won the legal battle in this matter. So, it appears that the petitioner is armed with a kabala in respect of the suit property executed and registered through court in pursuance of civil Court decree and is in possession through his tenant Pakistan Embassy in the knowledge and sight of the Government. Further, the learned Deputy Attorney-General representing the respondent No. 1 failed to explain the validity of enlistment of the suit property in the 'ka' list of abandoned property in contravention of section 5 of the Ordinance 54 of 1985. He also remained silent in the matter of possession of the suit property. However, the respondent No. 1 failed to come with the official file of the suit property in question to show their bonafide in the matter. Had it been filed we could at least see the genuineness of the claim of the respondent No. 1. On the other hand, the papers and documents filed by the petitioner as referred to in Annexures discussed above led us to hold that the petitioner as a bonafide purchaser for value entered into possession thereto before promulgation of President's Order 16 of 1972, the sheet anchor of the respondent's case, and the same has been enlisted in 'ka' list of the abandoned properties when a suit for specific performance of contract was pending in violation of section 5 of the Ordinance 54 of 1985 and, as such, the action of the respondent No. 1 in the matter of enlistment is found ex-facie illegal."

10. Leave was granted to consider the submissions, that in a case before the Court of Settlement the initial presumption is that the enlisted building is an abandoned property and that the onus lies on the claimant to show that it is not an abandoned property.
