It would have been taken for granted by the makers of the Constitution that the 'law' to which the citizens could have recourse for the protection of fundamental liberties assured to them by the Constitution would be a system of law that did not flout those fundamental rules. If it were otherwise, it would be misuse of language to speak of law as something which affords 'protection' for the individual in the enjoyment of his fundamental liberties, and the purported entrenchment of Articles 9(1) and 12(1) would be little more than mockery". The observation of the Privy Council fully applies in our case as the principles of natural justice were firmly established as fundamental rules of judicial procedure in our country from long before the present Constitution came into force, thus breach of the principles of fair hearing is a violation of fundamental right guaranteed by Article 31 and brings in the mischief of Article 26 rendering an action void and not voidable. Article 26 addresses Parliament and a law in violation of fundamental right is void. A law, which excludes the necessity of hearing, will be void under Article 31 and a fortiorari an action, which must have the backing of law, in breach of fair hearing, must be void in terms of Article 26 of the Constitution.</u>

<u>19. The legal position is, that when an action is void, it is a nullity and has no force in law and cannot be enforced. It not being voidable need not be avoided by taking any available legal proceeding. Pakistan Supreme Court in MO Ghani vs AN Mahmood, 18 DLR (SC) 463, quoted with approval the following passage from Corpus juris Seckmdum-</u>

<u>"Disobedience of, or resistance to, a void mandate, order, judgment, or decree, or one issued by a Court without jurisdiction of the subject matter and parties litigant, is not contempt, and where the Court has no jurisdiction to make the order, no waiver can cut off the rights of the party to attack its validity."</u>

20. Now, let us address the second aspect of the matter, i.e., whether this Court while sitting in its contempt jurisdiction can go into the question of voidness of the order complained of. We have already noted the submissions made by Mr. Rafique-ul-Huq, Dr Zahir and Mr Mahmudul Islam, Amicus Curiae and the submissions of the learned Advocates of the respective parties.

21. The crux of the submission made by Mr Rafique-ul-Huq is that if an order is void ab initio, i.e., the order passed by a Court without jurisdiction is a nullity, and violation of such order does not give rise to any liability in contempt and if the order is voidable, i.e., if the Court has initial jurisdiction to pass an order, the violation of that will amount to contempt even if it is subsequently found to be erroneous or irregular on merit. As against that Dr Zahir has made an extreme submission that no matter whether the order is void or valid any violation of any order passed by a Court would amount to contempt. Mr Mahmudul Islam has submitted that an order can be void if it is passed in breach of the principle of natural justice and an order can also be void ab initio if it is without jurisdiction. As opposed to that, Mr Akhtar Imam, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner, has relied on certain decisions which we have already noted earlier. He has relied on the decision reported in AIR 1958 (Punjab) 180 for the proposition that so long as the injunction order has not been vacated or modified by the Court granting it or has not been reversed on appeal no matter how unreasonable and unjust the injunction may be, the order must be obeyed and violation of the order of injunction cannot be excused on the ground that though the Court acted within its jurisdiction but the order that was passed was erroneous. Similarly, he has relied on the decision reported in AIR 1966 (Madras) 53 wherein it was held that flouting an order of Court lacking in territorial or pecuniary jurisdiction with the knowledge of the order and deliberately would render the party to the order liable for contempt. He has relied on two other decisions of Indian Jurisdiction. One is AIR 1949 (Lahore) 131 and the other is AIR 1974 (SC) 1471 and also he has relied on the case of 18 DLR 242 in support of his aforesaid contention as against that there is a decision reported in 18 DLR (SC) 463 which laid down the legal proposition that if an order is void it is a nullity and violation of such order does not give rise to any liability in contempt and Mr Mahmudul Islam has also taken us through some of the decisions which we have already noted earlier from which he substantiated the proposition that an order passed in violation of the principle of natural justice is also a nullity

22. Let us now examine this important legal aspect in the light of the submissions made and the decisions placed before us. It seems to us that Dr Zahir has made an extreme submission that any order of a Court if violated irrespective of whether it is void or voidable will amount to contempt. To substantiate his contention he did not place any decision before us.

23. We have studied the cases referred to and relied on by Mr. Imam and on a reading of the same it appears to us that the Lahore case and the Indian Supreme Court case do not support him rather go against him. Then remain the other three cases and the proposition laid down in those cases boils down to that if an order is passed by a Court with jurisdiction the violation of such order certainly gives rise to liability in contempt but in the Madras case in arriving at such a proposition their Lordships also noted that a distinction should be made between a lack of jurisdiction which does not go to the root of the power of the Court and a lack of jurisdiction which is basic to the very organization of Court or to the scope of its power and in that case it was canvassed that an order which lacks inherent jurisdiction violation of that does not amount to contempt of Court and it has been noted in that decision that absence of inherent jurisdiction of the Court may not give rise to contempt of Court and their Lordships had kept that question open in view of the fact that in that case the Court had acted within jurisdiction and thus rejected the contention that when the order is made by Court of jurisdiction it cannot be flouted on the ground that the order is erroneous or irregular. The same view is reflected in the case reported in AIR 1958 (Punjab) wherein also it was noticed by their Lordships that there is long line of decisions which laid down the proposition that if the order is void violation of the same will not give rise to any liability but they have not considered those decisions as in that case as a matter of fact it was found that the Court had jurisdiction to pass the injunction order and it cannot be violated on the plea that the order was erroneous unless it is vacated or modified by the Court granting it. On the other hand, the Lahore case and the case of the Indian Supreme Court do not help Mr Imam because in the Lahore case it has been held by the majority that the violation of a void order does not amount to contempt, however, improper or discourteous conduct may be because an order without jurisdiction is void and a void order binds nobody. Similarly, in the case of Nawabkhan [AIR 1974 (SC) 1471] it has been clearly held that if an order is null and void and a competent Court holds it invalid it operates from nativity, i.e., the impugned act or order was never valid. Thus, these two cases do not come in aid of Mr Imam to substantiate his point. On the other hand, in the case reported in 18 DLR (SC) 463 the Supreme Court reversed the decision of the High Court which has been relied on by Mr Imam, i.e., the case reported in 18 DLR 242, and the Supreme Court held that if an order is void the violation of the same is immune from an action in contempt and if an order is voidable the violation of the same will give rise to liability. Similarly, in the case reported in 1985 CriLJ 359 (Bom) it has been held by the Bombay High Court that if an order is passed without jurisdiction the non compliance of the same will not amount to contempt.

<u>24. From a review of all these decisions it appears that there are two lines of decisions. The first line of decisions is that if the order is void abilities it is a nullity in the eye of law and it has no existence of its own and non-compliance of the same does not give rise to any liability whatsoever in contempt. The other line of decisions is that when a Court acts within jurisdiction but erroneously or commits irregularity in passing an order such order so long it remains in force, i.e., unless it is vacated or modified by the Court itself or reversed in appeal, the violation of such order is contempt of Court. Thus, it appears that if one disobeys an order of the Court one does it at one's own peril and at an ultimate analysis if it is found that the order is void ab initio the violation of the same will not create any liability, whereas the position will be reverse in case of violation of a voidable order. The position has been very lucidly and succinctly stated in the case of Macfoy vs United Africa Co Ltd reported in (1962) AC 152 at 160 where on this point Lord Denning observed:</u>

<u>"If an act is void, then it is in law a nullity. It is not only bad, but incurably bad. There is no need for an order of the Court to set it aside. It is automatically null and void without more ado, though it is sometimes convenient to have the Court declare it to be so. And every proceeding which is founded on it is also bad and incurably bad, you cannot put something on nothing and expect it to stay there. It will collapse. But if an act is only avoidable, then it is not automatically void. It is only an irregularity which may be waived. It is not to be avoided unless something is done to avoid it. There must be an order of the Court setting it aside and the Court has a discretion whether to set it aside or not. It will do so if justice demands it but not otherwise."</u>

<u>25. Therefore, in that view of the matter it appears to us that while exercising contempt jurisdiction this Court is competent to examine the legality and validity of the order complained of because this Court working under the Constitution and having the obligation to defend, preserve and protect the Constitution cannot enforce an order or action which appears to be unconstitutional besides being void. The celebrated decision of Marbury vs Madison, 2 LEd 60 is an authority for this, though no authority is really required. Definitely it is the power, nay the duty, of this Court to see that the directions for the compliance of which petition has been made are constitutionally valid directions and this power cannot be denied to this Court on the analogy of an executing Court. Though contempt jurisdiction is availed of to enforce a writ of mandamus, this Court exercising jurisdiction under Article 108 cannot be equated with an executing court. Even an executing court will not execute a void decree or order and the Indian Supreme Court in Nai Babu vs Lala Ramnarayan, AIR 1978 SC 22, observed;</u>

<u>"It is true that a decree for eviction of a tenant cannot be passed solely on the basis of a compromise between the parties. The Court is to be satisfied whether a statutory ground for eviction has been pleaded which the tenant has admitted by the compromise. Thus dispensing with further proof, on account of the compromise, the court is to be satisfied about compliance with the statutory requirement on the totality of facts of a particular case bearing in mind the entire circumstances from the stage when the compromise is effected".</u>

26. When a compromise decree is challenged as a nullity in the course of its execution the executing court can examine relevant materials to find out whether statutory grounds for eviction existed in law. If the pleadings and other materials on the record make out a prima facie case about the existence of statutory grounds for eviction a compromise decree cannot be held to be invalid and the executing court will have to give effect to it."

<u>27. Therefore, we are of the opinion that in exercising jurisdiction of contempt, a Bench of this Court is competent to see if the order complained of is a valid order in the eye of law because unless the order is legal and valid it will not give rise to any legal consequences and violation of such order is immune from attack. The governing question in exercising the contempt jurisdiction is to see if the Court had the initial jurisdiction, i.e., the inherent competency, to entertain the writ petition and pass an order as has been done in the instant case or the Court lacked inherent jurisdiction. If the Court had no jurisdiction at all then any order passed by it is void abilities, i.e., a nullity, no nest, the violation of such order will not amount to contempt of court at all because there is no order of the Court in the eye of law. Thus, in exercise of contempt jurisdiction when the Court examines the voidness of the order it does not sit in appeal as contended by Mr Imam, rather it is the bound duty of the Court to see if the order complained of is a valid and legal order. If an order passed by a Court including this Court lacks inherent or total jurisdiction why an innocent member of the public should be burdened with the job of challenging the same before the higher Court for no fault of him or why a citizen should be compelled to comply with an order which is void ab initio. If this is allowed to go unabated, it will not enhance the dignity, authority or prestige of this Court or of any Court rather shake the public confidence in the institution which has been brought into existence to safeguard and protect the rights and interest of the people at large. In making this observation, we are not oblivious of the fact that if the order issued by a Court having jurisdiction in the matter, the violation of that certainly would give rise to liability and such violation must be visited with severe punishment.</u>

<u>28. On a review of the relevant decisions, we are of the opinion that the correct legal position has been stated by Mr Rafique-ul-Huq and Mr Mahmudul Islam. In respect of the contention of Mr Huq that the use of the word "void" or "voidable" is applicable to contract and they should not be used in other context is difficult to accept. It is true that the said expressions are frequently used in respect of contract. But nevertheless, an order of the Court can also be 'void' or 'voidable' and that aspect has nicely been described by Lord Denning MR as he usually does on any legal issue. The Pakistan Supreme Court has used these two expressions in Dr MO Gani's case [18 DLR (SC) 463] in this context as admittedly sometimes Courts pass 'void' order which is absolutely illegal and without jurisdiction and very frequently also pass 'voidable' orders which remain in full force until and unless it is vacated, modified by the Court itself or reversed by the appellate Court. We are, therefore, of the opinion that the Pakistan Supreme Court correctly used these expressions in explaining the legal position in the present context. Neither we nor Mr Huq could coin a better expression to cover the situation.</u>

<u>29. We have weighed the submission made by Dr Zahir. We are in great pain to disagree with him. If his submission is accepted then the Courts of law will become supernatural institutions in the country. We live in a democratic society and the Courts in our country derive their power and authority from the general people through their elected representatives. In a democratic polity where the Court derives its authority from the people, it cannot be above everything, it must discharge its functions in accordance with law and under the Constitution of the Republic. Therefore, it cannot be placed above everything, it cannot be attributed supernatural character and must be kept within its bounds. The Courts including the Superior Courts cannot be unanswerable to anybody. No more it can exercise Regal Authority. It is a Court of the people, by the people and for the people. So, a duty is cast upon all the Courts including the Superior Courts to act in accordance with law. We, therefore, do not find any substance in the submission of Dr Zahir. Thus, we are of the opinion that in a contempt proceeding the contemner is entitled to raise the question of voidness of the order, and if he is not allowed to do so, cause of justice will be impeded and innocent people or litigant will be visited with punishment for non-compliance of a void order which is nonest.</u>

<u>30. In the instant case, we have already found that the order complained of is void ab initio on two counts, namely,</u>

<u>(1) for violation of the principles of audi alteram partem which is deep-rooted in our jurisdiction and has got judicial recognition in Zakir Ahmed's Case [16 DLR (SC) 722] and thereafter consistently followed by both the Divisions of this Court;</u>

<u>(2) the impugned order also suffers from patent illegality in view of the fact that the Requisition and Acquisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982 made provisions for challenging legality of the requisition and acquisition order and for disputing the quantum of compensation and the jurisdiction of the Court is ousted.</u>

<u>31. Therefore, on that count also this Court has no jurisdiction to direct the respondents to pay compensation as early as possible at the present market rate as per provision of 1982 Ordinance because on perusal of the Ordinance it does not appear that any Court is authorised to award compensation for acquisition at the present market rate of the property. In the instant case the property was acquired in 1961-62 through LA Case No. 138/1961-1962 and 1982 Ordinance provides that in assessing compensation the present market rate as on the date of requisition shall be a relevant question to be considered by the Arbitrator but admittedly, the instant property was acquired in 1962 when the Emergency Requisition and Acquisition of Property Act, 1948 was in force and the 1982 Ordinance did not see the light of the day in 1961-62 and in giving that direction to award compensation in the light of the 1982 Ordinance this Court also lost sight of the provision of law as was prevailing in 1961-62. Besides, if the grievance is in respect of quantum of compensation then the writ petitioner must pursue her remedy under the Ordinance and giving a gobye to that cannot approach a civil court or this Court as the jurisdiction of civil Court is ousted by the Ordinance and the Court must apply the "hands off" doctrine. See 39 DLR (AD) 1.</u>

<u>32. Now, since both the parties extensively argued on merit, let us advert to that aspect of the case as well. The crux of the allegation is that the order dated 14-8-2001 was communicated to the contemner No. 1 on 26-8-2001 through lawyer's certificate. But it is positively contended by all the contemners in one voice that the structures standing on plot No. 753 was demolished by the RAJUK on 25-8-2001. The petitioner however, has disputed this contention of the contemners. Now, there is no dispute in the legal arena that the contempt proceeding is a quasi criminal proceeding and like any other criminal proceeding the onus is on the petitioner to prove the commission of the offence and like any other criminal proceeding the contemners are also entitled to get the benefit of doubt. In the affidavit-in-opposition, all the three contemners stated that they have started demolition work in Block 'J' at Baridhara on 23-8-2001 and it continued upto 30-8-2001. The contemners have annexed certain documents to show that the eviction process started on 23-8-2001 and it continued unabated till 30-8-2001. On the other hand, the contemners also referred to certain correspondences made by RAJUK with different authorities. The letters dated 28-8-2001 and 27-8-2001 written by RAJUK which are admitted by both the parties show that the eviction started on 23-8-2001 and continued till 30-8-2001 and admittedly, the case plot is situated in the northern side of Block 'J' at Baridhara and the positive contention of the contemners is that they continued the eviction work from northern side of Block 'J' and they have, on the 25th of August 2001, evicted the petitioner. To refute the contention, the petitioner in her affidavit-in-reply, annexed an 'affidavit' sworn by one Lieutenant Colonel M. Latifur Rahman to show that from 23-8-2001 demolition work started from the southern side of 'J' Block and he brought the sane to the notice of the contempt petitioner and immediately the contempt petitioner, that is, the writ petitioner, Mrs Razia Sattar, assured him that she would take up the matter before the High Court Division of the Supreme Court immediately as she was the lawful owner of the plot of the land and RAJUK had no authority to demolish her house whatsoever and admittedly, she filed the writ petition on 14-8-2001 and obtained an order in her favour restraining the respondents from evicting her from the case land, but from the statement made in paragraph No. 2 of the said affidavit it appears that this fact was not disclosed to him rather, on 23-8-2001 she stated that she will immediately bring the matter to the knowledge of this Court. It further appears that in paragraph No. 3 of the said affidavit it is stated that on 25-8-2001 he was shown this court's order by the contempt petitioner and he felt relieved on going through the same and suggested her to exhibit the same order written on boards on the entrance road of the house and as well as on its boundary wall which was done immediately. Therefore, if this assertion made is true then what happens, the order of this Court was shown to him on 25-8-2001 and on seeing this he suggested the petitioner to hang the notice in a Notice Board but admittedly, the case of the petitioner is that she applied for certified copy of the order dated 14-8-2001 on 26-8-2001 and got the certified copy on 28-8-2001. Therefore, by no stretch of imagination it can be said to be true and is ex facie false and concocted story because from the contempt petition it appears that admittedly she applied for certified copy on 26-8-2001 and the same was delivered on 28-8-2001. Therefore, before 28-8-2001 the said colonel could not have any opportunity of going through any such order of this Court and there was no possibility whatsoever on the part of the petitioner to hang any board containing the said order of this court. Therefore, it appears that the statement made in paragraph Nos. 1 and 2 of the said affidavit are nothing but a blatant lie and concocted story created to strengthen the case. Thus, we find substance in the submission of Mr Mahbubey Alam that this affidavit is nothing but an after-thought and is created for the purpose of this case. In the contempt petition also this fact is not stated. we do not find any earthly reason why such an important and material fact will be omitted by the petitioner in drawing up her application for contempt. Therefore, this affidavit does, not in fact, support the case of the petitioner, rather it demolishes her case. For the reasons stated above we also cannot put any credence on the statement of fact made by the deponent in paragraph No.3 of the said affidavit.</u>

33. Here it may also be mentioned that in the writ petition the petitioner has given the Plot No. as 753 but in the pleader's certificate the plot number has been mentioned as 5763 measuring an area of 28 decimals whereas the admitted position is that after her purchase she subsequently transferred about 8 decimals of land to her two sons and this fact was suppressed by her both in the writ petition as well as in this contempt petition from which it appears that the contempt petitioner is in the habit of telling lie. By supplementary affidavit the petitioner tried to establish the fact that the structures that were standing on the case land were let out to one Brigadier Sharif Aziz with effect from 1-2-2001 and in that agreement also she described herself as sole owner of the entire land, whereas she had already transferred 8 decimals of land to her two sons and that fact has been established beyond any doubt from the supplementary affidavit filed by the contemner No. 3. But in the writ petition she claimed the land to be more or less. 30 decimals. It further appears that the structures were let out at a monthly rental of Taka 35,000. Admittedly, the structures were semipucca structures and nowhere within the four corners of the case record she has ever stated as to whether she pays income tax. Even if it is assumed that the petitioner had no other source of earning then also the income derived from property becomes taxable. Therefore, she must have been an income tax payee. Her silence in this regard casts doubt about the quntum of rent.

34. In the Supplementary-affidavit-in-opposition dated 23-6-2002 to fortify her contention that the structures of the petitioner were demolished on 25-8-2001 she annexed a copy of the 'Daily Sangbad', dated 24-8-2001. From that it appears that the eviction started on 3rd of August, 2001 and continued till 25-8-2001. Here it should be mentioned that no affidavit-in-reply to the supplementary affidavit-in-opposition filed by the contemner No.1 has been filed by the petitioner. Therefore, the factual aspects which have been asserted in the supplementary affidavit-in-opposition remain uncontroversial. If these factual aspects are taken into consideration it appears that there is no doubt that the structures of the petitioner were demolished on 25-8-2001. In paragraph No. 17 of the said supplementary affidavit-in-opposition it has been positively stated by the condemners that the petitioner of the contempt petition was evicted by 25-8-2001 and subsequent to the eviction some of the unauthorized occupants again tried to raise constructions and to remove them RAJUK again requested to depute police and bulldozer to remove and demolish the pica building and structures and in the event of non-denial of this fact by the petitioner, it is established beyond any doubt that the petitioner was evicted from her land by 25-8-2001. Therefore, in this view of the matter, without entering into the controversy as to whether the lawyer's certificate or the certified copy of the order of this Court dated 14-8-2001 was served or not on 25-8-2001 and 28-8-2001 respectively it could be said that the eviction of the petitioner was carried out by the contemners on 25-8-2001 without any knowledge of the aforesaid order and this view of ours is also fortified from other facts and circumstances. It has already been noted that another owner of land filed writ petition No. 3500 of 2001 in which he obtained Rule and stay and that order of stay was vacated by this Division at the instance of contemner No. 1 on 14-8-2001. Here it may be noted that on that date incidentally the learned Advocate of the petitioner Mr Farid Ahmed was present in the Court Room when the stay was vacated. Being aggrieved by that order the aforesaid writ petitioner filed Miscellaneous Petition No. 519 of 2001 before the Appellate Division and at the time of hearing of that application also the learned Advocate Mr Farid Ahmed was present in the court room but did not disclose the fact that while moving the Writ Petition No. 3705 of 2001 before this Division he obtained an order of injunction against the contemners. This fact betrays normal human behaviour. It further appears from the supplementary affidavit that as soon as the Appellate Division passed an order for maintaining status quo the eviction of the petitioner of Writ Petition No. 3500 of 2001 was stopped at the instance of the contemner No.1 when he was so informed by the RAJUK's Magistrate that an order has been passed by the Appellate Division for maintaining status quo in respect of their land. Therefore, it was urged before us by Mr Mahbubey Alam that when the RAJUK stopped the eviction of the petitioner of Writ Petition No. 3500 of 2001 at the telephonic instruction of Chairman of RAJUK for what purpose and for what earthly reason they would proceed against the petitioner in evicting her from her land violating High Court's order. Moreover, there is no allegation against the contemners that they had any enmity or personal grudge against the petitioner. There is no such allegation against the contemners. Therefore, admittedly the contemners have no personal interest whatsoever in evicting the petitioner from the case land.

35. There is, however, another aspect of the case which has not been noticed by the learned Advocates of either of the parties. A copy of the Demand of Justice Notice has been annexed by the petitioner with the contempt petition as Annexure "D" where in paragraph No. 3 of the said Demand of Justice Notice it is asserted that the certified copy of the judgment was received on 26-10-2001 and the certified copy of the judgment was communicated to all the respondents on 26-10-2001 through courier service as well as by hand. Then, if this is true then the contempt petitioner has no cause of action. According to her own version, she had communicated the order on 26-10-2001 after the alleged eviction of her on 25-8-2001 and the same statement has been reiterated by the petitioner in paragraph No. 4 of the said notice. It might be a genuine printing mistake but at no point of time till to-day it has been said so. We have already pointed out that in the instant proceeding the contemners are entitled to get the benefit of doubt. In view of the assertion made in paragraph Nos. 3 and 4 of the Demand of Justice Notice it appears that the instant contempt petition seems to be a vexatious proceeding initiated only to harass and create pressure upon the officials of RAJUK.

36. Be that as it may, there is another aspect which also stares at the contempt petitioner. In the writ petition she has referred to the plot number as 753 whereas in the lawyer's certification which is annexed as Annexure 'B' to the contempt petition the plot number has been described as 5763 and the quantum of land has been described as more or less 30 decimals. Besides, from Annexure H(2), that is, a photograph annexed to the affidavit-in-reply it appears that in the hanging notice board the plot was also described as plot No. 5763 which is admittedly not the plot number which is mentioned in writ petition No. 3705 of 2001 and admittedly, the petitioner was not the owner of that plot.

In the light of our aforesaid discussions we do not find any merit in this Rule and accordingly, this Rule is discharged and the condemners are acquitted of the charges leveled against them.

End.

full_judgment:
This Rule obtained on an application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure by the plaintiff is directed against the judgment and decree dated 24-6-92 (decree signed on 1-7-92) passed by the Additional District Judge, 3rd Court, Mymensingh in Other Class Appeal No.368 of 1986 allowing the appeal by reversing the judgment and decree dated 13-8-86 (decree signed on 20-9-86) passed by the Assistant Judge, Gouripur in Other Class Suit No.15 of 1986 decreeing the suit in part.

2. The petitioner as plaintiff filed Other Class Suit No.15 of 1986 in the court of Assistant Judge, Gouripur for declaration against the opposite parties that the dismissal order dated 24-12-85 served on him is illegal, void, inoperative and not binding upon him and he is still in service of defendant corporation and there was a further prayer for reinstatement in the former post.

3. The case of the plaintiff is, that the plaintiff petitioner incurred displeasure of defendant opposite party No.2 in connection with the collection of taxes from him for his holding before he was elected Chairman of the Gouripur Pourashava and that he had enmity with the defendant opposite party No.15 in the matter of family affairs and in order to put him into a quandary, they managed to dismiss him from the service of the Pourashava vide dismissal order dated 24-12-85 issued under Memo No. 625 and served upon the plaintiff petitioner by the defendant-opposite party No. 2.

4. The further case of the plaintiff-petitioner is that since his appointment as Tax Collector he was discharging his duties very much honestly and diligently to the best of his capabilities. He further contended that he was given no show cause notice at all and he was given no personal hearing or pre-hearing before his dismissal from the service of the Pourashava in accordance with provisions of Local Council Servants (Efficiency and Discipline) Rules, 1968.

5. The defendant-opposite parties contested the suit by filing a written statement contending that the suit is not maintainable for want of cause of action, that the suit is barred by the principles of estoppel, waiver and acquiesence. That the suit is not maintainable inasmuch as the plaintiff-petitioner did not file an appeal under section 3 of the Municipal Committee (Appeals) Rules, 1960. Further case of the defendant-opposite parties is that he was dismissed from service after compliance with the requirements of law in that he was given show cause notice and after considering the reply thereto the plaintiff-petitioner was found guilty of misconduct as levelled in the letter dated 31-8-85 and Municipal Committees in a meeting held on 22-12-85 brought charge against the plaintiff-petitioner and decided to dismiss the plaintiff-petitioner from his service and authorised the Chairman, the defendant No.2, to take necessary action and in pursuance of that authority defendant No.2 vide letter dated 24-12-85 dismissed the plaintiff-petitioner from service on the grounds that he was found guilty of misconduct.

6. The plaintiff examined himself as witness in support of his case before the trial Court and the defendant-opposite parties-examined 4 witnesses including the defendant-opposite party No.15 in support of their case and the trial Court on consideration of the materials and evidence on record decreed the suit in part holding that the Pourashava did not comply with the provisions of Local Council Servants (Efficiency and Discipline) Rules 1968 and there has been violation of the principle of natural justice and, as such, set aside the order of dismissal dated 24-12-85 and directed the defendant-opposite parties to hold inquiry in respect of charges levelled against the plaintiff-petitioner by appointing an Inquiry Officer and to take appropriate action against the plaintiff-petitioner on the basis of the inquiry report of that committee.

7. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and decree of the trial Court the defendant-opposite parties preferred an appeal before the District Judge, Mymensingh which on transfer was heard by the Additional District Judge, 3rd Court, Mymensingh who allowed the appeal and dismissed the suit on 3 grounds namely, that the suit is not maintainable for want of notice under section 152 of the Pourashava Ordinance, 1977; that the suit is also not maintainable for not preferring any appeal under the provision of Local Council Servants (Efficiency and Discipline) Rule, 1968 and also on the ground that the plaintiff petitioner was given 2 show cause notices before his dismissal and, as such, the principles of natural justice was complied with.

8. The plaintiff petitioner being aggrieved by the said judgment and decree of the appellate Court below preferred an application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure before this court and obtained the present Rule.

9. Mr. Sk. Afzalur Rahman, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff-petitioners-submits that the finding of the appellate Court that the suit is not maintainable for want of service of notice under section 152 of the Pourashava Ordinance, 1977 is not tenable in law inasmuch as section 152 of the Pourashava Ordinance, 1977 does not contemplate that a notice is a must before filing of any suit against a Pourashava in the civil Court. He further submits with much emphasis that the provision of service of notice as provided in section 152 of the Pourashava Ordinance, 1977 is not mandatory, rather it is directory and for that purpose he relies on the decision reported in 39 DLR 145. His second submission is that in the instant case it is crystal clear from the materials and evidence on record that the defendant-opposite parties have dismissed the plaintiff-petitioner from service of Pourashava without complying with the provisions laid down in the Local Council Servants (Efficiency and Discipline) Rules, 1968 and as such, the order of dismissal is per se illegal and without jurisdiction. He finally, submits that admittedly in this case there has been a violation of the principle of natural justice and on that count also the impugned judgment is liable to be set aside.

10. Mr. Jashimuddin Ahmed, the learned Advocate appearing for  the defendant-opposite parties, submits that the provision of section 152 of the Pourashava Ordinance, 1977 is a mandatory provision and not directory and anyone who wants to file a suit against a Pourashava must comply with the provision of section 152 before he is entitled to approach the civil Court, and in support of his contention he relies on the decision reported in 46 DLR 295 which is a decision with regard to the interpretation of section 152 of the Pourashava Ordinance, 1977. The learned Advocate further submits that the said case has every manner of application in the facts and circumstances of the present case. To fortify his said submission the learned Advocate also relies on the case reported in 41 DLR 332. The learned Advocate further submits that the Local Council Servants (Efficiency and Discipline) Rules, 1968 provides for preferring an appeal against any order passed by a Pourashava against its employees and in the instant case the plaintiff-petitioner without preferring any appeal as contemplated in the Local Council Servants (Efficiency and Discipline) Rules, 1968 has approached the civil Court and on that count also the suit is not maintainable. The learned Advocate next submits that the Pourashava Ordinance, 1977 is a special Act and the Civil Procedure Code is a general law so the provision as contained in the Pourashava Ordinance will get preference to the provisions of Civil Procedure Code and if there be any conflict between the two the provision of the Pourashava Ordinance will prevail. In this connection he relies on a decision reported in 1988 BLD (AD) 66. The learned Advocate further submits that in the instant case as many as two show cause notices were served upon the plaintiff-petitioner and after complying with the provisions as laid down in the Local Council Servants (Efficiency and Discipline) Rules, 1968, the defendant-opposite parties have dismissed the plaintiff-petitioner from service and, as such, it cannot be stated by any stretch of imagination that there has been any violation of the principle of natural justice in the instant case.

11. The learned Advocate further submits that section 152 of the Pourashava Ordinance is not directory but mandatory. He submits that on a persual of the section itself it is crystal clear that this section contemplates that a plaintiff must state in the plaint itself that a notice under section 152 of the Pourashava Ordinance, 1977 has been served before filing of the suit and this shows that the notice is a must for filing a suit against the Pourashava. In this connection the learned Advocate also refers to and relies on a decision reported in PLD 1960 (Lahore) 488, wherein it has been held that when the affairs of the Municipality is managed by a public officer no suit will lie against him in respect of any act performed by him in his official capacity in the absence of notice under section 80 of the Code. In the instant case the defendant No.15 is the Secretary of the Pourashava who is admittedly a public servant and a suit cannot be filed against him without serving any notice under section 80 of the Code of Civil Procedure and on that count also that suit is not maintainable.

12. It appears on a perusal of the judgment of the appellate Court below that the appellate Court below has dismissed the suit and allowed the appeal on 8 counts. The first ground is, that the suit it not maintainable for non-compliance with the provision of section 152 of the Pourashava Ordinance or, in other words, non-service of notice on the Pourashava under section 152 of the Pourashava Ordinance disentitles the plaintiff to file the suit. The second ground on which the judgment of the trial Court was reversed is, that the Local Council Servants (Efficiency and Discipline) Rules, 1968, provides for preferring an appeal against the order passed by the Pourashava against its employee and in the instant case admittedly the plaintiff petitioner without preferring an appeal as contemplated in the Local Council Servants (Efficiency and Discipline) Rules, 1968 has instituted the suit and on that count also the suit it not maintainable for not preferring an appeal as contemplated by rule 12 of Local Council Servants (Efficiency and Discipline) Rules, 1968 by the plaintiff-petitioner. The third ground for dismissing the suit by the appellate Court is that the plaintiff petitioner was given chance to show cause and he was given as many as 2 chances to show cause and as such he was given full opportunities to defend himself before he was dismissed from service.

13. The learned Appellate Court below held that as many as 2 show cause notices were served upon the plaintiff petitioner and, as such, according to him the plaintiff-petitioner was given sufficient opportunity to defend himself. On a perusal of the materials and evidence on record it appears that the plaintiff petitioners was placed under supervision vide letter dated 19-8-1985 and he was asked to show cause within 3 days of the receipt of the said letter as to why he should not be removed from service. On receipt of the said letter the plaintiff submitted his reply on 29-8-1985 and on receipt of the said explanation the defendant No.2 suspended the plaintiff from his service with effect from 1-9-1985 vide letter dated 19-8-85 and he was directed to hand over the charge to one Abdur Rashid, Tax Collector-cum-Cashier of the said Pourashava. It appears from this letter that it contains 13 charges but there is no indication in this letter that the plaintiff was asked to explain his position in writing with regard to those charges nor any inquiry committee was constituted as is contemplated by the Local Council Servants (Efficiency and Discipline) Rules 1968. Thereafter vide letter dated 24-12-85 the plaintiff-petitioner was dismissed from service under Memo No.625/1 (2) dated 24-12-85 without giving him any opportunity to explain his position with regard to the alleged charges. It is crystal clear from the contents of the letter dated 24-12-85 that the Municipal Commissioners in a meeting held on 22-12-85 considered the charges brought against this plaintiff-petitioner and after considering the relevant records maintained by the Municipality found the plaintiff-petitioner guilty of the charges and decided to dismiss him from service for the alleged misconduct and authorised the defendant No.2, Chairman of the Pourashava, to take necessary action in that regard. So it is crystal clear from the materials and evidence on record that the plaintiff petitioner has been been condemned without giving any pre-hearing. It, thus, appears to me that in dismissing the plaintiff-petitioner from the service of the Pourashava the defendants have violated the principles of audi alteram partem. In this connection we may refer to a decision reported in 16 DLR (SC) 722 wherein it has been held that whenever any person or body of persons is empowered to take decisions after ex post facto investigation into facts which would result in consequences affecting the person, property or other right of another person, then in the absence of any express words in the enactment giving such power excluding the application of the principles of natural justice, the courts of law are inclined generally to imply that the power so given is coupled with a duty to act in accordance with such principles of natural justice as may be applicable in the facts and circumstances of a given case.

14. In the instant case the plaintiff-petitioner is an employee of a statutory corporation and his service is regulated by statutory rules. The Local Council Servant (Efficiency and Discipline) Rules, 1968 provides the procedure for holding an inquiry against its employees on the charges of inefficiency, misconduct and corruption and Rule 8 contemplates that where an employee is proceeded against under clause (a), or clause (b) or clause (c) of Rule 3, and the authority has decided that the case is for a major penalty, the authority shall appoint an officer, being senior in rank to the person proceeded against, to be inquiry officer and to conduct the proceedings.

15. Rule 8(2) provides that the Inquiry Officer shall hear the case from day to day, and no adjournment shall be given except for reasons to be recorded in writing. Rule 8(4) provides that the Inquiry Officer shall, within ten days of the conclusion of the proceedings, submit his findings and grounds thereof to the authority. Rule 9(1) provides that an employee against whom action is proposed to be taken under clause (b) or (c) or Rule 3 may be placed under suspension if, in the opinion of the authority, suspension is necessary or expedient.

16. Rule 3 postulates the grounds for penalty and Rule 4 sub-rule 1(a) and (b) classifies minor penalties and sub-rule 1(c) (d)(e)(f) and (g) classifies major penalties and Rule 6 sub-rule 5(a) provides that in cases calling for major penalty, the authority having power to impose the penalty shall frame a charge and communicate it to the accused together with a statement of allegations on which it is based and of any other circumstances which the authority proposes to take into consideration when passing orders on the case. Sub-rule (b) of Rule 6 provides that the authority shall require the accused, within a reasonable time, which shall not be less than seven days or more than fourteen days from the date the charge has been communicated to him, to put in a written defence stating at the same time whether he desires to be heard in person.

17. Sub-rule 5(c) of Rule 6 provides that if the accused so desires, or if the authority concerned so directs, an inquiry officer to be appointed under Rule 8 shall hold an oral inquiry at which oral evidence shall be heard as to such of the allegations as are not admitted, and the accused shall be entitled to cross-examine the witnesses against him, to give evidence in person and to have such witnesses called for the defence as he may wish, provided the inquiry officer may, for the reasons to be recorded in writing, refuse to call a particular witness or to summon or admit particular evidence.

18. It is contemplated by sub-rule 5(d) of Rule 6 that the proceedings shall contain a sufficient record and of the evidence and the Inquiry Officer's report of his findings and the grounds thereof.

19. Similarly, it is provided in sub-rule 5(e) of Rule 6 that when the authority having considered the report, has arrived at a provisional coalusion as to the penalty to be imposed, it shall so inform the accused and supply him with a copy of the report and call upon him to show cause within a reasonable time, which shall not be less than seven days, nor more than fourteen days, why the penalty proposed should not be imposed. The authority should take into consideration any cause shown by the accused before passing orders.

20. So it is apparent in the instant case that in dismissing the plaintiff-petitioner from the service of the Pourashava the authority of the Pourashava miserably failed to comply with any of the provisions as laid down in the Local Council Servants (Efficiency and Discipline) Rules, 1968 and in that view of the matter the finding of the appellate Court below that the plaintiff-petitioner was given sufficient opportunity to defend himself is absolutely erroneous and contrary to the materials and evidence on record and that finding of the appellate Court below cannot be sustained at all. In this connection we may also refer to a decision reported in 31 DLR (AD) 33 wherein it has been held that while it is open to a domestic Tribunal enquiring into the conduct of an officer to collect materials and examine witnesses behind the back of the officer concerned for the purpose of framing the charges, the principles of natural justice require of a tribunal that such witnesses must be allowed to be cross-examined by the delinquent officer for the purpose of giving probative value to the statements of these witnesses. The denial of such opportunity would render the trial ineffective for violation of the principles of natural justice.

21. The domestic Tribunal, if not so prescribed by the rules, may not take evidence strictly as required by the Evidence Act. It must, however, be remembered that the law requires that such tribunals should observe rules of natural justice in the conduct of the enquiry and if they do so their decision is not liable to be impeached on the ground that the procedure followed was not in accordance with that which obtains in a Court of Law. The Indian Supreme Court in the case of Mysore and others vs. Shivabasappa Shivappa Makapur reported in AIR 1963 (SC) 375, has also held that tribunals exercising quasi-judicial functions are not courts and that, therefore, they are not bound to follow the procedure prescribed for trial of actions in courts nor they are bound by strict rules of evidence. They can, unlike courts, obtain all information material for the points under enquiry from all sources and through all channels, without being fettered by rules and procedure, which govern proceedings in court. The only obligation which the law casts on them is that they should not act on any information which they may receive unless they put it to the party against whom it is to be used and give him a fair opportunity to explain it.

22. Lord Loreburn LC in the case of Board of Education vs. Rice and others reported in 1911 Appeal Cases 182, observed that the authority can obtain information in any way they think best, always giving a fair opportunity to those who are parties in the controversy for correcting or contradicting any relevant statement prejudicial to their view. This view was also reiterated by the House of Lords in the case of Local Government Board vs. Arlidge 1951 (Appeal Cases) 120. Our Appellate Division in an unreported case namely, Civil Appeal No.138 of 1977, has held that the order passed by the Screening Board also requires observance of the principles of natural justice as the law is silent as to exclusion of principle of natural justice. In that case it has also been held that whenever any person is likely to be affected adversely in respect of his property or other legal right in any ex-post facto investigation, he must be given a trial ensuring the elementary and essental principles of fairness. In the instant case we have already found that the Local Council Servants (Efficiency and Discipline) Rule, 1968, provides for the observance of principle of natural justice in the matter of taking any disciplinary action against an employee of a Pourashava and it has been found that the defendant-opposite parties have failed to observe those Rules in taking disciplinary action which culminated in the dismissal of the plaintiff-petitioner from the service. In this connection it may be stated that an employee of a Pourashava is not governed by the Rules of Master and Servant. The plaintiff petitioner is an employee of a statutory authority and it is expected that the statutory authority in taking disciplinary action affecting the right of the employee should observe the procedure as laid down in the Rule of Local Council Servants (Efficiency and Discipline) Rules, 1968. In the instant case we find that the defendant opposite parties have wilfully violated those provisions of the rules and in contravention of those rules held a meeting of the commissioners on 22-12-85 for considering the charges brought against the plaintiff-petitioner and on the basis of materials available on their record unilaterally found the plaintiff-petitioner guilty of the charges and authorised the chairman of the Pourashava to dismiss the petitioner from the services. The chairman, therefore vide his letter dated 24-12-85 dismissed the plaintiff-petitioner from the service of the Pourashava without affording him any opportunity to controvert the charges. It is, thus, clear that the said dismissal order is violative of the principles of natural justice.

23. We have already found that the second ground for setting aside the judgment of the trial Court and allowing the appeal is that the appellate Court below has found that there is provision for appeal in the Local Council Servants (Efficiency and Discipline) Rules, 1968 and the plaintiff-petitioner by passing that provision went to the civil Court to redress his grievance and on that count the appellate Court below found fault with the plaintiff petitioner and observed that non-compliance with Rule 12 which provides for an appeal disentitled the plaintiff-petitioner to file a suit before the civil Court.

24. Mr. Jashimuddin Ahmed, the learned Advocate appearing for the defendants-opposite parties, argues that non-compliance with Rule 12 of the Local Council Servants (Efficiency and Discipline) Rules, 1968, will stand as a bar on the way of the plaintiff-petitioner in seeking any relief before a civil Court. As against that the submission of Mr. Sk. Afzalur Rahman is that it is, a case in which there has been violation of the principles of natural justice, so, non-compliance with Rule 12 will not stand as a bar on the way of the plaintiff-petitioner in going to the civil Court. In a case reported in 13 DLR (SC) 105, it has been held that non-exhaustion of the remedy by way of appeal will not stand on the way of an aggrieved party in approaching the High Court in its writ jurisdiction when the order is attacked on the ground of want of authority. Similarly, in a case reported in 19 DLR 592, the High Court has held that nothwithstanding provisions of appeal made in the Sea Customs Act and Sales Tax Act, in a case where it is found that the relief contemplated by preference of such appeal is not equally effective, efficacious and inexpensive, the affected party can come for relief under the writ jurisdiction and article 98 imposes a bar to approach the court under writ jurisdiction if there is efficacious and inexpensive remedy but if the alternative remedy is not effective or efficacious the aggrieved party giving a go-by to the appeal can approach the Court. This proposition has been reiterated by the Supreme Court in the case reported in 22 DLR (SC) 98. In that case it has been held that ordinarily, a party in revenue matters should exhaust all his remedies by way of appeal before invoking the aid of the civil Court. But where the allegation of a party is that the impugned order is a nullity in the eye of law, there is ample authority that in such case the jurisdiction of the civil Court is not barred. In the instant case the plaintiff petitioner's case is that without observing the rule laid down in the Local Council Servants (Efficiency and Discipline) Rules, 1968, the defendants- opposite parties with malafide intention dismissed him from service and, as such, the order of dismissal is ex facie illegal and without jurisdiction and in that view of the matter the non-compliance with Rule 12 of the said Rules cannot stand as a bar in approaching the civil Court. There is another decision reported in 22 DLR (SC) 443 wherein it has been held that when an order passed by some authority suffers from an illegality which is apparent on the face of the record, an order in the nature of a certiorari could always issue, even though a right of statutory appeal had not been availed of. It cannot, therefore, be said as a general rule that wherever another remedy is provided by law the remedy of approaching the court under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act will not be available to an aggrieved party, In the case reported in 31 DLR 184, decided under the writ jurisdiction, it has been held that if the order passed 'on the face of it is violative of any provision of the constitution, it is without jurisdiction, and cannot be allowed to stand even though the person affected did not avail of the alternative available remedy. In that case it was observed that an alternative remedy was available but it was not availed of. Ordinarily, writ jurisdiction is not available to a person who does not seek alternative remedy provided by law but this provision may be waived if an impugned order is, on the face of it, without jurisdiction or is violative of any provision of the constitution. In another case decided by the Appellate Division which is reported in BLD 1988 (AD) 84, it has been held that if the writ jurisdiction is sought to be invoked raising purely a question of law or interpretation of statute, availability of alternative remedy will not stand in the way. This is the consistent view taken by the superior courts of this sub-continent including our Appellate Division and from a review of all these decisions it appears that be it in the writ jurisdiction or in the civil Court, non-compliance with alternative remedy provided by way of appeal will not disentitle a party to approach the civil Court seeking relief therein if the order is ex-facie bad, illegal and without jurisdiction. In the instant case we have already found that the defendant- opposite parties dismissed the plaintiff from the service without observing statutory rules and without giving him any opportunity to explain his conduct and on top of that without proving the allegations leveled against him. This dismissal order is, therefore, arbitrary which cannot withstand scrutiny of law and the order is ex-facie bad, illegal and without jurisdiction and in that view of the matter I find no substance in the submission made by Mr. Jashimuddin Ahmed that the non-availability of the forum of appeal under rule 12 of the Local Council Servants (Efficiency and Discipline) Rules, 1968 bars the instant suit.

25. Mr. Jashimuddin, the learned Advocate appearing for the defendant-opposite parties, found it difficult to substantiate his submission that there has been no violation of the principle of natural justice or that there has been no violation of the provisions of Local Council Servants (Efficiency and Discipline) Rules, 1968, in dismissing the plaintiff-petitioner from his service by order dated 24-12-85.

26. In the instant case, section 152 of the Pourashava Ordinance, 1977 is of much importance to determine the important question as to whether the suit is maintainable for want of service of notice. Mr. SK. Afzalur Rahman, the learned Advocate, appearing for the plaintiff petitioner, submits that this section is not mandatory rather it is directory and in support of his contention he relies on the decision reported in 39 DLR 145. On the other hand, Mr. Jashimuddin Ahmed, the learned Advocate appearing for the defendant opposite parties, with much emphasis, submits that the provision as contemplated in section 152 of the Pourashava Ordinance, 1977 is mandatory one and no one can approach the civil Court without complying with the provision of section 152 of the said Ordinance and he further submits that this very section came up for consideration before this court in a case reported in 46 DLR 295, wherein a Single Bench of this court after considering the import and tenor of section 152 of the Pourashava Ordinance, 1977 has held that the service of notice as contemplated in section 152 is a pre-condition for filing a suit against a Pourashava in a civil Court, and in support of his contention he also relies on another decision reported in 41 DLR 332. To fortify his submission Mr. Jashimuddin Ahmed relies on these two decisions. The 41 DLR case relates to section 109 of the Chittagong Port Authority Act which contemplates that no suit shall be brought against the trustees for anything purporting to be done under this Act, until the expiration of one month next after notice in writing has been delivered or left at the office of the Trustees or at the place of abode of such person, stating the cause of suit and the name and place of abode of the intending plaintiff, and unless such notice is proved, the court shall dismiss the suit. In view of the provisions of section 109(1) of the Chittagong Port Act, 1914, it was held that the court has no alternative but to dismiss the suit where the plaintiff fails to comply with the mandatory requirement of section 109(1) of the Act. In that case no notice was served as contemplated in section 109(1) of the Act and, as such, it was held that the trial Court rightly dismissed the suit for want of notice. In the context of Chittagong Port Act, 1914, it was held that section 109(1) of the said Act is mandatory. That does not necessarily mean that section 152 of the Pourashava Ordinance, 1977, is also a mandatory provision. So this case, in fact, does not help Mr. Jashimuddin Ahmed. Now we are to examine the true import and tenor of section 152 and see as to whether the provision of section 152 of the Ordinance is mandatory one. Section 152 of the Pourashava Ordinance, 1977 reads as under :

"No suit shall be instituted against a Pourashava, or against any commissioner, officer, or employee of a Pourashava in respect of any act done or purporting to be done in official capacity, until the expiration of one month next after notice in writing has been, in the case of a Pourashava, delivered or left at its office, and in the case of a commissioner, officer or employee, delivered to him or left at his office or place of abode, stating the cause of action and the name and place of abode of the intending plaintiff and the plaint shall contain a statement that such notice has been so delivered or left."

27. This very provision of section 152 of the Ordinance came up for consideration before a Single Bench of this court and the case has been reported in 46 DLR 295 wherein it has been held that notice under section 152 of the Pourashava Ordinance, 1977 is a prerequisite in all circumstance for institution of a suit against Pourashava for anything done in official capacity. That suit was instituted for permanent injunction restraining the Narayangonj Pourashava from interfering with the plaintiff's possession in the suit land. The case of the plaintiff was that he was the owner of the property recorded in his name in RS khatian which orginally appertained to CS plot No.278 and the contention of Pourashava was that the suit land was part of CS plot No.279 appertaining to khatian No.670 belonging to the Pourashava and the plaintiff who got his name mutated in the Pourashava papers by fraudulent means was an unauthorised occupant therein and, as such, liable to be evicted. Non-maintainability of the suit for want of notice under section 152 of the Pourashava Ordinance was also pleaded in the defence.

28. The learned Munsif decreed the suit holding that the suit land belonged to the plaintiff. On the question of maintainability of the suit he held that the notice issued upon the plaintiff by the municipality having not mentioned the suit plot and the defendants having no valid claim in respect thereof the notice under section 152 of the Pourashava Ordinance was not required to be served before institution of the suit. In the appeal preferred by the defendants the learned Subordinate Judge also arrived at concurrent findings including a finding that the issue of notice under section 152 before institution of the suit was not a necessity. Against the judgment of affirmance the Narayanganj Pourashava preferred a revisional application before the High Court Division. Only one point was urged before the High Court Division that is, that the act complained of was done in discharge of official duty and, as such, no suit can be filed without prior notice. On the other hand, it was submitted by the plaintiff that the action taken by the Pourashava having not been in relation to the property of the Pourashava, the action could not be held to have been in discharge of any official act and, as such, no notice was at all necessary. In deciding the question as to whether the prior notice is a must or not the learned Single Judge in interpreting section 152 of the Ordinance observed that section 152 of the Ordinance contemplates absolute prohibition. It is not a case in which the court would start with initial jurisdiction and then come to a finding whether the suit could be entertained at all. It is a case in which the suit could not at all be instituted without notice and without a statement to that effect in the body of the plaint. The learned Judge further observed that the notice under section 152 of the Ordinance is a pre-requisitite in all circumstances for institution of a suit against the Pourashava for anything done in official capacity. The learned Judge also held that notice under section 152 is a mandatory one.

29. For the interpretation of section 152 of the Ordinance it would be profitable for us if we try to discover the true import and tenor of the section. It appears that it is not a new provision. Similar provision was embodied in the Municipal Acts of different provinces of British India. Similar provision requiring prior notice for filing a suit against a municipality found place in the Municipal Act of this Sub-continent as early as 1854 and the said provisions have been interpreted by the superior Courts of this sub-continent for more than a century. There is a long line of decisions that a notice as contemplated in section 152 of the Ordinance may act as bar for the institution of a suit against a Pourashava if the act complained of is a past act and that the act complained of was done by the municipality within its statutory limit. Even in case of past act, the act complained of if it does not come within the perimeter of statutory limits, no notice is necessary at all. In the case reported in ILR 6 Calcuta 8 which was decided in 1880, it was held that section 87 of Bengal Act III of 1864 which is similar to the present section 152 of the Ordinance, 1977 is applicable only in those cases where the plaintiff claims damages or compensation for some wrongful act committed by the commissioners or their officers, in the exercise, or honestly supposed exercise, of their statutory powers. It has been further held that the notice in the earlier part of the section is meant to give the defendant an opportunity of making some pecuniary amends for the wrong, without incurring the cost of litigation. In the case reported in ILR (All.) Vol.1 269, in interpreting similar provision namely, section 43 of the Local Government Act, it was held that the notice previous to suing a Municipal Committee for a thing done by them under that Act required by section 43 of the Act is only necessary where compensation is claimed for the thing done. It was further held that the plea that notice was given as required by section 43 cannot be taken for the first time in special appeal. In the instant suit it is also found that the defendants have neither taken this plea of want of notice in their written statement nor they asserted that point before the trial Court. In the case reported in AIR 1939 (Lahore) 254 similar provision namely, section 49 of Punjab Municipal Act, Act 3 of 1911, came up for consideration. The Lahore High Court held that where a Municipal Committee has served notice on a person to remove structures on the ground that the land belonged to the Committee and that person brings a suit for a declaration that the site in dispute was owned and possessed by him without giving notice to the Committee, the suit is not barred by section 49. In another decision reported in PLD 1954 (Lahore) 599 the same view has been reiterated by the Lahore High Court about section 49 of the Punjab Municipal Act. In the case reported in ILR 22 Bombay 605, section 48 of the District Municipal Act (Bom. Act 11 of 1884) came up for consideration. Section 48(1) of the District Municipal Act (Born. Act 11 of 1884) runs as follows:

"No action shall be commenced against any municipality or against any officer of a municipality, for anything done, or purporting to have been done, in pursuance of this Act, or of the principal Act, without giving to such Municipality, officer, servant or person one month's previous notice in writing of the intended action and of the cause thereof, nor after three months from the date of the act complained of, and in the case of any such action for damages, if tender of sufficient amends shall have been made before the action was brought, the plaintiff shall not recover more than the amount so tendered, and shall pay all costs incurred by the defendant after such tender.",

That was a suit brought against a municipality to recover possession of a piece of land taken by it, for damages for pulling down a wall on the land, and for an injunction. It was held that as regards damages the suit came under section 48 of the District Municipal Act (Bom. Act 11 of 1884), but as regards possession and injunction notice of action was not necessary under the section. In another case which is reported in the same volume at page 637, it has been held that section 48 of the Bombay District Municipal Act does not apply to a suit for specific performance of contract or for breach thereof because such a suit is not an action for anything done or purporting to be done in pursuance of the Bombay District Municipal Act, for the Act, though it may give the Municipality power to make contracts, does not authorise them to refuse to perform them. There is yet another decision reported in the same volume which involves the interpretation of the said section 48 of the Bombay District Municipal Act (Bom. Act 11 of 1884). The fact of the case is, that the plaintiff was inamder of the village of Dakor. He filed an ejectment suit against the Municipality of Dakor, alleging that the Municipality had illegally and wrongfully encroached upon a portion of the Gomti Lake at Dakor by laying the foundations of a building which they intended to erect for the purpose of a dharmsala. The Municipality pleaded, inter alia, that the suit was bad for want of notice of action under section 48 of the Bombay District Municipal Act (Bom. Act 11 of 1884). It was held by a majority of the Full Bench that the provisions of section 48 of Bombay Act 11 of 1884 do not apply to actions for the possession of land brought against a Municipality.

30. Similarly, section 48 of the District Municipal Act (Bom. Act 11 of 1884) came up for interpretation before the Bombay High Court in the case reported in ILR 25 (Born) 142. In that case the plaintiffs sued the Municipality of Parola to obtain a declaration that a certain building erected by them had been built in accordance with, and not in contravention of, orders issued by the Municipality, and further, to obtain an injunction restraining the Municipality from pulling it down. The Municipality contended that the suit was not maintainable, as no notice of the suit had been given as required by section 48 of the District Municipal Act. Their Lordships after reviewing all the decisions of different High Courts of this sub-continent came to the finding that for the purposes of section 48 what the court has to look to is the real object of the suit, and the section required notice only when the suit is for an act already done or purporting to have been already done, under the powers conferred. In such case only can it be necessary for the plaintiff to give an opportunity to make amends for compensation, and in such cases, the delay necessitated by notice is comparatively immaterial. But when the suit is not for an act already done, but to prevent an act from being irremediably, irrevocably done, neither can amends be claimable, nor can delay be obligatory. It is impossible to hold that a mere notice, a requisition or a threat to do a thing in the future, even though it is issued or made under the powers, is an act already done, or purporting to have been done, and there is nothing else alleged in this case that can be alleged to have been done by the Municipality. A notice, therefore, does not appear to have been made an indispensable preliminary to such a suit by section 48 of the Act. Similarly, in the case of Mayandi vs. Mequhae reported in ILR 1878 2 Madras 214 in interpreting section 168 of the Madras Town Improvement Act, 1871 which required notice "when a suit is brought against the commissioner for anything done under the Act," it was held that no notice was required in a suit to recover the balance due under a contract, for a breach of contract was not to be regarded as a thing done under the Act. In the case of Flower vs. Local Board of Low Leyton (1877) 5 Chancery Division 347, Jessel, MR, observed that the real object of the action was to prevent the continuance of an intolerable nuisance which plaintiff said he had suffered through the acts of the defendants; acts which apparently depended on the exercise of their statutory powers. The section (38 and 39, vict., cap. 55; sec. 264), requiring notice for anything done or intended to be done or omitted to be done under the provisions of this Act, it was held, was intended to apply to an action at law for damages, and its object was to give an opportunity to a local authority to make payment or tender of compensation for the damage sustained, but could not be intended to apply to a case where the local authority was improperly pulling down a house, for instance, or stopping up a sewer, and if that were so, it was added, it would amount to a licence to every Local Board to do what injury they pleased while the month's notice was running.

31. From a review of all these decisions it appears to me that the law is well settled on this point that a notice is required if the act complained of is a past act of the Municipality and not for threatening injury and the notice is indispensable one in case of past action where the Municipal authority or officer acted within their statutory authority but when the Municipality or its officers acted beyond their jurisdiction no notice is required for the institution of a suit by the aggrieved party. Unfortunately, this long line of decisions of the superior courts of this sub-continent were not cited before the learned Judge and the learned Judge had no opportunity to consider those decisions and without considering those decisions his Lordship has arrived at a finding that it is a pre-requisite in all circumstances for institution of a suit against the Paurashava for anything done in official capacity.

32. We have already noticed that in section 152 of the Pourashava Ordinance the  immunity is conferred on the Pourashava  Commissioner, officers and employees in  respect of any act done or purporting to have been done in official capacity. Similar expression finds place in section 197 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. In section 197 of the Criminal  Procedure Code it has been provided that  sanction is necessary to prosecute a Judge, a  Magistrate or a public servant who is not  removable from his office save by or with the sanction of the Government if he is accused of any offence alleged to have been committed  by him while acting or purporting to act in the discharge of his official duty. If the alleged offence is committed in discharge of official duty sanction is necessary but if the alleged offence is committed not in discharge of official duty no sanction is required. In interpreting this section Indian Supreme Court has held that misappropriation of money by the chairman is not an act in discharge of official duty (AIR 1983 SC 64) . Similarly, in a case reported in 1983 Pakistan Criminal Journal 1413, it has been held that when a Magistrate uses filthy language against the complainant in a case before him he does not act within the official capacity. It has been held in a number of cases that a public officer can only be said to act or purport to act in the discharge of his official duties, if his act is such as to be within the scope of his official duty. See 52 CWN 567, AIR 1948 PC 128+156, 76 IA 10, AIR 1949 PC 117). In determining the question whether a person committed an act while acting or purporting to act in the discharge of his official duty is a question of fact which must be determined in each case on the basis of materials and evidence on record. So, if we examine the provisions of section 152 of the Pourashava Ordinance from this angle we find that a suit against municipality cannot be thrown away for want of notice if the allegation is that the act done by the Municipality or its employee was not an act done in their official capacity. If the act complained of is without jurisdiction and beyond the statutory powers it can not be treated or termed as an act done in their official capacity. This aspect of section 152 of the Pourashava Ordinance was not considered in the case reported in 46 DLR 295.

33. There is another aspect. In this connection we may refer to section 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure which provides that any civil Court has the jurisdiction to try all suits of civil nature excepting suits of which their cognisance is either expressly or impliedly barred. Privy Council in the well- known case of Secretary of State vs. Mask & Co. reported in AIR 1940 (PC) 105 held that it is settled law that the exclusion of the jurisdiction of the civil Courts is not to be readily inferred, but that such exclusion must either be explicitly expressed or clearly implied. Even if jurisdiction is so excluded, the civil Courts have jurisdiction to examine into cases where the provisions of the Act have not been complied with, or the statutory tribunal has not acted in conformity with the fundamental principles of judicial procedure.

34. This case laid down a great principle of law which is being consistently followed by all the superior courts of this sub-continent. In the case of Md. Latif vs. Province of West Pakistan reported in PLD 1970 (SC) 180, where in spite of the provisions of law imposing bar of suit, the Supreme Court of Pakistan held that since the allegation was that the impugned order was a nullity in the eye of law, the jurisdiction of the civil Court was not barred. Section 14A of the East Bengal (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act 1948 provides :

"14A. Except as expressly provided in this Act, no civil Court shall entertain any suit or application against any order passed or any action taken under this Act and all suits and appeals pending in any such Court against any order passed or any action taken under this Act shall abate with effect from the date of coming into force of the East Bengal (Emergency) Requisition of Property (Amendment) Ordinance, 1963,"
