In a case reported in 17 DLR 263 this court observed that a suit, of course, lies if the impugned order is wholly outside the purview of the East Bengal (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948, otherwise, the validity of any act done under the said Act cannot be challenged in a suit or in any other manner except as allowed under section 14A quoted above. In other words, in order to prosecute an independent suit it must be shown that the impugned order cannot be passed or that the order does not amount to an order under the Act, that is to say, the order itself is incompetent, There is, however, a vital distinction between an order which cannot be made or which cannot be described as an order made under the Act and an order made by a competent authority for a valid purpose (when the purpose of the order is an essential element of its validity) but tainted with some irregularity or illegality for non-observance of some provision of the Act. In the former case a suit will lie, but in the latter eventuality the grievance can only be agitated under section 14A.

35. There is ouster clause in the Frontier Crimes Regulation. Sections 10 and 60 of the Frontier Crimes Regulation are reproduced below:

"10 Restriction on jurisdiction of civil Court:—Civil Court shall take cognizance of any claim with respect to which the deputy commissioner has proceeded under section 8, sub-section (3), clause (a), clause (b) or clause (d).

60. Finality of proceedings under Regulation : Except as therein otherwise provided no decision, decree, sentence or order given, passed or made, or act done, under Chapter III, chapter IV, Chapter V or Chapter VI, shall be called in question in, or set aside by, any civil or criminal Court."

36. The provisions of these two sections were considered by the Supreme Court of Pakistan in the case of Abdul Rauf and others vs. Abdul Hamid Khan and others (17 DLR (SC) 515). In interpreting the provisions of these two sections Pakistan Supreme Court observed :

"We are quite familiar with the words "under the Act" or "under chapter " No order is an order passed "under the Act" if it was not passed in exercise of powers granted by the Act and was therefore without jurisdiction. In a particular Act the words "under the Act" or "under chapter" may not appear and words of similar import may be used. But whatever the phraseology employed, any provision in an enactment saying that orders passed under the enactment or by virtue of the powers conferred by the enactment would not be liable to challenge in a court of law has reference only to orders passed with jurisdiction. It can be stated as a general rule without reference to the language used in an enactment, that barring provisions like those with which we are here concerned apply only to orders passed with jurisdiction."

37. So from these decisions as well we get a guidance to interpret section 152 of the Pourashava Ordinance, 1977, and in view of these decisions it can be stated that the burden of notice imposed by section 152 can operate only when the action complained of is an action wain the statutory power and the bar will not operate when the action complained of is not an action within the statutory power. This aspect of the law was neither noted in the case reported in 46 DLR nor this aspect was considered by the learned Judge in interpreting section 152 of the Pourashava Ordinance, 1977.

38. There is another aspect of this case that it appears from the statement made in paragraph 6 of the plaint that the plaintiff petitioner made out a case of malafide against the defendant Nos. 2 and 15. It is needless to mention that it is well settled that the power conferred by or under any law must not be exercised malafide or for illegal purpose. No legislature grants powers for malfade exercise of its power and when such malafide is allowed then the civil Courts have the power to investtigate and give decision thereon. There is a long line of decisions on this point. In the case of Abdur Raouf and others vs. Hamid Khan and others reported in 17 DLR (SC) 515, the then Supreme Court of Pakistan considered a somewhat similar provision of Frontier Crime Regulation which ousted the jurisdiction of the civil Court. In that case certain proceedings were challenged before the civil Court on the ground of malafide. The lower court dismissed the suit. The High Court on appeal set aside the decree and remanded the case holding that the court had jurisdiction to try the suit. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal observing that" the decision of the question whether the civil Court had jurisdiction in the present case would depend on whether the impugned orders and proceedings were without jurisdiction. There is in this case an attack on the proceeding on the ground of malafide too. A malafide act is by its nature an act without jurisdiction. No legislature when it grants power to take action or pass an order contemplates a mala fide exercise of power. A mala fide order is a fraud on the statute. It may be explained that a mala fide order means one which is passed not for the purpose contemplated by the enactment granting the power to pass the order, but for some other collateral or ulterior purpose." Similarly in the case of the Federation of Pakistan vs. Saeed Ahmad reported in PLD 1974 (SC) 151, (168) Hamoodur Rahman, CJ explained the status of mala fide acts and observed. "In-deed mala fide acts stand on the same footing as acts done without jurisdiction. Similarly, acts coram non judice also stand on the same footing, because, these words literally mean that they have been done by an authority or a body exercising judicial or quasi-judicial powers which was not properly constituted even under the law under which it was set up and that its decision is not a decision of a competent authority. If this be so then such acts do not also qualify for validation and they have not been saved from scrutiny by the ouster clause, no matter how widely that ouster clause may be worded."

39. Similarly, our Appellate Division in the case of Kh. Ehteshamuddin Ahmed @ lqbal vs. Bangladesh and others reported in 33 DLR (AD) 154, considered the question of the Superior Courts authority in the matter of issuing writ of certiorari. It has been held that as a normal practice in a constitutional set-up in exercise of the writ jurisdiction, the superior Courts are competent to examine the proceedings or action taken by an inferior tribunal, but the position is altogether different in the case of Martial Law Court or Tribunal acting within the ambit of the Martial Law Regulations. Then their Lordships observed. "Of course, when a Martial Law Court or Tribunal has acted without jurisdiction or such court or Tribunal is not properly constituted, that is to say, is coram non-judice, or has acted mala fide, the power of the superior courts under Article 102 of the Constitution in an appropriate case may be exercised." In the same case it has been further held that this judicial power exists as long as the superior Courts exist. No ouster clause can operate to oust the jurisdiction of superior Court, unless the superior court itself is satisfied that by such ouster clause the jurisdiction is ousted because the actions that had been performed are not mala fide or in excess or in coram non judice.

40. The plaintiff in paragraphs 6 and 7 of the plaint made out a case of mala fide against defendant Nos. 2 and 15 and it appears from a perusal of the written statement filed by the defendant-opposite parties that there is no clear denial of the allegations of mala fide made by the plaintiff-petitioner against these two defendant-opposite parties. On top of that it appears that the plaintiff-petitioner as PW 1 also asserted the allegations of mala fide in his deposition before the trial Court and while cross-examining PW 1 the defendants have not challenged those allegations made by PW 1 in his examination-in-chief. We have already found that mala fide act is not an act in the eye of law and in the instant case the allegations of mala fide made by the plaintiff-petitioner remains unchallenged and this aspect of the case was neither considered by the trial Court nor by the appellate Court below and on this ground alone the impugned judgment can be set at naught.

41. In interpreting section 152 of the Pourashava Ordinance, 1977, we can also take help from section 80 of the Code of Civil Procedure. In that section it has been provided that two months' prior notice in writing is necessary to institute a suit against government or a "public officer" in respect of any act purporting to be done by such public officer in his official capacity". The superior courts of this subcontinent interpreted this expression in a number of cases. "Act purporting to be done in official capacity" has been interpreted in such manner that in a suit against a public officer, notice under this section is necessary only when the act in respect of which the suit is brought is purported to have been done by public officer in the official capacity. In this connection we may refer to the cases reported in AIR 1930 (All) 742, AIR 1934 (PC) 96 and AIR 1942 (Lahore) 287. In interpreting this expression of section 80 of the Code of Civil Procedure it has been held that a public officer can only be said to act purporting to the discharge of his official duty if his act is such as to lie within the scope of official duty and, as such, it has been held by the superior courts of this sub-continent in various cases that this section does not apply when at the time of institution of a suit the defendant has ceased to be a public officer, or where the action arises out of an insult or the use of defamatory language or assault on a subordinate by a public officer, or an assault on a witness by an investigating officer or unauthorised seizure of property or where no relief is sought against a public officer personally. It appears from a perusal of paragraph 16(Ka) of the plaint that in this particular case no relief has been claimed or pleaded against defendant No.15 who is the Secretary of the Pourashava. Since mala fide has been pleaded against defendant No.15, he has been made a party to give him an opportunity to refute the same although no relief is claimed against him by the plaintiff in the instant case. While interpreting the said section i.e. the amended section 80 of the Code of Civil Procedure it has been held in a number of cases by the superior courts of this sub-continent that when a public officer acts mala fide and dishonestly, law purported that such an act cannot be considered as an act done in the official capacity as a public officer. So, if we compare the provision of section 152 of the Pourashava Ordinance, 1977 with the amended section 80 of the Code of Civil Procedure, we find that a mala fide act or unauthorised act by the public officer or municipal corporation or committee does not come within the ambit of Pourashava Ordinance, 1977 and in case of such an act no notice as contemplated in section 152 of the Pourashava Ordinance, 1977 is at all required for filing a suit against the Pourashava.

42. While arguing the case Mr. Sk. Afzalur Rahman submitted that section 152 of the Pourashava Ordinance, 1977 is directory and not mandatory but he could not lay reason to substantiate his submission. Of course, he cited a decision reported in 16 DLR 722 and another case reported in 31 DLR 145 but on a perusal of these two decisions it appears that they have no manner of application in the instant case and they are not attracted at all and these two cases are not relevant at all. On the other hand, Mr. Jashimuddin Ahmed referred to section 152 itself and relied on the decision reported in 46 DLR 295 and submitted with much emphasis that the provision of service of notice as contemplated or incorporated in section 152 of the Pourashava Ordinance, 1977 is a mandatory provision of law and no one can file a suit against a Pourashava without complying with the provision as laid down in the said section. Section 152 of the Pourashava Ordinance makes it incumbent upon the plaintiff to state in the plaint that a notice as contemplated in the first part of section 152 of the Act has been served and this indicates that the intention of the legislature was that the notice should be a pre-condiction for filing a suit against a Pourashava. It appears from the decision reported in 46 DLR 295, that it was argued before the learned Judge that the provision of notice is not mandatory but merely directory as there is no consequential provision for breach of the requirement of notice. It appears from the observations made by the learned Judge in the case reported in 46 DLR 295, that the learned Judge found that the provision of service of prior notice before the institution of a suit against a Pourashava is a mandatory one on the ground that the language of the section itself prohibits institution of a suit without prior notice. In interpreting section 152 of the said Act the learned Judge is of opinion that, that section imposes an absolute bar on an intending plaintiff to go to the civil Court without service of notice under that section.

43. Mr. Jashimuddin Ahmed the learned Advocate for the opposite party, while arguing the case referred to the decision reported in 1988 BLD (AD) 66 and therefrom he tried to impress upon me that the Pourashava Ordinance is a special law and the provisions embodied in that Act shall get preference to other provisions of law that may be found in the Civil Procedure Code that is to say, section 152 of the Pourashava Ordinance will override any provision of the Civil Procedure Code. The learned Advocate, therefore, urged before me that if there is any conflict between section 152 of the Pourashava Ordinance and section 80 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the provisions of section 152 will prevail. On a perusal of the case reported in 1988 BLD (AD) 66, it appears that that case was under the Labour Law i.e. Employment of Labour (Standing Orders) Act 1965 and it was held by the Appellate Division in that decision that Employment of Labour (Standing Orders) Act, 1965 is a special law. It was further, held by their Lordships of the Appellate Division that since the plaintiff answers the description of a worker as defined in the Act, he can not go to the civil Court and must seek redress before the Labour Court. No one disputes the proposition of law laid down in that decision. None also disputes that Pourashava Ordinance is a special law. The moot question in this case is not whether the Pourashava Ordinance is a special law or not but to decide the true import and tenor of the provisions of section 152 of the Pourashava Ordinance. Thus I fail to understand how the case reported in 988 BLD (AD) 66, is relevant.

44. Mr. Jashimuddin Ahmed then argues relying on a decision reported in PLD 1960 (Lah) 488, wherein section 80 of the Code of Civil Procedure came up for consideration and relying on that decision he submits that in the instant case defendant No. 15 namely, the Secretary of the Pourashava, is a public officer and as such a notice under section 80 of the Code of Civil Procedure was a must before filing of the suit against him. The submission, in my opinion, has no substance in it. Firstly, the facts and circumstances of the case relied on by him is altogether different from the facts and circumstances of the instant case. In that case Municipal Committee was superseded by the Government and an administrator was appointed to run the affairs of the Municipal Committee and also to manage the property of the Municipal Committee. In that case the plaintiff filed the suit under section 54 of the Specific Relief Act praying for permanent injunction against the Municipal Committee but at the time of Institution of the suit the Municipal Committee was no more in existence. The plaintiff in that case did not serve any prior notice under section 49 of the Punjab Municipal Act as a suit for injunction could be filed without notice against the Municipal Committee. Section 49 of the Punjab Municipal Act reads as under :

"49. No suit shall be instituted against a committee, or against any officer or servant or a committee, in respect of any act purporting to be done in its or his official capacity, until the expiration of one month next after notice in writing has been, in the case of a committee, delivered or left at its office, and in the case of an officer or a servant, delivered to him or left at his office or place of above, stating the causes of action and the name and place of abode of the intending plaintiff; and the plaint must contain a statement that such notice has been so delivered or left.

Provided that nothing in this section shall apply to any suit instituted under section 54 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877."

45. The contention of the plaintiff that the suit was filed against the committee and no notice was necessary was repealed on the ground that it was not a suit against the committee but against the Administration of the Municipal Committee and administrator being a public officer as defined in section 2(1) (g) of the Act a notice as contemplated under section 80 of the Code of Civil Procedure was necessity and on that count the plaint of that suit was rejected and the suit was dismissed. The instant case is not a case against an Administrator of a Pourashava rather it is a case against the Pourashava itself and the case reported in PLD 1960 (Lah) 488 has no manner of application in the facts and circumstances of the case. The point decided in 1960 PLD (Lah), has lost its force in view of the amendment of section 80 of the Code of Civil Procedure in 1962. Under the amended section 80, a suit shall not fail for want of notice and the plaintiff shall not be entitled to any costs if settlement as regards the subject matter of the suit is reached or the government or public officer concedes the plaintiff's claim, within the period of two months from the date of institution of the suit. After amendment of 1962 the present position of law is that a notice is not a condition precedent for the suit. There is another aspect. Section 80 does not apply where no relief is sought against a public officer personally. In the present case no relief has been claimed by the plaintiff against defendant No. 15 and in that view of the matter also no notice is required under section 80 of Code of Civil Procedure.

46. I have already indicated earlier that if we examine section 152 of the Pourashava Ordinance along with other provisions of the enactment coupled with section 80 of the Code of Civil Procedure, section 197 of the Criminal Procedure Code, section 14A of the East Bengal (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948, it leads us to the irresistible conclusion that service of notice as contemplated in section 152 of the Pourashava Ordinance does not impose an absolute bar to the institution of a suit in a civil Court. In my opinion, a notice under section 152 of the Pourashava Ordinance is a must only when the act complained of is a past act of the Pourashava and the act is within its statutory limit. Then and only then a notice would be a pre-condition for filing a suit against a Pourashava. But if in a suit when past act of the Pourashava is not in question or the same is not an act within its statutory limit the notice under section 152 of the Ordinance is not a must and the suit will not fail for want of notice. If we interpret section 152 of the Pourashava Ordinance along with section 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure, we find that in a case where the plaintiff sues a Pourashava for its act and the act complained of is not within its statutory limit then the civil Court will have authority to entertain the suit and to examine itself to see if the allegations made by the plaintiff are correct or not and in that case non service of notice as contemplated by section 152 of the Pourashava Ordinance, 1977 will not be a bar and for this proposition I have already cited long series of decisions of Indian jurisdiction which started from 1854, and till today the same view holds the field in the Indian jurisdiction. Unfortunately, these decisions were neither cited nor discussed in the case reported in 46 DLR 295. The consistent view of all the superior courts of this sub-continent is, that in case of threatened injury no notice is necessary for filing a suit against a Pourashava. But the learned Single Judge took different view in the case reported in 46 DLR 295 without considering the long line of decisions on this point. In the case reported in ILR 22 (Born) 636, the Bombay High Court considered the similar provisions as contained in the Bombay Municipal Act and observed that the section requiring notice for anything done or intended to be done or omitted to be done under the provisions of the Act, was intended to apply to an action at law for damages, and its object was to give an opportunity to a local authority to make payment or tender of compensation for the damage sustained, but could not be intended to apply to a case where the local authority was improperly pulling down a house, for instance, or stopping up a sewer, and if it were so, it was added, it would amount to a licence to every local Board to do what injury they pleased while the month's notice was running. Similarly, in the case reported in ILR 25 (Bom) 142, the Bombay High Court considered section 48 of the District Municipal Act, 1884 which is similar to section 152 of Pourashava Ordinance, 1977. In that case Bombay High Court after considering all the leading cases on this point observed that for the purpose of section 48 what the court has to look to is the real object of the suit, and the section requires notice only when the suit is for an act already done or purporting to have been already done, under the powers conferred. In such case only can it be necessary for the plaintiff to give an opportunity to make amends or compensation, and in such cases, the suit is not for an act already done, but to prevent an act from being irremediably, irrevocably done. Neither can amends be claimable, nor can delay be obligatory. It is impossible to hold that a mere notice, requisition or a threat to do a thing in the future, even though it be issued or made under the powers, is an act already done, or purporting to have been done. A notice, therefore, does not appear to have been made an indispensable preliminary to such a suit, by section 48 of the Act.

47. Here it may be noted that our Appellate Division had the opportunity of considering the meaning of the expression "done, purported to have been done" as appeared in the Martial Law Regulation. In the case of Ehteshamuddin vs. Bangladesh reported in 33 DLR (AD) 154, it was contended by the learned Attorney-General that the expressions "done, purported to have been done" in exercise of the powers or in the purported exercise of powers have rendered the actions immune from attack. But this contention was repelled by the Appellate Division and it was observed that those expressions are merely legislative device to protect those actions which are done in the exercise of jurisdiction and in doing so some irregularities are committed. These are never meant to give protection to the acts which are clearly without jurisdiction or which are coram non judice. It was further held in that decision that 'malafide' act is by its nature an act without jurisdiction.

<u>48. Taking into consideration all these decisions I am of the opinion that it is not correct to observe that in every case a notice under section 152 of the Pourashava Ordinance is a must. I am also of the opinion that in case of a future action of the Pourashava no notice is required to be served on the Pourashava under section 152 of the Pourashava Ordinance, 1977. It is only when the act complained of is a past act and the same is within the statutory power of the Pourashava, notice under section 152 of Ordinance is a must for filing a suit against a Pourashava. But if the act complained of is a past act but the same is not within its statutory limit want of notice will not unsuite the plaintiff.</u>

49. In view of my aforesaid discussions I find that the interpretation given on section 152 of the Pourashava Ordinance, 1977 in the case reported in 46 DLR 295 is not applicable to the present case inasmuch as in that case future or threatened injury was in issue but in the instant case past act of the Pourashava is called in question. Facts of the case reported in 46 DLR 295 are quite different from the facts of the present case. So, in my opinion, the decision reported in 46 DLR 295 has no manner of application in the facts and circumstances of the present case. I have already found that the act complained of in the instant suit is a past act and the same is beyond the statutory limit of the Pourashava. I, therefore, find substance in this revisional application.

50. In the result the Rule is made absolute. The judgment and decree dated 24-5-1992 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 3rd Court, Mymensingh in Other Class Appeal No. 368 of 1986 are set aside and those of the Assistant Judge, Gouripur in Other Class Suit No. 15 of 1986 are restored.

51. In view of the facts and circumstances of the case there will be no order as to cost.

Send down the records at once.

End.

lawyer:
Abul Kalam Azad, Advocate -For the Petitioners. 
Al-Haj Md Abdur Rahman with Md Nurul Amin, Advocates -For the Opposite Parties.
parties:
Liakat Ali Sheikh & ors ------ Petitioners
vs.
Mahatabuddin and ors ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
This Rule is directed against the judgment and order dated 10-11-1997 passed by the Additional District Judge. First Court, Kushtia in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 18 of 1996 allowing the appeal and reversing the judgment and order dated 30-5-96 passed by the Senior Assistant Judge, Khoksha in Miscellaneous Case No. 22 of 1994 under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act dismissing the Miscellaneous Case.

2. Facts, in short, are that the present opposite Party No. 1 as petitioner filed Miscellaneous Case No. 22 of 1994 for preemption of the case land under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act against the opposite parties on the assertions that the petitioner of the aforesaid miscellaneous case is the co-sharer of the disputed holding recorded in SA Khatian No. 236 by way of inheritance. The petitioner's co-sharer Dr Aftab Uddin transferred the case land to the opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 on the basis of a heba-bil-ewaz deed dated 29-7-93 without any notice to the petitioner. Hence the case upon deposit of an amount of Taka 5,000 together with the statutory compensation.

3. The opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 entered appearance and contested the case by filing a written objection wherein they denied, inter alia, that the pre-emption case is not maintainable and that it is hopelessly barred by limitation. It is the further case of the opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 that the transferor opposite party No. 3 is the 'Fufato Bhai' of opposite party Nos. 1 and 2. Due to love and affection opposite party No. 3 executed and registered the above heba-bil-ewaz deed in favour of them and delivered possession of the case land in their favour on 29-7-93 within the knowledge of the petitioner. The petitioner's assertion that he came to know of the transfer on 1-7-94 is false and in any event the case is liable to be dismissed.

4. The trial Court recorded the evidence of 3 PWs as against one for the opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 and upon conclusion of the trial of the case he dismissed the case by his judgment and order dated 30-5-98. Against the said judgment and order the pre-emptor preferred appeal before the District Judge, Kushtia by filing Miscellaneous Appeal No. 18 of 1996 and on transfer of the appeal it was heard by the Additional District Judge, First Court; Kushtia who by the impugned judgment and order dated 10-11-97 allowed the appeal and reversed the judgment and order of the trial Court. The lower appellate Court allowed the preemption of the preemptor.

5. Being aggrieved by the impugned judgment and order dated 10-11-97 passed by the Additional District Judge, First Court, Kushtia in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 18 of 1996 the opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 in the original Miscellaneous case as petitioners moved this Court under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the Rule.

6. The opposite party No.1 has opposed the Rule.

7. There is no dispute that opposite party No. 2 is a co-sharer of opposite No.1 in the disputed holding. It is the definite case of the opposite party No.1 that the petitioners are strangers and that opposite party No. 2 without notice of the transfer in question to the opposite party No.1 made the transaction and that he came to know of the transfer effected by the heba-bil-ewaz only on 11-7-1994. The petitioners, on the other hand, have stated that they are 'mamato' brothers of the transferor opposite party No. 2. It appears from the judgment of the trial Court that he on reference to the oral evidence of the witnesses held that the petitioners are the 'Mamato' brothers of opposite party Nos. 1 and 2. Here the question of relationship by consanguinity comes in for consideration in view of clause (c) of sub-section 10 of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Clause (c) has excepted certain categories of persons who claim interest in a given land by way of heba-bil-ewaz. Clause (c) of section 96 (10) is as under:

"(C)-a transfer by bequest or gift (including Heba but excluding Heba-Bil-Ewaj) for any pecuniary consideration in favour of the husband or wife or the testator or donor or any relation by consanguinity within three degrees of the testator or donor."

Mr Nurul Amin, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner, submits that in the instant case the heba-bil-ewaz was made by opposite party No. 2 in favour of the petitioner upon receipt of one copy of the Holy Quran, one cap and a Jainamaj (prayer mat). It is contended by him that a copy of the Holy Quran, cap and a jainamaj (prayer mat) do not fall within the purview of pecuniary consideration as indicated in clause (c). They are all on pecuniary consideration and if a transfer is effected by a heba-bil-ewaz in exchange of the above 3 items in favour of a person who happens to be a close relation of the donor within three degrees of consanguinity then the transfer so made will not be liable for preemption. That heba-bil-ewaz effected in exchange of prayer-mat, cap and copy of the Holy Quran is not to be construed as having been made for pecuniary consideration and this has been decided in number of cases and in this connection the learned Advocate of the petitioners refers to the citations reported in 11 DLR 353 in the case of Shafique Mia and others vs Hafizuddin and others, 20 DLR 433 in the case of Syed Ali Gazi and others vs Akhaj Sardar and others, and 44 DLR 228 in the case of Mir Amanullah vs Mohammad Sharif and others. It is further argued by the learned Advocate of the petitioners that non-pecuniary consideration for making a transfer on the basis of a Heba-bil-ewaz will not be enough and the right of preemption of the preemptor cannot be resisted unless the donor and the donee stand in relationship with each other within 3 degrees of consanguinity. It is submitted by him that the petitioners are, as established by evidence on record, 'mamato' brothers Of the donor. Being the 'mamato' brother of the donor, the opposite party No.1 cannot preempt the land demised by the heba-bil-ewaz. To show that the petitioners are within 3 degrees of consanguinity, the learned Advocate of the petitioners refers to a decision reported in 48 DLR (AD) 88 in the case of Shamsu I Islam and others vs Badiuz Zaman@ Bablu and another. It is submitted by him that in the above case it was found by the Appellate Division while interpreting section 96(10)(c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act that a cousin sister's son is within 3 degree of consanguinity with the donor. It is contended by the learned Counsel for the petitioners that in the instant case the transferees are the maternal uncle's son of the donor which relationship is more nearer in degree to the donor compared to the cousin sister's son as indicated in the aforesaid decision. This being the position the interest of the petitioners acquired by the heba-bil-ewaz in question cannot be preempted.

8. Next submission of the learned Advocate for the petitioners is on the point of limitation which, as submitted by him, is dependent upon facts. It is submitted by him that the trial Court upon consideration of the evidence held that opposite party No.1 was very much aware of the transfer as well as the possession in the case land. Opposite Party Nos. 1 and 2 both are the residents of Kushtia town. It is contended by the learned Advocate of the petitioners that opposite party No.1 being a resident of Kushtia town like opposite pray No. 2 is stated to have learnt about the transfer from his son PW 1 on 1-7-1994. This fact of knowledge of the transfer has been discussed at length in the judgment of the trial Court after sifting the evidence of the witnesses. It is further argued by the learned Advocate of the petitioners that the lower appellate Court as the final court of facts did not discuss at all the evidence of the witnesses nor did the lower appellate Court dwell upon the evidence of the witnesses adduced on behalf of both the parties. He did not controvert the finding of the trial Court with convincing reasons and the heba-bil-ewaz documents alleged to have been executed by opposite party No. 2 in favour of several persons weighed heavily upon the mind of the lower appellate Court to allow the preemption case of opposite party No. 1. It is submitted by the learned Counsel of the petitioners that these documents have not been used in evidence by any party before the trial Court as well as before the lower appellate Court and there is no knowing as to on what basis the lower appellate Court made mention of these 13 Heba-bil-ewaz documents. It is further contended by the learned Counsel of the petitioners that the lower appellate Court had handed down a judgment which is not a judgment of reversal in the true legal sense of the term and such judgment is not in consonance with the requirements of law as laid down in Order LXI rule 31 of the Code of Civil Procedure and that, as such, the impugned judgment and order cannot be sustained in law.

9. Mr Amirul Islam, the learned Advocate of the opposite party No.1, submits that the lower appellate Court has rightly reversed the judgment and order of the trial Court upon correct appreciation of the evidence on record. In view of the decision referred to by the learned Advocate of the petitioner in 48 DLR (AD) 88 on the point of relationship by consanguinity, the learned Advocate of the opposite party No.1 found difficulty in asserting that the petitioners are beyond, 3 degrees of consanguinity with the donor ie the opposite party No. 2.

<u>10. It is a settled principle of law that a Heba-bil-ewaz executed in favour of the done in change of prayer mat, a cap and a copy of the Holy Quran is a document carrying no pecuniary consideration. This point has been made clear in the case reported in 11 DLR 353 of which I made mention earlier. In 20 DLR 433 it was held. "The word pecuniary means money and money alone. Therefore, the prayer mat, however valuable is not pecuniary consideration." Similar view appears to have been taken in the decision reported in 44 DLR 228.</u>

<u>11. The question now remains to be addressed is whether the petitioners being the done of the heba-bil-ewaz in question are within 3 degrees of consanguinity with the donor ie the opposite party No. 2. This question appears to have been adequately addressed in the decision reported in 48 DLR (AD) 88 wherein their Lordships of the Appellate Division were pleased to hold that cousin sister's son is within three degrees of consanguinity from the donor. In the instant case, the petitioners being the 'Mamato' brothers of opposite party No. 2 who is the donor, they are more nearer in degree with the donor than the cousin sister's son, So, the petitioners in the light of the Appellate Division Judgment are well within 3 degrees of consanguinity from the donor. The petitioners therefore, satisfied all the requirements of law as laid down in section 96(10)(c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and, as such, the transfer made to them on the basis of the Heba-bil-ewaz in question cannot be preempted. Regarding the question of the case being barred by limitation it is my considered opinion that the trial Court on proper appreciation of the evidence on record rightly held that the case as filed by the opposite party No.1 is barred by limitation. The lower appellate Court has not set aside this finding of the trial Court with sufficient and cogent reason. On perusal of the judgment of the lower appellate Court, I hold the view that the impugned judgment and order is not a proper judgment of reversal as per provisions of law as laid down in Order XLI rule 31 of the Code of Civil Procedure. To hand down a judgment of reversal, the lower appellate Court is required to consider the judgment and order of the trial Court and then reverse the finding of the trial Court with sufficient and cogent reasons. In my opinion, the judgment and order of the lower appellate Court has been passed in a perfunctory and slipshod manner.</u>

12. In this view of the matter the impugned judgment and order suffers from serious legal infirmity and, as such, it cannot be sustained in law.

13. In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs. The impugned judgment and order dated 10-11-1997 passed in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 18 of 1996 by the Additional District Judge, First Court, Kushtia, is hereby set aside and the judgment and order dated 30-5-1996 passed by the Senior Assistant Judge, Khoksha in Miscellaneous Case No. 22 of 1994 is affirmed.

14. Stay granted earlier by this Court is hereby vacated. Communicate the order at once to the Court concerned.

Send down the lower Court's records.

End.

lawyer:
Abdur Razzaque with Hassan MS Azim and Md Abdus Salam, Advocates-For the Petitioner. 
Hassan MS Azim with Md Abdus Satan? Advocates-For the Petitioner. (In WP 3288 of 2007) 
Masud R Sobhan with Fatema S Chowdhury and Md AFM Saiful Karim, Advocates-For the Petitioner fin WP 2864 of 2007] Shafiq Ahmed with Tanjib-ul-Alam, Advocates-For the Respondents.
parties:
Advocate AM Zia Habib Ahsan and others ----- Petitioners 
Vs.
Chittagong University & ors ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
SAN Mominur Rahman J: These Rules, arising out of three (3) writ petitions, are taken up together for disposal inasmuch as the facts are similar and issues involved are same.

2. In Writ Petition No. 3022 of 2007 the petitioner, Advocate Abu Md Zia Habib Ahsan, passed LL.B. preliminary examination in 1987 and then passed LL.B. final examination in 1990 and his final examination result was Gazetted by the Chittagong University on 3-5-92 bearing Memo No. 12360-64 and was placed in the 3rd Class under Roll No. 3754. The petitioner was given mark-sheets for LL.B. preliminary examination dated 14-8-1988 and LL.B. final examination dated 3-5-92. The Chittagong Law College, from which the petitioner appeared in the examination, issued the testimonial dated 29-6-92 confirming his passing of the LL.B. final Examination. The petitioner also obtained Provisional Certificate for Bachelor of LL.B. Degree dated 4-8-92. Therefore, the petitioner appeared before the Bangladesh Bar Council for enrolment as an Advocate and got the enrolment in due course and started his practice in the Chittagong District Court and became a member of the Chittagong Bar Association in 1993. Subsequently, 116 obtained permission to practice in the High Court Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh from the Bangladesh Bar Council in the year 1996 and is continuing as a practicing Advocate in the Chittagong District Court.

3. Advocate Jesmin Sultana is the petitioner in Writ Petition No. 3288 of 2007. She passed LL.B. preliminary examination and final LL.B. examination in 1990, result of which was published on 17th March, 1992. She appeared in the examinations from Comilla Law College and in due course she obtained Provisional LL.B. Degree Certificate dated 26-5-1992 and got enrolment as an Advocate with the Bangladesh Bar Council on 19-9-93 and started her practice in the Comilla District Court and then, on his application, the Bar Council permitted her to practice before the High Court Division on 18-1-1998. She is practicing as an Advocate in the Comilla District Court.

4. Mr Faisal Mahmud Faizee is the petitioner in Writ Petition No. 2864 of 2007. He obtained LL.B. Degree from Chittagong University appearing from Chittagong Law College, and obtained his Provisional LL.B. Certificate dated 10-12-90. He got himself enrolled as an Advocate with Bangladesh Bar Council on 16-10-1991 and practiced as Advocate in the Chittagong District Court and then got permission to practice before the High Court Division on 22-10-94. While practicing as an Advocate in the High Court Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh he was elevated to the Bench on 23-8-2004 as Additional Judge and thereafter, was appointed as permanent Judge of the High Court Division of the Bangladesh Supreme Court with effect from 23-8-2006.

5. In all these three Rules common facts, relevant for the purpose of disposal of these Rules, are that from a news item published in "the National Dailies including the Daily Star dated 4-3-07 under the caption "Mark Sheet Tampering : CU cancels certificates of Judge Faizee, 2350 others" petitioners came to know that Examination of 50 LL.B. examinees were cancelled and thereafter, on query, they came to know that by a Gazette notification dated 10-3-07 the writ petitioners LL.B. examination results were cancelled but they were not given any notice. The notification bearing No.- স্মারক নং-পনি/সিফবাস/০১/২০০৭/১৩৮৭/(৪২)dated 10-3-07, issued by the Controller of Examinations (in Charge), Chittagong University, contains the results cancelled by the Syndicate of the Chittagong University by a resolution taken in its Extraordinary meeting held on 3-3-07 pursuant to three notices issued on 1-3-07.

6. It appears from the impugned Gazette Notification dated 10-3-07 that (1) the result of Faisal Mahmud Faizee bearing Roll No. 3652 (Chittagong Law College) published in the Gazette bearing Memo No. Ex/14169-77 dated 16-11-90 of LL.B. final examination, 1989, and (2) the result of Jesmin Sultana bearing Roll No. 3321 (Comilla Law College) published in the Gazette under Memo No. Ex/11150-165 dated 19-3-92 relating to LL.B. final examination and (3) the result of Abu Md Zia Habib Ahsan bearing Roll No. 3754 (Chittagong Law College) published in the Gazette bearing Memo No. Ex/12346-55 dated 28-4-92 of LL.B. final examination of 1990, were cancelled along with others.

7. Materials on record show that the Chittagong University pursuant to a decision of the 416th meeting of the Syndicate held on 9-11-04 formed the second Inquiry Committee led by Prof. (Dr) Md Shamsuddin of Political Science to examine and to point out the anomalies or other discrepancies in the report of Prof. Saleh Committee, the first Inquiry Committee, earlier accepted in the 336th and 353rd meetings of the Syndicate, in respect of the irregularities in the result of the examinations in Degree Pass. Subsidiary, LL.B. Preliminary and Final, and Bed held during the period 1983-1992. The Second Inquiry Committee, submitted its report with comments as to the anomalies and discrepancies found by it. In completing the inquiry said second Committee divided itself into five(5) sub-committees, and each of which examined the results of different years and of different examinations: Sub-Committee i.e. Team No. V, with Kazi Mostain Billah of English Department and Mr Md Morshed Mahmud Khan of Law Department, was entrusted to examine the results of LL.B. and BEd for the year 1983 to 1992. The said second Inquiry Committee prepared its report on 5-9-06 and thereafter, the Chittagong University convened Syndicate's 439th (Extra-ordinary) meeting On 313-07 at 3-00 PM vide first notice dated 1-3-07 without agenda. Subsequently, the time of the meeting was changed from 3-00 PM to 10-00 AM on the same date i.e. 3-3-07 by another notice dated 1-3-07, with which the Agenda of the meeting was sent. Thereafter, the third notice was sent on 1-3-07 calling and convening the Syndicate's 439th Extraordinary meeting on 3-3-07 at 10-00 AM referring to the first notice. Out of 14, members of the Syndicate including the Vice Chancellor, 9 members attended the meeting. All those nine (9) members are University teachers. The rest five(5) members, who were not present, were outsiders. It has been submitted that the decision of cancellation of results of the examinees, is bad (1) because of absence of application of judicial mind (2) absence of any finding as to the involvement of the respective petitioners in the alleged erasement or alterations found in the Tabulation sheets, (3) for not giving an opportunity of hearing to the petitioners, thus violated the principle of natural justice, and also (4) for the inordinate delay in taking the decision by the Syndicate. The meeting as called and convened by the notices, all dated 1-3-07, is bad in the eye of law for non service of notices upon the other five(5) members of the Syndicate, as well as for not providing two (2) days' interval between the time of issuance of the notice and time of holding the meeting.

8. The petitioner of the Writ Petition No. 3022 of 2007 through supplementary affidavit annexed Photostat copy of the Gazette Notification bearing No. 12360-64 dated 3-5-92, by which he was declared to have passed the LL.B. Final Examination, by the Chittagong University to meet the denial of the respondent-University, as to the existence of said gazette notification dated 3-5-1992. The petitioner of Writ-Petition No. 2864/2007 filed photo-copy of the second inquiry report through a supplementary affidavit.

9. The respondent Nos. 1-4 entered appearance by filing powers jointly. However, only on behalf of the respondent No. 1 affidavits-in-opposition and supplementary affidavits have been filed in each of the writ-petitions, denying the cases of the respective writ petitioners mentioned hereinabove, contending, amongst others, that the Chittagong University Syndicate has, in fact, implemented the decisions taken in the 336th and 353rd Syndicate meetings held on 10-10-98 and 13-8-99 respectively, as to the results, on consideration of the Saleh Committee reports, by taking the impugned decision in the 439th Syndicate meeting (Extraordinary) held on 3-3-07, wherein the reports of both the Inquiry Committees were considered and the said decision has been gazette on 10-3-07 under the impugned. Memo No. পনি/সিফবাস ০১/২০০৭/১৩৮৭/(৪২). The second Inquiry Committee was formed by the Syndicate in its 416th meeting held on 9-11-04 and the report of the said committee dated 5-09-06 has been considered in the Syndicate's meeting held on 3-3-07. Pursuant to a complaint dated 1-12-1993 made by Professor MA Khaleque against 14 students of the Department of Philosophy, the Syndicate formed an Inquiry Committee in its meeting dated 14-4-94, which committee submitted its report on 18-5-94 and on the basis of which action was taken against the corrupt officials of the office of the Controller of Examinations and in the report irregularities in respect of the examinations of several Departments as well as in the publication of the results were mentioned and some of the officers of the respondent-Controller of Examinations were found at fault and accordingly, the Syndicate in its 287th meeting held on 21-12-04 took decision to carry out a detailed and in-depth enquiry and thereafter, the first Inquiry Committee headed by Professor MA Saleh was formed by the Syndicate in its 301st meeting held on 25-4-96. The said Saleh Committee prepared its final report on 15-5-99 and the said final report was considered by Syndicate in its 353rd meeting held on 13-8-99 and decision was taken to cancel the result of the Examinees against whom anomalies, easement, etc. were found in the Tabulation sheets. The said Saleh Committee earlier submitted two (2) interim reports and the second interim report was considered in the Syndicate's 336th meeting held on 10-10-98. Though the decision was taken for implementation of the Syndicate's decision taken on 13-8-99 for cancellation of the results of examinees, which were found to be irregular, but due to influence of some corrupt and unscrupulous officials of the Chittagong University and also because of political influence the said decision of the Syndicate could not be implemented. It was found that the irregularities in the Tabulation she ester carried out by staff of the Controller of Examinations' office, and that anti-corruption cases were initiated against the corrupt officials involved in the tampering of results and charge sheets have been submitted and the cases are pending before the Special Judge, Chittagong. The respective petitioners obtained the certificates through tampering with the marks in the Tabulation sheets with the help of some corrupt, dishonest, unscrupulous officers of the office of the Controller of Examinations, including the Controller of Examination himself, and that the provisional certificates as well as the mark sheets in reference are not genuine documents, inasmuch as the University do not have any record of such mark-sheets and the provisional certificates and that Mr Latif, the Controller of Examination, along with some dishonest officials, who were dismissed from service, issued the certificates illegally and that the Gazette notification dated 3-5-92 showing That the petitioner of Writ Petition No. 3022 of 2007 has passed the LL.B. Final Examination is a fake certificate, since the said notification has been obtained and procured by the petitioner in connivance with some corrupt, dishonest and unscrupulous officials of the Office of the Controller of Examinations including the then Controller of Examinations Mr MA Latif who appears to have signed the fake Gazette showing that the petitioner in WP No. 3022/07 has passed the final LL.B. Examination and that action taken by the Chittagong University, on the basis of the decision of the Syndicate meeting held on 3-3-07 is good and taken in accordance with law and Regulations of the University and the decision relates to an administrative action, hence not be interfered with by any Court and that as the writ petitions contain disputed question of fact, the writ applications are not maintainable and the Rules are liable to be discharged.

10. The learned Advocates, appearing in the respective Rules, made similar submissions and adopted the submissions of each other. The learned Advocates, on behalf of the respective petitioner, submitted that the impugned decision of cancellation of the results in reference is bad being against equity inasmuch as there was inordinate delay in taking the impugned decision against the petitioners. In elaborating the submissions, it has been submitted that the impugned cancellation of result of the petitioners relates to the examinations held in 1990 and June and July 1991 and which were published in 1990 and 1992 respectively. Thus there was a delay of around 17/15 years in taking the impugned decking by the Chittagong University and for which the petitioners are neither at fault nor in any way involved or otherwise responsible. From the record it has been revealed that the University authority initiated the enquiry as early as in 1994 and took the decision for holding an enquiry and that in 1996 the first Inquiry Committee was formed and the said committee submitted its final report in May, 1999 which was considered by the Syndicate in its meeting held on 13-8-99 and took decision for cancellation of the results of examinees, against whose results irregularities were found, but no action was taken to implement the decision and the University, remained silent for years. In the affidavits-in-opposition as well as in the supplementary affidavits filed by the respondent No. 1-University it has been asserted that because of some corrupt officials of the office of the Controller of Examinations and also due to undue influence from the political arena the decision taken on 13-8-99 by the Syndicate could not be implemented. Thereafter, the second Inquiry Committee was formed by the Syndicate in its 416th meeting held on 9-11-04 and the said second inquiry Committee submitted its report dated 5-9-06 as per terms of reference and thereafter, on 3-3-07, the Syndicate took the impugned decision for cancellation of the results in its Extraordinary meeting. Thus it appears that delay in taking action in reference is due to the default or inefficiency on the part of the University authority. Because of such inordinate delay the petitioners should not be punished, inasmuch as the petitioners in the meantime has settled themselves in their professional life entering into the worldly affairs with their families including their children, achieving status and dignity in the society and that 17/15 fruitful years of the petitioners should not be allowed to be wasted at the instance i.e. negligence, of the respondent No. 1-Chittagong University. The process of life cannot be reversed after lapse of 17-15 years and this Court should not ignore the principle of equity, which is in favour of the petitioners. For the inordinate delay due to inaction and inefficiency on the part of the University in taking disciplinary action against the wrongdoers, the petitioners not being found to be in any way involved or responsible for such delay or the alleged wrongdoings, the principles of estoppel is applicable against the University authority in the instant case. Thereafter, the University authority now cannot take any action against the petitioners disadvantageous to the success and achievements which the petitioners gained during said 17-15 years, having no knowledge about the fault and negligence on the part of the University. The University authority, in the facts and circumstances, acted illegally in cancelling the results of LL.B. Degree of the petitioners being hit by the principle of estoppel.

11. The learned Advocates, on issue of delay and estoppel, relied on an Indian decision in the case of Kin Maxey Charan vs Rohil Khand University, Bareilly, reported in AIR 1982 All. 122, wherein the writ petitioner was shown to have passed BA part-I and on the basis of which she proceeded in her education and passed BA part-II and also LL.B. examination and then it was detected that actually she failed in the BA Part-I examination held in 1982, and she was informed by the University on 27-11-84 that she failed in the BA part-I examination and her result of BA Part-II of 1983 was cancelled. The Allahabad High Court made the Rule absolute on contest observing, amongst others, that the Court will not permit the petitioner to suffer for the mistake and negligence of the University authority and that the said case was a fit case, in which the principle of promissory estoppels should be applied to the respondents, because it was at their instance the petitioner has improved her position and has put in many years in her studies, which cannot be allowed to go waste.

12. The learned Advocate appearing for the contesting respondents submitted that the facts and circumstances of that Maxey Charan case, are not similar to the instant case, hence not applicable and that in the instant case the chronology of the events shows that the University authority was not at default but because of certain corrupt officials of the University, the decision of the Syndicates meeting held on 13-8-99 could not be implemented earlier and that the University authority has the right and authority to correct any mistake at any point of time and that in the instant case the mistake relates to the corrupt acts of easements/alterations made in the Tabulation-Sheets and that both the Inquiry Committees have rightly pointed out the anomalies/easements found in the Tabulations Sheets in their respective reports and on consideration of the enquiry reports, both of Saleh Committee and of Shamsuddin Committee, the Syndicate has arrived at its decision in accordance with law and Regulations of the University and hence the cancellation of the result cannot be challenged, mores when the action taken is a disciplinary action and taken in its administrative capacity. Therefore, the principle of estoppels is not applicable, inasmuch as the delay was not intentional.

13. The learned Advocate for the respondents relied on an Indian decision in the case of the Bihar School Examination Board vs Subash Chandra Sinha and others, reported in 1970(1) SCC 648, wherein it has been observed that in the matters relating to examination result, normally the decision of the authority should not be interfered with and such decision does not stand the test of natural justice and that the action taken being an administrative action, does not call for any interference by any Court of law. On the same point, the learned Advocate also relied on a decision in the case of Associated Provisional Pictures House Ltd vs Wednesbury Corporation, reported in 1947(2) All ER 680.

14. On behalf of the petitioners, next sub-mission was made on the issue of principle of natural, justice, which has not been complied with in canceling the results of the petitioners. It has been submitted that the cancellation of the results is, in fact, a grave punishment inflicted upon the petitioners, so as to say that their entire life was put to ruination by the impugned decision and that in arriving at such decision the petitioners were not given any opportunity of hearing and no notice as to the enquiries held by the University authority was issued upon them and the Inquiry Committees have neither examined the petitioners nor gave any opportunity of hearing to the petitioners to defend their respective cases. Such act on the part of the University authority is also against the principle of fair play. The learned Advocates submitted that the application of the principle of natural justice is an inherent right and in any case wherein a person is put to suffer any punishment, such punishment cannot be awarded without providing an opportunity to defend by such person and that the Superior Courts of the Sub-continent consistently discouraged such arbitrary action and always favored the petitioner aggrieved person. On this issue of natural justice, the learned Advocate relied on the decision in the case of Zakir Ahmed vs Dhaka University, reported in 16 DLR 361, which decision was upheld by the Supreme Court of Pakistan in the case of University of Dhaka vs Zakir Ahmed, reported in 16 DLR(SC) 722, and the decision in the case of the Principal, Chittagong Medical College and others vs Shahrayar Murshed and others, reported in 48 DLR (AD) 33. Their Lordships of the Appellate Division in the case of Chittagong Medical College (48 DLR), referring to the decisions, in the case of (1) Ridge vs Baldwin, reported in 1964 AC 40 (Law, Reports 1964), wherein it has been observed that the exact requirements in any case, principles of natural justice cannot precisely be defined and that they depend in each case on the circumstances of that case, and (2) the Supreme Court case of Zakir Ahmed reported in 16 DLR (SC) 722, wherein it is observed that fair opportunity to the person sought to be affected to correct or contradict any relevant statement prejudicial to him should be given, in other words, in order to act justly and to reach just ends by just means, the Courts insist that the person or authority should adopt such elementary and essential principles, observed that:

"in saying so we are not unmindful of the necessity of maintaining discipline in educational institutions or other institutions or departments where the maintenance of discipline is essential for the orderly conduct of the institution or department concerned nor are we unmindful of the fact that persons in charge, particularly of educational institutions, must be given fullest authority to correct those placed in their charge in the same manner as a parent or guardian would be able to do. But even so, we find it difficult to accept the contention that they must also be free from the necessity of acting in a manner which excluded every reasonable possibility of unfair action."

15. Quoting from the decision of Zakir Ahmed vs University of Dhaka (16 DLR 361) it has been submitted on behalf of the petitioners that:

"from the standpoint of urgency of action to be taken the cases of indiscipline are categorized in two heads and that the first head will comprise those cases in which action is called for immediately in the interest of maintenance of discipline and the fact of indiscipline is committed in presence of the person empowered to take action and that in such cases issuance of show cause notice will be a meaningless formality and may be dispensed with without any prejudice or violence to the principle of Audi Alteram Parton and that there is however other class of cases, where action is to be taken on the basis of information or evidence to be collected, after the offending act has taken place.

and that in such case notice of show cause should be issued and such issuance of show cause notice cannot be said to be subversive of discipline. In the said Zakir Ahmed's case (16 DLR) their Lordships have quoted from Tucker JS in the case of Russell vs Duke of Norfolk:

"There are, in my view, no words which are of universal application to every kind of enquiry and every kind of domestic tribunal. The requirements of natural justice must depend on the circumstance of the case, the nature of the inquiry, the rules under which the tribunal is acting, the subject matter that is being dealt with, and so forth."

Relying on the judgment of the Supreme Court reported in the case of Zakir Ahmed, 16 DLR SC 722, it has been submitted that the general conscience of judicial opinion in order to ensure elementary and essential principles of fairness, the person sought to be affected must at least be made aware of the nature of the allegation against him and he should be given a fair opportunity to make any relevant statement putting forward in his case to correct or controvert any statement brought forward to his prejudice.

16. The learned Advocate appearing for the respondent Chittagong University submitted that the cases cited do not bear the same facts as in the instant case and those were the cases in which disciplinary action was taken against the petitioner but in the instant case no such disciplinary action has been taken against the petitioners and in the instant case the anomalies as found in the Tabulation Sheets are in issue to which the petitioners were not required to be examined and that ex-facie the anomalies as appearing in the Tabulation sheets are for the benefit of the petitioners and the action taken by the University is an administrative/disciplinary action, therefore not to be interfered with by any Court of law. Thus the principle of natural justice is not applicable.

The learned Advocates appearing for the petitioners submitted that admittedly neither any notice was served upon the petitioners in taking the impugned decision by the Syndicate in its meeting held on 3-3-07 nor any enquiry has been initiated against the respective petitioners alleging their involvement in the anomalies /easements/alterations appearing in the Tabulation sheets and thus there is no finding as to the involvement of the petitioners, not to speak of any finding of guilt there against, in the alleged easement /alteration of the marks appearing in the respective Tabulation sheets but the impugned decision of cancellation of the results of the respective petitioners is based only on the anomalies/erasements/overwritings appearing on the Tabulation sheets and that the impugned decision has affected the respective life, livelihood and future, in respect of income and the social status and dignity of the petitioner, and that their status and dignity in the eye of the society have fallen low leading to their civil death and, as such, the action of the Chittagong University is arbitrary, irrational and unreason-able and cannot be maintained. 19. The learned Advocate appearing for the contesting respondents submitted, that the notice having been issued on 1-3-07 and the meeting having been held on 3-3-07 ex-facie there was two (2) days interval between the dates of issuance of the notices and date of the meeting as held as required for convening an Extraordinary meeting of the Syndicate.
