Further, in absence of a finding that the marks appearing in the Tabulation sheets have been found to be incorrect on comparison of said marks with any other valid documents, the results, cannot be cancelled on ground of the alleged erasements/overwritings on the Tabulation sheets.

The learned Advocate appearing for the contesting respondents surmised that it is not probable that except the beneficiary examinees anyone else will try to erase or alter the marks in the Tabulation sheets and that the easement and alteration, etc on the Tabulations sheets were done in collusion with the officials of the office of the Controller of Examinations as well as with the help of the Controller of Examinations itself as has been found on inquiry. The learned Advocate submitted that the notices for the meeting as issued were in accordance with law and therefore, the meeting as held was also lawful and consequently, decision taken therein cannot be questioned it was also submitted by the learned Advocate for the contesting respondents that the enquiry reports were not challenged earlier at any riling of time, though those were prepared as far back in 1999 and 2006. In reply thereto, on behalf of the petitioners, it has been submitted that those reports were internal materials of the University and were not disclosed to the petitioners at any point of time and thus, the petitioners had no knowledge about those Inquiry Reports, since prepared without notice.

21. In support of the contention that the marks appearing in the Tabulation sheets reflect the correct one and that if required can be corrected, the learned Advocates for the petitioners referred to the statements of the Court witnesses. The Court Witness No. 1 Mr MA Khaleque, has stated that the correction may be made on the Tabulation sheets, however on such correction in the Tabulation sheets, the tabulator must put his signature. In most cases after the result. is published in the Gazette, the marks sheets were issued by authority and the marks appearing on the mark sheets should correspond with the marks appearing in the Tabulation sheets and in the instant case the inquiry committee has examined the Tabulation sheets only and there being no other document, containing the marks in reference, available, the marks appearing on the Tabulation sheets could not be compared and therefore, it cannot be said that the marks appearing in the mark sheets are identical to the marks appearing in the Tabulation sheets are not correct or that the marks appearing in the Tabulation sheets are not correct. The Tabulation sheets show that the petitioners got the pass marks in the examination.

22. Perused the writ petition, affidavits-in-opposition and supplementary affidavits filed by the respective parties.

23. Considered the submissions of the learned Advocates of the respective parties. Also perused the decisions cited, with which we are in respectful agreement.

<u>24. The respective petitioners appeared in their respective LL.B. final examinations and the respective results were published in the year 1990 and 1992. The writ petitioner Advocate Abu Md Zia Habib Ahsan and the writ petitioners Advocate Jesmin Sultana procured marks-sheets and the provisional LL.B. Degree Certificates and the writ petitioner Faisal Mahmud Faizee, hereinafter referred to as Mr Faizee, procured the provisional LL.B. Degree certificate. They also procured the testimonials from their respective law colleges. Thereafter, they appeared before the Bangladesh Bar Council and got enrolled themselves as Advocates with permission to practice in the District Courts and thereafter, in due course, on their prayers they were permitted to practice in the High Court Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh and thus they became Advocates of the High Court Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh. Mr Ahsan Habib started his practice in the Chittagong District Court, Advocate Jesmin Sultana has been practicing in the Comilla District Court and Mr Faizee started practicing in the Chittagong District Court. Mr Faizee subsequently moved to Dhaka to practice in the High Court Division of Bangladesh Supreme Court and in course of time was elevated to the Bench as Additional Judge of the High Court Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh and subsequently appointed as permanent Judge of the High Court Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh. Thus they have been carrying on their professional life and settled themselves in the society with status and dignity with their family members. The Chittagong University by the impugned Gazette Notification bearing Memo No. পনি/সিফবাস/০১/২০০৭/১৩৮৭/(৪২) dated 10-3-07, pursuant to the decision of the Chittagong University Syndicate taken in its 439th meeting (Extraordinary) held on 3-3-07, called and conveyed by notices dated 1-3-07, cancelled the results of the petitioners. The respective petitioners being aggrieved moved this Court with their respective writ petitions, on which Rules were issued. In order to get ourselves clarified as to the (1) sanctity of the Tabulation sheets, (2) the procedure adopted in canceling the results, we have taken statements of (1) Mr ASM Abdul Khaleque, Professor, Department of Philosophy Chittagong University, as Courts witness No. 1, who was a Tabulator in respect of LL.B. preliminary examination, 1989, and (2) Mr Morshed Mahmud Khan, Associate Professor, Department of Law, Chittagong University, as Court's witness No. 2 and (3) Dr M Badiul Alam, the Vice-Chancellor of Chittagong University, as Court's witness No. 3. Mr Md Morshed Mahmud Khan is one of the members of the 2nd Inquiry Committee, who along with another member examined the anomalies and submitted report in respect of the LL.B. and B.Ed. examinations. Dr M Badiul Alam, Vice-Chancellor, presided over Syndicate's 439th Extraordinary meeting held on 3-3-07, in which the impugned decision for cancellation of the results was taken.</u>

25. From the record it reveals that the Chittagong University authority, on receipt of allegation of malpractice in the publication of results, took decision in the year 1994 for holding inquiry in respect of the irregularities alleged to have been committed in the publication of the results of the examination held in between 1983 and 1992, and accordingly, on 25-4-96 in the 301st meeting of the Syndicate the first Inquiry Committee was formed led by Dr MA Saleh, Professor of Chemistry, to enquire into the irregularities in the examinations of the university held during period 1983 to 1992 and the said committee, apart from submitting two interim reports, submitted its final report on 15-5-99 showing irregularity in respect of one hundred and eleven (111) LL.B. Examinees apart from thousand other examinees of different courses for the period 1986 to 1992 and that thereafter, the said report was accepted in the Syndicate's 353rd meeting and decision was taken therein for publishing the results making corrections through gazette cancelling the results of the examinees against whose results irregularities were found and to informing the failed examinees through letters about their result but the said decision of the Syndicate was not implemented and thereafter, on 9-11-2004 in the 416th meeting of the Syndicate, second Inquiry Committee was formed led by Dr Md Shamsuddin, to probe into the allegations raised in the newspapers and to examine the Prof. Saleh enquiry report dated 15-5-1999, submitted earlier and accepted by the syndicate in its 353rd meeting held on 13-8-1999, and that the said second Inquiry Committee prepared its report on 5-9-2006 as per terms of reference and that the Syndicate considered the said report of the second Enquiry Committee, prepared on 5-9-2006, as well as the report of the first Inquiry Committee in its Extraordinary meeting held on 3-3-07, wherein the impugned decision for cancellation of the results was taken and accordingly, the cancelled results was published vide gazette notification dated 10-3-07. It appears from impugned gazette notification dated 10-3-07 that (1) Mr Abu Md Zia Habib Ahsan (Roll No. 3754, Chittagong Law College) appeared in the LL.B. final examination, 1990 and his result was published in the Gazette Notification bearing Memo No. Ex/12346-55 dated 28-4-92 and that (2) Ms Jesmin Sultana (Roll No. 3321 Comilla Law College) appeared in LL.B. final examination, 1990 and her result was published in the Gazette notification bearing Memo No. Ex/11150-165 dated 19-3-92 and that (3) Mr Faisal Mahmud Faizee (Roll No. 3652, Chittagong Law College) appeared in the LL.B. Final Examination, 1989 and his result was published in the Gazette Notification bearing Memo No. Ex-14169-77 dated 26-11-90 and thus it appears that the petitioners have passed in due course and their results were published accordingly, but the Chittagong University, after about 17 and 15 years, have cancelled the results of the writ petitioners.

<u>26. From the statements made before this Court by the Vice Chancellor and two other teachers of the Chittagong University, as Court witness, as well as from the materials placed before us, it has been established that for such inordinate delay the writ-petitioners had no hand and the Chittagong University is responsible for the delay, either because of its negligence or inefficiency. The Chittagong University has made enquiries into the alleged irregularities and anomalies in the results in different examinations held during 1983 to 1992 on receipt of a complaint and found that the then Controller of Examinations as well as the few other officers of the office of the Controller of Examinations were responsible for the irregularities/anomalies and accordingly, actions were taken against them and that the matter was also reported to the Anti-Corruption Authority, which initiated cases, which tare pending. It also appears from the records that the mark sheets and the provisional certificates were issued by the concerned officers of the University but the Chittagong University Authority claims that those were issued unauthorized. Since admittedly the delay of 17/15 years in cancelling the results of the writ petitioners is due to inefficiency or negligence or mistake of the University Authority and that the writ petitioners have gained advantages during those 17/15 years, and there was no fault or involvement of the petitioners in such inordinate delay in taking decision and such gains as well as the period of 17/15 years cannot be reversed by the University authority, hence the University authority cannot be allowed to take advantage of such delay putting the writ petitioners in irreparable disadvantage. So many years of the petitioners cannot be allowed to be wasted. Equity is in favour of the petitioners, the principle of estoppel is in favour of the petitioners. This view also gets support from the superior Courts of the Sub-continent and in a decision of Indian Jurisdiction in the case of Km Maxey Charan vs Rohilkhand University, reported in AIR 1992 Allah 122, wherein it has been observed that:</u>

<u>"Many useful years of the petitioner cannot be allowed to be wasted at the instance of the University. It is too late in the day for the University to ask the petitioner to appear in BA part-I examination or any of the papers of the said course. On the assurance of the respondents contained in the mark sheet, she had secured admission and passed in future classes also. This process cannot be reversed now after a lapse of many years. Thus Court cannot be oblivious to the principle of equity which is in favour of the petitioner. Had the University done its part or the petitioner had been guilty in any manner, she would not be permitted to rely on promissory estoppel. But in view of the conduct of the University and for the reasons stated in this judgment, it is fit case in which the principle of promissory estoppels should be applied to the respondents because it is at their instance that the petitioner has improved her position and has put in many years in her studies which now cannot be allowed to go waste."</u>

<u>In this Allahabad case the petitioner was informed after four (4) years that she failed in the BA Part-I examination. In deciding the said Allahabad case, another decision in the case of Sri Netrapal Singh vs Rohilkhand University (Writ Petition No. 1515 of 1989), judgment pronounced on 7-2-90, has been discussed, wherein the petitioner, after having passed MSc and after having applied for a job was not given the BSc degree, and when he approached the University he was asked to appear in supplementary examination in Physics paper of BSc Part-II and that he was given marks sheet, in which he was shown to have passed BSc Part-II examination and then, after a gap of many years, the petitioner was informed that he had failed in BSc Part-II examination and he could not be admitted in MSc Part-I course but he appears to have passed MSc course in the meantime and that on the basis of aforesaid facts it was held by the Division Bench that the same was a fit case to which the principle of estoppels should be applied against the University and that it was too late in the day for the University to withhold the BSc degree of the petitioner, on the ground that he failed in BSc Part-II examination.</u>

<u>27. Considering the facts and circumstances of the instant case and the decisions of the said Allahabad case, discussed above,, and having found that the Chittagong University and its officers are solely responsible for the inordinate delay of said 17/15 years in taking the impugned decision on 3-3-07 and the publication of the impugned gazette notification dated 10-3-07 and there being no finding as to the involvement of the petitioners in said delay, we are of the view that the Chittagong University, after 17/15 years of declaration of the results of the petitioners, cannot cancel the petitioners results by the impugned decision of the Syndicate taken in its Extraordinary meeting held on 3-3-07, which was published by the impugned gazette notification on 10-3-07. The University is barred both in equity and by the principle of estoppel and cannot be allowed to cancel the results of the respective writ petitioners putting them in disadvantageous position to face civil deaths in the society.</u>

28. The learned Advocate appearing for the contesting respondents raised objection against scrutiny of the impugned decision of the Syndicate canceling the results by this Court in its writ jurisdiction, submitting, amongst others, that the action of the University is an administrative decision and that such disciplinary action as taken falls within four corners of the powers given to the University authority and in support of his submission he has relied on a decision, in the case of the Bihar School Examination Board vs Subhas Chandra Sinha and others, reported in 1970(1) Supreme Court Cases 648. The said case arose from the decision of the Patna High Court. In the said case the Secondary School Examination held in March 1969 was in issue. The candidates of the said examination appeared at various centers including one, namely Hanswadih Centre. On the basis of a newspaper report dated 22-7-69 an enquiry was held and the results of the examinees of the said Hanswadih Centre were not declared and cancelled on the ground of unfair means practiced on a large scale at the said centre and that the examinees of said centre were allowed to appear at the Supplementary Examination to be held in the same year i.e. in September, 1969. Some of the examinees challenged the cancellation order. It was found that in the said examination the percentage of the successful candidates in all the examination centres, except the Hanswadih Centre, was around 50%, whereas the percentage of success in the said Hanswadih Centre was above 90%. The High Court gave finding that the high percentage did not give rise to a suspicion that unfair means were practiced and that the examinees were not given a chance to show cause, and that the materials on which the Chairman of the Board passed the order were not disclosed to the examinees and hence the High Court interfered therein on the ground that the principle of natural justice and airplay were not observed. The Rule was made absolute and the Supreme Court of India allowed the appeal filed there against on the ground that it was not a case of any particular individual, who is being charged with adoption of unfair means, but the conduct of all the examinees or at least a vast majority of them at a particular centre. The Supreme Court in allowing the appeal observed that:

"If it is not a question of charging any-one individually with unfair means, but to condemn the examination as ineffective for the purpose it was held. Must the Board give an opportunity to all the candidates to represent their cases? We think not. It was not necessary for the Board to give an opportunity to the candidates if the examinations as a whole were being cancelled. The Board had not charged anyone with unfair means so that he could claim to defend himself. The examination was vitiated by adoption of unfair means on a mass scale. In these circumstances, it would be wrong to insist that the Board must hold a detailed inquiry into the matter and examine each individual case to satisfy itself which of the candidates had not adopted unfair means. The examination as a whole had to go."

29. In coming to that decision their Lordships of the Supreme Court of India have satisfied themselves by examining some of the answer scripts of that Hanswadih Centre and it was found that students had assistance froth outside source. Therefore, the conclusion that unfair means were adopted was vindicated. In the instant case, the facts are different, in that, out of several hundred LL.B. examinees results of only 50 LLB examinees of different centers were cancelled. by the impugned decision dated 3-3-07 published in the Gazette notification dated 10-3-07. As per report of the Daily Star dated 4-3-07 results of 2350 examinees were cancelled by the Syndicate. In the judgment of said Bihar Board's case reliance was placed on Ghanshyam Das Gupta's case reported in 1962 (3) Supp SCR 36, wherein result of three candidates were cancelled and the Court held that they should have received an opportunity of explaining their conduct and that if any particular person is to be proceeded against he must have a proper chance to defend himself and this did not obviate the necessity of giving an opportunity even though the number of persons proceeded against was large. It was also observed in said Ghanshyam Das Gupta's case therein that:

"While we do not wish to whittle down the requirements of natural justice and fair play in cases where such requirement may be said to arise, we do not want that this Court should be understood as having stated that an inquiry with a right to representation must always precede in every case, however different."

30. Both the learned Advocates for the petitioners and the contesting respondents relied on the aforementioned decisions. The learned Advocate for the respondent-University asserted that since anomalies have been found in respect of large number of examinees the question of issuance of show cause notices upon them was dropped and he relied on the decision in the case of the Bihar School Examination Board (1970)(I)SCC 648) referred to above.

<u>31. It appears from the aforementioned judgments that the Courts are not debarred from scrutinizing the decisions of University affecting rights of students without affording an opportunity to defendant themselves. Thus, we do not find any substance in the submission made by the learned Advocate for the contesting respondents that the impugned decision of the Chittagong University is not to be interfered with by this Court. The learned Advocate also relied on the case of Associated Provincial Picture Houses reported in 1947(2) All ER 680 in support of his contention that disciplinary action taken by the University should not be interfered with by Courts of law To meet this point, we may profitably refer to the observations made by their Lordships of the Pakistan Supreme Court in the case of Dhaka University vs Zakir Ahmed, reported in 16 DLR (SC) 722, which runs as under:"</u>

<u>"32. We are not impressed by the argument that such interference by Courts of Law with orders passed by educational institutions in the interest of maintenance of discipline would defeat the very purpose for which these institutions exist or that it would stultify the powers of the authorities in charge of educational institutions or prevent them from taking any action against student misconduct. The Universities and educational institutions generally are armed with abundant powers of disciplinary action against the recalcitrant students and the Courts are in no way minded to deprive them of their powers but all that they are entitled to insist upon in the interest of fairness is that the minimum requirements of fairness must be observed, by them before such action is taken, for it is equally important to remember that unfair action may cause greater harm to the prestige of the heads of educational institutions, who are expected to be loco parentis to the students and may seriously undermine the authority which they claim to possess over the students placed in their charge"</u>

32. As to scrutiny in the matter of administrative actions taken by University or educational institutions, the application of principle of natural justice has been approved in the said Zakir Ahmed's case (16 DLR SC 722) by the Supreme Court of Pakistan holding that:

"This Court has already had occasion to point out in at least three cases, namely, in the cases of the Chief Commissioner, Karachi vs Dina Sohrab Katrak (8), Faridsons Limited vs Government of Pakistan (9), and Abdur Rahman vs Collector and Deputy Commissioner Bahawalnagar and others. (10), that in all proceedings by whomsoever held, whether judicial or administrative, the principles of natural justice have to be observed if the proceedings might result in consequences affecting the person of property or other right of the parties concerned. This rule applies even though there may be no positive words in statute or legal document whereby the power is vested to take such proceedings for in such cases this requirement is to be implied into it as the minimum requirement of fairness."

33. Our Appellate Division in the case of Chittagong Medical College vs Shahrayar Murshed, reported in 48 DLR (AD) 33, has approved the application of the principle of natural justice in actions taken by the educational institutions against the students and in affirming the judgment of the High Court Division, their Lordships of the Appellate Division observed:

"The High Court Division in its judgment observed that although the point regarding the jurisdiction and authority of the Principal was raised but it was not seriously pressed by the learned Advocate for the writ petitioners and it was conceded that the Principal of the College being in the position of loco parents and responsible for internal administration and maintenance of discipline was authorized to impose a punishment upon a recalcitrant student in an appropriate case. As to the question of expulsion forever, the learned Judge observed that it is the most severe punishment so as to ruin the educational career of a student and therefore, great care and caution is called for in taking such a measure. The High Court Division, however, finally made the Rule absolute upon finding that the respondents having not been given any opportunity to show cause to explain the allegations made against them, there has been a violation of the principle of natural justice in awarding the punishment of expulsion forever and, as such, the said punishment cannot be legally sustained".

34. In deciding the said case, the Appellate Division also relied on the following paragraphs from the said Zakir 'Ahmed's case reported in 16 DLR (SC) 722.

"Nevertheless, the general consensus of judicial opinion seems to be that, in order to ensure the "elementary and essential principles of fairness" as a matter of necessary implication, the person sought to be affected must at least be made aware of the nature of the allegations against him, he should be given a fair opportunity to make any relevant statement putting forward his own case and "to correct or controvert any relevant statement brought forward to his prejudice." Of course, the person, body or authority concerned must act in good faith, but it would appear that it is not bound to treat the matter as if it was a trial or to administer oath or examine witnesses in the presence of the person accused or give him facility for cross examining the witnesses against him or even to serve a formal charge sheet upon him. Such a person or authority can obtain information in any way it thinks fit, provided it gives a fair opportunity to the person sought to be affected to correct or contradict any relevant statement prejudicial to him. In other words, "in order to act justly and to reach just ends by just means" the Courts insist that the person or authority should have adopted the "elementary and essential principles" unless the same had been expressly excluded by the enactment empowering him to so act."

"It has to be examined in the light of the aforesaid principle whether the appellants had acted justly to reach just ends by just means. In order to qualify for the same the minimum that is required to be proved is that the respondents were made aware of the allegations against him and they were given a fair opportunity to make any relevant statement putting forward their own case and to correct or controvert the statements which are used against them to their prejudice. The High Court Division found that the materials before it were not sufficient to hold that the respondents were served with any notice as would satisfy the requirements of a fair opportunity. Of all the findings made by the High Court Division we think the most significant is, to quote from the judgment itself, that "there is nothing to show from the record that any notice was issued and or served on the petitioners asking them to show cause as to why the proposed disciplinary action should not be taken against them".

35. On the issue of natural justice, we may profitably refer to an Indian Supreme. Court decision in the case of Union Carbide Corporation vs Union of India, reported in AIR 1992 SC 248, wherein their Lordships have observed:

"While Shri Nariman understandably strongly relies on these observations as the law of the case, Shri Shantibhushan seeks to deny them any binding force on the ground that they were passing observations, inasmuch as the question of validity of the settlement was not before the Court in Saint case (AIR 1990 SC 1480). Shri Shantibhushan relied upon several pronouncements of this Court viz National Textile Workers Union vs PR Ramakrishnan (1983) 1 SCC 228; (AIR 1982 SC 75), Institute of Chartered Accountants vs LK Ratna (1986) 4 SCC 537 (AIR 1987 SC 71), K1 Shepahard vs Union of India, (1987 4 SCC 431 : (AIR 1988 SC 686), RB Shreeram Durga Prasad vs Settlement Commissioner, (1989) I SCC 628 : (AIR 1989 SC 1083) and HI Trehan vs Union of India (1989) 1 SCC 764: (AIR 1989 SC 568) to emphasize the imperatives of observance of natural justice and the inevitability of the consequences that flow from a non-compliance of the requirements of a pre-decisional hearing."

<u>36. These are all accepted principles. Their wisdom, verity and universality in the discipline of law are well established. Omission to comply with the requirements of the rule of Audi Alterarn Partem, as a general rule, vitiates a decision. Where there is violation of natural justice no resultant or independent prejudice need be shown, as the denial of natural justice is, in itself, sufficient prejudice and it is no answer to say that even with observance of natural justice the same conclusion would have been reached. The citizen "is entitled to be under the rule of law and not the rule of discretion" and "to remit the maintenance of constitutional right to judicial discretion is to shift the foundations of freedom from the rock to the sand". But the effects and consequences of non-compliance may alter with situational variations and particularities, illustrating a "flexible use of discretionary remedies to meet novel legal situations". One motive" says Prof. Wade "for holding administrative acts to be avoidable, where, according to principle, they are void may be a desire to extend the discretionary powers of the Court". As observed by Lord Reid in Wiseman vs Borneman, 1971 AC 297, natural justices should not degenerate into a set of hard and fast rules. There should be a circumstantial flexibility."</u>

37. The Vice-Chancellor has given statement before this Court to the effect that:

৩। পরীক্ষার ফলাফল বিষয়ে সিদ্ধান্ত গ্রহণের সংক্রান্তে সংশ্লিষ্ট পরীক্ষার্থীদের কোন নোটিশ দেয়া হয় নাই। কারণ বিশ্ববিদ্যালয় ফলাফল সংশোধন করার অধিকার সংরক্ষণ করে।

৪। প্রশ্ন : পরীক্ষা সংক্রান্ত সিদ্ধান্ত নিতে যে বিলম্ব হয়েছে তার জন্য কি সংশ্লিষ্ট পরীক্ষার্থীরা কোনভাবে দায়ী?

উত্তর : এই প্রসেসের সাথে পরীক্ষার্থীদের কোন সম্পৃক্ততা নেই।

৫। প্রশ্ন: এই পরীক্ষার ফলাফলের অনিয়ম কে বা করা হয়েছে? এ বিষয়ে কি কোন তদন্ত করেছেন?

উত্তর: তদন্ত করা হয়েছে এবং তদন্তে দোষীদের বিরেুদ্ধে মামলা হয়েছে। দোষীরা সংশ্লিষ্ট কর্মকর্তা এবং তাদের চাকুরী হতে বরখাস্ত করা হয়েছে।

৬। প্রশ্ন : সেই তদন্তে কোন পরীক্ষার্থীকে কি দোষী সাব্যস্থ করা হয়েছে?

উত্তর : ঐ তদন্তে কোন পরীক্ষার্থীদের বিরুদ্ধে কোন অভিযোগ আনা হয় নাই।

৭। প্রশ্ন: সংশ্লিষ্ট পরীক্ষার্থীদের বিরুদ্ধে কোন তদন্ত হয়েছে কি?

উত্তর : না, তাদের বিরুদ্ধে কোন প্রসিডিং ড্র করা হয় নাই।

38. Mr Md Morshed Mahmud Khan, one of the members of the 2nd Inquiry Committee, has stated before this Court that :

১। কেইস সংক্রান্ত এল,এল,বি, পরীক্ষার ফলাফল ইনকোয়ারী করার সময় সংশ্লিষ্ট পরীক্ষার ফলাফলের গেজেট এব টেবুলেশন বই দেখেছি এবং তার ভিত্তিতেই রিপোর্ট তৈরী করেছি।

২। টেবুলেশন শীটে যে অনিয়ম দেখা যায়, সে পরিপ্রেক্ষিতে পরীক্ষা নিয়ন্ত্রকের অফিসের কর্মকর্তাদের জিজ্ঞাসাবাদ করেছি।

৩। প্রশ্ন : জিজ্ঞাসাবাদে কি উত্তর পেয়েছেন?

উত্তর : উত্তরে কর্মকর্তাগণ জানান তাহারা এই অফিসে নতুন। টেবুলেশন শীটের অনিয়ম সম্পর্কে তাদের কোন জ্ঞান নেই। আমরা আর অন্য কাহাকে জিজ্ঞাসাবাদ করি নাই।

টেবুলেশন শীটে (ক) ২ জন টেবুলেটরের, (খ) পরীক্ষা ফলাফল কমিটির চেয়ারম্যান এবং (গ)মেম্বারদের (ঘ) পরীক্ষা নিয়ন্ত্রকের এবং (ঙ) উপাচার্য মহোদয়ের সই স্বাক্ষর থাকা দরকার।

১০। আমরা যে টেবুলেশন শীট দেখেছি তাতে সকলের সই স্বাক্ষর ছিল না। শুধুমাত্র পরীক্ষা ফলাফল কমিটির চেয়ারম্যান মহোদয়ের সই স্বাক্ষর ছিল।

39. Mr. ASM Abdul Khaleque, one of the tabulators, has stated before this Court that :

প্রশ্ন: (৩) টেবুলেশন শীট কিসের ভিত্তিতে তৈরী করা হয়?

উত্তর: পরীক্ষার পর প্রার্থীদের পরীক্ষার খাতায় প্রাপ্ত নম্বর আমাদেরকে সরবরাহ করা হয়, তার ভিত্তিতে টেবুলেশন শীট তৈরি করা হয়। পরীক্ষার খাতা সরবরাহ করা হয় না। এলএলবি পরীক্ষার খাতা দুজন পরীক্ষক দেখেন ভিন্ন ভিন্ন ভাবে এবং তাদের দেয়া নম্বর দুটি গড় করে টেবুলেশন শীটে উঠানো হয়।

প্রশ্ন: (৪) টেবুলেশন শীট কে সংরক্ষণ করেন?

উত্তরঃ টেবুলেশন শীট পরীক্ষা নিয়ন্ত্রকের অধীনে সংরক্ষিত থাকে।

প্রশ্নঃ (৫) টেবুলেশন শীট কোথায় রাখা হয়?

উত্তরঃ টেবুলেশন শীট সংরক্ষনের জন্য ষ্ট্রং রুম নির্দিষ্ট করা আছে এবং উহা পরীক্ষা নিয়ন্ত্রকের অধীনে থাকে।

প্রশ্নঃ যে ঘরে বসে এবং যে সময়ে টেবুলেশন শীট তৈরী করা হয় সে সময়ে সেখানে কি সাধারন লোকের প্রবেশাধিকার আছে?

উত্তরঃ না, নেই। কন্ট্রোলার অব একসামিনেশন এর অনুমতি ব্যতিরেকে কারো প্রবেশাধিকার নেই।

প্রশ্নঃ টেবুলেশন শীটে কি ভুলত্রুটি সংশোধন করা যায়?

উত্তরঃ হ্যাঁ। টেবুলেশন শীটে ভুল থাকতে পারে এবং তা সংশোধন করা যায়। তবে ভুল সংশোধন করা হলে টেবুলেটরের সই স্বাক্ষর থাকবে।

প্রশ্নঃ (১) পরীক্ষার টেবুলেশন শীটে কোন ভুল ত্রুটি কখনো দেখেছেন কি?

উত্তরঃ হ্যাঁ। ১৯৮৯ সনের এলএলবি প্রিলিমিনারী পরীক্ষা টেবুলেশন শীটে আমি একটি ভুল সংশোধন করেছি এবং সেখানে আমার সই স্বাক্ষর আছে।

<u>40. From the statements quoted above it is proved that no inquiry has been made by the Chittagong University to find out involvement or guilt of the petitioners in the alleged acts of erasement/overwritings in the Tabulation sheets and that no notice as to holding of the inquiries, as held, was given to the petitioners and that the petitioners were not involved in the process of delay in taking the decision.</u>

<u>41. In the instant case, the impugned cancellation of the result was made on the basis of two enquiry reports. From the materials on record, the statements of the Vice Chancellor and the member of the 2nd Inquiry Committee, quoted hereinabove, and the submissions made by the learned Advocates of the respective parties, it appears that admittedly the respective petitioners were not given any opportunity of hearing either by the Inquiry Committees or by the University Authority before taking the impugned decision of cancellation of their results, though they have been affected and put to face irreparable loss and injury. In the absence of finding of any guilt, fault or involvement of the petitioners in the alleged easement/ alteration/overwriting on the Tabulation sheets, the impugned cancellation of the results is against equity, principles of natural justice and airplay.</u>

<u>42. Considering the decisions discussed hereinabove and in the facts and circumstances of the instant case, we cannot but hold that the principles of natural justice and airplay are applicable in the instant case and as those principles have not been followed, the impugned cancellation of the results of the petitioners is illegal and cannot be sustained.</u>

<u>43. From the materials on record it appears that second Inquiry Committee only perused the Tabulation sheets and the first Inquiry Report. No other material was available before the 2nd inquiry Committee on the basis of which it could come to any conclusion that the marks appearing on the Tabulation sheets are not correct. However, comment, as to the correctness of the marks appearing on the Tabulation sheets, has been made by one of the sub-committees of the 2nd Inquiry Cronkite to the effect that there were easements and re-writings of marks on the Tabulation sheets and those were accepted as correct marks and that the examinees were not found to be at fault for the same. It further appears that the Tabulation sheets, which have been placed before the second Inquiry Committee, were not proper, inasmuch it is the requirement that in case of LL.B. results the Tabulation sheets should contain signatures of (1) two tabulators (2) Chairman of the Examination Result Committee and (3) the members of the said Committee, (4) Controller of Examination and (5) the Vice-Chancellor. Mr Md Morshed Mahmud Khan, the Court witness No. 2, one of the members of the second Inquiry Committee and who has seen the Tabulation sheets, has stated before this Court that the Tabulation sheets which he has seen contained only the signature of the Chairman of the Examination Result Committee and that there was no other signature in the said Tabulation sheets. Further, it has been found from the statement given by Mr MA Khaleque, the Court witness No.1 quoted above, that there may be corrections in the Tabulation sheets and if a correction is made on the Tabulation sheets, the tabulator must put his signature against the correction made, and that the Tabulation sheets are being kept in a strong-room under the control of the Controller of Examinations and that there is no scope for outsiders to have any access to the Tabulation sheets, without permission of the Controller of Examinations. The contents of the copy of the report submitted by the second Inquiry Committee, annexed to the supplementary-affidavit in Writ Petition No. 2864 of 2007, do not show that the writ petitioners were examined or served with any notice in connection with the alleged easement and or alteration of marks of the Tabulation sheets at any point of time. The Vice-Chancellor Dr M Badiul Alam, as Court witness No. 3, also stated before this Court that the examinees concerned were not given any notice to explain themselves, before taking the impugned decision of cancellation of the results of the writ petitioners. Thus, it appears that though the writ petitioners were affected by the impugned cancellation of the results yet they were not given any notice or opportunity of hearing and the impugned decision has been taken arbitrarily behind their knowledge. There is also no statement from the respondents that the issuance of show cause notices upon the writ petitioners, prior to taking the impugned decision, would have defeated the decision or would have jeopardised the interest of the University in any way. It is found that the marks contained in the mark-sheets and in the Tabulation sheets are same and not different and that the mark sheets were issued soon after the publication of the results by the concerned officials of the University. In such circumstances, it is now too late to say that the marks appearing in the Tabulations Sheets are not correct, in spite of the fact that there are easements and over-writing in the Tabulation-sheets. In the absence of any other legal document with which the marks appearing in the mark sheets supplied to the writ petitioners, could be compared and found to be not same, the said marks cannot be said to be not correct. Similarly, the marks appearing in the Tabulation-sheets in reference, in the absence of any legal document containing the marks obtained by the examinees with which the said marks can be compared, cannot be questioned and should be treated as correct for all practical purposes.</u>

<u>44. In the premises, we are of the view that the correctness of the marks contained in the Tabulation sheets, maintained by the University authority, cannot be questioned now. The Tabulation sheets were produced by the University before this Court, attested Photostat copy of which has been kept with the records of the respective cases, show that the University authority do not take proper care in preserving the Tabulation sheets in accordance with Rules or provisions made therefore. The impugned decision for cancellation of results only on the ground that there are easements and overwriting in the petitioners' marks appearing in the Tabulation sheets, in the absence of any finding or proof that these marks are not correct, is simply based on presumption and therefore, is bad in the eye of law.</u>

<u>45. The learned Advocates for the writ petitioners also challenged the validity of the notice for holding the Extraordinary meeting of the Syndicate asserting that, as per University rules and regulations, for calling and convening an Extraordinary meeting of the Syndicate at least 2 days' interval has to be provided in between the issuance of the notice and the holding of the meeting. It appears that in the instant cases three (3) notices were issued on the same date i.e. on 1-3-07, in calling and convening the meeting held on 3-3-07. First notice under Memo No. C /SN/2/1561(13) dated 1-3-07 was issued without Agenda, but stating that the agenda would be sent subsequently, and fixing the meeting to be held at 3-00 PM on 3-3-07 under Memo No. C/SN/2/ 1563(13) was sent enclosing the agenda but changing the time of the meeting from 3-00 PM to 10-00 AM on 3-3-07. Thereafter, the third notice was issued on 1-3-07 under Memo No. C /SN /2/1566(13) containing that the meeting would be held at 10-00 AM on 3-3-07. The proceeding of Syndicate meeting held on 3-3-07) copy annexed to the Writ Petition No. 2864 of 2007 as Annexure-B, shows that the meeting stated at 10-00 AM on 3-3-07. Thus it appears that requirement of 2 days' interval in between the issuance of the notice and the holding of the meeting was not complied with, inasmuch there could be no interval of two days, for that matter 48 hours, between the issuance of the notices at different times on 1-3-07 and holding of the meeting at 10-00 AM on 3-3-07. Further, it appears from the materials on record that there are 14 members in the Syndicate including the Vice-Chancellor, of which 9 members belong to the Chittagong University and the rest five (5) members are outsiders and no material could be placed before us to show that the notices of the meeting were issued or served upon the said five (5) outside members. It also appears from proceeding of the Syndicate meeting held on 3-3-07 that only the 9 Syndicate members, belonging to the University only, were present. Thus, we are of the view that the notices of the meeting held on 3-3-07 were not duly issued and/or served upon the five (5) outside members. Accordingly, the Syndicate's Extraordinary meeting dated 3-3-07 as called, convened and held was not proper, in the absence of issuance/service of notices on the five (5) members of the Syndicate and for not providing required "two days' interval" between the issuance of notice and holding of the meeting. Thus, the extraordinary meeting of the Syndicate held on 3-3-07 was not proper and therefore, the impugned decision taken in said meeting held on 3-3-07 is bad in the eye of law.</u>

46. The action taken by the Chittagong University as per decision of the Syndicate members appears to be bad for non-application of mind in that by the impugned gazette notification dated 10-3-2007 the result of Habib Ahsan published in the Gazette Notification No. Ex-12346-55 dated 28-4-92, which relates to his getting referred in one subject has been cancelled. The Gazette Notification bearing Memo No. 12360-64 dated 3-5-92, by which said Habib Ahsan has been declared to have passed the LL.B. Final Examination, has not been cancelled and, as such, his result declaring him passed remained unchallenged and unaltered. It is to be noted that Habib Ahsan categorically stated that the result showing him passed in the LL.B. Final examination was published in the gazette notification bearing Memo No.12360-64 dated 3-5-1992 but the Chittagong University could not produce any Memo containing "same number and date" to show the claim of Habib Ahsan was incorrect. The copy of the said gazette notification bearing Memo No. 12360-64 dated 3-5-92 has been enclosed as Annexure-4 to the Supplementary Affidavit dated 5-6-07. The said Memo dated 3-5-1992 having not been cancelled, the impugned notification dated 10- 3-07 so far relates to cancellation of result of Habib Ahsan is of no legal effect. The respondent-University did not produce any gazette notification bearing Memo No. 12360- 64 dated 3-5-92 to show that the copy of the gazette notification dated 3-5-92 produced by Habib Ahsan is forged or not genuine. The Syndicate though accepted the recommendations of the second Inquiry Committee but failed to take into consideration the comments made at pages 152 and 155 of the report, wherein it has been clearly written that : "

“অনেক টেবুলেশন শীটে টেবুলেটরদের ও সহি নেই। ফলে ফলাফলে অনেক কাটাছেড়া রয়েছে কিন্তু সই নেই। তাই ছাত্রদের দোষ নেই বিধায় ঘষামাজা কাটাকাটিকে সঠিক হিসাবে ধরিয়া নেয়া হইয়াছে।”

Photocopy of report has been annexed as Annexure-I to the Supplementary Affidavit of the petitioner of WP No. 2864/07.

47. These facts prove the non-application of mind in taking the impugned decision of cancellation of results by the Syndicate.

<u>48. Considering the aforesaid facts and circumstances of the case, we are constrained to observe that the University Authority, for that matter the Syndicate members, did not act bonfire and or applied their mind in taking the impugned decision of cancellation of the results of the examinees, including the writ petitioners, in spite of the fact that the University Authority claims to be the loco parents of the students. The University authority was so unmindful to realise that by the impugned decision it attempted to ruin the family lives of the examinees concerned, in that the petitioners having had established themselves in the social life through achievements of so many years, were put to face civil death in their worldly life and that there could be hardly any "way or time for them to settle themselves again in the society after so many years. The writ petitioners, two of them are practicing as lawyers and the third petitioner Mr Faizee, while practicing in the High Court Division, was appointed as permanent Judge of the High Court Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh, a noble and dream office. Because of such unmindful, inconsiderate and unkind decision of the Syndicate the said Mr Faizee has been compelled to tender resignation from the office of Judge of the High Court Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh and thus he has suffered irreparable loss and injury, which cannot be adequately compensated with money or otherwise. The sufferings of the petitioners are irreparable, and particularly the future of Mr Faizee has been ruined, and the Chittagong University is solely responsible for the same. We may profitably refer to a softer case in the Indian Jurisdiction in the case of Rabindra Nath Ghosal vs University of Calcutta and others, reported in All India Educational Cases (1950-91)(4) AIEC 666 wherein the publication of the result of an examinee delayed by six years has been held by the Calcutta High Court as an act of criminal neglect. We do not find any reason why, in the instant case, the decision of the Syndicate, for that matter of the Chittagong University, in canceling the results of the petitioners along with others after about 17/15 years should not be termed as an act of criminal neglect.</u>

<u>49. In view of the findings that (1) the notices dated 1-3-07 calling and convening the Syndicate's Extraordinary meeting held on 3-3-07 not being proper, since not served on five (5) out of fourteen (14) members of the Syndicate, the meeting as held suffers from illegality, (2) there was violation of the principles of natural justice in cancelling the results, (3) there was no proper application of mind of the syndicate members in taking the decision for cancellation of the results, (4) there is no proof of involvement of the writ petitioners in the alleged erasement and overwriting in the. Tabulation sheets, (5) there is no proof that the marks appearing in the Tabulation-sheets are incorrect and (6) there was inordinate delay in passing impugned decision of cancellation of the results, for which the University is solely responsible and is hit by the principle of estoppel and equity, so the petitioners should not be punished. Thus, we find merit in the respective Rules.</u>

<u>Accordingly, the respective Rules in (1) WP No. 3022 of 2007, (2) WP No. 3288 of 2007 and (3) WP No. 2864 of 2007 are made absolute there will be cost of Taka 20,000 in each Rule against the University. The impugned cancellation of the results of the petitioners of (1) WP No. 3022 of 2007, (2) WP No. 3288 of 2007 and (3) WP No. 2864 of 2007, published in the impugned Gazette Notification No. পনি/সিফবাস/০১/২০০৭/১৩৮৭(৪২) dated 10-3-2007, pursuant to the impugned decision taken by the Chittagong University Syndicate in its meeting held on 3-3-07 canceling their results is declared to be without lawful authority and of no legal effect. The respondents are directed to correct and rectify the impugned Gazette Notification dated 10-3-2007 in terms of this judgment and order, declaring that the petitioners (1) Abu Md Zia Habib Ahsan, (2) Jesmin Sultana and (3) Faisal Mahmud Faizee has passed the LL.B. Degree examinations, through gazette notification, within thirty (30) days of receipt of copy of this judgment and order.</u>

End.

parties:
Abdul Khaleque Sarnamat  ----- Appellant
vs.
Abdul Khaleque Sarnamat and another  ----- Respondents.
case_source: (From judgment and order dated 5th June, 1990 passed by the High Court Division, Barisal Session in Writ Petition No. 29 of 1988).
full_judgment:
ATM Afzal CJ : This appeal by leave arises out of a proceeding under section 95 and 95A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 and is directed against the judgment and order dated 5th June 1990 passed by a Divisor Bench of the High Court Division (Barisal Session) in Writ Petition No. 29 of 1988 making the Rule absolute and declaring that the order of the Additional Commissioner, Khulna Division dated 24-3-1988 in Redemption Appeal No. 213 of 1985 was of no legal effect.

2. Admitted facts of the case are that respondent No. 1 purchased one acre of land from the appellant by a registered kabala dated 24-6-1967 (Annexure "A" to the writ petition) for a consideration of Taka 2,000.00. On the same date he executed a registered agreement to reconvey the kabala land (Annexure "B" to the writ petition) if the consideration money was repaid within 4 years from that date. The appellant filed Miscellaneous Case No. 1227 of 1972-73 in the Court of the then Sub-Divisional Officer, Barisal (South) to get the land redeemed.

3. During the pendency of the said proceeding the appellant filed Title Suit No. 287 of 1979 in the Second Court of Munsif, Barisal for specific performance of contract on the basis of the aforesaid agreement for reconveyance which was dismissed on 17-4-1980 on the ground that the suit was barred by limitation. The appellant took an appeal, Title Appeal No. 120 of 1980, which was also dismissed by the District Judge, Bakergonj on 26-6-1981.

4. It appears from the Paper Book that the proceeding started by the appellant under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act for redemption of the disputed land was dismissed by the CO (Revenue), Bakergonj by his order dated 3-2-1983 passed in Miscellaneous Case No. 922 BK/73-74 and appeal from the said order was also dismissed by the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) on 1-7-1985 and upon a further appeal the Additional Commissioner, Khulna by his order dated 24-3-1988 allowed the appeal and ordered for redemption of the land as prayed for by the appellant in his Miscellaneous case. As already noticed the order of the Additional Commissioner, Khulna Division was set aside by the High Court Division by the impugned judgment and order passed in Writ Petition No. 29 of 1988.

5. The High Court Division in the impugned judgment observed that as the date of reconveyance expired on 1-3-1972 before the President's Order No. 88 of 1972 came into force on 3-8-1972, the transaction on the basis of Annexures "A" & "B" to the writ petition could not be treated as a mortgage transaction in the light of the decision in Bangladesh vs. Haji Abdul Gani Biswas 32 DLR (AD) 233 and the appellant was not entitled to get back the case land on the basis of section 95A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act.

6. Leave was granted to consider the submission that the High Court Division upon an erroneous view of section 95 and 95A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and the decision referred to above as also the facts of the case erred in holding that the appellant was not entitled to get back the case land.

7. There is no dispute that the appellant sold the land to respondent No. 1 by kabala dated 24-6-1967 and the agreement for reconveyance of the said land executed on the same day stipulated a period of 4 (four) years from the said date, that is to say, the time for reconveyance expired on 23-6-1971. The question for consideration is whether the aforesaid transaction is attracted by section 95A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act.

8. Mr. TH Khan, learned Advocate for the appellant, has argued that it does and the principles enunciated in 32 DLR (AD) 233 do not defeat the appellant's right of redemption under section 95 of the said Act. Mr. AK Badrul Huq, learned Advocate for respondent No. 1, has, however, contested the submission made on behalf of the appellant.

9. Section 95A was inserted by President's Order No. 88 of 1972 which came into force on 3-8-1972 and following certain amendments therein made by President's Order No. 136 of 1972 and President's Order No. 24 of 1973, it reads thus :

95A. Treatment of Certain Transaction as Usufructuary Mortgage. Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force, any transfer of a holding or of portion or share thereof, either by way of an out and out sale with an agreement to reconvey or where the transferor receives from the transferee any consideration and the transferee acquires the right to possess, and to enjoy the usufruct of, such holding or portion or share thereof for a specified period in lieu of such consideration, shall notwithstanding anything contained in the document relating to the transfer, be deemed to be a complete usufructuary mortgage for a period not exceeding seven years and the provisions of section 95 shall apply to such transfer whether made before or after the date of commencement of the State Acquisition and Tenancy(Second Amendment) Order, 1972 (President's Order 88/72).

10. In 33 DLR (AD) 233 this Division decided as follows :

Our conclusions, therefore, are that the President's Order Nos. 88 and 136 of 1972 and No. 24 of 1973 are all valid legislation for effecting necessary amendments in the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and those laws cannot be attacked on the ground of ultra vires; (2) any transfer of a holding or part thereof by a raiyat either by way of out and out sale with an agreement to reconvey or where the transferor receives from the transferee any consideration and transferee acquires the right to possess and enjoy the usufruct, shall notwithstanding anything contained in the document relating to the transfer, be deemed to be a complete usufructuary mortgage for a period of maximum 7 years and the provisions of section 95(4) and (5) shall apply to such transfers; (3) and such transfers are not to be understood in the light of the Transfer of Property Act because those are to be understood in the light of the enactment in question: (4) those transactions which are subsisting on the date of promulgation of President's Order No. 88 of 1972 are hit by section 95A including the transaction entered into by way of an out and out sale with an agreement to reconvey, made whether before or after the promulgation of President's Order No. 88 of 1972: and (5) as for the transactions which are not alive before the promulgation of President's Order No. 88 of 1972 they are concluded by the transactions past and closed.

11. Reading the provisions of section 95A and our decision above it cannot be denied that the transactions in the present case (by way of an out and out sale with an agreement to reconvey) shall be deemed to be a complete usufructuary mortgage and it must be said that the High Court Division was wrong in holding that the transaction "cannot be treated as a mortgage transaction in the light of the above decision". But then the question will still be that to attract the application of section 95A the transaction must be a subsisting one on the date of promulgation of President's Order No. 88 of 1972 (3-8-72) and the transactions which are not alive on that date are to be treated as transactions past and closed. This is precisely what has been laid down in clauses (4) and (5) of paragraph 11 of the judgment quoted above.

<u>12. In the instant case, the parties agreed by the transaction in question that the period of mortagage will be for 4 years beginning from 24-6-1967. So, the transaction cannot be said to be alive and subsisting on the date of promulgation of President's Order No. 88 of 1972, i.e. on 3-8-1972. It was a transaction past and closed. Mr. TH Khan wanted us to interpret section 95A as laying down that notwithstanding anything contained in the document relating to the transfer the same should be deemed to be a complete usufructuary mortgage for a period of 7 years and, in that view of the matter, he submits that the transaction was subsisting on 3-8-1972. We find it plainly difficult to accept his submission. The import of the provision of section 95A is that whatever may be the period mentioned in the document the mortgage will be deemed to be for a period "not exceeding seven years." The intention of the law is to limit the period of mortgage to 7 years. In this connection reference may be made to section 95(1) which also stipulates that the period of complete usufructuary mortgage, which (alone) a raiyat is permitted to enter into, shall not exceed seven years which prior to the amendment in 1969 was fifteen years. This does not mean that the parties cannot or could not make a transaction for less than seven years and that in such a case also, section 95A contemplates mortgage for seven years. Admittedly, the mortgage in the present case was for 4 years and the period having already expired long before 3-8-72, section 95A will have no application to the transaction which was past and closed.</u>

13. Mr. Khan also argued that since the transaction in question has been found to be a complete usufructuary mortgage under section 95A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, the appellant was entitled to seek for redemption of the said mortgage and the doctrine of 'transaction past and closed' did not apply. In support of his contention he referred to Abu Bakkar vs. Nazir Ahmed 34 DLR (AD) 237. We have perused the said decision and found that the same does not help the appellant. In that case plaintiff-appellant filed a suit in 1964 for redemption of the suit land which was transferred by him to the defendant-respondent under a registered instrument dated 11 November, 1953. Question arose whether the document: in question was a kot mortgage or an out and out sale with a condition for reconveyance on repayment of the consideration within a period of 5 years. The trial Court held the transaction to be an out and out sale and dismissed the suit but on appeal the learned Subordinate Judge found the transaction to be a complete usufructuary mortgage, the consideration of which was already satisfied by the usufruct of the land and accordingly, decreed the suit for redemption. The decree was, however, set aside by the High Court Division taking the view that the suit was barred by limitation as well as by the doctrine of transaction past and closed. Leave was granted to consider whether the suit was barred by limitation as well as by the doctrine of transaction past and closed as held by the High Court Division.

14. In that case this Division held contrary to the High Court Division that the transaction in question was a complete usufructuary mortgage as found by the Subordinate Judge and that the suit filed by the plaintiff for redemption within a period of 60 years from the date of accrual of his right of redemption was not barred by limitation. Nothing has been said with regard to the other question as to whether the transaction was past and closed in view of the finding that the document in question was one of mortgage and not of sale with a condition for reconveyance. There is nothing in that judgment which is contradictory to paragraph 11 as quoted above of the decision reported in 32 DLR (AD) 233. In the facts of the present case the view that has been taken that the transaction in question was not subsisting on the date of promulgation of President's Order No. 88 of 1972 as per the guideline set out in the 32 DLR case does not in any way seem to be in conflict with the decision cited i.e. 34 DLR (AD) 237.

15. Although not very material for the purpose of the decision in the case there is an error in the impugned judgment of the High Court Division which need be corrected. On behalf of the writ-petitioner-respondent, it was argued that although the time for reconveyance ended on 24-7-1971 the period would be extended till 1-3-1972 in view of the Bangladesh (Legal Proceedings) Order, 1972 President's Order No. 12 of 1972. The High Court Division accepted the contention which appears to be plainly wrong inasmuch as President's Order No. 12 of 1972 has no application in case of a private document. The learned Advocates of both the sides agree that President's Order No. 12 of 1972 was wrongly invoked in the facts of the case. This wrong invocation, however, does not affect the merit of the decision because whether it was 24-6-1971 or 1-3-1972 the fact remains that President's Order No. 88 of 1972 came into force long after both the dates i.e., on 3-8-1972.

16. The High Court Division although was not correct in making some findings as noticed above but the decision given by it ultimately following 32 DLR case was correct. TH Khan has been fair enough to concede that if the transaction is construed to be a mortgage for 4 years only and not 7 years as mentioned in section 95A then he has no case because in that case it will be governed by the principle of transaction past and closed as laid down in 32 DLR case.

17. In view of the discussion above we find no merit in this appeal which is accordingly dismissed with cost.

End.

lawyer:
Md. Nurul Amin, AKM Shahidul Huq, Advocates—For the Petitioners.
Faruque Ahmed with Nasrin Ferdous and Roushan Praveen, Advocates—For the Opposite Parties.
parties:
Abdul Gani Master being dead his heirs Abu Taher and others ----- Defendant-Petitioners
Vs. 
Ayub Ali Mollah and ors ----- Plaintiff-Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
By this Rule the Opposite Parties were called upon to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and decree dated 7-6-1989 passed by the learned District Judge, Chandpur, in Title Appeal No. 101 of 1985 dismissing the appeal and affirming those dated 31-7-1985 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge), Chandpur in Title Suit No. 182 of 1982 decreeing the suit should not be set aside and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. Facts necessary for disposal of the Rule are that the schedule 3 land to the plaint belonged to Hafez Ali Akbar who entered into an oral contract for sale of the said land for a consideration of Taka 26,000 in favour of the plaintiff in the month of Baishak 1362. Said Hafez Ali Akbar on receipt of entire consideration money handed over possession of the said land in favour of the plaintiff who started possessing the land and during his possession Hafez Ali Akbar died in the year 1965 leaving behind the defendant Nos. 1-9 as his heirs. During possession of the plaintiff the SA Khatian in respect of the said land was prepared in his name and he also paid rent and had been in possession more than 12 years. The plaintiff requested the defendant Nos. 1-9 to execute and register a sale deed pursuant to the said oral contract but they refused. By virtue of continuous possession for more than 12 years there was created title by adverse possession in favour of the plaintiff as against the defendants. Thereafter, the plaintiff came to know that the defendant Nos. 1-5 had executed and registered a sale deed in respect of schedule 3 land to the plaint dated 6-6-1980 in favour of the defendant Nos. 10-13 (the present petitioner). Thereafter, the plaintiff instituted the instant suit being No. 206 of 1980 in the Court of learned Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge), Chandpur for declaration of title by way of adverse possession and for further declaration that the deed dated 6-6-1980 executed by the defendants Nos. 1-5 in favour of the defendants Nos. 10-13 to be void, collusive and not binding upon the plaintiff, that the suit was subsequently renumbered as Title Suit No. 182 of 1982.

3. The defendants Nos. 10-13 contested the suit by filing Written Statement denying the material statements made in the plaint and contending, inter alias that the suit land belonged to Bondey Ali. The heirs of Hafez Ali Akbar sold the suit land to the defendants. After the death of Hafez Ali Akbar the defendants Nos. 1-9 used to possess the suit land as of their own right, title and interest. During their possession, the defendant Nos. 1-5 sold the suit land in favour of the defendants Nos. 10-13 and since purchase they had been in possession in the suit land. The predecessor of the defendants Nos. 1-9 or the defendant Nos. 1-5 had never transferred the suit land in favour of the plaintiff. The defendants Nos. 1-5 had never entered into an agreement for sale of the suit land as alleged in the plaint. The plaintiff got recorded his name in the SA record without having any basis. The plaintiff got no right title and possession in the suit land and there created no right of adverse in their favour with these averments he prayed for dismissal of the suit.

4. The learned Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge), Chandpur framed the following issues:

(i) Is the suit maintainable in its present form?

(ii) Has the plaintiff right, title, interest and possession in the suit land?

(iii) Is the impugned deed that stood in favour of the defendant Nos. 10-13 by the defendants Nos. 1-5 dated 6-6-1980 void, illegal without jurisdiction, fraudulent, collusive and not binding upon the plaintiff?

(iv) To what relief, if any, is the plaintiff entitled to get?

5. The plaintiff examined 4 PWs and the defendants Nos. 10-13 examined equal number of witnesses.

6. The learned Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge), Chandpur upon consideration of the evidence on record decreed the suit by the judgment and decree dated 31-7-1985.

7. Being aggrieved by the said judgment and decree the defendants Nos. 10-13 preferred Title Appeal No. 101 of 1985. That appeal was heard by the learned District Judge, Chandpur who by the impugned judgment and decree dated 7-6-1989 dismissed the appeal with costs and affirmed those dated 31-7-1985 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge), Chandpur, in Title Suit No. 182 of 1982.

8. Having felt aggrieved by the impugned judgment and decree, the defendants Nos. 10-13 have obtained the instant Rule.

9. Mr Md Nurul Amin, the learned Advocate for the petitioners, took me to the judgments of both the Courts below and also the evidences on record and submitted that to acquire title by adverse possession the plaintiff had to make out a case of his entry into the suit land wrongfully and to continue his possession in the suit land for more than 12 year with hostile assertion of right but, in the instant case, such an averment has neither been made in the plaint nor any evidence has been adduced by the plaintiffs. He submitted that the PW 1 himself failed to make out any case of acquiring his title by adverse possession in the suit land. He further submitted that the other PWs simply testified that on the basis of oral agreement, the plaintiffs were parted with possession and they continued that possession. Mr. Nurul Amin submitted that the evidences of PWs if be read together those do not constitute any title by adverse possession.

10. Mr Faruque Ahmed, the learned Advocate for the opposite parties, submitted that the judgment and decree impugned in this Rule is a judgment of affirmance and both the Courts below have concurrently found title in favour of the plaintiffs by adverse possession and this Court in revision is not entitled to interfere unless any case of non-consideration of any evidence or no reading of any evidence or misreading of any evidence are made out.

11. Mr Md Nurul Amin at this stage took me to the judgments of the learned District Judge, Chandpur and pointed out that the learned District Judge utterly failed to discuss and consider any evidence on record and simply made a ditto with the judgment pronounced by the trial Court. He further submitted that no issue was framed upon the question of acquisition of title by adverse possession and he submitted that unless any issue is framed the decree if passed would be a nullity. In support of his contention, he relied upon the case law of Niropoma Ritchel vs Md Abdul Jalil Miah and others, reported in 41 DLR 467. He further submitted that possession on the basis of an agreement if be relied upon that also does not acquire any title unless a kabala is registered and possession is handed over on the strength of the said kabala. He submitted that in the instant case it is not the case of plaintiff that any kabala was made pursuant to the oral contract. Mr Nurul Amin cited the case law of Banabir Purkayastha alias Bhanu vs Alekjan Bibi and others, reported in 34 DLR (AD) 98. He has drawn attention to the evidence of PW 1 and submitted that PW 1 hopelessly failed to adduce any evidence in support of his possession and in absence of any evidence adduced by the PW 1, the other evidences as adduced by the PW 2-PW 4 did not constitute any title in favour of the plaintiff. In support of his arguments he relied upon the case of Jobeda Khatun vs Hamid Ali, reported in 40 DLR (AD) 101 relevant page 105 pares 9 and 11. On the other hand, Mr Faruque Ahmed contended that the possession of the plaintiffs having been supported by PW 2 - PW 4 from 1955 those are sufficient to create title by adverse possession in favour of the plaintiff. He relied upon the case of Mahmood Alam and others vs Moklesur Rahman Bhuiya reported in 54 DLR 523 and also relied upon the case law of Jalil Miah vs Niropoma Ritchel, reported in 49 DLR (AD) 61. He submitted that the facts of the instant case are quite identical with the facts of case law of Mahmood Alam (Md) and another vs Moklesur Rahman Bhuiya, reported in 54 DLR 523. He further submitted that although no issue was framed upon the question of acquiring title by adverse possession but that will not disentitle the plaintiff from getting relief on relying upon the case law of Hachina Begum and others vs Mosammat Mahfuza Akhter and others, reported in 1996 BLD 374.

12. I have heard the learned Advocates of both the parties at length. I have gone through the judgments recorded by the Courts below very meticulously and also have gone through the evidence on record very carefully.

13. On perusal of the plaint it appears that at paragraph 4 of the plaint the plaintiff made some averment to the effect that the suit land belonged to Hafez Ali Akbar Ali who entered into a contract for sale of the suit land at a consideration of Taka 2600 in favour of the plaintiff and on receipt a the said consideration money had handed over possession in his favour and since then he had been continuing his possession in the suit land. It is further stated that after taking over possession he sold out some earth from the suit land, made the same suitable for cultivation and thereafter started possessing the same by cultivating crops. Save and except these averments no other averments are available in the plaint to constitute title by adverse possession. In paragraph No. 7 of the plaint it is stated that Hafez Ali Akbar died in 1965 leaving behind the defendants Nos. 1-2 and 6 as his sons and the defendant No. 3, 4, 5, 7, 8 and 9 to be his daughters. In paragraph No. 8 it has been stated that during his possession in the suit land, the defendants Nos. 1-5 collusively executed and registered the kabala deed in question in favour of the defendants Nos. 10-13 in respect of the suit land on 6-6-1980. He came to know about the kabala on and from 11-6-1980 and filed the suit. Save and except this averment there is no other averment available in the plaint to acquire title by adverse possession.

14. Adverse means obstruction to one's interest, unfavorable, harmful or detrimental or prejudicial. Adverse possession means hostile possession which is expressly or impliedly in denial of the title of the true owner. Such possession must be actual and exclusive under a claim of right adequate in continuity, in publicity and in extent so as to show that it is adverse to the true owner. Such possession in denial of title of the true owner must be peaceable, open and continuous. It must he open and hostile enough to be capable of being known to the party interested. Before a right can be acquired or lost by adverse possession, it must have been the subject of possession by a man without title as against the person with the rightful title.

<u>15. In the instant case, on perusal of the evidences on record I find that there is no such evidence adduced by the plaintiff asserting his possession expressly or impliedly in denial of the title of true owner. The plaintiff himself, on oath, at the trial, adduced evidence but had failed to adduce any evidence in support of his claim and acquiring title by adverse possession. Mr Faruque Ahmed candidly admitted the fact that due to the fault of the learned Advocate, who conducted the case on behalf of the plaintiff, before the trial Court, had unintentionally failed to adduce any evidence from the lips of the plaintiff in support of his possession. PW 2 Kazi Abdus Sobhan adduced evidence in support of talk of sale by Ha fez Ali Akbar with the plaintiff and adduced evidence in support of payment of consideration of Taka 2600 and further added that the plaintiff had been in possession in the suit land since 1362 but did not adduce any evidence in support of title and possession of the plaintiff in the suit land. PW 3 Fazlul Haque Patwary testified that the suit land belonged to Hafez Ali Akbar from whom the plaintiff had purchased the same in 1362, 27th Baishak at Taka 2600. That consideration money was paid and the plaintiff was handed over possession in the suit land and since purchase he had been in possession. PW 4 Abul Kalam did not adduce any evidence in support of the plaintiff's possession in the suit land. On perusal of the evidences as discussed above there is no averment made in the plaint that the plaintiff entered into the suit land with hostile assertion of his title and continued his possession adversely against the defendant. It is his simple case that he entered into the suit land on the strength of an oral agreement and paid the full consideration money. In the case of Ibrahim Khan and others vs Muhammad Afsar Khan, reported in PLD 1960 Azad Jammu and Kashmir page 26, a similar question arose for decision wherein the fact was that one Afsar Khan filed a suit for declaration against the appellant claiming that he was in adverse possession of the suit land for more than 12 years on the basis of agreement for sale. The suit was contested stating, inter alias, that the possession of Muhammad Afsar Khan could not be treated as adverse to others on the basis of an agreement for sale as Afsar Khan's possession under the contract for sale was of a permissive in nature and could not be treated as adverse possession. The learned Subordinate Judge held that Afsar Khan's possession was not adverse possession and the learned District Judge held the possession of Mohammad Afsar Khan was adverse and had ripened into ownership. In the reported decision the finding of the District Judge was set aside and the decision of the Subordinate Judge was restored. The observation of their Lordships were as under: "When a contract for sale is executed it does not bestow any right of ownership on the person in whose favour it is executed until a regular sale deed is executed. A promise who is allowed to take possession of the land before a regular sale deed is executed merely holds it on behalf of the promissor and if the promissor is not willing to part with possession the promise cannot compel him in law to part with possession." Their Lordships further held in that decision that possession under a defective sale deed is different from a possession under a contract for sale. In that case he is not entitled to consider himself to be the owner, as it is yet to get a proper sale deed executed in his favour to become an owner in the true sense of the term and his possession cannot be considered as hostile to the promissor. If the starting of his possession was found on the basis of agreement, then the plaintiff lawfully went to possess by virtue of a contract for sale. But that cannot be declared adverse possession.</u>

<u>16. In the case of Banabir Purkayastha alias Bhanu vs Alekjan Bibi and others, reported in 34 DLR (AD) 98 a common question came for decision, whether possession on the basis of a contract creates a title and it was held by our Appellate Division that unless a decree on the basis of contract is given and is completed by execution of the kabala, no title accrues in favour of the purchaser and hence the question of possession becomes secondary. In a suit of this nature possession is not linked up with the main claim of the suit, as the title does not accrue on the passing of the decree. Here in the instant case the evidences adduced by PW 2 and PW 3 in support of possession became secondary, in view of the fact that mere possession, asserted by them, in their evidences, is not linked up with the main claim of adverse possession in the suit and those evidences do not create any title by adverse possession. It is to be also held that lawfully possession and claiming adverse possession are two distinct and separate things. The most essential elements of adverse possession is the possession of a property by a person having no right over the property and such possession must be adverse to the true owner. The question of adverse possession in a case has to be determined from the specific averments made in the plaint. In the instant case, as I have seen, that no such averment has been made in the plaint asserting title by adverse possession. It is really surprising to note that the decree has been passed declaring title by adverse possession without framing any issue on such vital question of law and fact. On my query, Mr. Faruque Ahmed submitted that mistakenly that issue could not be framed by the trial Court and as well as the appellate Court. In view of the above, the plaintiff if he found to be in possession on the basis of the oral contract that possession cannot be considered to be adverse possession against the true owner. The learned District Judge was not justified in finding adverse possession without framing any issue on the point. The Courts below were not justified in declaring title by adverse possession and the decisions arrived at by the courts below are liable to he set aside. The case law reported in 54 DLR 523, cited by Mr Faruque Ahmed is quite distinguishable from the facts of the instant case. In the case reported in 54 DLR 523, possession was handed over in favour of the plaintiff on the basis of contract and thereafter, the plaintiff constructed pucca homestead upon the said land and continued possession for more than 12 years. Thereafter, another transfer was made and the transferee continued in possession more than 12 years. Taking into consideration that aspect this Court held possession to be adverse possession. But the fact of that case is quite distinguishable from the facts of the instant case and that decision does not come to any assistance to the plaintiff-opposite party. The case law reported in 1996 BLD 375 being not at all relevant for decision of this case and the fact of that case being distinguishable from the fact of the instant case, the same is kept out of consideration. From the facts and circumstances and the discussions made above, it is my considered view, that the learned Sub-ordinate Judge being the trial Court and the learned District Judge being the appellate Court have committed an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning a failure of justice declaring title of the plaintiff by adverse possession in the suit land without being based on any proper pleading and as well as any evidences on record.
