The finding and decision arrived by the learned District Judge are although concurrent in nature but those are perverse and not sustainable in law. Those decisions having been arrived at without being based on any evidence on record are set aside. In view of the above I find merit in the Rule.</u>

17. In the result, the Rule is made absolute, however, without any order as to costs. The impugned judgment and decree dated 7-6-1989 passed by the learned District Judge, Chandpur, in Title Appeal No. 101 of 1985 dismissing the appeal and affirming those dated 31-7-1985 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge), Chandpur in Title Suit No. 182 of 1982 decreeing the suit are hereby set aside. The suit stands dismissed however without any order as to costs.

The office is directed to send down the lower Court's record at once.

End.

lawyer:
AB Siddique, Advocate—For the Petitioner. 
Goutom Kumar Roy, Advocate—For Opposite Party No. 1.
parties:
Lutfunnessa @ Lutfa Begum ----- Petitioner
vs.
Abdul Halim Khan and others ----- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
This Rule calls in question the legality and propriety of the judgment and decree dated 27-10-1998 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Faridpur, in Title Appeal No. 216 of 1991 reversing those of dated 10-8-1991 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Artha Rin Adalat, Faridpur, in Title Suit No. 30 of 1975 remanding the suit to the trial Court for fresh trial.

2. Short facts leading to this Rule are that on 7-4-1975 the opposite party No. 1 as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 30 of 1975 in the First Court of Subordinate Judge, Faridpur, impleading the petitioner and opposite party Nos. 2-52 as defendants for declaration of title in the property described in the Schedule of the plaint.

3. The plaintiff's case, in brief, is that the suit land had originally belonged to Faridpur Chowdhury Estate Ltd. Abdul Latif Khan and others were the tenants under them. Due to arrears of rent the Estate filed Rent Suit No. 2307 of 1941 in the then Court of Munsif, Faridpur Sadar, Faridpur against Abdul Latif Khan and others. The suit was decreed. Consequently, the suit property was auctioned under Rent Execution Case No. 1587 of 1941. The defendant No. 12, Kamrunesa Khanam purchased the first lot in the said auction sale and got possession on 8-5-1944. Subsequently, she sold out 51 decimals of land to the plaintiff under plot Nos. 12/1331 and 12/1332 by a registered kabala deed dated 28-6-1974. The defendant No. 12 permitted defendant No. 5 (herein petitioner) to reside in her dwelling house, but she fraudulently mutated her name in Municipal holding. Hence, the suit.

4. Defendant Nos. 1, 2-5, 46, 49 and 50 contested the suit by filing a joint written statement denying all the material allegations made in the plaint contending, inter alia, that their predecessor was the owner and possessor of the suit property who died leaving behind her husband Abdul Latif Khan, sons and daughters namely, defendant Nos. 1, 2, 4-5 and Abdus Salam Khan, the predecessor of the defendant Nos. 9-21 before RS record. So, the suit property was rightly recorded in their names.

5. On the pleadings different issues were settled including the issue of maintainability.

6. In course of trial, the plaintiff examined 4(four) witnesses and contesting defendants examined 3(three) witnesses to prove their respective case.

7. Eventually, the learned Judge of the trial Court by the judgment and decree dated 10-8-1991 dismissed the suit holding that the suit is not maintainable under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act.

8. On appeal, the learned Judge of the Court below by the judgment and decree dated 27-10-1998 reversed those of the trial Court and sent the suit back on remand for fresh trial.

9. Feeling aggrieved the petitioner obtained the present Rule.

10. Mr AB Siddique, the leaned Advocate appearing for the petitioner, supports the Rule and submits that there were sufficient materials on record to arrive at a conclusive decision in the appeal without remanding the suit to the trial Court. He adds that the plaintiff prayed for declaration of his title without possession in respect of unspecified share in the suit property, there-fore, the trial Court rightly dismissed the suit. He adds that the Court of appeal below acted illegally in remanding the suit to the trial Court with the decision to obtain a fresh evidence, both oral and documentary, from the parties. In support of his contention, the learned Counsel refers the case of Atikullah and others vs Zafala Begum and others reported in 54 DLR (AD) 74, wherein it is held:

"Remand as contemplated under Order XLI, rule 23 of the Code of Civil Procedure was not a matter of course or to fill in the lacuna in any party's pleading."

11. He also refers the case of Superintendent Engineer (Distribution), Power Development Board, Jangalia, Comilla and others vs Madhumati Cinema Ltd Comilla and others reported in 54 DLR (AD) 170 wherein it is held:

"Although the provision of remand should not be exercised to cure any defect or filling up any lacuna in the pleadings of the parties or the case of the parties but in order to decide the material issue concerned in the suit, the order of remand was warranted in the facts and circumstances of the case."

12. The learned Counsel also refers the case of Golam Rahman vs Hazera Khatun reported in 47 DLR (AD) 108 wherein it is held:

"The suit ought not to have been remanded for giving an opportunity to amend the plaint for making out a new case of adverse possession."

13. He refers the case of Md Abdus Sattar and others vs Lalon Mazar Sharif and Seba Sadan Committee and others reported in 2004 BLD (AD) 125 wherein it is held:

"Remand cannot be allowed as matter of course to filling the lacuna of the case of any party. The appellate Court relied upon inadmissible evidence namely, report of the Advocate Commissioner. Report itself is no evidence, unless the Advocate Commissioner deposes on oath before the court, the same is evidence."

14. He further refers the case of Khairunnesa vs Atar Banu and others reported in 10 BLC (AD) 25 wherein it is held:

"It is the settled principle of law that a remand order is never to be made to fill up the lacuna in the case of any party and a remand order should not be made on fanciful or unnecessary ground. The remand order of the High Court Division in the present case seems to be unnecessary because the High Court Division itself is competent to decide the dispute in revision on the basis of evidence on record. From the close scrutiny, discussion and evaluation of the deposition of the defence witnesses, it is apparently clear that they could not disprove the case of the plaintiff. Rather, indirectly they admitted the case of the plaintiff and her predecessor-in-interest. It appears that the High Court Division without any cogent and legal reason has set aside the concurrent findings and decisions of the Courts below. The lower appellate Court dismissed the appeal discussing the evidence on records both oral and documentary in detail and, as such, the order of remand made by the High Court Division does not carry any legal meaning rather, it is fanciful."

15. The learned Counsel lastly submits that the Court of appeal below without considering the evidence on record illegally observed with some remarks which materially affected the merit of this Case, thereby the Court of appeal below committed an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice.

16. Mr Goutom Kumar Roy, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite party No. 1, without filing counter-affidavit opposes the Rule and submits that after considering the evidence on record the Court of appeal below rightly remanded the suit to the trial Court for fresh trial. He adds that by such order neither of the parties will be prejudiced rather, the plaintiff will get the chance to prove his case with out going to further suit. According to him, in such case the order of remand passed by the Court of appeal below is justified. In support of his contention, he refers the case of Chand Mohammad vs Md Golam Rasul reported in 3 BLC 381 wherein it is held:

"The plaintiff having failed to comply with the direction of the appellate Court to make the suit as a partition suit by amendment, the trial Court has rightly dismissed the suit as the appellate Court after due consideration and for the ends of justice gave an opportunity to the plaintiff to amend the suit and to change the nature of the suit and it becomes obligatory on the part of the plaintiff to follow the direction of the appellate Court."

17. He also refers the case of Chand Mia being dead his heirs Rehana Khatun and others vs Md Shamsuddin and others reported in 5 BLC (AD) 163 wherein it is held:

"The suit was found not maintainable by the trial Court for want of possession of the plaintiff in accordance with the proviso to section 42 of the Specific Relief Act when the appellate Court found fault with the finding of possession arrived at by the trial Court holding that the reasons of the trial Court suffered from discrepancy and the appellate Court also found that the Assistant Custodian was a necessary party and thus the appellate Court did not give any independent finding on possession or decided the matter imp leading the party in the suit itself and the said Court had sent back the case on remand to the trial Court for deciding it on all points after holding the trial afresh which has not occasioned any miscarriage of justice and, as such, it was not proper for the High Court Division to interfere with the order of remand while exercising revisional jurisdiction."

18. The learned Counsel further refers the case of Syed Abdul Mannan being dead his heirs(a) Syed Abdul Barek and others vs Md Mujahar Ali Mridha and others reported in 2 MLR 317 wherein it is held:

"When the trial Court dismissed the suit on discussion of evidence on record, the appellate Court's finding in favour of the proof of possession of the plaintiff as well as the order for sending the suit on remand for affording opportunity of adducing fresh evidence by both sides is held to be improper in the facts and circumstances of the case. Open remand is ordered so as to avoid any cause of prejudice to either party"

19. He further refers the case of Mohammad Hossain vs Monowara Begum and others reported in 2 BLC (AD) 124 wherein it is held:

"The suit was instituted by the plaintiff-respondents claiming themselves to be government servants and challenged the order directing them to apply for giving appointment afresh. Although the defendant contested the suit but could not prove his case as the prayer for shifting the date of hearing was refused and the suit was decreed and on appeal the appellate Court sent the case on remand to the trial Court giving the defendant a chance to prove his case holding that civil Court had jurisdiction to try the suit and the High Court Division endorsed the said view in civil revision. Since the petitioner could not get any opportunity to adduce evidence before the trial Court, it is the trial Court who will decide the case afresh after giving an opportunity to the defendant to adduce evidence and will also consider afresh the issue as to the maintainability of the suit in civil Court because of the plea of bar under the Provisions of the Administrative Tribunal Act."

20. In the case of Pasanta Kumar Mani and others vs Sree Radha Krishna Chowdhury reported in 4 MLR (AD) 356 wherein it is held:

"The trial Court has to give its findings based on reasoning and write judgment in accordance with law when the decisions of the trial Court are not based on any reasoning as to the points at issue. In such a situation the order for remand is justified because the trial Court judge must know and rectify himself how to write judgment property.

21. Mr Roy lastly submits that after considering the evidence on record, the Court of appeal below has rightly remanded the suit, so the same calls for no interference by this Court.

22. In order to appreciate the submissions advanced by the learned Counsels, I have gone through the revisional application, other materials on record and given my anxious consideration to their submissions.

23. Now, the question that calls for consideration is, whether the Court of appeal below committed any error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice in passing the impugned judgment and decree and remanding the suit to the trial Court for fresh trial.

24. To appreciate the question involved in this Rule, the provisions of Order XLI, rules 23, 24 and 25 and section 107 of the Code of Civil Procedure which deal with the remand of a case by the Appellate Court, may be extracted here.

"23-Where the Court from whose decree an appeal is preferred has disposed of the suit upon a preliminary point and the decree is reversed in appeal, the Appellate Court may, if it thinks fit, by order, remand the case and may further direct what issue or issues shall be tried in the case so remanded, and shall send a copy of its judgment and order to the Court from whose decree appeal is preferred, with directions to re-admit the suit under its original number in the register of civil suits, and proceed to determine the suit; and the evidence (if any) recorded during the original trial shall, subject to all just exceptions, be evidence during the trial after remand.

24-Where the evidence upon the record is sufficient to enable the appellate Court to pronounce judgment, the appellate Court may, after resetting the issues, if necessary, finally determine the suit, notwithstanding that the judgment of the Court from whose decree the appeal is preferred has proceeded wholly upon some ground other than that on which the appellate Court proceeds.

25-Where the Court from whose decree the appeal is preferred has omitted to frame or try any issue, or to determine any question of fact, which appears to the appellate Court essential to the right decision of the suit upon the merits, the appellate Court may, if necessary, frame issues, and refer the same for trial to the Court from whose decree the appeal is preferred, and in such case shall direct such Court to take the additional evidence required.

Section 107 of the Code runs as follows:

107(1)-Subject to such conditions and limitations as may be prescribed, an Appellate Court shall have power-

(a) to determine a case finally:

(b) to remand a case; (c) to frame issues and refer them for trial; (d) to take additional evidence or to require such evidence to be taken. (2) Subject as aforesaid, the appellate Court shall have the same powers and shall perform as nearly as may be the same duties as are conferred and imposed by this Code on Courts of original jurisdiction in respect of suits instituted therein."

25. From a plain reading of the above stated provisions of law it is clear that under Order XLI, rule 23 of the Code there can be no remand unless the following conditions exist: (a) that the entire suit and not a portion of it has been disposed of by the trial Court; (b) that the disposal must be on a preliminary point; (c) and that the preliminary point on which the suit is decided has been reversed by the appellate Court.

26. Order XLI, rule 24 of the Code enjoins that where the evidences on record are sufficient, the appellate Court is competent to determine the suit finally and there is no need for remand.

27. Order XLI, rule 25 of the Code lays down that only specific issues can be sent to the trial Court for findings and not for re-trial of the entire suit and the appeal is to be heard under Order XLI, rule 26 of the Code.

28. Under section 107 of the Code, the appellate Court is vested with the power to determine a case finally and also to remand the case. Sub-section 2 of section 107 of the Code lays down that the appellate Court shall have the same powers and shall perform as nearly as may be the same duties as are conferred and imposed by this Code on Courts of original jurisdiction in respect of suits instituted therein.

29. It appears that the learned Judge of the Court of appeal below sent back the suit on remand for fresh trial but I find that the learned Judge took notice of the evidence oral and documentary on record but as a last court of facts failed to weigh and sift the same and to decide the same finally and should not send the suit back on remand for fresh trial.

30. On perusal of the record of the case it appears that in the instant case all the evidences and materials were before the lower appellate Court who itself could have disposed of the appeal finally.

<u>31. It is settled principles of law that unnecessary order of remand entails hardship, agony of fresh hearing and additional expenditure and the same is to be deprecated and discouraged as it tends to delay the administration of justice far from advancing its course.</u>

32. The Pakistan Supreme Court and the Appellate Division of our Supreme Court decided the question of the order of remand in a good number of cases.

33. The Supreme Court of Pakistan in the case of Pramotha Nath Chowdhury and seventeen others vs Kamir Mondal and others reported in 17 DLR (SC) 392 held:

"a remand cannot be lightly ordered if the evidences on record is sufficient for the appellate Court to decide the question itself. There can be no bar to the Court doing so."

34. The Appellate Division, in the case of Probodh Ranjan Shome vs Md Easin reported in 1980 BSCR 457 observed that:

"It is well settled that remand orders are not to be made as a matter of course. When there is sufficient evidence on record, remand of a case to the trial Court for fresh hearing is not called for."

35. In the case of Dr Razia Khatun vs Banu Guha and another reported in 1986 BLD (AD) 135 it was observed by the Appellate Division:

"The long line of judicial decisions is to the effect that the remand order should be avoided as far as possible and even the Privy Council in some cases observed that indiscriminate order of remand tantamount to shirking the responsibility."

36. In the case of Abdul Awal Khan vs Md Sadu Mia and others reported in 1986 BLD (AD) 156 the Appellate Division held:

"when evidences on all material points are there on record, the revisional court is not justified in sending the case back to the Court below for reconsidering the matter."

37. In the case of Abdul Mannan and others vs Akram Ali and others reported in 43 DLR (AD) 124 it was held by the Appellate Division:

"both oral and documentary evidence having been available on record there was no necessity for the remand as ordered by the High Court Division."

<u>38. In the case of Haji Mustafiqur Rahman being dead his heirs Kabir Ahamed and others vs A Kader reported in 3 BLC (AD) 38 wherein it is held:</u>

<u>"It is well settled that remand orders are not to be made a matter of course, it should be avoided as far as possible."</u>

<u>39. In view of the discussion made above and the preponderant judicial views emerging out of the authorities referred to above I am of the view that the lower appellate Court was fully competent to decide the case by itself as the evidence and other materials on record were sufficient to enable it come to a final decision without entailing the parties with unnecessary trouble and expenses and the appellate Court shirked its responsibility and thus committed an error of law resulting in an error in remanding the suit to the trial Court for fresh trial and delivery of fresh judgment.</u>

40. Having regard to the facts I hold that the submissions advanced by the learned Counsel for the opposite party No. 1, may hold good before the Court of appeal below at the time of disposal of the appeal.

<u>41. Having considered the facts and circumstances of the case I am of the view that the ends of justice will be met if the matter is remitted to the Court of appeal below for final disposal of the matter on merit and then pass whatever order or orders it thinks appropriate in the interest of justice. However, the petitioner and the opposite party No. 1 are at liberty to place their respective case on merit in the Court of appeal below.</u>

42. In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to cost. The impugned judgment and decree dated 27-10-1998 passed in Title Appeal No. 216 of 1991 is hereby set aside and the suit is sent back on remand to the Court of appeal below for disposal on merit touching all points.

43. The order of stay granted earlier by this Court stands vacated.

44. The learned Judge of the Court of appeal below is directed to dispose of the appeal expeditiously preferably within 3 (three) months from the date of receipt of this order.

Send down the record of this case at once with a copy of judgment for information and taking necessary action.

End.

lawyer:
Mahbubey Elahi, Deputy Attorney-General ------ For the Petitioner. 
Fida M Kamal, Advocate ------ For the Respondent No.2.
parties:
Commissioner Customs, Excise and VAT ------ Petitioner
Vs.
Customs Excise and VAT Appellate Tribunal and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Syed Amirul Islam, J: In this Rule an interesting question of law has been raised by the VAT Department namely, as to whether the Appellate Tribunal constituted under section 196 of the Customs Act is authorised to pass an ad interim order on admission of an appeal under section 42 of the VAT Act.

2. The respondent No.2 company is manufacturer of various kinds of glass jar and they imported certain "machineries & spares" for BMRE for their industry. At the time of importation the respondent No. 2 paid the usual taxes and VAT and after importation of the materials they obtained rebate under section 9(1) (WMMA) of the VAT Act. Subsequently, it was adjusted by the VAT authority on the ground that these parts were not imported for BMRE rather for reconstruction and repair of their plant. Against that order the respondent No. 2 moved this Court by filing an application under Article 102 of the Constitution which was registered as Writ Petition No. 1680 of 2001 but that writ petition was summarily rejected by this Court holding that an appeal lies under section 42 of the VAT Act against the impugned order and the appellate authority is also competent to pass ad-interim order. There after the respondent No. 2 filed an appeal before the Appellate Tribunal against the self same order and the Tribunal on admission of the appeal stayed the impugned order on an application of the respondent No. 2 and that order is under challenge in this Rule.

3. The respondent No. 2 entered appearance and filed an affidavit-in-opposition wherein they have contended that the Appellate Tribunal is authorized by the law to pass an ad-interim order pursuant to the authority vested in them by section 42 of the VAT, read with section 196B of the Customs Act which provides for procedure for disposal of the appeal filed under section 42(1) of the VAT Act, 1991.

4. Mr Mahbubey Elahi, the learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing for the petitioner, submits that the Appellate Tribunal is not invested with the power to pass any such ad-interim order under section 42 of the VAT Act inasmuch as no such power has been conferred upon the Appellate Tribunal pursuant to that section. Mr Mahbubey Elahi, referring to the provision of section 36(2) of the Industrial Relations Ordinance, 1969 submitted that wider power was conferred upon the Labour Court under section 36(2) of the Industrial Relations Ordinance hereinafter called "the IRO" and that section came up for consideration before the Appellate Division in the Pubali Bank's case which is reported in 44 DLR (AD) 40 wherein the Appellate Division on examination of the provisions of section 36 of the IRO arrived at a finding that the Labour Court set up under section 35 of the IRO has no power of passing an ad interim order by way of granting an ad interim injunction or stay on an order impugned before it and it has been specifically observed by the Appellate Division in the said decision that only limited power as specifically conferred by sub-section (2) of section 36 on the IRO can be exercised by the Labour Court. The learned Deputy Attorney-General further fortified his submission by relying on the decision of the Appellate Division reported in 49 DLR (AD) 44 which is a case under the Administrative Tribunal Act, 1980 and in that case also the Appellate Division after considering the provisions of section 4 read with section 6 of the Administrative Tribunal Act arrived at a finding that the Appellate Tribunal constituted under the Administrative Tribunal Act has no inherent power to grant interim relief in respect of a case pending before if for final adjudication and so also is the case with the Administrative Appellate Tribunal as they are not courts proper. The learned Deputy Attorney-General finally submits that the powers conferred on the Administrative Appellate Tribunal are much wider than the powers conferred on the Appellate Tribunal under section 42 of the VAT Act read with section 196B of the Customs Act and, as such, the Appellate Tribunal is not authorised by law to pass an interim order.

5. Mr Fida M. Kamal, the learned Counsel appearing for the respondent No. 2, made a lengthy argument before us. He has taken us through the provisions of section 42 of the VAT Act and sections 196B, 196C of the Customs Act and then submitted that the impugned order is not an unreasonable or unfair order. It is a very reasonable order and the tribunal after admitting the appeal had passed the order by giving cogent reason to save the respondent No.2 from undue harassment of the authority. The learned Advocate further submits that the VAT official is bent upon the respondent No.2 evident from the fact that they instead of filing any application before the Tribunal challenged the order before this Court though the appeal is pending before the Tribunal. The learned Advocate further submits that the instant writ petition is incompetent and not maintainable because the same issue could be agitated by them before the Tribunal itself. The learned Counsel further submits that in view of the facts and circumstances of the case the petitioner does not come within the ambit of an aggrieved person at all inasmuch as at the end of the day if the appeal is dismissed they will be able to  the disputed amount but, on the other hand, if the appeal is allowed the huge amount claimed by them if realised at this point of time may force respondent No. 2 to go out of business as the respondent No.2 is passing through financial crisis. The learned Advocate referring to the provisions of section 42 of the VAT Act read with the provisions of section 196B of the Customs Act submits that the Appellate Tribunal has all comprehensive authority and power to pass the final order as it thinks fit after hearing the parties, so also it has the authority to pass an ad interim order if it is just and convenient in the facts and circumstances of the case. The learned Counsel drawing our attention to the facts and circumstances of the case submits that in the instant case it is just convenient to stay the impugned order otherwise due to paucity of fund the respondent No. 2 will not be able to carry on the manufacture of the goods. The learned Counsel further submits that the Appellate Tribunal pursuant to the provision of section 196B of the Customs Act can pass an order after giving the parties to the appeal an opportunity of being heard and order as it thinks fit confirming, modifying or annulling the decision or order appealed against, therefore, it can not be said that the Tribunal is devoid of any power to pass an ad interim order in the interest of justice and for the sake of convenience. The learned Advocate also submitted that the instant writ petition is premature because it is against the ad-interim order and the substantive matter is still pending before the Tribunal and since there is time limit provided for under sub-section (4) of section 42 of the VAT Act, the VAT Department ought to have resolved the dispute before the Tribunal without invoking the writ jurisdiction against an interim order. The learned Advocate further submits that the Tribunal although has some of the trappings of the court yet it is neither a court under the Civil Court Act or under the Civil Procedure Code but nevertheless it is a special tribunal and as special tribunal can pass such order as it thinks fit on admission of an appeal. The learned Advocate further submits that right to file an appeal is a substantive right and there is no dispute in the case that that the Tribunal is invested with the power to hear and determine the appeal under section 42 of the VAT Act and if that proposition is accepted it can not be agitated by the petitioner that the Tribunal has no power to pass an ad interim order which of necessity must be read with the substantive power and in support of his contention he relied on the decision reported in PLD 1971 (SC) 242 and PLD 1975 (SC) 32. The learned Advocate referring to the provision of section 196C(7) and (8) of the Customs Act submits that the Appellate Tribunal for the purpose of discharging its functions has the same powers as are vested in a Court under the Code of Civil Procedure and any proceeding before the Appellate Tribunal shall be deemed to be a judicial proceeding within the meaning of sections 193 and 228 and for the purpose of section 196 of the Penal Code and the Appellate Tribunal shall be deemed to appear for all purposes of section 196 of the Penal Code and the Appellate Tribunal shall be deemed to be a Civil Court for all purposes of section 195 and Chapter XXVI Criminal Procedure Code. Therefore, it is evident that the Tribunal have authority to pass an ad interim order under section 42 of the VAT Act.

6. The learned Advocate distinguished the decisions relied on by the learned Deputy Attorney-General namely, the Pubali Banks case and the 9 DLR case. Mr FM Kamal submits that Pubali Bank's case is a decision in respect of a labour legislation but yet in deciding the matter the Appellate Division considered the case reported in PLD 1971 (SC) 242 and kept the matter open in the majority judgment delivered by Mr Justice MH Rahman, and the point was not taken up by Mr Justice Mostafa Kamal in his judgment and their discussion was only in respect of the power conferred on the Labour Court by section 36(2) of the LRO. Similarly, he submits that the case reported in 49 DLR (AD) 44, also should be distinguished inasmuch as that is a decision under the Administrative Tribunal Act, 1980 and in the case the learned Counsel appearing for the petitioner, in fact, advanced argument on the doctrine of inherent power and that submission was repelled by the Appellate Division on the ground that the power has to be conferred expressly and no such power was conferred upon the Appellate Administrative Tribunal to stay an order appealed against before it and that the Tribunal is constituted under Article 117 of the Constitution which deal with the service matter in respect of the persons in the Service of the Republic and the Tribunal can not act beyond the scope of section 7(1) thereof so far exercising its authorities under the Civil Procedure only in respect of the matters expressly provided therein. The learned Advocate then submits that in the instant case the Appellate Tribunal is invested with the power to dispose of the appeal finally and therefore, the power to grant interim relief by suspending wholly or partially is incidental or ancillary to the main appellate jurisdiction. The learned Advocate in support of his contention also relies on the decision reported in 71 ITR (SC) 815 wherein the Indian Supreme Court was considering a similar provision as contained in section 254(1) of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1961 which is in similar terms of section 196B(1) of the Customs Act, and held that the section confers on the Appellate Tribunal powers of the widest amplitude in dealing with an appeal before it. It was argued in that case that the Appellate Tribunal can not pass any order of stay as the same power has not been expressly conferred on it. The contention was negative by the Indian Supreme Court and it was observed that the Appellate Tribunal must be held to have the power to grant stay as incidental or ancillary to its Appellate jurisdiction. It was further observed that when section 254 confers appellate jurisdiction, it impliedly grants the power of doing all such acts or employing such means, as are essentially necessary to its execution and that the statutory power carries with it the duty in proper cases to make such orders for staying proceeding as will prevent the appeal, if successful, from being rendered nugatory.

7. Mr FM Kamal also relied on a decision reported in 52 DLR 360 wherein one of us was a party and in interpreting the provisions of section 193 of the Customs Act, it was held that the Appellate authority has the power to pass any order including an appropriate ad interim order.

8. After hearing the parties the matter was fixed for delivery of judgment on 22-1-2002 and at that time the provision of section 42(2) caught our eyes when we requested the learned Attorney-General to address us and also appointed Mr Mahmudul Islam, the former Attorney-General, as amicus curiae and they appeared before us on 3-3-2002 when the matter was again heard.

9. Mr Hasan Ariff, the learned Attorney-General, candidly submits that on perusal of the provision as contained in section 42(2) of the VAT Act it is clear and obvious that as soon as an appeal is filed the impugned order is automatically stayed. The learned Attorney-General further submits that an appellate authority like the Tribunal has ample power to pass an ad interim order staying the order appealed against during the pendency of the appeal.

10. Mr Mahmudul Islam, the learned Advocate appearing as amicus curiae, submits that he would fully agree with the submission of the learned Attorney-General but for the decision reported in 49 DLR (AD) 44. He further submits that in case of Appellate Administrative Tribunal much wider power has been conferred on them even then the Appellate Division considering the relevant provisions of the Administrative Appellate Tribunal has no authority to pass an ad interim order in an appeal during the pendency of the same before it. Mr Mahmudul Islam, the learned amicus curiae , has taken us through the different provisions of the Customs Act, Income Tax Ordinance and VAT Act and referring to the schemes of the aforesaid Acts submits that they provide for quick disposal of an appeal and consequently, no power has been conferred upon the appellate authorities to pass an ad interim order because if the appellate authority fails to dispose of the appeal within the time limit as provided by sub-section (4) of section 42 the appeal shall be deemed to have been allowed. Mr Mahmudul Islam further submits that as an administrative measure department concerned automatically stays the order appealed against and does not take any step to implement the same during the pendency of the appeal before the Appellate forum and therefore, there is no necessity of passing an ad interim order for staying the operation of the impugned order.

11. Initially, when the Rule was heard the learned Deputy Attorney-General tried to support the Rule on strength of the decision reported in 44 DLR (AD) 40 and 49 DLR (AD) 44 but ultimately, when his attention was drawn to the provision of sub-section (2) of section 42 of the VAT Act he shifted from that position and frankly conceded that in compliance with the provision of sub-section (2) of section 42 the order appealed against is automatically stayed and the department during the tendency of the appeal do not press for implementing the order appealed against. The learned Attorney-General submits that the Appellate Tribunal is also of necessity invested with the power to pass an ad interim order in a proper case. We have already noticed that the Pubali Bank's case has been decided on the basis of the provisions of the Industrial Relations Ordinance, 1969. The Labour Court is constituted under section 35 of the LRO and the substantive power is vested in the Labour Court pursuant to section 35 and the procedural power is provided by section 36(2) of the IRO. The Appellate Division considering the scheme of the Act found that there is no occasion for the Labour Court to come across any situation where they can require to pass an ad interim order during the tendency of a case. In this connection it may be mentioned that IRO is a consolidated Act which provides for, amongst others, maintenance of peace in the industrial sector and there are substantive provisions in the Act for raising industrial dispute by the employer vis-a-vis the employee. On the other hand, the Labour Court can assume jurisdiction under section 25 of the Employment of Labour (Standing Orders) Act, 1965 in respect of dismissed worker and section 25(c) of the said Act provides that the Labour Court can decide a matter after hearing the parties. Taking these sections into consideration the Appellate Division in the Pubali Bank's case arrived at a positive finding that there is no such power conferred upon the Labour Court to pass an ad interim order and Mr Mahmudul Islam also did not bank on this decision while arguing as amicus curiae. He, however, heavily relied on the decision reported in 49 DLR (AD) 44 that is the case of Qumrul Hasan which was decided under the provision of the Administrative Tribunal Act. We have carefully gone through the decision and it appears that on the strength of earlier decision of the Appellate Division on the same point which are reported in 44 DLR (AD) 111 and 45 DLR (AD) 106, the Appellate Division observed that the Administrative Tribunal has no doubt all the trappings of a Court but is not a Court proper, which exercises all judicial powers of the Court provided under the Code of Civil Procedure. Therefore, the Administrative Tribunal or Administrative Appellate Tribunal are not Courts proper, for the purpose of exercising all the power and authorities exercisable by the Civil Court under the Code of Civil Procedure. To meet this contention, however, it was argued on behalf of the appellant that provision of sections 4 and 6 of the Act has an inherent authority to grant any stay of the order complained against, pending final adjudication in the matter but this contention was repelled by the Appellate Division on the ground that sections 4 and 6 of the Administration Tribunal Act do not contain in express terms that those Tribunals may grant any interim relief in respect of a lis pending before it. The contention of the Appellate Division was based on the ground that since neither the Appellate Tribunal nor the Administrative Appellate Tribunal are Courts proper within the meaning of the Civil Court Act or under the Civil Procedure Code they have no inherent jurisdiction to pass any such interim order but unfortunately, in the said decisions the case of the Indian Supreme Court as reported in 1971 ITR (SC) 815 and PLD 1971 (SC) 242 and PLD 1975 (SC) 32 were neither cited nor the Appellate Division had the occasion to consider the ratio decidendi of these decisions.

12. In this connection we may also refer to the decision relied on by Mr Feda M. Kamal namely, in the case reported in PLD 1971 (SC) 242. In this case the Pakistan Supreme Court had the occasion to interpret section 18 of the West Pakistan Control of Good as Ordinance of 1959 which provides for an appeal to the Commissioner under section 18. In that case also it was argued as has been urged before us, that the Appellate Authority had no jurisdiction to pass an ad interim order as the same has not been conferred upon the Appellate Authority expressly by the provision of section 18 of the said Ordinance but the Pakistan Supreme Court expressed the view that the power to suspend the operation of an order passed by a Tribunal is ancillary to the power conferred upon the Commissioner by section 18 to discharge the person complained against on final adjudication:

13. In the case reported in PLD 1975 (SC), 32 a similar question was raised whether a social security Court in session of an appeal under section 59 of the West Pakistan Employees Social Security Ordinance, 1965 has in the absence of an express provision for the purpose, jurisdiction to stay execution of order appealed against. It was argued that by that section it was not the intention to bring the Social Security Court on a par with an ordinary Civil Court so as to make it possible to the former to invoke the provisions of Order XXXIX rules 1 and 2 nor it can lay claim to any other provision of law to suspend the execution of the order appealed against. But the Pakistan Supreme Court repelled that argument on the ground that when the Social Security Court has power to reverse the order appealed against in its entirety it will have also the power to suspend the operation of the order during the tendency of the appeal. It was further observed that the exercise of that power is incidental or ancillary to the appellate jurisdiction which is conferred upon it. The aforesaid two decisions indicate that a Special Tribunal of limited jurisdiction can stay or suspend an order appealed against during the tendency of the appeal not necessarily under Order XXXIX, rule 1 C.P.C nor under inherent jurisdiction rather this is a power which is incidental or ancillary to the main appellate jurisdiction. In the Kamrul Hasan's Case [49 DLR (AD) 44], the Appellate Division considering the provisions of sections 4 and 6 of the Administrative Tribunal Act rejected the contention that the Appellate Administrative Tribunal has inherent power to grant an ad interim relief. The reason assigned by the Appellate Division is that the jurisdiction provided in section 4 of the Administrative Tribunal Act and that of the Appellate Tribunal in section 6 do not contain in express terms that those Tribunals may grant any interim relief in respect of a case pending before it. Their Lordships of the Appellate Division also observed that the rules framed under the Act also do not authorise the Tribunals to grant any interim relief. In reiterating the said legal position the Appellate Division relied on their two previous decisions namely, the cases of Mujibur Rahman vs Government of Bangladesh and others 44 DLR (AD) 111 and Kazi Nazrul Islam vs Bangladesh House Building Finance Corporation 45 DLR (AD) 106. In arriving at such a finding the Appellate Division also duly took into consideration the provision of section 7(1) of the Act. Although it is not specifically spelt out in the decision as to whether the scheme of the Act was considered, but on a reading of the decision it becomes clear and obvious that the scheme of the Act was behind their Lordships' minds. It becomes clear if we see the purpose and scheme of the Act. Even if C.P.C were applicable in its entirety then also there could be no occasion to grant stay or injunction as for example when a case is filed against dismissal order there is no scope to grant injunction. Similarly, in case of a transfer, promotion, etc also no order of stay could be passed on the ground of balance of convenience. From a careful reading of the aforesaid two decisions of the Appellate Division it appears that in Pubali Bank's case the question was kept open by the Appellate Division in respect of the power of the Appellate authority. But about appellate Administrative Tribunal it was held that Appellate Administrative Tribunal has no power to grant any interim relief during the pendency of the appeal. But unfortunately, the cases reported in 71, ITR (SC) 815, PLD 1975 (SC) 32 and PLD 1971 (SC) 242 were neither cited nor considered in Kamrul Hasan's Case. But no consideration of those cases have no bearing because we have noticed that the decision is based on the provisions of the Administrative Tribunal Act and the scheme of the Act also does not contemplate such power.

<u>14. Now let us see what is the position in the VAT Act, 1991. Section 42(1) provides for filing of an appeal against any order or decision given by a VAT official. Sub-section (2) of section 42 provides that at the time of filing of the appeal certain portion of the disputed amount has to be deposited. Sub-section (4) puts a time limit and if the appeal is not heard within the stipulated time by the appellate authority the appeal shall be deemed to have been allowed after the expiry of the deadline. In interpreting sub-section (2) of section 42 all the learned Advocates agreed that on filing of the appeal with the necessary deposit of a portion of the disputed amount, the impugned order is automatically stayed and there is no scope for the VAT officials to press for the payment of the disputed amount during the pendency of the appeal. So far so good. But when it comes to the passing of an interim order Mr Mahmudul Islam, the learned amicus curiae, differs with all other learned Advocates and he submits that there is no necessity of investing the Appellate Tribunal with the power to pass any interim order inasmuch as the impugned order is automatically stayed. But the learned Attorney-General and Mr Kamal in a chorus submitted that when at the end of the day the Appellate Tribunal can reverse the impugned order in its entirety, it can also pass any interim order which is just and convenient at the beginning of the day. The canon of interpretation is that a fiscal statute must be strictly construed and if a provision is capable of two or more interpretations the one which is more favourable to the citizen must be accepted. In the 71 ITR case, the Indian Supreme Court on consideration of the provision of section 254(1) of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1961 observed that the Appellate Authority is invested with wide power including the power to grant stay during tendency of an appeal before it. We have compared the provisions of section 254(1) of the Indain Income Tax Act with those of section 196B(1) of the Customs Act, 1969. It appears that the power conferred on the Appellate Tribunal by section 196B(1) is much wider in scope than the power conferred on the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal by section 254(1) of the Indian Act. Therefore, it appears to us that if at the end of the day the Appellate Tribunal can knock down the order appealed against why they should be helpless to pass any ad interim order during the tendency of the appeal in the interest of justice and also for the sake of convenience. Here it must be mentioned that this power is exercised by the Appellate Tribunal as it is reasonably incidental or ancillary to the main appellate jurisdiction and not under the provisions of the Civil Procedure Code. If the Appellate Tribunal is not allowed to exercise this incidental or ancillary jurisdiction it becomes a meaningless and helpless creature of the statute and the VAT payee appellants will have no means to resist the onslaught of the VAT officials. Let us take the example of this case. In the instant case, rebate taken by the respondent No. 2 is disputed by the department and therefore they adjusted Taka 7,840,997.85 from the current account register of the respondent No.2 and that order has been subsequently affirmed by the Commissioner of (Appeal) by his order dated 17-4-2001 and the respondent No. 2 thereafter filed the second appeal before the Appellate Tribunal and after admission of the appeal filed an application to stay the operation of the impugned order till disposal of the appeal when by the interim order dated 15-5-2001 the Tribunal stayed the order appealed against. If the order is not stayed, in addition to the amount already adjusted a further amount of Taka 47,58,657,45 is to be adjusted. The respondent No.2 alleged that they are in financial difficulty and if the entire amount is adjusted before final hearing of the appeal they will not be able to run the factory and they will be compelled to go out of business. So, in this case the balance of convenience is in favour of the respondent No. 2. Besides, as soon as the appeal is admitted, the impugned order is automatically stayed. In spite of that the department has filed writ petition calling in question the legality and propriety of the order dated 15-5-2002 passed by the Tribunal and the motive behind that is that if the said order is declared to be illegal they will be able to adjust the remaining portion of the amount in the current account of the respondent No. 2. If in such circumstances the Appellate Tribunal becomes helpless to pass an interim order the appellant is bound, t suffer and the purpose of setting up of the Tribunal will be frustrated to a great extent which can not be the intention of the Parliament. Besides, our experience shows that both the Customs Department and VAT Authority have a common tendency to press for implementation of the order appealed against during the tendency of the appeal and in such circumstances the provision for deposit of a portion of the disputed amount amounts to double jeopardy to the appellant. Earlier the provision of section 193 of the Customs Act came up for consideration before a Division Bench in the case of Shawn Apparels. Ltd (52 DLR 316) wherein one of us was a party. In that case it was observed that the Commissioner (Appeal) can pass an interim order during the tendency of the appeal. In view of our aforesaid discussions we are inclined to hold that the powers conferred on the Appellate Tribunal pursuant to the provisions of section 196B(1) of the Customs Act are of widest amplitude and it can pass an ad interim order during the tendency of an appeal which is reasonably ancillary and incidental to the main appellate jurisdiction. The view taken by us also gets support from the case reported in PLD 1973 Karachi 383, wherein in interpreting Article 201 of the 1972 Constitution of Pakistan it was held that where a court has power to pass an order finally it will generally have the power to do so by way of interim measure unless such a power is either expressly or by necessary implication excluded. The power conferred upon the Appellate Tribunal under section 196B(1) of the Customs Act, leads us to the irresistible conclusion that the Tribunal can pass an interim order pending hearing of the appeal before it. The provisions of the VAT Act read with the relevant provision of the Customs Act do not show that there is an express bar in making any interim order or by necessary implication.</u>

In the result, the Rule is discharged, however, without any order as to cost.

End.

lawyer:
Khondaker Mahbubuddin Ahmed with SR Khosnabish, Advocates -For the Petitioner 
Nikhilesh Dutta, Deputy Attorney-General with Nahid Mahtab, Assistant Attorney-General -For the Respondents
parties:
Ruhul Mannan Helali ------ Petitioner
vs.
Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh & others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Abdus Salam Mamun J: This Rule Nisi was issued under Article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh calling upon the respondents to show cause, why the second proviso to section 4 of the Muslim Marriages and Divorces (Registration) Act, 1974 (Act No. LII of 1974) introduced by Ordinance No. XLIX of 1982 (Annexure-A(1) and the Muslim Marriages and Divorces (Registration) Rules, 1975 (Annexure-E), particularly Rules 3, 4 and 10 thereof, and the order contained in Notification No. 1121- Bichar- 7/2N-23/98 dated 3-2-2000 (Annexure-D) purporting to appoint respondent No. 6 as Nikah Registrar for three Unions of the petitioner's area should not be declared to have been enacted and issued without lawful authority and to be of no legal effect and why the said proviso to section 4 of Act No. LII of 1974 and the Rules framed there under should not be struck down as void and order in Annexure-'D' should not be cancelled.

2. Facts of this Writ Petition, in short, are that the petitioner has passed Kamel in 1995 and Faazil in 1987 and was appointed a temporary Nikah Registrar in 1986 and as permanent Nikah Registrar on 12-2-1988 for six Unions, viz, Uttar Dhurang, Dhakhin Dhurang, Lemshikhali, Koiarbeel, Baraguph, Ali Akbar Deil under Kutubdia Police Section, Cox's Bazar having his office at Baraguph, in the centre of the Kutubdia island. He has registered about 700 marriages each year, on an average. He possesses an unblemished record. His licence is governed by section 4 of the Muslim Marriages and Divorces (Registration) Act, 1974 (Act LII of 1974) as amended by Ordinance No. XLIX of 1982.

3. Suddenly by Order No. 602-Bichar-7/2N-23/98 dated 13-10-98 the respondent No. 1 has excluded three Union Parishads namely, Ali Akbar Deil, situated in the extreme south and Uttar Dhurang and Dhakhin Dhurang Union Parishads situated in the extreme North from the area of his Licence and gave Licence to the respondent No. 6 for these three Union Parishads as Nikah Registrar on purely temporary basis. The respondent No. 1 has also issued another letter bearing the same number and on the same date granting Licence to the respondent No. 6 for the Union Parishads named Ali Akbar Deil and Baraguph on temporary basis, vide Annexure B and B(1).

4. In the Writ Petition No. 3312 of 1998 the petitioner has challenged issuance of temporary Licence to the respondent No. 6 before this Hon'ble Court where a Rule was issued and operation of impugned order was stayed vide Order dated 26-10-1998. But after hearing, this Court has been pleased to discharge the Rule along with some other Rules heard analogously, Vide Annexure-C. The petitioner thereafter filed a petition praying for leave to appeal against the said Judgment before the Appellate Division of the Hon'ble Supreme Court of Bangladesh being Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 1148 of 1999.

5. After disposal of the said Writ Petition the respondent No. 1 has issued an order bearing No. 1121 / Bichar-7/2N-23 /98 dated 23-2-2000 purporting to withdraw/cancel the order No. 602-Bichar-7 /2N-23 /98 dated 13-10-1998 in respect of All Akbar Deil and Baraguph Union Parishads, Annexure-D maintaining the other Licence for Ali Akbar Deil, Uttar Dhurang and Dhakkin Dhurang.

6. Granting Licence in favour of the respondent No. 6 in respect of the three Union Parishads situated in the extreme north and extreme south of Kutubdia island has very adversely affected the functioning of the petitioner as Nikah Registrar inasmuch as while passing through the central area (from one part of his area to other part) respondent No. 6 illegally registers marriages solemnised within the area of the petitioner thereby causing financial loss to the petitioner.

7. Since the Muslim Marriages and Divorces (Registration) Act, 1974 does not provide for constitution of any Advisory Committee with function to decide upon fixation of areas for which Nikah Registrar may be licensed the Rules 3, 4 and 10 of the Muslim Marriages and Divorces (Registration) Rules, 1975 framed by SRO No. 231-L/75/798- GIV /IV-2/74 dated 1-7-1975 are ultra vires. Rule 10 has undergone amendments time and again arbitrarily.

After amendment of Rule 10 in 1997 Orders have been passed at different times during 1998, 1999 and 2000 granting Licences in Pourashavas in some cases for one ward, in some cases for two Wards and in some cases for three Wards while in rural areas Licences have been granted in some cases for 5 Unions and in some cases for one, two or three Unions, vide Annexure-G series, most arbitrarily and adopting the pick and choose policy according to the sweet will of the Government. These Licensings are done and changes made without caring to notice the conveniences and inconveniences of Nikah Registrars.

8. The office of a Nikah Registrar is an employment and source of income providing means and sustenance of his family and the income depends upon the number of marriages and divorces of the people living in the area under Licence and the population is also not same in the urban and rural areas. A dense City Corporation, municipal or pourashava ward contains greater number of people than the whole of an Union Parishad. Density of population again varies in the rural areas and non-Muslim population is also a factor to be considered in determining area. There must be some guidelines in determining the area considering the number of Muslim population instead of Wards or Unions as the basis of granting Licence and allocating areas.

9. From 1975 onwards Rule 10 has been repeatedly amended without providing any guideline to be followed by the Government resulting in arbitrariness in granting Licences and discrimination of pick and choose in allocating areas. The Muslim Marriages and Divorces (Registration) Rules, 1975 is discriminatory, made in violation of the fundamental rights enshrined in Articles 27 and 31 of The Constitution the Muslim Marriages and Divorces (Registration) Rules, 1975, in particular Rule 10, is liable to be struck down.

10. Under the then existing Rules in 1988 the petitioner was granted Licence for the whole of Kutubdia island and subsequent granting Licence to the respondent No. 6 for one Union at the extreme south and two Unions at the extreme north curtailing those from the licensed area of the petitioner and keeping him in between was arbitrary and malafide and not sustainable in law. The order dated 13-10-1998 (Annexure-B) appointing the respondent No. 6 as Nikah Registrar bifurcating the area of the petitioner is liable to be struck down being arbitrary and malafide. Section 2 of the Ordinance No. XLIX of 1982 and the Muslim Marriages and Divorces (Registration) Rules, 1975, particularly Rule 10, is liable to be declared to have been made without lawful authority and of no legal effect being violative of Articles 27 and 31 of the Constitution.

11. The petitioner had thereafter annexed the SRO No. 273-Ain/2002 dated 2-10-2002 by way of Supplementary Affidavit stating that the Rule 10 has undergone further amendment and the latest position of Rule 10 is as follows:

"10. Jurisdiction-Notwithstanding anything contained in these Rules or in any licence granted under these Rules, an area for which a Nikah Registrar may be licensed shall be-

(a) in the case of a City Corporation, not more than one ward;

(b) in the case of a municipality of-

(i) category 'A' not more than one ward;

(ii) category 'B' not more than two wards; and

(iii) category 'C' not more than three wards; and

(c) in other cases, not more than one union."

12. Mr Khondaker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, the learned Senior Advocate appearing for the petitioner, has taken us through the Writ Petition and Annexure thereto and submits that the second proviso to section 4 of the Muslim Marriages and Divorces (Registration) Act, 1974 was inserted in the year 1982, during the Martial Law, vide Ordinance No. XLIX of 1982 giving the Government unlimited and unqualified power to extend, curtail or otherwise alter the limit of any area for which a Nikah Registrar has been licensed thus paving the way for arbitrary exercise of power and the Government has exercised power arbitrarily by amending the Rules, called the Muslim Marriages and Divorces (Registration) Rules, 1975, especially the Rule 10. This Rule has repeatedly been amended without any guideline at the sweet will of the Government causing inconveniences to the petitioner and other licensees the second proviso to section 4 of the Act together with Rules, particularly Rules 3, 4 and 10, are liable to be struck down being violative of Articles 27 and 31 of the Constitution. According to him, Licence to a Nikah Registrar should be given on the basis of pre-determined population and not on the basis of Wards or Unions.

According to Mr Ahmed, when the Rules, called the Muslim Marriages and Divorces (Registration) Rules, 1975, were framed and published by SRO No. 231-L/75/798 G IV/IA-2/74 on 1st July, 1975 to carry into effect the purposes of the Muslim Marriages and Divorces (Registration) Act 1974 (Act No. LII of 1974) in accordance with section 14 of the Act, the 2nd proviso of section 4 was not there in the Act at that time and, as such, the rationale worked behind the framing of the Rules have been demolished by the subsequent amendment, ie, the 2nd proviso to section 4 introduced in 1982 and, as such, the Act and the Rules are not in conformity to each other and that is why Rule 10 has been subject to arbitrary exercise of power, time and again. Had there been specific guidelines to exercise the unlimited power of the Government, the Government would be obliged to work in accordance with set norms and principles and the petitioner along with other Licensees would find reasons in the executive actions of the Government.

Mr Ahmed next submits that the geographical bounds and limits are, of course, necessary to avoid overlapping by one Nikhah Registrar on the area of another Nikah Registrar but equality of Nikah Registrars must be established as the same class removing discrimination. According to him, the latest amendment too is discriminatory inasmuch as it provides one Nikah Registrar for a Ward in the City Corporation, one for an Union Parishad, one for a Ward of 'A' category municipality. But in a 'B' category municipality a Nikah Registrar can hold two Wards and in a 'C' category municipality three Wards. There is no rationale why a Nikah Registrar in a municipality shall hold two or three wards, and another Nikah Registrar in the same municipality should hold one Ward and again, why two or three Wards in the municipality as against one Union Parishad in the rural area. On the other hand, the population in a Ward of the Dhaka City Corporation, he argued, is not same with another ward of any other City Corporation or municipalities and it may be altogether different with relation to an Union Parishad. The income of Nikah Registrars differs depending on the population, especially the Muslim population, on the number of marriages and divorces. The Nikah registrars being members of the same class should be treated equally in accordance with Articles 27 and 31 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh.

13. In support of his contentions Mr Khondaker Mahbubuddin Ahmed has relied upon the cases of Satwant Singh Sawhaney vs Assistant Passport Officer, reported in AIR 1967 SC 1863, State of West Bengal vs Anwar Ali Sarkar and another, reported in AIR 1952 SC 75, Dr Nurul Islam vs Bangladesh, reported in 33 DLR (AD) 201, Bangladesh vs Safiuddin Ahmed and others, reported in 50 DLR (AD) 27.

Mr Ahmed lastly, submits that though the 2nd proviso to section 4 of the Muslim Marriages and Divorces (Registration) Act 1974 together with Rule 10 of the Muslim Marriages and Divorces (Registration) Rules, 1974 have undergone judicial scrutiny but constitutionality of the same have not been challenged so far and those have not been seen from the Constitutional point of view, especially in the perspective of Articles 27 and 31 of the Constitution.

During hearing Mr Ahmed has produced a copy of the Judgment of Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 1148 of 1999 where their Lordships have been pleased to refuse leave on 6-3-2002 holding that in view of amendment to section 4 and Rule 10(2) no interference was called for.

14. According to Mr Ahmed, issuance of two Licences to respondent No. 6 under the same Memo number and on the same date one for two Wards and another for three Wards curtailing the same from the petitioner and subsequent cancellation of one Licence by the same authority evidenced recklessness on the part of the Government and arbitrary exercise of power.

15. The respondents did not file any Affidavit-in-opposition. Mr Nikhilesh Dutta, the Learned Deputy Attorney General appearing for the respondents, submits that the second proviso to section 4 of the Muslim Marriages and Divorces (Registration) Act, 1974 has given the Government unfettered power to extend, curtail or otherwise alter the limit of any area for which a Nikah Registrar has been licensed, whenever it deems fit so to do and when the Government takes any action in exercise of this power, an existing Nikah Registrar has got no right to challenge it. According to the Learned Deputy Attorney-General, the petitioner being a Licensee cannot challenge the authority of the Licensor and, as such, the Writ Petition is not maintainable.

According to the Learned Deputy Attorney General, Section 14 of the Act, 1974 has given the Government ample power to make Rules and the government has amended the Rule 10 time to time according to the exigencies by exercising this power and the Rule 10 as it stands now is good and calls for no interference. The point of equality, according to him, has been decided in the case of Sk Abdus Sabur.

16. Second proviso to section 4 of the Muslim Marriages and Divorces (Registration) Act, 1974 is quoted below.

"Provided further that the Government may, whenever it deems fit so to do, extend, curtail or otherwise alter the limits of any area for which a Nikah registrar has been licensed. Vide Ordinance XLIX of 1982."

17. From mere reading of the 2nd proviso to section 4 of the Muslim Marriages and Divorces (Registration) Act, 1974 introduced in 1982, it appears that plenary powers has been given to the Government to extend, curtail or otherwise alter limit of an area for which a Nikah registrar has been licensed whenever it deems fit so to do.

The phrase "whenever it deems fit so to do" sounds like the phrase, "the king can do no wrong."

But in the case of Anowar Hossain Chowdhury vs Bangladesh, reported in 41 DLR (AD) 165 their Lordships have observed that "the King is not above the law but under the law."

Apparently, the 2nd proviso to section 4 has placed the Government above the law.

18. In some other laws, like the Pourashava Ordinance, 1977 the Government has been given plenary powers to extend, curtail or otherwise alter the limit of any municipality (section 4(b) of the Pourashava Ordinance, 1977) but this power was made subject to the limitation by providing a pre-condition in the words: "The Government may, in the prescribed manner". Thus, the plenary powers in this section of the Pourashava Ordinance, 1977 is plenary but not absolute, for, it must be exercised in the "prescribed manner". So, this is the check and balance of power. Where there is power that power must be exercised with some restrictions and in a prescribed balanced manner to the knowledge of all.

19. This principle was followed in making similar provisions under section 3 of the Local Government (Union Parishad) Ordinance, 1983 that the Deputy Commissioner shall exercise the plenary powers to extend, curtail or otherwise alter the limit of an Union Parishad "in the prescribed manner".

But there is no "prescribed manner" in section 4 of the Muslim Marriages and Divorces (Registration) Act, 1974 and the Rules framed there under also do not provide any "prescribed manner" for the exercise of unlimited power.

20. The 1st proviso to section 4 provides that "not more than one Nikah Registrar shall be licensed for any one area." Here the deciding factor is the "area" but this word or term or notion "area" has not been defined either in the Act or in the Rules framed under the Act, namely, the Muslim Marriages and Divorces (Registration) Act, 1974 and, as such, "area" is a vague and indefinite term having tendency towards arbitrariness. What was an area in 1975 is not an area in 2003. Area has been changed without defining the area itself.

This area has been determined by the Government from time to time in exercise of the power conferred by section 4 but without any" prescribed manner" or guidelines for exercise of such power in determining the area.

21. The Learned Deputy Attorney-General submits that the Act in its section 14 has delegated power to the Government to make Rules and the Government has framed Rules in 1975 as it stands now with latest amendments. Section 14 is quoted below:

"14. Power to Make Rules (1) The Government may, by notification in the official Gazette, make rules to carry into effect the purposes" of this Act.

(2) In particular and without prejudice to the generality of the foregoing power, such rules may provide for-

(a) qualifications to be required from persons to whom licence under section 4 may be granted:

(b) fees payable to a Nikah Registrar for registration of a marriage or divorce:

(c) any other matter for which rules are required to be made."

22. This section empowers the Government to make Rules in particular: (a) qualifications of persons for issuing licence of Nikah registrar; (b) Fees of Nikah Registrar; (c) any other matter for which Rules are required to be made. It shows that Rules in particular and with priority is framed relating to qualifications of Nikah Registrars, their fees and for any other matter that may require a Rule. The Rules making authority, ie, the Government, has made provisions for qualification, etc. of candidates in Rule 6 and relating to fees in Rule 18. From the qualification of a Nikah Registrar, it appears that the candidate must possess Alim Certificate from a Madrasha Board and be a resident of the area in which the vacancy occurs. In January 2002 this condition has been relaxed substituting the word 'preferably' and hence it now stands that "preferably he be a resident of the area" and aged between 21 to 40 years.

23. Fees of a Nikah Registrar, on the other hand, as provided by Rule 18 is sealed from both ends, ie, minimum Taka Thirty and maximum Taka three thousand on the basis of Taka five for the dower of every one thousand taka or part thereof. This fees for registration is payable by the bridegroom and apart from this prescribed fees he can charge taka ten as commission fee, traveling allowance taka one per mile and out of the fees realised the Nikah Registrar shall deposit annually in the Government Treasury an amount of Taka three thousand in case of a Ward of a City Corporation, taka one thousand in case of a Ward of a municipality and Taka five hundred in case of an Union Parishad. This is the income of the Government out of the marriages and divorces registrations in the country apart from the licence renewal fees.

24. The petitioner in this Writ Petition has stated that he would register at least 700 marriages a year in six Union Parishads under his Licence before curtailment. In a densely populated area like a Ward of a City Corporation or a Municipality the rate of marriages could be much higher. This is not the amount of money that the Nikah Registrars are earning or depositing to the Government that we are concerned but the potential couples they are getting directly in touch by virtue of their offices and positions on the very auspicious moment of the couples of starting their conjugal lives. These Nikah Registrars are all educated people, at least Alim degree holders and fortunate section in the society. The existing system has given them that opportunity to render valuable services to the society though direct contact with the bride and the bridegroom at the prime time of starting their conjugal lives which evolves child births as natural consequences. The Nikah Registrars may perform their duties by making the couple whom they solemnise or whose marriage they register, understand the importance of family planning, health and hygiene, child bearing, child care, nutrition, child education, etc taking the couple in a place in the precinct of the festivity ancillary to the solemnisation and registration of marriages. They may hand over literatures, booklets on these subjects to the couple, supplied to them by the Government to be delivered to the couples on the day of solemnisation and registration of marriages as gifts from the Government.

25. The Government acting through the Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Ministry of Education, the Ministry of Women and Children Affairs, Religious Affairs and the Social Welfare in their concerted efforts can work on and achieve these goals through these Nikah Registrars approaching the couple directly.

26. "Social Justice" is our Pledge in the preamble and fundamental principle of state policy under Article 8 of the Constitution. In the modern judicial system social justice has got immense importance and that was crystallised by their Lordships in the case of Bangladesh Soya-Protein Project Limited vs Ministry of Disaster Management, reported in 2002 BLD 378 in the following words: "The Courts are always alive to the paramount public interest, either in upholding the decision of the Government even to the prejudice of an individual or in case of striking down as arbitrary or unreasonable, the public interest element is always, the criteria for doing so. The Courts all over the world in deciding an issue give importance always to the overall interest of the people at large which commensurate with the sense of social justice."

27. Mr Khondaker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, learned Senior Advocate has argued on the equality of the Nikah Registrars before law as enunciated in Article 27 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh.

Article 27 reads as under:

"All citizens are equal before law and are entitled to equal protection of law."

28. There are different attributes in the Constitution to this Article, such as Articles 10, 28(2), 29(2), 40, etc. Article 10 provides that "steps shall be taken to ensure participation of women in all spheres of national life." Article 28(2) provides that "Women shall have equal rights with men in all spheres of the state and of public life". Article 29(2) provides that "No citizen shall on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth, be ineligible for, or discriminated against in respect of, any employment or office in the service of the Republic" and Article 40 provides that "subject to any restrictions imposed by law, every citizen possessing such qualifications, if any, may be prescribed by law in relation to his profession, occupation, trade or business shall have the right to enter upon any lawful profession or occupation and to conduct any lawful trade or business."

As we have seen the required qualification of a Nikah Registrar, under Rule 6 is a Alim Certificate from a Madrasha Board, age between 21-40 years and preferably, a resident of the area in which vacancy occurs. There are many women Madrashas, called Mahila Madrashas, in the country producing Alim Certificate holders under Madrasha Board and competent to function as Nikah Registrars.

According to Mr Ahmed, the office of a Nikah Registrar is an employment and if this is an employment the women have their equal right to the employment under the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh.

29. To our query, the learned Deputy Attorney-General has informed the court that there are 6,500 Nikah Registrars all over the country and if Articles 28(2) and 40 together with Article 27 were complied with a good number of them, in a square deal, should be women Nikah Registrars. Their approach on the aforesaid matters could be more appealing and effective. Discrimination on sex is prohibited by the Constitution and under Article 40 they are since possessing the same qualifications are entitled to equal opportunity.

30. The scope for discrimination is there in the Rule for selection of candidates. Rule 5 provides that whenever a vacancy occurs of a Nikah Registrar or a new office is created the Registrar may with the approval of the Government issue licence to a qualified person to act on purely temporary basis until a Nikah Registrar is licensed by the Government on regular basis. He shall then invite applications for grant of permanent licence within one month. The Registrar shall place all applications received before the Advisory Committee for consideration and selection of candidates. The Advisory Committee shall select three candidates in order of priority and the Government may grant licence to any one of the three selected candidates, or may, for any special reason, grant licence to any other person from amongst the other candidates. Rule 5 A provides, notwithstanding anything contained in rule 5 any person acting as temporary Nikah Registrar under rule 5(1) and completed two years as such Registrar be granted licence if he fulfils the required qualification.

This Rule prima facie shows arbitrary exercise of powers and functions of the District Registrar and the Government. The temporary Nikah Registrar will be appointed by the District Registrar (with the approval of the Government) and the temporary Nikah Registrar shall be granted permanent Licence after two years. So, why invitation of applications from others for the same office? The pertinent question is, on what basis the temporary Nikah Registrar was appointed who shall be given permanent licence after two years? The selection procedure was the sweet will of the District Registrar and the Government who accords approval. And again, if the temporary appointee shall be given permanent licence what is the utility of having an Advisory Committee under Rule-3? Under Rule-4 the functions of the Advisory Committee is to advise the Government in regard to the selection of candidates for grant of licence. How this committee will advise the Government in matters of selection of candidates in the absence of specific procedure? How they shall select three candidates from among the equals in order of priority and what is the priority criteria? And what is the necessity of such selection when the Government can appoint any one from the selected three and even, on special reason, any other person? What is special reason? In the Warrant of Precedence a Member of the Parliament ranks the top of other members of the Advisory Committee but in Rule-3 he/she ranks the last, how? Why a Member of Parliament should waste his/her time and energy when his/her advice has got little or no bearing and only to put a seal of endorsement to a temporary Nikah Registrar selected by the District Registrar from before?

31. It is also apparent that there is no guidelines to determine the territorial jurisdiction of a Nikah Registrar under the law or the Rules and Rule 10 as it stood at the time of filing this Writ Petition and stands now is a subject of arbitrary exercise of executive power, Mere reference to Ward or Union cannot suffice in the given time and circumstances, especially, on the point of view of equality Article.

32. Mr Ahmed submits appointment of Nikah Registrars on the basis of certain and determined number of Muslim population within specific territorial bounds both in urban and rural areas could ensure equality among the Nikah Registrars before law within the meaning of Article 27 of the Constitution. According to him, the office of a Nikah Registrar is an employment and equal opportunity should be had for all Nikah Registrars they being all equal in requisite qualifications and status.
