We find force and substance in his submissions in this respect and find also the equality is equally extended to the womenfolk.

33. Rule 19 provides procedure before registration of marriage. A Nikah Registrar shall examine the parties for satisfying himself as to the affecting of marriage or shall examine two witnesses who were present at the solemnisation of the marriage. If the woman be pardanashin, her duly authorised vakil shall be examined instead of herself.

This Rule is defective and lacking in material particulars. The first and foremost duty of a Nikah Registrar should be to satisfy himself that the contracting parties, namely, the bride and bridegroom have attained the age of majority and are above the age of 18 years. If one or both of them are minor and not competent to undertake responsibilities of conjugal lives he should at once refuse to register the marriage and maintain the same in his register book. This is the first step to restrain child marriage and reduce mortality rate at child bearing, child delivery and infant mortality. But the Rule has dispensed with the duty of the Nikah Register by providing to examine two witnesses whereas the marital obligation under the Muslim law is a contractual obligation and the contracting parties have to bear their own responsibilities and none else and that is why the Muslim law has provided that the proposal and acceptance must both be expressed at one meeting. A marriage without witness will not render the marriage void but a marriage without consent is void ab initio. Mr Justice Kemaluddin Hossain, the former Chief Justice of Bangladesh, in the case of Siddique Ahmed vs Gani Ahmed, reported in 33 DLR (AD) has found this term 'Pardanashin' to be social disability of a woman and unfortunate.

34. Vakil was a class of lawyers who existed during the Sultani and Mughal period wherefrom the word 'Vokalatnama' has derived, practicing right from the Dadar Nizamat Adalat and Sadar Dewani Adalat to the bench of Munsif (chowki) in the rural areas. They were the fore-runners of modern Advocates. In 1926 by the Indian Bar Council Act the post and service of vakils have been abolished. This word vakil is still occurring in Rule 19 only to characterise a woman to be Pardanashin and to be examined in place of the bride. During the colonial period the womenfolk of our country were reluctant to appear before the alien white or unknown people and the Farshi words 'Pardanashin', 'vakil' have got importance in social arena. This word 'Pardanashin' found place in the Indian Contract Act at the time of its making in 1872. Now a days, these two words vakil and Pardanashin are obscure, obsolete and almost obscene for those who are going to marry by maintaining ceremonial congregation and festivity at the expense of huge money. The condition of womenfolk has also improved in the rural areas to a great extent both in education and social perspective. This process, hopefully will continue. A daughter is not Pardanashin if she can read and write and if she cannot read and write, that is a curse upon the parents and the society.

35. The Nikah Registrar must examine both the bride and bridegroom directly and without any via-media and apart from taking their consent must talk about family planning, health, hygiene, child bearing, child education, child health, etc as part of solemnisation and registration of marriage. There is nothing for hesitation to talk about on matters which are natural consequences of marriage contracted by an adult male and an adult female knowing the consequences very well. Mulla has quoted the definition of a Muslim marriage from Hedaya and Baillie, that "Marriage (Nikah) is a contract which has for its object the procreation and the legalising of children" (Sir DF Mulla, Principles of Mohammedan Law, page 223). This may restrain forcible marriages and if the Nikah registrar/notices/ lack of consent from either party to the marriage he/she must refuse to register the marriage and make entry in the register book, for, consent is the cardinal factor in a contract. A Muslim Marriage is out and out a contract which must be performed by the party himself or herself and none can substitute it. This rule 19 was made under section 7 of the Act and the Rule making authority has utterly failed to translate intentions of the statute.

36. From Rule 21 it appears that if a Nikah Registrar has refused to register a marriage the person may prefer an appeal to the District Registrar. But the basic point is missing as to under what circumstances the Nikah Registrar must refuse to register a marriage and under what circumstances a Nikah Registrar should refuse to register a marriage. Procedure relating to appeal and its disposal also is laid down specifically in the Rules.

37. Training of Nikah Registrars has been provided in Rule 34 but there is again no guidelines where, when and how the training will be conducted and on what matters. Whether any training has taken place till 1975, ie, after making the Rules is also not known. There are many subjects to be transacted in regular training courses such as, restraining child marriage, forcible marriage, effective family planning approach, health and hygiene, child bearing, child heath, child education, etc. but the existing Rules are inept, in cohesive and inadequate to cope with the needs of the time and the people and, as such, lost its utility.

38. We have taken judicial notice of the fact that a huge number of Writ Petitions and litigations have arisen out of and under this Act and the Rules due to their ambiguity, inefficacy and inadequacy.

A law should not be such in nature that draw a lot of people in the Courts from all over the country but shall be such that mitigates woes and disputes and reduces litigations.

39. In the case of the State of West Bengal vs Anowar Ali Sarkar and another, referred to above and cited by Mr Khondaker Mahabubuddin Ahmed, his Lordship Fazal Ali, J, held that "if an Act is unable to fulfill the requirements of the Constitution it will have to be suitably redrafted in order to conform to the requirements of the Constitution". Mukherjee J, held that "If a legislation is discriminatory and discriminates one person or class of persons against others similarly situated and denies to the former the privileges that are enjoyed by the latter, it cannot but be regarded as "hostile" in the sense that it effects injuriously the interests of that person or class."

We are inclined to hold that the Muslim Marriages and Divorces (Registration) Rules, 1975 are discriminatory and hostile to the womenfolk of the country having same qualifications of Alim Certificate and also between Nikah Registrars of the same class and the selection of candidates for Nikah Registrars are also defective, discriminatory and arbitrary.

Competitive examinations are an essential requirement in public employment.

40. Mukherjee, J in this case has further held that "when the statute itself makes a discrimination without any proper or reasonable basis, the statute would be invalidated for being in conflict with equal protection clause, and the question as to how it is actually worked out may not necessarily be a material fact for consideration."

<u>41. In the case of Satwant Sing Sawhani vs Assistant Passport Officer and others, referred to above, their Lordships have held that "A law would be void, if it discriminates or enables an authority to discriminate between the persons without just classification."</u>

<u>42. Under Rule 10, in its present form, there is the ceiling to the maximum limit saying that not more than two Wards or not more than three Wards in case of municipalities and no reason is there why one shall get two or three Wards in the municipality and the other only one Ward or one Union. This rule enables the executive authority to discriminate against persons without just classification in allocation one Ward to one Nikah Registrar and three Wards to another Nikah Registrar.</u>

43. The question and necessity of having specific guidelines in matters relating to service was exhaustively discussed in the case of Dr Nurul Islam vs Bangladesh, referred to above and the same question arose in the case of Bangladesh vs Shafiuddin Ahmed and others, reported in 50 DLR (AD) 27 and their Lordships have been pleased to hold that "In the absence of any guideline the respective committees themselves devised their own procedure. The committees, without being provided with any uniform guidelines, yardsticks or principles were thus vested with unguided and arbitrary powers or at least being provided with a scope for arbitrary exercise of powers which is in conflict with equal treatment of candidates, with equal protection of law and with equality of opportunity of all citizens in respect of employment."

Their Lordships have further held that "the guidelines should be laid bare by an official Notification. In the absence of any guideline the authorities are vested with arbitrary powers offending equality Clauses contained in Articles 27 and 29(1) of the Constitution."

The Muslim Marriages and Divorces (Registration) Rules, 1975 was published by SRO and, as such, bare, but we find it ineffective, inefficacious and untenable.

44. As regards the Subordinate Legislation, it was held in the case of Kundeswari Ausadhaly vs Bangladesh, reported in 28 DLR 63 that "A subordinate Legislation can be struck down as being invalid if it conflicts with an Act of Parliament under which it was made. It may also be declared unconstitutional if it is seen to violate any provisions of the Constitution."

45. Sheik Abdus Sabur's case, reported in 41 DLR (AD) 30 and cited by the Learned Deputy Attorney-General to support Rule 10(b)(ii) and (iii) is not applicable in the instant case for, all Nikah Registrars are in the same class having same requisites. The argument that a Licensee cannot challenge actions of the Licensor also does not hold water.

46. We have noticed that this 2nd proviso to section 4 together with relevant Rules have undergone Judicial Scrutiny, especially in the cases of Latifur Rahman vs Bangladesh, 49 DLR 434, Moulavi Md Khorshed Alam vs Bangladesh, 50 DLR (AD) 82, Fazlur Rahman and others vs Bangladesh, 53 DLR 237, Kazi Syed Shamsul Hoq vs Bangladesh, 5 BLC 366, Abdul Halim Khan vs Bangladesh, 2 BLC 335.

In the case of Moulavi Khorshed Alam the Writ was filed against curtailing of area under Licence of the petitioner. The Rule was discharged holding that the 2nd proviso to section 4 of the Act authorises the Government to extend, curtail or otherwise alter the limit of any area for which a Nikah Registrar has been licensed. Relying upon the case of Kazi Md Amirul islam vs Bangladesh, reported in 1996 BLD (AD) 110 their Lordships have further held that the Rule 10 was directory and not mandatory.

The Appellate Division found that the Learned Judges of the High Court Division had taken the correct view.

In Latifur Rahman's case the question of Government's authority to curtailment arose and was held that the Government has the authority to exclude certain area but notice to show cause should be served upon the existing Nikah Registrar.

In the case of Ahsan Ullah, reported in 52 DLR 168 it was held that impugned Notification (curtailing area) did not offend principle of natural justice. The Government is well within its administrative power to create any new area and in such case no show cause notice was necessary.

In the case of Fazlur Rahman and 38 others, this petitioner himself was one of the petitioners against curtailment of area under his Licence and appointment of respondent No. 6 as new Nikah Registrar and it was held that "Neither the principle of natural justice nor question of vested right arises in the way of passing an order for curtailment of the area of jurisdiction of the petitioner within the permissible limit of area."

In the case of Abdul Halim Khan it was found that "the Government has unlimited power to extend, curtail or alter the limit but the area will not be less than the area mentioned in Rule 10".

We are in respectful agreement with these decisions and find that under the existing system the Government may extend, curtail or otherwise alter the limit of a Nikha Registrar whenever thinks fit so to do and Rule 10 is the instrument to exercise this unlimited power of 'so to do' arbitrarily. Theory of violation of natural justice will not apply in such a case nor the question of vested right will arise.

But it also appears that in those reported cases question of constitutionality of second proviso to section 4 of the Act and the Rules did not arise and no occasion arose to examine them from the Constitutional point of view.

47. The case of Dr S Motiur Rab vs Bangladesh reported in 42 DLR (AD) 126 can be referred to in this respect. Their Lordships held that "the previous Judgment is admissible to show the assertion of the petitioner but is not binding if the new issues that have been raised had no occasion to be considered in the previous proceeding".

In this proceeding the issues are new and different.

48. We have also noticed that in this case and in some other cases the Principle of res judicata and constructive resjudicata were found by their Lordships applicable in proceedings under Writ Jurisdiction.

<u>49. In view of 2nd proviso to section 4 of the Muslim Marriages and Divorces (Registration) Act, 1974 and Rules 3, 4, 5, 6, 10, 18, 19 and 34 we are prompted to quote from Lord Denning; "It is no longer necessary for the Judges to wring their hands and say "there is nothing we can do about it". Whenever the strict interpretation gives rise to an absurd and unjust situation, the Judges can and should use with good sense to remedy it by reading words in, if necessary, so as to do what Parliament would have done, had they had the situation in mind". Lord Denning, The Discipline of Law, page 16.</u>

50. It was held in the case of ETV vs Bangladesh and others, 10 BLT (AD) 108 = 54 DLR (AD) 130 that "The Court under Constitutional mandate is duty bound to preserve and protect rule of law. The cutting edge of law is remedial and the art of justice has to respond so that transparency wins over opaqueness".

51. We have given our anxious consideration and find that if the words "in the prescribed manner" are inserted there in section 4 of the Muslim Marriages and Divorces (Registration) Act, 1974 omitting the phrase "whenever thinks fit so to do" like section 4 of the Pourashava Ordinance, 1977 and section 3 of the Union Parisad Ordinance, 1983 and if the "manner" is specifically provided in the Rules the second proviso to section 4 may hold good. It is not necessary to strike down this proviso. Interpretation of statute is necessarily in favour of maintaining the statute, if possible.

52. But the existing Rules, in view of our above discussion, are inept, in cohesive, inadequate, ambiguous and ineffective having tendency to pick and choose policy, arbitrariness, absurdities and require to be remodeled and redrafted in the given situation and demand of time with sound thought and modern look with special reference to Articles 10, 28(2), 29(2), 27, 31 and 40 and the Warrant of Precedence and the Muslim Marriages and Divorces (Registration) Rules, 1975 (Annexure-E to the Writ Petition) is therefore, struck down being unconstitutional.

53. The second part of the Rule (Annexure-D) to the Writ Petition does not merit and hence discharged.

In the result, the Rule is made absolute in part without any order as to costs.

End.

case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 17th December 2000 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 62 of 2000 with Writ Petition No. 5362 of 2000)
full_judgment:
Md Fazlul Karim J: All these appeals by leave arose out of the same and single judgment and order of the High Court Division making the Rules absolute in Writ Petition Nos. 62 of 2000 and 5362 of 2000 declaring the impugned order in Memo dated 27-9-1998 Annexure 'K' issued by the respondent No. 1 and the impugned decisions under item Nos. 12 and 13 as adopted/taken at the meeting of the Standing Committee comprising of writ respondent Nos. 3, 5 and 6 on 2-6-1999 and 20-9-1999 contained in the minutes (Annexure 'M') and of the gradation list issued and published by respondent Nos. 2 and 8 in the Bangladesh Gazette on 23-11-1999 placing writ-respondent Nos. 11-79 in serial Nos. 115 to 183 therein (Annexure 'N') and the remarks under clause 9 of the gradation list against the names of the writ petitioner-respondents to be unconstitutional, void and without lawful authority and further directing the writ respondent Nos. 1-10 to follow the final gradation list published on 1-10-1990 (Annexure H) relating to the writ-petitioner-respondents and other writ respondents.

2. The facts relevant for disposal of these appeals are common as detailed in those writ-petitions, inter alia, that the Writ-petitioner Nos. 1 and 2 and Writ-Petitioner Nos. 3-10 of Writ Petition No. 62 of 2000 were appointed on 30-9-1976 and on 17-12-1976 respectively and the writ petitioner Md Abdus Salam of Writ Petition No. 5362 of 2000 was appointed on 17-12-1976 as the Assistant Engineer (Civil) of Roads and Highways. All these appointments were on ad-hoc basis for six months or till regularisation of service by the Public Service Commission, briefly the PSC. This period was extended from time to time. The PSC published an advertisement on 30-3-1978 and in that advertisement it was mentioned that the Assistant Engineers of Roads and Highways Department who were appointed on ad-hoc basis might apply for regularisation of their service. The writ petitioner No. 1 Md Halim Miah of Writ Petition No. 62 of 2000 and the writ petitioner Md Abdus Salam of Writ Petition No. 5362 of 2000 applied for regularisation of their service. Subsequent advertisement of similar nature was made by the PSC on 1-4-1978 and the Writ-petitioners Nos. 2-10 of Writ Petition No. 62 of 2000 applied for regularisation of their service. All the writ petitioners thereby made their first appearance at the interview before the Public Service Commission on those dates and came out successful. Because of their success at their first appearance before the commission, the service of all writ petitioners were regularised on 9-3-1979. The Government on the recommendation of the Council Committee and in consultation with the PSC issued a Memorandum dated 22-4-1984 (Annexure K-2) providing that seniority of ad-hoc appointees, after regularisation, would be counted from the date of their ad-hoc appointment. The ad-hoc appointments of the writ-petitioners and others were quite different from the ad-hoc appointments made before 1972 and regular scales of pay, yearly increments and efficiency bar crossing were allowed to them from the very beginning and the period of appointment was extended far beyond six months and thereby clearly indicating that the appointments of the writ-petitioners were, in fact, quasi-permanent. The memo of the Establishment Division dated 23-8-1973 in its paragraph 3 provided that besides the appointment mentioned in Regulations 39 and 40 of the PSC the Government decided that all appointments under the Government of Bangladesh shall be made on ad-hoc basis till decision of the Government on the report of the Administrative and Service Reorganisation Committee and the repatriation of Bangladeshi employees stranded in Pakistan. The paragraph 4 of the aforesaid memo further provides for regular yearly increments.

3. A meeting of the council committee was held on 16-11-1985 vide (Annexure D) wherein the matter of counting of ad-hoc service was discussed and it was pointed out that the ad-hoc appointees who, after such appointment did not apply or appear at the interview before the Public Service Commission and were not removed from service by the concerned Ministry and Department, the benefits of their service cannot be denied to them as it was decided in the circular dated 22-4-1984 (Annexure K-2) which remained in force being unchanged. The question of giving seniority to the ad-hoc appointees was considered in a subsequent meeting held on 26-11-1988 by the Public Service Commission wherein it was decided that if the ad-hoc appointees had appeared at the interview with outside candidates when applications were invited, after ad-hoc appointment for filling up the said posts and the ad-hoc appointees could not become successful at the interview before the Public Service Commission, their seniority would be counted from the dates of their regularisation later on and others' seniority would be counted from the date of their ad-hoc appointment. The Public Service Commission, the Ministry of Communication and the Department of Roads and Highways made enquiries for a long time but did not find evidence of the failure of the writ petitioners before the PSC and accordingly, the PSC vide letter dated 22-9-1986 vide Annexure F requested the Ministry of Communications to obtain an undertaking from the ad-hoc appointees who did not fail at any interview before the PSC. The writ petitioners gave undertakings that they did not fail at any interview before the PSC. Thereafter, the names of the writ petitioners along with others, who became successful, were sent to the standing committee in early part of 1989 for placement of their names at the appropriate place of the gradation list for finalisation. Accordingly, the Standing Committee at its meeting held on 10-4-1989 finalised the question of seniority of the writ petitioners and other ad-hoc appointees and final gradation list was published in Bangladesh Gazette on 1-10-1990 (Annexure H) wherein the seniority of the writ petitioner-respondents were counted from the date of their ad-hoc appointments.

4. In the meantime Ad-hoc Service Counting (Seniority Determination) Rules, 1990 was published in Gazette Notification dated 8-11-1990 vide Annexure K and the relevant provisions of Rule 4 are quoted below:

"জ্যেষ্ঠতা নির্ধারণ কতিপয় কর্মকর্তার এডহক চাকরিকাল গণনা (১) নিম্নবর্ণিত কর্মকর্তার জ্যেষ্ঠতার নির্ধারণ তাহাদের এডহক চাকরিকাল এই বিধিমালার বিধান অনুযায়ী গণনা করা হইবে যথা :

ক) ৯ই এপ্রিল ১৯৭২ এর পূর্বে কোনো পদে এডহক ভিত্তিক নিযুক্ত হইয়া উক্ত তারিখ এবং ১২ ই মে ১৯৮৩ এর মধ্যে যে কোনো সময় একই পদে নিয়মিতভাবে নিযুক্ত কোনো কর্মকর্তা ।

খ) ৯ই এপ্রিল ১৯৭২ হইতে ১২ ই মে ১৯৮৩ পর্যন্ত সময় সীমার মধ্যে কোনো পদে এডহক ভিত্তিক নিযুক্ত হইয়া উক্ত সময় সীমার মধ্যে যে কোনো সময় একই পদে নিয়মিতভাবে নিযুক্ত কোনো কর্মকর্তা ।

২/ উপবিধি (১) এ যাহা কিছুই থাকুক না কেন নিম্নবর্ণিত ব্যক্তিগণ উক্ত উপবিধিতে উল্লিখিত সুবিধা পাইবেন না যথা:-

(ক) এডহক ভিত্তিক নিযুক্ত হওয়ার সময় সংশ্লিষ্ট পদের জন্য প্রচলিত নিয়োগ বিধি বা নিয়োগ নীতিমালার শর্ত মোতাবেক নিযুক্ত হন নাই এমন কর্মকর্তা ।

(খ) উক্তরূপ নিযুক্ত হওয়ার সময় সংশ্লিষ্ট পদের জন্য শিক্ষাগত যোগ্যতা ছিল না এমন কর্মকর্তা ।

(গ) নিয়মিতভাবে নিযুক্তির জন্য কমিশন কর্তৃক পরিচালিত পরীক্ষার বা সাক্ষাৎকারে প্রথমবারে উহার সুপারিশ লাভে ব্যর্থ হইয়াছে এমন কর্মকর্তা ।

5. According to the said Rule 4(I), the ad-hoc appointees who were appointed on ad-hoc basis from 9-4-1972 to 12-5-1983 and were regularised during this period, would count their seniority from the dates of their respective appointment on ad-hoc basis. The ad-hoc appointees appointed between 9-4-1972 to 12-5-1983 and regularised in service within this period would count their seniority from the date of their ad-hoc appointment with the exception that the ad-hoc appointees who failed to get recommendation by the PSC for regularisation in the first time shall not be entitled to claim seniority from the date of the ad-hoc appointment as provided in rule 4(2)(Gha). The seniority of the writ petitioners was thus counted from the date of their ad-hoc appointments from 30-9-1976 and 17-12-1976 respectively. Because of the writ petitioner's success at the first appearance in the interview before the Public Service Commission between the period from 9-4-1972 and 12-5-1983 they are similarly situated and all of them are entitled to have their seniority counted from the date of their ad-hoc appointment and no discrimination can be made with others.

6. The Ministry of Establishment vide its memo dated 30-12-1990 (Annexure B) gave its interpretation to Rule 4(2)(Gha) of Ad-hoc Service Counting Rules, 1990 which runs thus:

“ধারা (২)(ঘ) এ বলা আছে এডহক তারিখ হইতে জ্যেষ্ঠতা গণনা করার সুবিধা তাহারাই পাইবেন না যাহারা অন্যান্য শর্তাবলীর মধ্যে নিয়মিতভাবে নিযুক্তির জন্য কমিশন কর্তৃক পরিচালিত পরীক্ষা বা সাক্ষাৎকারে প্রথম বারে ইহার সুপারিশলাভে ব্যর্থ হইয়াছেন এমন কর্মকর্তা । এই প্রথম বার বলিতে নিয়মিতভাবে নিযুক্তির জন্য কমিশন কর্তৃক পরিচালিত পরীক্ষার/সাক্ষাৎকারের মাধ্যমে সংশ্লিষ্ট প্রার্থী যে পরীক্ষায় বা সাক্ষাৎকারে প্রথম উপস্থিত হইয়াছিলেন, সেইটাই তাহার জন্য প্রথম পরীক্ষার/ সাক্ষাৎকার হিসাবে গণ্য হইবে এবং উক্ত পরীক্ষায়/ সাক্ষাৎকারে কৃতকার্য হইলেই তিনি এডহক নিয়োগের তারিখ হইতে জ্যেষ্ঠতা পাইবেন”।

The Ministry of Establishment thus interpreted rule 4(2)(Gha) stating that first interview faced by an ad-hoc appointee will be, for him, the first time mentioned in rule 4(2)(Gha) and the same was re-iterated on 18-9-1994.

By Annexure C dated 18-9-1994 the Ministry of Establishment gave its opinion reiterating the earlier position vide Annexure B dated 30-12-1990. The memo dated 18-9-1994 reads as follows:

“এডহক চাকরি গননা (জ্যেষ্ঠতা নির্ধারণ) বিধিমালা ১৯৯০ এর ৪ (২)(ঘ) বিধি সম্পর্ক অত্র মন্ত্রণালয়ের ৩০-১২-১৯৯০ইং তারিখের স্মারক মারফতে প্রদত্ত মতামতই যথার্থ । তবে কোন কর্মকর্তা পিএসসি পরীক্ষায় হাজির হয়ে উত্তীর্ণ না হয়ে থাকেন যে ক্ষেত্রে তিনি উক্ত বিধির আওতায় এডহক নিয়োগের তারিখ হইতে জ্যেষ্ঠতা পাবেন না । "

Mr Mahmudul Islam, the learned Counsel appearing for the appellants, has submitted with reference that the provision under section 4 of the Administrative Tribunal Act, 1980 that the Administrative Tribunal having exclusive jurisdiction to determine the terms and conditions of service including the question of violation of the fundamental right and that the respondent not having challenged the Service Counting (Determination of Seniority) Rules 1990 as ultra vires the Constitution, grievances raised in the writ petition are regarding the terms and conditions of service, the writ petition is not maintainable. Mr Mahmudul Islam, the learned Counsel further submitted with reference to the decision of Bangladesh vs Shafiuddin Ahmed reported in 50 DLR (AD) 27 that the violation of the fundamental right by action in the nature of interpretation of rules which are not by law, can be agitated before the Tribunal which is the supplementary role as opposed to violation of fundamental right by law could only be challenged in the High Court Division. Mr Mahmudul Islam, the learned Counsel, submitted that in order to have the judicial review of any order the same must be legislative one and not executive one in order to have the force of law. Mr Mahmudul Islam further submitted with reference to the appointment letter dated 17-12-1976 which are for 6 months only or until duly regularised by the Public Service Commission whichever is earlier and the writ petitioner-respondents having continued as the ad-hoc appointees but did not appear before the Public Service Commission at the first examination held in March 1977 pursuant to the amended advertisement, otherwise, under the general principle of seniority provided in Establishment Manual Volume 1, ad-hoc appointees will continue to their seniority from the date of recommendation by the Public Service Commission i.e. from the date of regularisation.

18. The learned Counsel further submitted that the submission of the learned Counsel for the writ-petitioner as to the question of violation of the fundamental right under Articles 27 and 29 of the Constitution does not arise in the instant case as the impugned order sought to interpret the concerned Rule 4(2)(Gha) of the Ad-hoc Appointment (Counting and Determination of Seniority) Rules 1990 which is purely a case determining the gradation as per law and yin's of which has not been challenged in this case but is purely relating to terms and conditions of service. The appropriate relief of which would be to take resort to the Administrative Tribunal set up under Administrative Tribunal Act, 1980 as contemplated under Article 117(2) of the Constitution rendering the writ petition not maintainable inasmuch as resorting to the Article 102 of the Constitution in the matter of seniority of service is of no avail and, as such, the writ petition is liable to be dismissed which has been used as a camouflage in order to invoke the writ jurisdiction.

19. The writ-petitioners have impugned the gradation list prepared by giving interpretation to the concerned Rule 4(2)(Gha) and the said interpretation of the word 'law' has not been contemplated under Article 152 of the Constitution which is intended to deprive their seniority from the date of their ad-hoc appointment and the decisions thus infringed their fundamental rights guaranteed in Articles 27 and 29 of the Constitution.

20. In the case of Mujibur Rahman vs. Bangladesh reported in 44 DLR (AD) 111 it has been held:

"I do not think that the Tribunals have been vested with the power of judicial review in our Constitution. What is "judicial review" in our Constitution? It is the power of the High Court Division under Article 102 of the Constitution to issue certain orders, directions, etc. upon a person performing any function with the affairs of the Republic or of a local authority. While the right to move the High Court Division in accordance with Article 102(1) for the enforcement of the fundamental rights conferred by Part III is itself a fundamental right and is guaranteed by Article 44(1), the right of judicial review under Article 102(1) is neither a fundamental right nor a guaranteed one. And the right of judicial review is neither an all-weather remedy nor a remedy for all wrongs. It is available only when "no other equally efficacious remedy is provided by law". Delay will defeat this remedy. Directions, etc. will ensue only from undisputed facts. Disputed questions of fact will not be entered into. It does not lie to enforce mere technicalities. It is not a substitute for money relief. Nor can all wrongs be remedied by judicial review. See Article 103(3) barring any interim or other order in relation to any law to which Article 47 applies. The laws referred to in Article 47 embrace a wide variety of property rights, professional, occupational, trade and business rights, almost all-embracing in sweep and depth. Some notice is to be given and some considerations need be given while passing an interim order in judicial review (Article 102(4)). Article 102(5) excludes from the purview of judicial review a Court or tribunal established under a law relating to the defence services of Bangladesh or any disciplined force (comparable, but not alike, to Articles 33 and 227(4) of the Indian Constitution) or a tribunal to which Article 117 applies. This power of judicial review, i.e. power to issue some directions etc. upon some persons, with all its attendant technicalities, was never conferred upon the Tribunals under clauses (a), (b) and (c) of Article 117 of our Constitution. This power is the exclusive preserve of the High Court Division under Article 102(1)".

This Court also held that:

"Within its jurisdiction the Tribunal can strike down an order for violation of principles of natural justice as well as for infringement of fundamental rights, guaranteed by the Constitution, or of any other law, in respect of matters relating to or arising out of sub-clause (a), but such tribunals cannot, like the Indian Administrative Tribunals in exercise of a more comprehensive jurisdiction under Article 323A (see SP Sampath Kumar vs Union of India, AIR 1937 SC 386 (Para 16) and JB Chopra vs. Union of India, AIR 1987 SC 357 (Para 2), strike down any law or rule on the ground of its constitutionality. A person in the service of the Republic who intends to invoke fundamental right for challenging the vires of a law will seek his remedy under Article 102(1), but in all other cases he will be required to seek remedy under Article 117(2).

An aggrieved person may, out of desperation or just for taking a sportive chance in the summary writ jurisdiction, allege contravention of some fundamental right which may turn out to be frivolous or vexatious or not even remotely attracted in his case. The Court is, however, to be on guard so the great value of the right given under Article 102(1) is not frittered away or misused as a substitute for more appropriate remedy available for an unlawful action involving no infringement of any fundamental right."

21. The position has not been changed by the decision reported in 50 DLR (AD) 27 in the case of Bangladesh vs Shafiuddin Ahmed wherein following the decision in the case of L Chandra Kumar vs Union of India reported in AIR 1997 SC 1125 holding, inter ilia, that "Subordinate Judiciary or Tribunal created under ordinary legislation though cannot exercise power of judicial review of legislative action to the exclusion of the High Court and the Supreme Court, there is no constitutional prohibition against their performing a supplemental as opposed to substitutional role in this respect and accordingly, held that "The supplemental as opposed to substitutional role of the Tribunals constituted under Article 117 of the Constitution was already exceeding that and permitted to in the Mujibur Rahman's case and no power of judicial review under Article 102 was conceded to the Tribunals in that case. The writ-petitioner on the one hand, advanced two-fold arguments first, the interpretation given by the Establishment Ministry is a law' within the meaning of Article 152 of the Constitution which comes squarely within the preview of the aforesaid decision which held:

"We see no reason why in our country as well the void created by the absence of law and rules under Article 133 cannot be filled up by executive power under Article 55(2) expressed to be taken in the name of the President (Article 55(4)). Such exercise of power is not unknown or without precedent in our jurisdictions. Referring to section 241(3) of the Government of India Act, 1935 and Article 178 of the Constitution of Pakistan, 1956 and relying upon the case of Pakistan vs Sheikh Abdul Hamid, PLD 1961 SC 105 = 13 DLR (SC) 100, it was held by the Supreme Court of Pakistan in the case of Province of West Pakistan vs Din Muhammad, PLD 1964 SC 21 = 16 DLR (SC) 58, that an administrative instruction, though not specifically described as "order making a rule" contained in a memorandum issued by an authority competent to alter or amend rules can be as effective and binding as statutory rules. In the Abdul Hamid case and in the case of Md Naseem Ahmed vs Azra Feroze Bakth, PLD 1968 SC 97 = 20 DLR (SC) 78, it was held that administrative instructions which have the precision of rules and are general in nature in their application to any particular service or services may have the force of law. These decisions, which we have no reason to depart from, are even more favourable to members of the service of the Republic in our country than to those in India, because the Supreme Court of India held that where a Rule is not made under constitutional or statutory authority, it is a mere administrative instruction, having no force of law (Satyavir vs Union of India AIR 1986 SC 555). There is no cause of action for breach thereof (Union of India vs Majji, AIR 1977 SC 757; Sethi vs Union of India, AIR 1975 SC 2164; Mehta vs Union of India, AIR 1977 SC 1673). Unless such breach constitutes a violation of some statutory or constitutional provisions. Contrarily, following the decisions of our jurisdiction, administrative decision on service matters emanating from the authority competent to frame or amend rules and conforming to the specifications laid down in Abdul Hamid's case may have the force of law, a breach whereof constitutes a cause of action challengeable on any ground whatsoever, before the Administrative Tribunal or the High Court Division under Article 102(1) of the Constitution, according as the cause of action may be."

And the decision reported in 1955 SCR 735 pages 745-46 held that:

A distinction is sought to be made by the learned Counsel between an "existing law" as defined in Article 366(10) and a law-in-force and it is argued that though an order can come within the definition of existing law it cannot be included within the expression law-in-force as used in Article 372. It is argued next that even if the word "law" is wide enough to include an order, that order must be a legislative and not a mere executive order promulgated by an administrative authority and in support of this contention the learned Counsel has relied on a number of cases decided by the Privy Council and the different High Courts in India."

22. The appellants also referred to the 'Rules of Business' which allocates the function including the interpretation of law to the Establishment Ministry. Following the earlier decision of Pakistan Supreme Court the petitioners allege that this Division held that administrative instructions and guidelines given by the authority competent to make rules will have the force of law if it has the generality of the rules.

23. In the instant case, the appellants, however, have contended that to be treated as 'law' the action must be an legislative act. When an interpretation of a law is given it may either be the judicial when given by a Court of law or administrative when given by the administrative authority in order to have the force of law. In the said decision the Indian Supreme Court clearly laid down that an order must be legislative and not executive before it is to be treated within the definition of law. The writ petitioners further argued that in the Rules of Business the function of making rules and interpreting rules by the Establishment Division has been separately shown in item 3 of schedule II and item 8 of schedule IV relating to the allocation in favour of the Ministry of Establishment so that interpretation of rules cannot be treated as making of the rules. Although the word 'interpretation' has been used as a common parlance but in effect it is the clarification/ opinion as expressed in the decisions explaining the particular provision of the rules for giving effect thereof.

24. The writ petitioner-respondents further argued that the judicial review by the High Court Division is a basic structure theory that contemplates that no amendment of the Constitution effecting the basic structure or feature of the Constitution is permissible and the plea of basic structure would be available if the ouster clause of Article 117(2) was introduced in the Constitution by way of amendment. Article 117(2) has been originally incorporated in our Constitution conferring the power of judicial review subject to the limitation of Article 117(2).

25. The writ petitioner-respondents, however, relied on the observation of this Division in the case of Bangladesh vs Azizur Rahman reported in 46 DLR (AD) 19 wherein the vires of the Rules 4(1)Ka, 4(1)Kha, and 5(2) of the Ad-hoc Appointees (Counting and Determination of Seniority) Rules, 1990 was unsuccessfully challenged but held that "when the question of fundamental right invoked therein has been so linked up with the facts and statutory rules that the question of fundamental right cannot be extricated for, exclusive consideration in a petition for enforcement of fundamental right, we, therefore, found that the High Court Division rightly held the writ petitions to be maintainable under Article 102(2) of the Constitution."

26. Concerned Rule 4(2)(Gha) of the Ad-hoc Appointees (Counting and Determination of Seniority) Rules, 1990 as interpreted in the resolution dated 18-8-1998 and Memo No.RHE/6P-4/98-674 dated 15-10-1998 issued by the Ministry of Communication, Roads and Railway Division, RHE section, was challenged as ultra vires of the fundamental rights guaranteed under the Constitution and have been declared to be without lawful authority in the case of Mriganka Prashad Banta vs Bangladesh reported in 5 BLC 112. In the said decision though the vires of Rule 4(2)(Gha) has not been challenged but the interpretation of Rule 4(2)(Gha) was challenged as violative of the fundamental rights of the writ petitioners as guaranteed under Articles 27 and 29 of the Constitution. The High Court Division accordingly held that:

"We hold that the writ petition may be maintainable in view of the observation made by Honourable Appellate Division in the decision reported in 46 DLR (AD) 19 in respect of writ petitions filed earlier challenging the Rules of 1990 although elements are distinct in the present case to invoke the jurisdiction of the Administrative Tribunal under Article 117(2) of the Constitution. In view of above detailed discussion we see no violation of Articles 27 and 29 of the Constitution vide Annexure E and F as alleged. We further find that proper and quite literal clarification with no ambiguity was given vide Annexure G i.e. resolution dated 18-8-98 that 37 ad-hoc appointees including writ petitioners recommended vide memo dated 27-5-77 (Annexure-B) will not be entitled to get seniority from the date of their Ad-hoc appointment as they failed to get recommendation at the first opportunity from the PSC in the examination or interview held by it as per Rule 4(2) Cha. We therefore do not see any merit in the Rule."

27. Thus from the above discussion it is clear that the right to move the High Court Division under Article 102(1) for the enforcement of the fundamental rights guaranteed under the Chapter 'Fundamental Rights of the Constitution' is itself a fundamental right and guaranteed under Article 44(1) thereof. But the right to judicial review under Article 102(2) of the Constitution is neither a fundamental right nor a guaranteed right but could be sought for under certain set conditions enumerated therein for certain specified relief or reliefs set forth therein which have been to some extent spelt out in the decision in the Mujibur Rahman's case as quoted above.

<u>28. In the instant case, no vires of the Rules has been challenged but certain decisions taken at the meeting of the Standing Committee and the placement in the gradation list and publication in the official gazette have been challenged by way of an application under Article 102(2) of the Constitution. The right of judicial review under Article 102(2) of the Constitution is neither a fundamental right nor a guaranteed right. Similarly, the judicial review of an administrative action is neither an all-weather remedy nor a remedy for all wrongs but is available only when there is no other equally efficacious remedy. The writ petitioners have challenged the impugned decisions alleged to have infringed their fundamental right guaranteed under Articles 27 and 29 of the Constitution, but in view of the provision of Article 117(2) of the Constitution the Parliament has set up the Administrative Tribunal Act, 1980 for exercise of the functions enumerated in Article 117(1) i.e. by setting up of the Administrative Tribunal to exercise the jurisdiction in respect of matters relating to or arising out of the terms and conditions of persons in the service of the republic, etc. Article 117(2) provides that no Court shall entertain any proceeding or make any order in respect of any matter falling within the jurisdiction of such Tribunal. Section 4 of the Administrative Tribunal Act, 1980 specifically provides how the jurisdiction under Article 117(1) is conferred to any other Court. In the case of 44 DLR (AD) 111 it has further been cautioned that an aggrieved person may, out of desperation or just for taking a sportive chance in the summary writ jurisdiction, allege contravention of some fundamental right which may ultimately turn out to be frivolous or vexatious or not even wrongly attracted in the case and asked to be a ground so that great value of the right given under Article 102(1) is not frittered away or misused on the pretext of alternative remedy. The question of enforcement of fundamental right is not available in the case as the questions involved in the impugned decisions are mere clarification of the rules for giving effect thereto and, as such, the assumption of jurisdiction under Article 102(2) of the Constitution for ventilating certain grievances regarding terms and conditions of service of the writ petitioners pursuant to the impugned decisions has never been contemplated. On our examination of the impugned order we do not think that any question of fundamental right is involved in the case so as to allege that the same cannot be extricated for exclusive consideration in the petition for enforcement of fundamental rights.</u>

29. The appellants have argued that no right has been accrued to the writ petitioners on the basis of a gradation list prepared upon alleged wrong interpretation of Rules 1990 inasmuch as no vested right has accrued to the writ petitioners as they did not avail the benefit under the rules by not appearing at the examination.

<u>30. The writ petitioner-respondents argued that they have been given the benefit of their ad-hoc service in determining inter-se seniority in the gradation list of 1990 and were given promotions on that basis, as such they have a vested right which cannot be defeated by a fresh interpretation made in 1998 and by the gradation list prepared in 1999. If the interpretation of rule 4(2)(Gha) given in 1990 and 1994 are correct, the writ petitioners would be entitled to the benefit of their ad-hoc service irrespective of any question as to vested right. But the question is, whether the plea of vested right is available if that earlier interpretation of 1990 and 1994 are found wrong?</u>

31. In support of their plea of vested right the writ petitioners have relied on the cases of Himayetullah vs Pakistan reported in PLD 1969 SC 407, Shoib vs Bangladesh reported in 27 DLR 315 and Shahbaz vs Crown reported in PLD 1956 FC 46 = 8 DLR (FC) 20. In all these cases, it has been held that an authority having passed an order can cancel or withdraw it only so long the order has not been carried into effect or given effect to and the writ petitioners argue that they having enjoyed the seniority pursuant to the earlier interpretation of rule 4(2)(Gha), that interpretation cannot be upturned. The appellants, however, argue that in order to be a vested right, it must first be a right and a right flows from either common law or a statute and no right can flow contrary to such common law or statute and in such case no question of vested right can arise. In this regard, the appellants refer to the provision of rule 7 of the Ad-hoc Rules of 1990 which runs as follows:

৭ ৷ বিধিগত জ্যেষ্ঠতা ও প্রাপ্ত পদোন্নতি রক্ষণঃ (১)বিধি 8 উল্লিখিত সুবিধা প্রাপক কোন কর্মকর্তার জ্যেষ্ঠতাসংস্থাপন মন্ত্রণালয়ের ২২শে এপ্রিল, ১৯৮8 তারিখের অফিস স্মারক নং এমই(আর-২)এস-৩৪/৮৪-৭৮(৫০০)এর উপর ভিত্তি করিয়া, এই বিধিমালা প্রবর্তনের পূর্বে নির্ধারণ করা হইয়া থাকিলে উহা, এই বিধিমালার সহিত সামঞ্জস্যপূর্ণ হওয়া সাপেক্ষে কার্যকর থাকিবে এবং উক্তরূপ নির্ধারণ এই বিধিমালার অধীন করা হইয়াছে বলিয়া গণ্য হইবে ৷

It thus appears that so much of the gradation list of 1990 has been rendered valid as is consistent with the provisions of the Ad-hoc Rules of 1990 and any entry in the gradation list on the basis of wrong interpretation of any provision of the Ad-hoc Rules of 1990 cannot have any legal validity or effect and cannot give rise to any right far less a vested right.

32. The appellant contend that the decisions cited by the writ petitioners have no application in the present case. In Himayetullah's case (PLD 1969 SC 407) the Pakistan Supreme Court found that the President had the power to fix the salary of Himayetullah and he fixed the salary and the fixation was communicated to Himayetullah which created a right in Himayetullah to receive the salary and, as such, the fixation of the salary could not be rescinded.

33. In Shoib's case (27 DLR 315) the Government has the power under President's Order 16 of 1972 to release a property from the list of abandoned property and the Government having released the property a vested right accrued in exercise of that power could not subsequently supersede the order of release.

34. In Shahbaz's case (PLD 1956 FC 46) the Government remitted the sentence of the accused under section 401 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and ordered release of the accused on a certain date, but before that date the Government cancelled the order. The Federal Court held that Government had power under section 21 of the General Clauses Act to cancel the order till the order has taken effect and in the case the cancellation was valid as it was passed before the order took legal effect by release of the accused.

<u>35. In all these cases, the original orders were legally passed creating rights and those orders could not be rescinded when those were given effect to. On the contrary, in the instant case, the gradation list of 1990 was prepared upon a wrong interpretation of rule 4(2)(Gha) and, as such, it could not create a legal right in favour of the writ petitioners and accordingly, the plea of vested right could not be alleged to have accrued to the writ petitioner-respondents.</u>

36. The writ petitioners urged that they were given promotion in view of their seniority. The gradation list of 1990 shows that those who were regularised in 1977 were promoted to the post of Sub-Divisional Engineers in 1983 and the writ petitioners who were regularised in 1979 were promoted to that post in 1985. Thus, before the publication of gradation list of 1990 the writ petitioners were given promotion in recognition of their claimed seniority on the basis of their ad-hoc service.

37. Mr AW Bhuiyan, appearing for the writ petitioner-respondents, argued that the ad-hoc appointments in these cases were of different nature inasmuch as the ad-hoc appointees were given scale of pay, while ad-hoc appointments generally are made on lump-sum salary. This distinction is not relevant as the writ petitioners are claiming seniority on the basis of Ad-hoc Rules of 1990 which were made for the benefit of ad-hoc appointees of the specified period and the exception of rule 4(2)(Gha) is equally applicable to them.

38. Mr. Bhuiyan argued that rule 4(2)(Gha) has to be interpreted having regard to the purpose of the Ad-hoc Rules of 1990 which, according to him, is to give benefit to the ad-hoc appointees of the specified period and he cited the decision of Alembic Chemical Works Co vs Workmen, reported in AIR 1961 SC 647. There cannot be any dispute regarding the principle laid down in the decision. But the substantive provisions of the Rule clearly shows that the benefit was restricted to those who did not have the opportunity of regularisation and availed the opportunity when it came and there is no scope to interpret the provision to extend it to all the ad-hoc appointees of the specified period as it would render the provision of rule 4(2)(Gha) redundant.

39. Mr Bhuiyan further argues that if the benefit was not intended to be given to all why the Rules speak of the period up to 12-5-1983. The Ad-hoc Rules of 1990 have been made for all cadre services of the Republic and there were ad-hoc appointments in other departments/ cadres within the period up to 12-3-1983 and required regularisation through the PSC within that period and hence that date of 12-5-1983 has been selected.

40. Mr Bhuiyan has taken exception to the use of the "এড-হক ভিত্তিক নিয়োজিত পদকে শূন্য গণ্য করে "  in Annexure K1b. But no exception can be taken to the phrase as no regular appointment can be made unless a post is treated to be vacant. The posts were vacant from the point of view of regular appointment though these were temporarily being occupied by ad-hoc appointees. Therefore, those posts were notionally treated as vacant for the purpose of regular appointment.

41. Mr Bhuiyan also refers to rule 5(2) of the Ad-hoc Rules of 1990 and claims that the seniority of the writ petitioners is protected by rule 5(2). This sub-rule provides that for the purpose of seniority of the ad-hoc appointees covered by 4(2)(Kha) the period of service will be counted from the date of ad-hoc appointment, but this sub-rule is not applicable to those who are covered by rule 4(2)(Gha) and this sub-rule does not in any way modify the provision of rule 4(2)(Gha).

42. Mr Rafique-ul Huq referred to the decision of AB Mohiuddin Ahmed reported in 49 DLR 353. But this decision is under appeal, this Division having granted leave to appeal on 12-1-2002 in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.440 of 1996.

43. The general principles of seniority is that a member of the service of the Republic would count his seniority from the date of his regular appointment on being recommended by the PSC and the period of service as an ad-hoc appointee would not be counted for seniority. When Bangladesh came into being as an independent State, in its early days a large number of ad-hoc appointments were made and examination/interview by the PSC could not be regularly held and the good numbers of ad-hoc appointees did not have appointments to get themselves regularised through the PSC. In 1983 seniority rules were framed providing further that the general principles of seniority would be followed in cases not covered by the said rules. As a good number of appointees on ad-hoc basis were not regularised so long, the Government, however, issued Memorandum dated 22-4-1984 providing that the ad-hoc appointees appointed during the period between 29-4-1972 and 12-5-1983 and regularised through the PSC within that period would count their seniority from the date of their ad-hoc appointment with a rider clause that an ad-hoc appointee who at any time was rejected for not being regularised by the PSC but regularised later on would count their seniority from the date of their regular appointment. Accordingly, a gradation list was prepared for the ad-hoc appointees of the Roads and Highways Department and published in the Gazette on 1-10-1990.

44. On 8-1-1990 the Ad-hoc Rules of 1990 were promulgated providing rule 4(1) for covering the period of ad-hoc service in determining seniority of the members of the service of the Republic, However, Rule 4(2) made certain exception of which rule 4(2)(Gha) is relevant in this case. Rule 4(2)(Gha) is quoted below:

(২) উপ-বিধি (১) এ যাহা কিছু থাকুক না কেন, নিম্ন বর্ণিত ব্যক্তিগণ উক্ত উপবিধিতে উল্লিখিত মুনাফা পাইবেন না , যথা -

………………………………………………………….

(ঘ) নিয়মিতভাবে নিযুক্তির জন্য কমিশন কর্তৃক পরিচালিত পরীক্ষা বা সাক্ষাৎকারে প্রথমবারে উহার সুপারিশ লাভে ব্যর্থ হইয়াছেন এমন কর্মকর্তা ৷

45. The dispute now turns on the কমিশন কর্তৃক পরিচালিত পরীক্ষা বা সাক্ষাৎকারে প্রথমবারে উহার সুপারিশ লাভে ব্যর্থ হইয়াছেন৷ The writ petitioners, though appointed on ad-hoc basis prior to 1977 but were regularised in 1979 on being recommended by the PSC, claim that প্রথমবারে উহার সুপারিশ লাভে ব্যর্থ refer to the examination or interview in which the ad-hoc appointee first appeared before the PSC and not the first examination or interview held by the PSC after their appointment on ad-hoc basis and interpretation to that effect have been given by the authority so long until the impugned decision and not the first examination/ interview held by the PSC after their appointment on ad-hoc basis as given by the impugned order.

46. The Ministry of Establishment as well, so long holding the view as that of the writ petitioners and interpreted the said provision in 1990 and 1994 and gave seniority to the writ-petitioner-respondents accordingly from the date of their ad-hoc appointments. On the other hand, the appellants contend that প্রথমবারে উহার সুপারিশ লাভে ব্যর্থ refers to the first examination or interview held by the PSC and those who did not appear in the first chance and/or failed to get the recommendation of the PSC first time would come within the mischief of rule 4(2)(Gha).

47. The Establishment Division adopted the very interpretation and accordingly, prepared the gradation list in 1999 whereby the writ-petitioners were allegedly denied the benefit of ad-hoc service in determining seniority.

48. The appellants in support of their contention referred to a decision reported in 5 BLC 112 in the case of aforesaid Mriganka Prashad Banta vs Bangladesh wherein the writ petitioners though qualified at the first examination/interview but were not recommended in the first opportunity have not been selected for regular appointment have moved the High Court Division and have challenged the resolution dated 18-8-1988 wherein the Standing Committee gave a clarification with its opinion to the effect that

“২৭-৫-৭৭ ইং তারিখের সুপারিশের যে ৩৭ জন এডহক কর্মকর্তা নিয়মিত করা হয়েছেন তারা এই বিধিমালার 8(২)(ঘ)নং বিধি অনুযায়ী এডহক চাকরির জ্যেষ্ঠতা পাবেন না………………………………কারণ তারা কর্মকমিশনের সুপারিশ লাভ প্রথম বার ব্যর্থ হয়েছেন ৷

49. The High Court Division held that the writ-petitioners were not entitled to the benefit of their ad hoc appointment as they failed to get recommendation in the first opportunity, which view was upheld by this Division in CP No.105 of 2000.

50. This decision supports the proposition of the appellants of this case that from the intent, spirit and letter of the provision of law it is apparent that an ad hoc appointee must not only appear at the first available examination/interview but also get the recommendation at the first chance, which is the sound interpretation of the words প্রথমবারে উহার সুপারিশ লাভ প্রথমবার ব্যর্থ হয়েছেন এমন কর্মকর্তা৷ Otherwise, as per previous interpretations of Rules of 1990 there would not be any end to appearances of the ad hoc appointees who would appear before the PSC at their sweet will and would get the seniority from the date of their ad-hoc appointments upsetting the seniority list all the time.

51. In 5 BLC case, the learned Attorney-General as well submitted that the writ petitioners could not bank on Establishment Ministry's letter dated 30-12-1990 containing a clarification that one will get the seniority from the date of ad-hoc appointment on mere success or pass in the examination/interview held by the PSC at the first opportunity when the provisions of Rule 4(2)(Gha) are apparently clear and unambiguous. Impugned resolution dated 18-8-1998 by the standing committee followed by the PSC itself contains no ambiguity in its decision and opinion about correct literal meaning of Rule 4(2)(Gha) vide impugned memo dated 15-10-1998.

52. In the case of Bangladesh vs Md Azizur Rahman reported in 46 DLR (AD) 19 the writ petitioners therein being certain Assistant Engineers of Bangladesh of different cadre services, namely, Roads and Highways, Public Works and Public Health challenged the vires of the Bangladesh Ad-hoc Appointees (Counting and Determination of Seniority) Rules, 1990 as ultra vires of Articles 27 and 29 of the Constitution as under the said rules seniority of the ad-hoc appointees is to be counted under the Rules then in force from the date of their regular appointment on the basis of recommendation of the Public Service Commission. In the said case High Court Division found the classification made in Rule 4(1)(Ka) to be lawful and constitutional but held that the classification made in Rule 4(1)(Kha) to be discriminatory and, as such, violative of Articles 27 and 29 of the Constitution. Similarly, rule 5(2) giving seniority to ad-hoc appointees from the date of ad-hoc appointment and not from the regular appointment adversely affecting the writ petitioner's right to equal opportunity was declared unconstitutional. Under the Rules the ad-hoc appointees were divided into two classes, one under rule 4(1)(Ka) i.e. those who were appointed at any time before 9th April, 1972 on ad hoc basis but were regularised at any time by 12th May 1983 and the others under rule 4(1)(Kha) i.e. those who were appointed an ad-hoc basis from 9th April, 1972 to 12th May 1983 and were regularised under this period. Rule 5(1) provided that the officers of the first category would count their seniority from 9th April 1972 and Rule 5(2) provided that the officers in the 2nd category would count their seniority from the dates of their respective appointments on ad-hoc basis.

53. This Division while allowing the appeal in the aforesaid decision found that "The main ground of the classification is to do justice to a large number of ad-hoc employees appointed during this period as a matter of policy as well as of necessity, by giving benefit of continuous ad-hoc service and this benefit has been equally given to both the writ petitioners and the respondents. So, the doctrine of severeability is not applicable to their case as it is same to others."

54. In the said decision though the issue regarding the interpretation of rule 4(2)(Gha) was passingly mentioned as contravention thereof in cases in which some of the ad-hoc appointees who did not appear before the PSC at all but were regularised under the. Regularisation Rules, 1983 have been granted seniority from the date of their ad-hoc appointments. Rule 4(2)(Gha) provide, that most ad-hoc appointees who failed to get a recommendation from the PSC at the first opportunity stand excluded from the benefit of seniority from the date of their ad-hoc appointments. The learned Counsel though argued that those ad-hoc appointees who did not appear before the PSC come under the category i.e. those who failed to get recommendation of the PSC but the learned Additional Attorney-General wants to restrict sub-rule (Gha) only to those ad-hoc appointees who appeared before the PSC but failed to get a recommendation at the first chance and those who could not appear before the PSC due to circumstances detailed in sub-rule (Gha). But ultimately, the issue which is dependent upon certain factual determination of certain question was left undecided in the decision as no decision was called for in those appeals.

55. The appellants invoked the Heydon's mischief rule and contend that the history of the legislation should be gone into to find the mischief sought to be remedied in order to resolve the dispute. They referred to Maxwell, 12 Edition at page 40 describing the mischief rule. Maxwell cited several cases of application of the said rule and the appellants referred to the case of Smith vs Hughes, [1960]1 WLR 830. In this case, a law was promulgated prohibiting prostitutes from soliciting in the streets. Some persons were prosecuted for soliciting from balconies and windows of buildings overlooking streets. Question arose whether soliciting from balconies and windows was covered by the law. Having regard to the mischief sought to be remedied, the Court held balconies and windows of building were covered by the law.

56. The appellants contend that one of the reasons for making the Ad-hoc Rules of 1990, as recognised in the decision of Azizur Rahman reported in 46 DLR (AD) 19, was want of opportunity for the ad-hoc appointees to get regularised as examination/interview by the PSC was not regularly held. The appellants contend that because of this reason, the ad-hoc appointees were given the benefit if they had availed the first opportunity.

57. They refer to the change of the language from the Memorandum dated 22-4-1984 to the one made in rule 4(2)(Gha) and contend that one cannot be "rejected" (the language used in the Memorandum) unless one appeared before the PSC, but failure to obtain recommendation as the language of rule 4(2)(Gha) may occur by appearing and failing or by simply not appearing.

58. The appellants refer to the orders of ad-hoc appointment dated 30-9-1976 and 17-12-1976. In these two orders it was clearly stated that the appointment was for a period of six months or till regularisation by the PSC, whichever is earlier and in condition No. 3 of the orders it was mentioned that the ad-hoc appointees may appear before the PSC when it holds the examination/interview if the ad-hoc appointees want to remain in the service.

59. The writ-petitioner-respondents contend that there was no such compulsion as they were allowed to continue in service. In answer to that the appellants referred to two letters, one dated 21-7-1977 by which the PSC intimated the Ministry of Communication the names of the candidates recommended for regular appointment after holding the examination/interview in 1977 and the other dated 18-10-1977 by which the Chief Engineer of the Roads and Highways Department wrote to the Ministry of Communication stating that the service of the ad-hoc appointees not recommended for regular appointment stood terminated, but as they are continuing for years and in the interest of the development works their services may be continued till further recommendation by the PSC. It was further mentioned that these ad-hoc appointees are not getting salary because of expiry of tenure of service and the matter may be considered on urgent basis.

60. In view of these, the contention of the writ petitioners that there was no compulsion on the part of the ad-hoc appointees to appear before the PSC at the first opportunity is without any substance. The interpretation given by the Establishment Ministry in 1990 would permit the ad-hoc appointees to appear before the PSC at their sweet will and such a position tends to uncertainty as well cannot be accepted as contemplated under the said rule.

61. The said rule as well concerned about the ad-hoc appointees for the period between 9th April to 12th of May 1983 to the various posts of different departments/cadres including the present post for uniform application of the rules to all cadres but no exception has been made in depriving the privilege under this rule to an employee who has not appeared in the first time at the examination or interview and failed to obtain recommendation.

62. The writ-petitioners though appointed on 27-12-1976 but did not appear at the examination held in 1977 pursuant to the amended notification dated March 1977 to appear in the examination in 1979 and were regularised from the date of ad-hoc appointment. The appellants have referred to the decision of Mriganka Prashad Barua and others vs. Ministry of Communication and others reported in 5 BLC 112 wherein the writ petitioner appeared in the first examination/interview held by the PSC and was not included in the first recommendation but was included in the second recommendation on the basis of the first examination/interview by the PSC when subsequently the Department requested selection of few more for regular appointment. The High Court Division found that the writ petitioner was not entitled to the benefit of his ad-hoc appointment as he failed to get recommendation in the first opportunity which was maintained by this Division. In that view of the order as well as an ad-hoc appointee must not only appear in the first examination/interview but also must get the recommendation in the first chance in order to avail the advantage of the said rule.

63. The writ petitioners, particularly Mr Rafique-ul Huq, the learned Counsel appearing for Abdus Salam, respondent in CA 70 and 72 of 2002, argued that the first advertisement was made by the Public Service Commission on 2-7-1976 (Annexure S of CA 71 /2002). By further advertisement on 5-8-1976 (Annexure S 2) the number of the posts was increased. These advertisements were made when they were not even appointed on ad-hoc basis and, as such, the same is not applicable to the writ petitioners who were appointed on 30-9-1976 and 17-12-1976. There was further advertisement for the posts in the Forest Department on 10-3-1977 (Annexure S 3). In that advertisement, there was corrigendum to the earlier advertisement for the posts of Roads and Highways Department increasing the number of posts in that Department. According to the writ petitioners, this corrigendum has been made in such a way that it would escape notice. Further, in none of that advertisement it was mentioned that the ad-hoc appointees may apply. But in the advertisement dated 1-4-1978 it was mentioned that the ad-hoc appointees, if any, may apply and the writ petitioners applied for and got recommended and regularised and, according to them, this was the first examination/interview available to them and they availed. The appellants, however, point out to an official correspondence dated 10-3-1976 wherein the Ministry of Communication referring to the last advertisement of 1977 informed the Chief Engineer that the ad-hoc appointees may apply to the PSC, if not applied earlier and contends that this Memo in the usual course was circulated and was known to all concerned. As regards the other contention of the writ petitioners, they argue that in the orders of appointment on ad-hoc basis dated 30-9-1976 and dated 17-12-1976, it was clearly mentioned in clause 3 that the ad-hoc appointees apply to the PSC when the PSC advertise for regular appointment and, as such, it was not necessary to mention in the advertisements made in 1976 and 1977 that the ad-hoc appointees may apply. But once the examination/interview was held and some of the ad-hoc appointees did not appear or did not get recommendation leading to the liability of losing employment, the question could arise whether they could appear before the PSC in the second examination/interview and, as such, it was mentioned in the advertisement of 1978, to remove any doubt, that the ad-hoc appointees may apply and from this no conclusion can be made that the advertisements in 1976 and 1977 did not apply to the ad-hoc appointees. The expression if any" in the advertisement of 1978 is important and can be understood to mean "if any who did not appear earlier". The appellants placed before this Division an analysis of the gradation list of 1990 from which it appears that out of the 47 persons appointed on ad-hoc basis on 30-9-1976, 24 are in the department and in the gradation list of 1990. Of them 19 were regularised through the PSC on 6-8-1977, 3 were regularised through the PSC on 9-3-1979 and 2 were regularised on 30-6-1983 under the Regularisation Rules of 1983. Out of the 120 persons appointed on ad-hoc basis on 17-12-1976, 60 are in the department and in the gradation list of 1990 and out of them 43 got regularised through the PSC on 6-8-1977 and 17 got regularised through the PSC on 9-3-1979. The appellants argue that overwhelming number of persons appointed on ad-hoc basis on 30-9-1976 and 17-12-1976 appeared in the first examination/interview and the contention of the writ petitioners that they were not aware of the advertisement of March, 1977 or that this advertisement did not relate to them is untenable.

<u>64. In view of the above discussion we are of the opinion that fundamental rights of writ petitioners guaranteed by the Constitution under Articles 27 and 29 have not been infringed or violated by the impugned decisions (Annexures K1 and M).</u>

<u>In this regard reference may be made to the decision reported in 46 DLR (AD) 19 wherein, on equality before law, it was observed:</u>

<u>"The term equality before law should not be interpreted in its absolute sense to hold that all persons are equal in all respects disregarding different conditions and circumstances in which they are placed or special quality and characteristics which some of them may possess but which are lacking in others. In fact, the term means that all persons are not equal in all respects and that persons similarly situated should be treated alike. Equal protection of law is a guarantee that similar people should be dealt with in a similar way and that people of different circumstances will not be treated as if they were the same."</u>

<u>"Guarantee of equal opportunity in respect of employment is available at this stage of initial appointment and of promotion. Merely because chances of promotion of the writ petitioners may be said to have been affected by the impugned Rules of 1990 would not amount to denial of equality of opportunity in respect of the employment as chances of promotion are not condition of service We see no violation of Articles 27 and 29 of the Constitution in the present case."</u>

<u>65. In view of the above, even on merit of the case as discussed above, there was no violation of any fundamental right as alleged and the High Court Division acted illegally in declaring the impugned order dated 27-9-1998 and the impugned decisions as adopted/taken at the meeting of the standing committee on 2-6-1999 and 20-9-1999 containing the minutes and of the gradation list published in Bangladesh Gazette on 23-11-1999 placing the writ-respondent Nos. 11-79 in serial No. 115 to 183 therein and the remarks under clause 9 of the gradation list against the names of the writ petitioner-respondents to be unconstitutional or void or without any lawful authority.</u>

66. Accordingly, the impugned order dated 27-9-1998 and the impugned decision adopted at the meeting of the Standing Committee dated 2-8-1999 and 20-9-1999 containing minutes and of the gradation list published in the Gazette dated 23-11-1999 placing the writ-respondent Nos. 11-79 in serial Nos. 115-183 and the remark in clause 9 in the gradation list do not suffer from any illegality or infirmity for any interference.

In the result the appeals are allowed without any order as to costs and the impugned judgment and order making the Rules absolute are hereby set aside.

End.
